Ibn Wahb said: Mālik related to me that Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn had grown weak and stayed behind from the pilgrimage. He would instruct anyone who went on pilgrimage to observe al-Qāsim’s guidance, his clothing, and his way of conducting himself, then report these to him so that he might follow al-Qāsim’s example.

Ibn Wahb said: Mālik related to me that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: “If I had any authority in the matter, I would appoint al-Qāsim to the caliphate.”

He said: “Al-Qāsim related few ḥadīths and gave few legal opinions.”

ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥasan al-ʿAsqalānī related to me: Ibn al-Mubārak related to us, from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Mawhab, who said: I heard al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad. A man asked him about several matters. When the man had finished, al-Qāsim said to him: “Do not go away saying, ‘Al-Qāsim said this is the truth.’ But if you are compelled to act on it, then do so.”

Abū Ṣāliḥ related to me: al-Layth related to me, from Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd, from al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad, who said: “People of Iraq, by God, we do not know much of what you ask us. For a man to live ignorant, yet know what God, Mighty and Glorious, has imposed upon him, is better than for him to say of God, Mighty and Glorious, and His Messenger what he does not know.”

Muḥammad ibn Abī Zukayr related to me: Ibn Wahb informed me: I heard Mālik mention al-Qāsim’s saying, “For a man to live ignorant is better than for him to say of God, Mighty and Glorious, what he does not know.” Mālik said: “These are words one may accept.” Then he mentioned Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq and the merit with which God, Mighty and Glorious, had singled him out and endowed him. Mālik said:

“Abū Bakr would say in that time, ‘I do not know.’” Mālik said: “And he would not say this—”

“I do not know.”

Zayd ibn Bishr and ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to me. They said: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying:

“I heard Mālik and other people of learning relate from Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd that he heard al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad say: ‘People of Iraq, by God, we do not know everything you ask us about. For a person to live ignorant, while knowing what God—Mighty and Majestic—is obligated upon him, is better for him than to speak about God—Mighty and Majestic—without knowledge.’”

Muḥammad ibn [Abī] Zukayr related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb related to us from Mālik, who said: “I heard him relate that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: ‘If any part of this authority were mine, I would entrust it only to al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad.’” Mālik said: “At that time, Yazīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik had already been appointed heir to the throne.”

He said: Ibn Wahb related to us, saying: “When al-Qāsim and ʿUmar met—and ʿUmar was then governor of Medina—ʿUmar said to al-Qāsim: ‘We have surplus food and goods with us; take them.’ Al-Qāsim replied: ‘I will not deprive anyone of anything.’ I asked Mālik: ‘Was ʿUmar an emir at that time?’ He said: ‘Yes.’”

Muḥammad ibn Abī Zukayr related to us, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Mālik related to us from Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd, who said: “Al-Qāsim would scarcely ever contradict anyone in his session or find fault with him. One day Rabīʿa spoke at al-Qāsim’s session at length. When al-Qāsim left, leaning on me, he turned to me and said: ‘May you be bereft of all but yourself! Do you think people were unaware of what this companion of ours is saying?’”

Ibn Bukayr related to us, saying: al-Layth related to me from Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd, who said: “Rabīʿa ibn Abī ʿAbd al-Raḥmān would sometimes give a legal opinion in al-Qāsim’s session ibn Muḥammad’s session. Al-Qāsim would turn to me and say: ‘The best of people, if what Rabīʿa says is true.’”

Saʿīd ibn Asad related to us, saying: Ḍamrah related to us from Rajāʾ ibn Abī Salamah, from Ibn ʿAwn, who said: “I have met no one more capable than three men: Rajāʾ ibn Ḥaywah in Syria, al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad in the Ḥijāz, and Ibn Sīrīn in Iraq.” He meant that they did not go beyond what they knew and did not presume to speak from their own opinion.

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmmār related to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī related to us, saying: “I heard Mālik ibn Anas say: ‘Al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad did not relate even a hundred hadiths.’”

Saʿīd ibn Asad related to me, saying: Ḍamrah related to us from Ibn Shawdhab, from Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd, who said: “We knew no one in Medina whom we preferred over al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad.”

Ibn Abī Zukayr related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb related to us, saying: Mālik related to me: “Sometimes there would be a dispute between al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad and a man over something, and al-Qāsim would say to him: ‘This thing you want to dispute with me about is yours. If it is rightfully yours, take it and do not discuss it with me. And if it is mine, you are absolved of it, and it is yours.’”

“Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb related to us, saying: Ḥammād ibn Zayd related to us from Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd, who said: ‘Al-Qāsim was once asked a question. He said, “I do not know.” Then he said: “By God, for a person to live ignorant after knowing what God—Mighty and Majestic—is owed by him is better than speaking without knowledge.”’” And from Ayyūb, who said: “Al-Qāsim was once asked about a matter and said:

‘I do not know. We do not know everything you ask us about. If we knew, we would not conceal it from you, and it would not be lawful for us to conceal it from you.’”

“Suleymān ibn Yasār”

Muḥammad ibn [Abī] Zukayr related to us, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying:

“Mālik related to us: Sulaymān ibn Yasār was among the most knowledgeable people in this town concerning the Sunan, and he was one of the people of learning. He would speak in his session; but when talk became plentiful and he heard the din, he would take his sandals and leave them.” I asked Mālik: “While he was in his session?” He said: “Yes.” He added: “Ibn al-Musayyab was a stern man who pelted people with pebbles.”

Ibn Wahb said: Mālik related to me, saying: “Sulaymān ibn Yasār was one of the learned people after Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, and he often agreed with Saʿīd. Saʿīd would not dare challenge him.”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us, saying: Sufyān related to us, saying: ʿAmr ibn Dīnār related to us, saying: al-Ḥasan ibn Muḥammad informed me: “In our view, Sulaymān ibn Yasār had better understanding than Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab.” He did not say “more versed in jurisprudence.”

Ibn Bukayr related to us, saying: al-Layth related to me from Yazīd ibn Abī Ḥabīb: A man asked Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab about something. He said: “Did you ask anyone besides me?”

“He said: ‘Yes.’ ‘Who?’ ‘ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār.’ ‘And what did he tell you?’ He said: ‘Such-and-such.’ He said: ‘Go to Sulaymān ibn Yasār and ask him, then tell me what he says.’ The man asked him, and Sulaymān said: ‘The matter is such-and-such.’ I told Ibn al-Musayyab.

“Ibn al-Musayyab said: ‘ʿAṭāʾ is a judge, and Sulaymān is a mufti.’”

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Maslamah related to us from Mālik, from Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd, from Bukayr ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ashajj, from al-Nuʿmān ibn Abī ʿAyyāsh, from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār, who said:

“ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ said to me: ‘You are only a judge.’”

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān related to us, saying: ʿAbd Allāh related to us, saying: Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd related to us from Bukayr ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ashajj, from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār: “ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar said to me: ‘You are only a judge, not a mufti.’”

“ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr”

Zayd ibn Bishr al-Ḥaḍramī and ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿImrān al-Khuzāʿī related to us. They said: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Abī al-Zinād informed me from Hishām ibn ʿUrwah, who said: “I never heard my father give his opinion about anything. Sometimes he would be asked about such a matter and say: ‘This is purely the ruler’s affair.’” He said: “My father also said:

‘Whenever I have related’—Zayd said: ‘Whenever I have informed’—anyone of anything from knowledge that his understanding cannot reach, that knowledge becomes a source of error for him.’”

Zayd ibn Bishr, ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, and Yūnus related to me. They said: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Yaḥyā ibn Ayyūb informed me from Hishām ibn ʿUrwah: ʿAwn ibn ʿAbd Allāh said: “Tell me something from your father.” Hishām said: “I began to relate to him traditions of the Sunan. He said: ‘Not his unusual reports; ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUrwah related to me from ʿUrwah, from ʿĀʾishah, that she wrote to Muʿāwiyah ibn Abī Sufyān: “If you fear God—Mighty and Majestic—He will suffice you; but if you fear people, they will avail you nothing against God—Mighty and Majestic. So fear God.”’ Hishām said: “ʿUtbah ibn ʿAbd Allāh related to me: ‘I was imprisoned with your father, and he laughed.’ I said: ‘What makes you laugh?’ He replied:

“‘You are referring us to the people who have full mastery.’” Hishām said: “He was speaking only from ʿĀʾishah.”

“Hishām said: ‘My father used to say: “We were once the youngest among our people, but today we are elders; you are now the youngest, and you will become elders. So learn knowledge, and you will lead your people by it, and they will need you.”’” “By God, people kept asking me until I had forgotten.”

“Hishām said: ‘My father would summon me, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUrwah, and my brothers ʿUthmān and Ismāʿīl—and another whom Hishām named—and say: “Do not make things difficult for me in front of people. When we are alone, ask me.” He would relate to us, beginning with divorce, then divorce by mutual release, then pilgrimage, then sacrificial animals, and then such-and-such. Then he would say: “Go over it with me again.” He was amazed at my memory.’

“Hishām said: ‘By God, we learned from him not even one part out of a thousand of his hadiths.’”

Ḥarmalah related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Lahīʿah related to me from ʿUqayl ibn Khālid, who said: “I heard Ibn Shihāb say: ‘I came to Egypt to visit ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Marwān, and I was relating from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab.’ He said: ‘Ibrāhīm ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Qāriẓ said to me: “Why do I hear you relate only from Ibn al-Musayyab?” I said: “Indeed.” He said: “You have left out two men of your own people, of whom I know no one who relates more hadiths than they do: ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr and Abū Salamah ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān.”’ He said: ‘When I returned to Medina, I found ʿUrwah to be a well that buckets could not muddy.’”

Ḥarmalah related to us, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, from Ibn Lahīʿah, from Abū al-Aswad, who said: “One night ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh came to ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr. ʿUrwah began relating to him, and ʿUbayd Allāh began to laugh. ʿUrwah thought that ʿUbayd Allāh was laughing in mockery, and said: ‘What makes you laugh?’ He replied: ‘You relate to me from ʿĀʾishah and bring me to the people in the open, while others refer us to the bankrupt.’”

Saʿīd ibn ʿUfayr related to us, saying: Yaʿqūb ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to me from his father, from Ibn Shihāb, who said: “I used to seek knowledge from three men: Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, who was the most versed in jurisprudence of all people; ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, who was an ocean that buckets could not muddy; and ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh. Whenever I wished to obtain from him some knowledge that I could not find with anyone else, I would obtain it.”

Ḥasan al-Ḥulwānī related to me, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us, saying: Maʿmar informed us from al-Zuhrī, who said: “I encountered four oceans of Quraysh: ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh, Abū Salamah ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, and Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab. As for Abū Salamah ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, he used to debate Ibn ʿAbbās, and thereby gained a great deal of knowledge.”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us, saying: Sufyān related to us from al-Zuhrī, who said:

“ʿUrwah would draw people together around his hadith.” Sufyān said: “As for ʿUmar, he related to us: ‘We came to ʿUrwah, and he said: “You have come to me, so receive knowledge from me.”’”

Saʿīd ibn Asad related to me, saying: Ḍamrah related to us from Ibn Shawdhab, who said:

“When the dates were ripe, ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr would29 … People would enter and eat and carry some away. Whenever he entered it, he would repeat this verse until he left it: ‘If only, when you entered your garden, you had said, “What God wills! There is no power except through God.”’ (Qurʾān 18:39).”

ʿUrwah would recite a quarter of the Qurʾān each day, looking into the codex, and would pray through it at night. He did not miss this practice except on the night his leg was amputated; he resumed it the following night.

Abū al-Nuʿmān related to us, saying: Ḥammād ibn Zayd related to us from Hishām ibn ʿUrwah, from his father, who said: “My sons, ask me, for I have been left alone until I nearly forgot. When I am asked about a hadith, I bring to mind a hadith from my day.”

Al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Walīd ibn Mazīd related to me, saying: My father informed me: Abū ʿAmr said: “A boil appeared on the sole of his foot—that is, ʿUrwah’s—and what was wrong with him worsened until his leg was sawn off.” He said: “When his leg was sawn off, ʿUrwah said: ‘O God, You know that I have never walked on it toward anything evil.’”

Nūḥ ibn al-Haytham al-ʿAsqalānī related to us, saying: al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rāfiʿ ibn Durayd related to us from his father, who said: “ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr came to al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, and a gangrenous sore appeared on his leg. The physicians agreed that it must be amputated, and that if they did not do so, it would kill him. He sent to al-Walīd asking him to send the physicians to him.

“He sent me with them. They said: ‘We will give you a sedative.’ He asked: ‘Why?’ They replied: ‘So that you do not feel what we do to you.’ He said: ‘No; go ahead with it.’ They sawed through his leg with a saw. They proceeded from one limb to another until they had finished with it, then cauterized the wound.

“When he saw it in their hands, he took it and said: ‘Praise be to God. As for the One who made me bear this: He knows that I never walked with you toward anything forbidden.’” ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rāfiʿ [ibn] Durayd—or another of our elders—said: “ʿUrwah ordered that it be washed, perfumed with camphor, shrouded, and wrapped in a velvet cloak; then he sent it to the cemetery.”

Ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥīm related to me, saying: I heard ʿAlī say: I heard Sufyān say:

“Ibn al-Zubayr was killed when he was seventy-three.” He said: “Ibn Ṣafwān and Ibn Muṭīʿ ibn al-Aswad were killed with him.” He was asked: “Where was ʿUrwah?” He replied: “In Mecca. When he was killed, ʿUrwah went to Medina with the wealth, deposited it there, and went to ʿAbd al-Malik. He arrived before the courier and before the news reached him. When he reached the door, he said to the doorman: ‘Tell the Commander of the Faithful that Abū ʿAbd Allāh is at the door.’ He said…”

“‘Who is Abū ʿAbd Allāh?’ He said: ‘Tell him: Abū ʿAbd Allāh.’ He went in and said: ‘There is a man here with the marks of travel upon him. He says, “Tell the Commander of the Faithful that Abū ʿAbd Allāh is at the door.” I asked him, “Who is Abū ʿAbd Allāh?” He said, “Tell him: Abū ʿAbd Allāh.”’ He said: ‘That is ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr. Admit him.’ When he saw him, he moved aside to make room for him. He began asking him questions, then said: ‘How is Abū Bakr?’—meaning ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr. He replied: ‘He has been killed ﵀.’ ʿAbd al-Malik got down from the bed and prostrated. Al-Ḥajjāj wrote to him that ʿUrwah had left and had the wealth with him. ʿAbd al-Malik spoke to him about this, and he said: ‘Will you not leave the man alone until he takes up his sword and dies with honor?’ When he saw this, he wrote to al-Ḥajjāj: ‘Leave the matter alone.’”

“Sālim ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar”

Zayd ibn Bishr and ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to me. They said: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying:

“Mālik related to me from Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd, who said: ‘I asked Sālim ibn ʿAbd Allāh about something I had heard from him: “Did you hear it from Ibn ʿUmar?” He said: “Once, yes—and more than a hundred times.”’”

ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb related to us, saying: Yaʿqūb related to me: “I was told that al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik wrote to Zayd ibn Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, asking him to pledge allegiance to ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn al-Walīd and renounce Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik. Zayd ibn Ḥasan was afraid of al-Walīd and agreed to his request. When Sulaymān became caliph, he found Zayd ibn Ḥasan’s letter to al-Walīd about this. He wrote to Abū Bakr ibn Ḥazm—who was governor of Medina—saying: ‘Summon Zayd ibn Ḥasan and show him this letter. If he acknowledges it, write to me to that effect. If he denies it, bring him forward and have him swear an oath on the pulpit of the Messenger of God ﷺ—that he neither wrote this letter nor ordered it.’ He said: Abū Bakr ibn Ḥazm sent for him…”

“Abū Bakr ibn Ḥazm summoned him and read the letter to him. He said: ‘Give me until the evening prayer; I will seek God—Mighty and Majestic—for guidance.’ Zayd ibn al-Ḥasan then sent to al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad and Sālim ibn ʿAbd Allāh to consult them. He had Rabīʿah join them, related the matter to them, and said: ‘I did not feel safe from al-Walīd taking my life if I had not agreed to his request. I did write this letter. Do you think I should swear an oath?’ They said: ‘Do not swear, and do not defy God—Mighty and Majestic—at the pulpit of the Messenger of God ﷺ. We hope that God—Mighty and Majestic—will save you through your truthfulness.’ So he acknowledged the letter but did not swear. Abū Bakr wrote informing him of this.

“Sulaymān wrote to Abū Bakr, ordering him to strike Zayd a hundred lashes, strip off his cloak, and make him walk barefoot. ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz detained the messenger from Sulaymān’s army and said: ‘Do not leave until I speak to the Commander of the Faithful about what he has written concerning Zayd ibn Ḥasan. Perhaps I can put his mind at ease and persuade him to set aside this letter.’ The messenger remained, and Sulaymān fell ill. ʿUmar said to the messenger: ‘Do not leave, for the Commander of the Faithful is ill.’

“When Sulaymān’s bier was carried out and authority passed to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, he called for the letter and tore it up.”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us, saying: Sufyān related to us from Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd, who said: “A son of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar was asked about something, but he did not know anything about it. A man said to him: ‘I consider it remarkable that you, the son of a rightly guided leader, should be asked about something and have no knowledge of it.’ He replied: ‘By God, what is more grave in God’s sight—and in the sight of those who convey from God, Mighty and Majestic—is for me to speak without knowledge or to relate from someone trustworthy.’”

Yūnus ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to me, saying: Ashhab informed me from Mālik, who said: “Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab said: ‘ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar was the son of ʿUmar who most resembled him, and Sālim ibn ʿAbd Allāh was the son of ʿAbd Allāh who most resembled him.’” Mālik said: “In Sālim ibn ʿAbd Allāh’s time, no one resembled the righteous people of the past more than he did in his asceticism and moderation in living. He wore a garment for two dirhams and bought a bundle of firewood for its load.”

Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik said to Sālim, seeing how handsome he was: “What do you eat?” He said: “Bread and oil, and when I find meat, I eat it.” He asked him: “Do you crave it?” He said: “If I do not crave it, I leave it until I do.”

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr related to me, saying: Sufyān related to us from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz al-ʿUmarī, who said: “When Sālim’s stipend came, if he had a debt, he paid it; then he gave some of it away and donated some of it. He then set aside his household’s expenses and kept whatever remained for pilgrimage, God willing, and for the lesser pilgrimage, God willing.” Saʿīd related to me, saying: Sufyān related to me from a shaykh among the people of Medina, who said: “Sālim said: ‘If I could find nothing for pilgrimage but a tailless donkey, I would make the pilgrimage on it.’”

“ʿUmar ibn Khaldah al-Zuraqī”

Hishām ibn Khālid al-Sulāmī related to us, saying: Abū Mushir related to us, saying: Mālik ibn Anas related to us, saying: Rabīʿah ibn Abī ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to me: “Ibn Khaldah—and what an excellent judge he was—said to me: ‘Rabīʿah, I see that you give legal opinions to people. When a man comes to you with a question, do not make it your aim to get him out of the predicament he has fallen into; let your aim be to…’”

“…”

“[Let] your concern be to extricate yourself from what he asked you about.”

QABĪṢA IBN DHUʾAYB

I read to Muḥammad ibn Ḥumayd. He said: Salama and ʿAlī ibn Isḥāq told me, both from ʿImrān ibn Abī Kathīr, who said:

I came to Syria, and there was Qabīṣa ibn Dhuʾayb, who had brought a man from Iraq and admitted him to ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān. The man related to him, from his father, from al-Mughīra ibn Shuʿba, that he had heard the Prophet ﷺ say:

“The caliph is not to be adjured.”

He said: The man was clothed, given money, and generously rewarded. He said: Something troubled me about it, so I came to Medina and met Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib. I told him the story, and he struck his hand against mine, then said: “May God fight Qabīṣa! How could he sell his religion for a fleeting world? By God, there is no woman of Khuzāʿa sitting in her house who has not memorized the words of ʿAmr ibn Sālim al-Khuzāʿī to the Messenger of God ﷺ:

O God, I appeal to Muḥammad

by the pact of our forefather and his ancient father,

“Was the Messenger of God ﷺ to be adjured, but the caliph not to be adjured? May God fight Qabīṣa! How could he sell his religion for a fleeting world!”

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to us from Saʿīd ibn Abī Ayyūb, who said: Jaʿfar ibn Rabīʿa told me, from Rabīʿa ibn Zayd, from Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAbd Allāh, who said: I entered upon Umm al-Dardāʾ, and Qabīṣa ibn Dhuʾayb was with her. I said to him, “Abū Saʿīd…”

Ibn Rabīʿa, from Rabīʿa ibn Zayd, from Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAbd Allāh, who said: I entered upon Umm al-Dardāʾ, and Qabīṣa ibn Dhuʾayb was with her. I said to him, “Abū Saʿīd…”

Ḥarmala ibn Yaḥyā told me: Ibn Wahb told us, from Ibn Lahīʿa, who said:

Yazīd ibn Abī Ḥabīb told me that Qabīṣa ibn Dhuʾayb was born in the Year of the Elephant.

Ibn Lahīʿa said: Whenever Ibn Shihāb mentioned Qabīṣa ibn Dhuʾayb, he would say: “He was one of the scholars of this community.”

ABŪ SALAMA IBN ʿABD AL-RAḤMĀN

Abū Ṣāliḥ related to us. He said: al-Layth ibn Saʿd told me, from Ibn al-Hād, from al-Mundhir ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī al-Ḥakam, who said:

His nephew proposed to a cousin of his, and they quarreled over some matter. The young man said, “She is divorced if I marry her before I eat the male palm spathe”—the ghaḍīḍ is the male palm’s spathe. Then they regretted what had happened, and al-Mundhir said, “I will bring you a clarification of this.” He said: I went to Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib and said to him: “A man proposed to his cousin, and some matter arose between them. He said, ‘She is divorced if I marry her before I eat the ghaḍīḍ.’” Ibn al-Musayyib said:

“He is not liable for anything. He divorced what he does not possess.”

Then I asked ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr, and he said:

“He is not liable for anything. He divorced what he does not possess.”

Then I asked Abū Salama ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān about it, and he said:

“He is not liable for anything. He divorced what he does not possess.”

Then I asked Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām, and he said:

“He is not liable for anything. He divorced what he does not possess.”

Then I asked ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUtba about it, and he said: “He is not liable for anything. He divorced what he does not possess.” Then I returned to the group and told them what I had asked about.

Abū Muḥammad ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad al-Miṣrī related to us. He said: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī al-Zinād related to us. He said: Abū al-Zinād said:

I met among the jurists and scholars of Medina, whose opinions we accept and whose authority people follow, Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr, al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad, Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, Khārija ibn Zayd, ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUtba, and Sulaymān ibn Yasār, along with a group of other elders of their standing, people of learning and merit.

Ḥarmala told me: Ibn Wahb informed us. He said: Ibn Lahīʿa told me that ʿUmāra ibn Ghaziyya related to him that Ibn Shihāb related to him, saying: al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad said:

“If you want ʿĀʾisha’s traditions, you should go to ʿAmra bt. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, for she is among the people most knowledgeable about ʿĀʾisha’s traditions. She was raised in her care.”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us. He said: Sufyān related to us. He said: I heard al-Zuhrī relate from Abū Salama, who said:

“If I had sat with Ibn ʿAbbās, I would have drawn much knowledge from him.”

Sufyān said: On another occasion, he said, “a great deal of knowledge.”

Abū Saʿīd Yaḥyā ibn Sulaymān told me: Aḥmad ibn Bashīr told me. He said: Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid related to us, saying:

One day Abū Salama ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān walked between me and al-Shaʿbī. Al-Shaʿbī said to him, “Who is the most learned of the people of Medina?” He replied:

“A man walking between you two.”

Abū Bakr related to us. He said: Sufyān related to us. He said: ʿAmr related to us, saying: Abū Salama ibn…

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān said: “I am more learned than whoever has urinated.” Ibn ʿAbbās replied: “In al-Mubārak.”

ʿAmr ibn Khālid related to us, from Ibn Lahīʿa, from Ibn al-Aswad, who said:

Abū Salama was with a group, and they saw a flock of sheep. He said: “O God, if it is in Your prior knowledge that I am to be caliph, let us drink their milk.” When he reached them, they were all billy goats.

ʿUBAYD ALLĀH IBN ʿABD ALLĀH IBN ʿUTBA

Ibn Bukayr related to us. He said: Yaʿqūb related to us. He said: I heard my father say:

I heard ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz say: “What I narrated from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUtba is more than what I narrated from all the people combined.”

Ibn Bukayr related to us. He said: Yaʿqūb related to me, from Ḥamza ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUtba ibn Masʿūd, who said:

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz used to say: “If ʿUbayd Allāh were alive, I would not have issued a decision except on his opinion. I would have wished to have one day with ʿUbayd Allāh in exchange for such and such.”

ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿImrān told me: Ibn Wahb related to us. He said: Yaʿqūb told me, from his father, who said:

I used to hear ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUtba say: “I have never heard a report intending to retain it without retaining it.”

Muḥammad ibn Abī Zakīr told me: Ibn Wahb informed me, from Mālik, who said: I heard him relate:

ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUtba was among the learned people, with abundant knowledge. Ibn Shihāb used to serve him, even handing him things. Ibn Shihāb would accompany ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUtba ibn Masʿūd, even drawing water for him.

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us. He said: Sufyān related to us. He said: I heard al-Zuhrī say:

“When I sat with ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUtba, I felt as though I were in the company of an ocean.”

Al-Ḥumaydī said: Sufyān related to us, saying:

A brother of ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh came to al-Zuhrī while we were with him. They were discussing that ʿUbayd Allāh used to compose poetry, and al-Zuhrī said: “ʿUbayd Allāh did compose poetry. Can one who has something in his breast refrain from giving it vent?” Sufyān said: Then al-Zuhrī recited these verses by ʿUbayd Allāh:

“Convey from me to ʿIrāk ibn Mālik … If you two do not do so, then to Abū Bakr

What do you want with a man of sixty years

for what he did when he was twenty or ten?

If I wished, more than one would speak out against you,

openly—or, he said, I have it in confidence.”

“If I neither command nor forbid you two,

I would laugh at him until he presses on and grows bold.

“Touch the dust of the earth, from which you two were created… The people feared no evil greater than arrogance.

“Were it not for fear of God, and forbearance toward you two,

I would reproach you with a reproach more bitter than embers.”

Saʿīd ibn Kathīr ibn ʿUfayr told me. He said: Yaʿqūb ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān told me, from his father:

ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUtba entered upon ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz—who was then governor of Medina—and greeted him. ʿUmar was turned toward ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān, and the two of them did not return his greeting. He said:

“Touch the dust of the earth, from which you two were created,

and in it is the return and the journey to the gathering.

“Do not be amazed that you should come and speak:

the people have never been filled with an evil worse than arrogance.

“If I wished, more than one would speak out against you,

openly—or, he said, I have it in confidence.

“If I neither command nor forbid you two,

I would laugh at him until he presses on and grows bold.”

The two turned toward him and apologized to him.

Abū Zayd ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī al-Ghamr related to us. He said: Yaʿqūb ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Zuhrī related to us, from his father, from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, who said:

“If ʿUbayd Allāh were alive, I would not have issued a decision except on his opinion.”

Abū Zayd told me: Yaʿqūb told me, from his father, that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said one day:

“I would have wished to have a day with ʿUbayd Allāh in exchange for such and such. If ʿUbayd Allāh were alive, I would not have issued a decision except on his opinion.”

Through the same chain: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said:

“What I heard—or what I narrated—from ʿUbayd Allāh alone is more than what I heard from all the other people.”

ʿABD AL-MALIK IBN MARWĀN

Ibn Numayr related to us. He said: Ḥafṣ related to us. He said: al-Aʿmash related to us, saying:

Abū al-Zinād related to us, saying: The jurists of the people of Medina were counted as four: Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān, ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr, and Qabīṣa ibn Dhuʾayb.

Saʿīd ibn Asad related to us. He said: Ḍamra related to us, from Rajāʾ ibn Abī Salama, from ʿUbāda ibn Nussī, who said:

Ibn ʿUmar was told, “You, the elders of Quraysh, are nearing extinction. Whom should we ask after you?” He replied: “Marwān has a son who is a jurist; ask him.”

MUḤAMMAD IBN KAʿB AL-QURAẒĪ

“Saʿīd ibn Abī Maryam related to us. He said: Nāfiʿ ibn Yazīd informed us. He said:

Abū Ṣakhr related to us, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muʿtab—or Mugīth ibn Abī Burda—from his father, from his grandfather, who said: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say:

“From one of the two soothsayer clans will emerge a man who will study the Qurʾān as no one after him will study it.”

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr related to us. He said: Yaʿqūb ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to us, from his father, who said:

I heard ʿAwn ibn ʿAbd Allāh say: “I have never seen anyone more knowledgeable about interpreting the Qurʾān than al-Quraẓī.”

Zayd ibn Bishr related to us. He said: Ibn Wahb informed me. He said: I heard Ibn Zayd say:

My father used to say: “If only Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī would be a little gentler and ease up on himself.”

I heard Muḥammad ibn Fuḍayl say:

Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb had companions who were among the people most knowledgeable about Qurʾānic exegesis. They used to gather in the mosque of al-Rabadha. An earthquake struck them, and the mosque collapsed upon them; they all died beneath it.

ʿAṬĀʾ IBN YASĀR

Zayd ibn Bishr related to us. He said: Ibn Wahb told me. He said: Ibn Zayd told me, from his father, who said:

We used to sit with ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār. My father and Abū Ḥāzim said: “We have never seen a man who was a greater adornment to the mosque of the Messenger of God ﷺ than ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār.” My father used to say: “If I were asked, ‘Of the people you have known, whom would you most wish to have live for you?’”—and he had known ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar and others—“I would say:

‘ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār.’” He said: My father used to say: “I have never seen anyone with a better dream vision than him.” He said to me: “Abū Usāma, I was told, ‘We will pull you three times, then place you in the highest division.’” He said: Then he was struck by pleurisy in Alexandria, and then— It struck him a second time, then struck him a third time, and that was when he died.

Zayd related to us. He said: Ibn Wahb informed me. He said: Ibn Zayd told me, from his father, who said:

Whenever I saw ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār in a gathering while I had some worldly need, I preferred sitting with him to attending to my need.

Abū Yūsuf Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us. He said: Zayd related to us, saying:

Ibn Wahb related to us. He said: Ibn Zayd told me, saying:

Abū Ḥāzim used to say: “I have never seen a man more constant in attending the mosque of the Messenger of God ﷺ than ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār. ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār and Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb did not take charge of expenses for [anything]; whatever they wanted, they placed in their wives’ hands and said, ‘Fear God, and take good care of your livelihood and your household.’”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us. He said: Sufyān related to us, saying:

ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār was one of the well-known companions of Abū Hurayra.

NāFIʿ IBN JUBAYR

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us. He said: Sufyān related to us, from Misʿar, who said:

It was mentioned that a roasted chicken had been prepared for Nāfiʿ ibn Jubayr. A beggar came, and he gave it to him. Someone reproached him about it, and he said: “I seek something better than it.”

Abū Bakr related to us. He said: Sufyān related to us, from Misʿar, who said:

Al-Ḥajjāj spoke to Nāfiʿ ibn Jubayr and mentioned Ibn ʿUmar. Al-Ḥajjāj said: “Was he the one who said such and such? If I had not struck off his head…” Nāfiʿ said to him: “God intended better for you than what you…”

“intended for yourself.” Al-Ḥajjāj said: “You are right.”

Al-Ḥajjāj said: “And ʿUmar, who says that people will soon recoil from their rulers—may God protect me lest that happen to me and to you—is he … and what would he have done had he lived to see that?” He said: “With the sword, like this and like that.” Sufyān gestured to his right and left. Nāfiʿ said: “Indeed, he was among the best of your governors.” He said:

“You are right.”

NUʿAYM AL-MUJМIR

Saʿīd ibn Abī Maryam related to us. Mālik informed us, saying:

Nuʿaym al-Mujmir sat with Abū Hurayra for twenty years.

Ibn Bukayr related to us. He said: al-Layth related to us, from Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd, who said:

“When you find the Medinan diligent and the Iraqi moderate, no two men will surpass them.”

YAZĪD IBN ʿABD ALLĀH IBN QUSAYṬ

ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿImrān and Aṣbagh ibn al-Faraj related to us, both saying: Ibn Wahb related to us. He said: Abū Ṣakhr told me that Ibn Qusayṭ related to him, saying that he heard Abū Hurayra say:

“I would not like to have a hundred she-camels, all with black pupils”—meaning camels—“and forgo washing on Friday.” This is the wording of ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz.

Abū Bishr told me. He said: Saʿīd ibn ʿĀmir told me, from Shuʿba, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-ʿAsqalānī, who said:

I heard Yazīd ibn Qusayṭ say: I heard Ibn ʿUmar say: “Nothing interrupts the prayer; ward them away from it.”

ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Shaqīq related to us. ʿAbd Allāh related to us. He said: Ḥaywa informed us— Ibn Shurayḥ said: Abū Ṣakhr informed me that he heard Yazīd ibn Qusayṭ say:

that he heard Abū Hurayra say: “There is no ablution required of one who sleeps sitting with his knees drawn up, nor of one who sleeps standing, nor of one who sleeps prostrate, until he lies down. When he lies down, he performs ablution.”

[K̲h̲ārija ibn Zayd ibn Thābit]

ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Saʿd related to us; my paternal uncle related to us; my father related to us, from Ibn Isḥāq, who said:

Yaḥyā ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī ʿAmra al-Anṣārī related to me, saying:

I heard K̲h̲ārija ibn Zayd ibn Thābit say: “By God, I remember myself when we were young lads in the time of ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān.”

[Al-ʿAbbās ibn Sahl ibn Saʿd]

ʿUbayd Allāh related to us; my paternal uncle related to us; my father related to us, from Ibn Isḥāq, who said:

Al-ʿAbbās ibn Sahl ibn Saʿd, a brother of Banū Sāʿida, related to me. I heard him say: “I was a man in the time of ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān.”

[Haramī ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Wāqifī]

ʿUbayd Allāh related to us; my paternal uncle related to us; my father related to us, from Ibn Isḥāq, who said: Haramī ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Wāqifī was born during the lifetime of the Messenger of God ﷺ—and lived to see the Companions when they were numerous.

[Rīḥān ibn Yazīd al-ʿĀmirī]

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Mak̲h̲ramī related to us; Abū Dāwūd Shuʿba related to us, from Saʿd ibn Ibrāhīm, who said: I heard a Bedouin Arab—never have I seen an Arab Bedouin like him—called Rīḥān, reporting from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr.

NEWS OF ʿUMAR IBN ʿABD AL-ʿAZĪZ

Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmar related to us; Sufyān related to me, saying: I heard Ayyūb say:

Al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik said to ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr: “What is ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz like with you?”—as though he had not praised him as highly as expected. He replied: “He is a righteous man, and I love the righteous.”

Saʿīd ibn ʿUfayr related to us; Yaʿqūb related to me, from his father, that ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Marwān sent his son ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz to Medina to be educated there, and wrote to Ṣāliḥ ibn Kaysān asking him to keep an eye on him. “ʿUmar used to go regularly to ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh, hearing knowledge from him. ʿUbayd Allāh heard that ʿUmar was disparaging ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. ʿUmar came to him while he was standing in prayer. ʿUmar sat down and did not leave until he had finished two rakʿas. Then he turned to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz and said: ‘When did you hear that God was displeased with the people of Badr after having been pleased with them?’ ʿUmar understood what he meant and said: ‘I ask your pardon. By God, I will not do it again.’ After that, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz was never heard mentioning ʿAlī except favorably.”

“Saʿīd related to me; Yaʿqūb related to me, from his father: ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Marwān sent his son ʿUmar to Medina to be educated there, and wrote to Ṣāliḥ ibn Kaysān asking him to keep an eye on him. ʿUmar used to attend the prayers regularly, but one day he was late for prayer. Ṣāliḥ asked: ‘What detained you?’ He replied: ‘My hairdresser was smoothing my hair.’ Ṣāliḥ said: ‘Has your love of having your hair smoothed reached the point that you prefer it to prayer?’ He wrote to ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz and told him about this.

“ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz sent a messenger to him, and would not speak to him until he had shaved his hair.”

“Saʿīd related to me; Yaʿqūb related to me, from his father, who said: When ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz used to let his garments trail and was extravagant with his perfume, a whole measure of cloves would go into his perfume. I saw ambergris on his beard like salt. But when the caliphate came to him, he abandoned that and dressed simply.

“He said: Riyāḥ ibn ʿUbayda told me—and he was a merchant from among the people of Basra who did business with ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz—that, while ʿUmar was in Medina, he ordered him to buy him a lined silk robe. ‘I bought it for ten dinars and brought it to him. He felt it and said: “I find it coarse.” When he became caliph, he ordered me to buy him a wool robe for one dinar. I did so and brought it to him. He kept putting his hand inside it and saying: “How soft it is!” I said: “How strange! Yesterday you found lined silk coarse, and today you find wool soft!” He said: “That was one circumstance, and this is another.”’”

Yūnus ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us, saying: Ashhab informed me, saying: Mālik said:

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz entered a church in Syria where his wife Fāṭima was. He spread over her a worn silk garment that he was wearing, then struck her thigh and said: “Fāṭima, our nights in Dābiq were more comfortable than we are today”—reminding her of a life she had forgotten. She struck his hand with a forceful blow, pushing it away from her, and said: “By my life, it is because today you have more power than you had then.” This affected him— that is, he became stern-faced—and he went to a place at the far end of the church where Yazīd had stood, saying in a sorrowful voice: “Fāṭima, I fear the Fire! Fāṭima, I fear the Fire! Fāṭima, I fear”—6:15 “if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous day”—6:15—in a sorrowful voice. Fāṭima wept and said: “O God, protect him from the Fire!”

Muḥammad ibn Abī Zukayr related to us, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Mālik related to me, saying: I have heard that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: “This morning I have nothing to do with these affairs except the occasions God has decreed for me in them.”

Muḥammad ibn Abī Zukayr also related to me; Ibn Wahb informed me; Mālik related to me:

When ʿUmar was appointed, people came to him. When they saw that he gave them only what he gave the general public, they dispersed from him. Then he drew near to himself the scholars whom he approved of.

“Saʿīd related to me; Yaʿqūb related to me, from his father, who said: When ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz became caliph, he relinquished the estates that had been in his possession. In his hands were al-Mukaydis, Mount al-Wars in Yemen, Fadak, and estates in al-Yamāma. He relinquished all of them and returned them to the Muslims, except for a spring at al-Suwaydāʾ which he had brought forth using his own funds. Its yield came to him each year: one hundred and fifty dinars, sometimes less and sometimes more. One day Muzāḥim told him that his family’s provisions had run out. He said: ‘Wait until our yield comes to us.’

“It was not long before Muzāḥim brought the price of his mule, a sack of ṣayḥānī dates, and a sack of ʿajwa dates, and poured them out before him. His family heard about this and sent him a young son. The boy scooped some dates for himself and went away. It was not long before we heard him burst into tears. Then he came toward the dinars. ʿUmar said: ‘Hold his hands!’ Then he raised his own hands and said: ‘O God, make them hateful to him, as You made them beloved to Mūsā ibn Nuṣayr.’ Then he said: ‘Let him go.’ It was as though he saw scorpions in them. Then he said: ‘Look for the blind old man from al-Jazīra who runs “to the mosque before dawn. Buy him a mount: neither a large one that would overpower him nor a small one that he would be too weak to manage.’ They did so. Then he said to Muzāḥim: ‘As for what remains, do as you see fit with it and spend it on your family.’”

Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb related to us; Jarīr ibn Ḥāzim related to us; al-Mughīra ibn Ḥakīm related to us, saying: Fāṭima, daughter of ʿAbd al-Malik and wife of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, said to me: “Mughīra, there may be people who pray and fast more than ʿUmar, but I have never seen anyone more fearful of his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, than ʿUmar. When he prayed the night prayer, he would sit in his mosque and raise his hands, and keep weeping until sleep overcame him. Then he would wake, and continue with his hands raised, weeping until sleep overcame him.”

Saʿīd ibn Asad related to us, saying: Ḍamra related to me, from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ḥamla, from Abū al-Ak̲h̲nas, who said: I was standing with K̲h̲ālid ibn Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya in the mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis when a young man came, wearing short garments. He took K̲h̲ālid by the hand and turned to him. The young man said to K̲h̲ālid: “Is there an evil eye upon us?” I said: “Yes, upon both of you there is an eye from God.” The young man’s eyes filled with tears. He pulled his hand from K̲h̲ālid’s, then went away.

He said: I asked K̲h̲ālid: “Who is that?” He replied: “That is ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, the son of the Commander of the Faithful’s brother.” ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān was then in Bayt al-Maqdis, and he said:

“By God, if your life is long, you will see him as an imam of right guidance.”

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān related to us, saying: ʿAbd Allāh related to us; al-Awzāʿī related to us, from Abū al-Ak̲h̲nas, who said: I was with K̲h̲ālid ibn Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya in the courtyard of Bayt al-Maqdis. A man approached him, took K̲h̲ālid by the hand, and said: “K̲h̲ālid, is there an “evil eye upon us?” I found it striking that he said, “K̲h̲ālid,” so I said: “Yes, upon both of you there is an ear from God that hears, and an eye that sees.” He pulled his hand from K̲h̲ālid’s and trembled. I said:

“K̲h̲ālid, who is this?” He replied: “This is ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. If your life is long, you will soon see him as a just imam—or an imam rightly guided.”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us, saying: Sufyān related to us, from a man who said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz told al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik something. He said to him: “You lie.” ʿUmar replied:

“I have not lied since I learned that lying harms those who practice it.”

Zayd ibn Bishr related to us, saying: Ibn Wahb informed me, saying: al-Layth ibn Saʿd related to me, from Abū al-Naḍr al-Madanī, who said: I met Sulaymān ibn Yasār as he was leaving ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. I asked him: “Have you come from ʿUmar?” He replied:

“I asked: ‘Do you consider him learned?’ He said: ‘Yes.’ I said: ‘By God, he is the most learned among you.’”

Zayd related to us; Ibn Wahb related to us, saying: al-Layth related to me that Ibrāhīm ibn ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz told him that he heard his father say to Ibn Shihāb: “Whenever you present something to me, I find that I have already heard it—except that you retain it better than I do.”

“Ibn Bukayr related to me, saying: al-Layth ibn Saʿd related to me, from ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Abī Salama, from Ṭalḥa ibn ʿAbd al-Malik al-Aylī, who said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz entered upon Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik while he was caliph, and his son Ayyūb was with him “and was heir apparent to the Muslims, having been designated to succeed him. A man came to him seeking an inheritance30 from one of the caliphs’ wives. Sulaymān said: ‘I do not think women inherit any share of real estate.’ ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: ‘Glory be to God! Then where is the Book of God?’ Sulaymān said: ‘Boy, go and bring me the register of ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān that was written about this matter.’ ʿUmar said to him: ‘It is as though you had sent for the Qurʾān on my behalf.’ Ayyūb said: ‘By God, a man who says something like this in the presence of the Commander of the Faithful is likely to speak, and then not realize until his head has parted from him.’ ʿUmar said to him: ‘If that comes into your hands, or comes into the hands of someone like you, what they bring upon those people will be more severe than what you feared might befall them from this.’ He said [Sulaymān to Ayyūb]: ‘Glory be to God! Who would have thought that Abū Ḥafṣ would say this!’ ʿUmar said: ‘By God, Commander of the Faithful, if his ignorance of this is a burden upon us, then our forbearance toward him is not.’

Ibn Bukayr related to us, saying: al-Layth related to me, from ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Abī Salama, from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿUmar ibn Ḥafṣ ibn ʿĀṣim ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Salama, who said: ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: I said to my father, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, about some of the property of his family that I saw him repeatedly returning.

“I said to him: ‘Father, carry out what you intend. By God, I do not care if the pot boils over with you and me in it for this.’ He said: ‘My son, by God, I am training people as one trains a difficult mount. I want to begin with a course of action that is right, but I fear it will be rejected unless I display alongside it some desire for worldly gain. If they turn away from this, they will not persist in that. If I live, I will carry out “what I intend, and if I die, God knows my intention.”

Ibn Bukayr related to us, saying: al-Layth related to me, saying: ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to me, from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿĀṣim, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz’s maternal uncle, who said: We came to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz when he was appointed caliph. People came to him from every place. He sat on the pulpit, praised God, and lauded Him. Then he said: “To proceed: people, return to your lands. I shall forget you here, but remember you in your lands. I have appointed governors over you; I do not say that they are the best among you. If a governor wrongs someone under his authority, that person has no need to ask my permission [to bring a complaint]. Whoever does not—may I never see him! By God, if I had kept this wealth from myself and my family and then begrudged it to you, I would indeed be miserly. By God, were it not that I might revive a sunna and act according to what is right, I would not wish to live for even a single breath.”

Ibn Bukayr related to us, saying: al-Layth related to me, from ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿUmar ibn Ḥafṣ, from a man of Wāsiṭ called Shayba ibn Musāwir, who said: I heard ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz address us after he was appointed caliph and sat on the pulpit. He praised God and lauded Him, then said: “To proceed, people: God did not send “a messenger after your Messenger, nor did He send down any book after the Book He sent down to him. Whatever God declared lawful through the words of His Messenger is lawful until the Day of Resurrection, and whatever God declared forbidden through the words of His Messenger is forbidden until the Day of Resurrection. Know that I am no innovator; I follow. I am no judge; I implement. I am no better than any one of you, but I am the one of you most able to bear the burden. Yet no one may be obeyed in disobedience to God. Have I made you hear? Have I made you hear?”

Saʿīd ibn Asad related to us; Ḍamra related to us, from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ḥamla and Ibn Shawk̲h̲ab, who said: ʿUmar ibn [al-Walīd ibn] ʿAbd al-Malik wrote a harsh letter to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. ʿUmar wrote back to him: “More unjust and oppressive than I am is the man who appointed the Thaqafī client over Iraq, giving him authority over their lives and property. More unjust and oppressive than I am, and more heedless of God’s covenant, is the man who appointed Qurra over Egypt, a boorish, uncouth fellow. More unjust and oppressive than I am, and more heedless of God’s covenant, is the man who appointed ʿUthmān ibn Ḥayyān over the Ḥijāz, where he recites “poems from the pulpit of the Messenger of God ﷺ. Your mother used to frequent the taverns of Ḥimṣ, and Dīnār ibn Dīnār bought her and sent her to your father, who impregnated her. What a wretched embryo, and what a wretched child! Then she gave birth to you, a tyrant, doomed to misery. I have nearly sent someone to shave your forelock. What a wretched forelock!”

Saʿīd related to us, saying: Ḍamra related to us, from Rajāʾ ibn Abī Salama, who said: ʿAnbasa ibn Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ said to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz—when he had cut off the stipends of the Companions, the Umayyad Companions—“Commander of the Faithful, I see a matter that can be set right only by considering the estate.” He replied: “You are on the right course, Abū Khālid. But think often of death, for if you place it in the midst of much, it will make it little; and if you place it in the midst of little, it will make it much. You are on the right course, Abū Khālid.”

Saʿīd related to us; Ḍamra related to us, from Rajāʾ, from al-Walīd ibn Hishām, who said:

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya came to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz and presented him with a debt of four thousand dinars. ʿUmar promised to pay it off on his behalf and said to him: “Appoint your brother al-Walīd ibn Hishām as your agent, and return to your family.” Al-Walīd said: “I pursued the matter of collecting it.”

He said: “Then ʿUmar said to me: ‘I have changed my mind about paying four thousand dinars on behalf of a single man—unless I knew that he had spent them on something good.’ I said: ‘Commander of the Faithful, then what of what we used to say: that it is among the qualities of a believer to fulfill what he promises?’ He said to me: ‘Woe to you, ibn Hishām! You have put me in this position.’”

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz al-Dhuhlī related to me: “Ḍamra related to us, from ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Abī al-Khaṭṭāb, from ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, who said: He said to me Rajāʾ ibn Ḥaywah said: “I have never seen anyone more complete in manly virtue than your father. One night I stayed up with him, and the lamp grew dim. He said to me, ‘Do you see that the lamp has grown dim?’ I said, ‘Yes.’” He continued: “Beside him was a sleeping attendant. He said, ‘Shall I wake him?’ I said, ‘No, let him sleep.’

“I said, ‘Then shall I get up myself?’ He said, ‘No. It is not part of a man’s virtue to put his guest to work.’

“He put down his cloak, then went to a hanging flask of oil, took it, and tended the lamp. Then he put the flask back in its place and returned to me. He said, ‘I got up as ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, and I came back as ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz.’”

[Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz told me: Ḍamrah related to us, from al-Sarī ibn Yaḥyā, from Riyāḥ ibn ʿUbaydah, who said: “I saw a man walking with ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, leaning on his hands. I thought to myself, ‘This man is rude.’ When ʿUmar had finished praying, I asked, ‘Who was the man who was just leaning on your hand?’

“He said, ‘Did you see him, Riyāḥ?’ I said, ‘Yes. I had thought you were a righteous man.’

“He said, ‘That was my brother al-Khiḍr. He gave me the good news that I would rule and act justly.’”

Abū ʿUmayr told me: Ḍamrah related to us, from ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Abī al-Khaṭṭāb, from ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, who said: Rajāʾ ibn Ḥaywah said to me, “I have never seen a man more complete in manly virtue than your father. One night I stayed up with him…”

The lamp was shining, then it grew dim. He said to me, “Rajāʾ, the lamp has grown dim, and an attendant is asleep beside us.” I said, “Shall I wake the attendant?” He said, “He has fallen asleep.”

I said, “Then I shall get up and tend it.” He said, “It is not part of a man’s virtue to put his guest to work.” He laid a woollen cloak over himself, went to a flask containing oil, poured some into the lamp and tended it, then returned. He said, “I got up as ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, and I came back as ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz.” Ḍamrah said: “Manly virtue is keeping oneself above every base trait.”

[Abū ʿUmayr told me: Ḍamrah related to us, from Ibn Abī Ḥamlah, from Abū al-Akhnas, who said: “I was sitting with Khālid ibn Yazīd in the courtyard of Bayt al-Maqdis when a young man wearing patched garments came up and took Khālid by the hand. He said, ‘Is there an eye watching?’ Abū al-Akhnas said: I hastened to say, ‘May there be upon you two an eye from God that hears and sees.’ He said:

“The young man’s eyes welled up, and he released Khālid’s hand and went away. I asked, ‘Who is this?’

“He said, ‘This is ʿUmar ibn al-ʿAzīz, the nephew of the Commander of the Faithful. If you and he live long enough, you will surely see him as an imam of guidance.’”

Hishām ibn ʿAmmār told me: Yaḥyā ibn Ḥamzah related to us, from Sulaymān, that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said to his sons: “Would you like me to appoint each of you over an army, so that you might set out with the post bells ringing for you?” His son Ibn al-Ḥārithiyyah said to him, “Why ask us when you are not going to do it?” ʿUmar said, “I know that this carpet of mine will come to ruin, and I would hate for you to soil it with your slippers. How, then, could I entrust you with my religion, for you to soil it in every army!”

Hishām ibn ʿAmmār told me: Yaḥyā ibn Ḥamzah related to us, from ʿAmr ibn Muhājir, that ʿUmar had a candle lit for him while he was occupied with the Muslims’ affairs. When he had finished dealing with their affairs, he extinguished it and then lit his own lamp.

ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿImrān told me: Ibn Wahb related to us, saying: Ibn Abī al-Zinād’s son informed me, from his father, who said: “I heard Maslamah ibn ʿAbd al-Malik say: ‘May God have mercy on my uncle. By God, he died without ever reaching the distinction of receiving a generous gift. By God, he held fast to the front of his shirt, then suffered hardship in this world until he departed from it.’ Then he raised his voice and said: ‘That abode of the Hereafter We assign to those who seek neither exaltation in the earth nor corruption; and the final outcome is for the God-fearing.’” (28:83)

[Ibn Bukayr told us: Yaʿqūb told me: I heard my father say:

“ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said, ‘Heat for me the water with which I will bathe for Friday prayer.’ They said, ‘Commander of the Faithful, by God, we have no firewood to kindle.’ They took the ewer to the kitchen—the Muslims’ kitchen—and then brought it back to him. They said, ‘Here is the ewer, Commander of the Faithful; it is boiling.’ He said, ‘Did you not tell me that you had no firewood? Perhaps you took it to the Muslims’ kitchen?’ They said, ‘Yes.’ He said, ‘Call the kitchen steward.’ When the steward came, he said to him, ‘Were you told this was the Commander of the Faithful’s ewer and then kindled a fire beneath it?’ He said, ‘No, by God, Commander of the Faithful. I did not put a single stick under it. It was only embers which, had I left them, would have gone out and turned to ash.’ He said, ‘How much did you pay for the firewood?’

“He said, ‘Such and such.’ ʿUmar said, ‘Pay him its price.’”

Ibn Bukayr told us: Yaʿqūb told me: I heard my father say:

“One day ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said, ‘I wish I had some honey from Sīnīn or Lebanon.’ His wife, Fāṭimah daughter of ʿAbd al-Malik, heard him and sent one of her servants—or one of her clients—to Ibn Maʿdīkarib, who was the governor of that region, with the message, ‘The Commander of the Faithful has taken a fancy to honey from Sīnīn or Lebanon.’ He sent her a large quantity of honey. When the honey reached her, she sent it to ʿUmar and said, ‘This is what you wished for the other day, Commander of the Faithful.’ He said, ‘I can just imagine you, Fāṭimah: when you heard that I had taken a fancy to this honey, you sent one of your clients or one of your servants to Ibn Maʿdīkarib.’

“He ordered that the honey be taken out to the market and sold, and its price was deposited in the Muslims’ treasury. Then he wrote to Ibn Maʿdīkarib: ‘Fāṭimah daughter of ʿAbd al-Malik sent you word that I had taken a fancy to honey from Sīnīn or Lebanon, and you sent it to her. By God, if you do such a thing again, you will never work for me again, and I will never look upon your face.’”

Ibn Bukayr and Abū Zayd related to us a similar account. They said: [Yaʿqūb related to us, from his father:

“ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz went to his father, who was caliph, to ask him for clothes. He said, ‘Father, clothe me.’ He replied, ‘Go to al-Khiyār ibn Riyāḥ al-Baṣrī. I have clothes with him; take whatever you like.’ He went to al-Khiyār ibn Riyāḥ and said, ‘I asked my father for clothes, and he sent me to you, saying that I have clothes with al-Khiyār ibn Riyāḥ—Sanbulānī or Qaṭarī clothes.’ He said, ‘These are what the Commander of the Faithful has with me. Take some of them.’ ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar returned to his father, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, and said, ‘Father, I asked you for clothes, and you sent me to al-Khiyār ibn Riyāḥ. He brought me clothes that are neither my clothes nor…”

…my people’s clothes.” He said, “That is what we have with the man.” ʿAbd Allāh went away, but just as he was about to leave, his father called him and said, “Would you like me to advance you one hundred dirhams from your stipend?” He said, “Yes, Father.” He advanced him one hundred dirhams. When his stipend was paid, the amount was charged against him and deducted from it.”

Ḥarmalah related to us: Ibn Wahb related to us: al-Layth related to me, from Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd and others, that some people from Medina came to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. He began asking him about the people of Medina. He said, “What became of the poor people who used to sit in such-and-such a place?” He replied, “They have left it, Commander of the Faithful.” He said, “And what became of the poor people who used to sit in such-and-such a place?”

He replied, “They have left it, and God has enriched them.” Among those poor people was a man who sold balls of thread to travellers. ʿUmar asked after him, and they said, “God has freed us from selling them, through what ʿUmar gives us.” Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd said: ʿUmar then asked, “What became of Busr ibn Saʿīd?” He replied, “He is well, Commander of the Faithful.” ʿUmar said, “Still in the two garments I knew him in?” He replied, “Yes, in his two garments.” ʿUmar said, “By God, if Busr ibn Saʿīd and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Malik are in Paradise at the same rank, I would rather live as ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Malik lives and be with him at his rank than live as Busr ibn Saʿīd lives and be with him at his rank.”

Ḥarmalah told me: [Ibn Wahb informed us: al-Layth related to me that Abū al-Naḍr told him: “I secretly asked one of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz’s relatives to tell him, ‘There is pride in you; you are conceited.’ This was said to him. ʿUmar replied, ‘Tell him: How badly you have thought of me, if you imagine that I am so scrupulous about the dinar and the dirham out of fear of God, yet I would commit the greatest of sins by riding it! Pride is the Mantle of the All-Merciful, and I would be contending with Him for it. Rather, when I was a boy among my people, they would enter upon me without permission, tread on my bedding, and take from me what people take from a brother over whom they have no authority. When I was appointed to office, I had to choose: either let them continue treating me as they had before, while opposing them whenever they opposed the truth, or bar them from my door and my presence so that they would restrain themselves from me and from what I feared for them, lest I embolden them against myself and expose them to punishment and discipline. That is what led me to this.’”

Ḥarmalah told me: Ibn Wahb related to us: al-Layth related to me, saying:

[A shaykh informed me, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Zakariyyā, that he visited ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz—having felt concern for him because he had heard of the hardship that had come upon ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz’s family. They spoke for a while, then he said, “Commander of the Faithful, I have seen you do something. On what grounds have you deemed it lawful?” He asked, “What is it?” He said, “You pay one of your officials one hundred dinars a month, two hundred dinars a month, or more than that.” ʿUmar said, “I consider that little for them if they act according to God’s Book and the Sunna of His Prophet. I want to free their hearts from worry about their livelihood and their families.” Ibn Abī Zakariyyā said, “You have done well. I have also been told that hardship has come upon your family, and you are the greatest among them in service. Consider what you have judged lawful for one of them, and draw the same stipend yourself, so that you may provide more generously for your family.” He replied, “May God have mercy on you. I know you intended only good, and that you were concerned by some of what you hear about our circumstances.” Then he placed his right hand on his left arm and said, “This bone has grown only from the wealth of God. By God, if I can help it, I will never put any of it back into it again.”

Ḥarmalah told me: Ibn Wahb informed us: al-Layth related to me, from Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Jumaḥī, from Muḥammad ibn Qays, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz’s storyteller, who said: “One day Muzāḥim came out to us and said, ‘The Commander of the Faithful’s family needs some money, and I do not know where to get it or from whom to borrow it.’ I said, ‘If I had more at my disposal, I would offer it to you.’ He asked, ‘How much do you have?’ I said, ‘Five dinars.’ He said, ‘By God, five dinars will suffice.’ I gave them to him. Then men from ʿUmar’s lands came to him with dates. Muzāḥim passed by me, delighted, and said:

“‘We have received some property from one of our lands; we shall repay you those five dinars now.’ He went in, then came out with one hand on his head, saying, ‘May God magnify the reward of the Commander of the Faithful! May God magnify the reward of the Commander of the Faithful! May God magnify the reward of the Commander of the Faithful!’ We said, ‘Yes indeed. May God magnify his reward. What is the matter?’ He said, ‘He ordered that this property that came from one of his lands be deposited in the treasury. I do not know how he managed to find the five dinars for me and repay me.’”

ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to us—Ibn Wahb—who said: Yaʿqūb ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to me, from his father, from Ziyād, the client of Ibn ʿAyyāsh, who said: “If only you had seen me when I visited ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz on a cold night. There was a brazier in his house, and ʿUmar was occupied with his writing. I sat warming myself by the brazier. When he had finished writing, ʿUmar came over and sat with me beside the brazier, although he was caliph. He said, ‘Ziyād ibn Abī Ziyād?’ I said, ‘Yes, Commander of the Faithful.’

“He said, ‘Tell me a story.’ I replied, ‘Commander of the Faithful, I am no storyteller.’ He said, ‘Then speak.’ I said:

“‘Ziyād…’ He said, ‘What about him?’ I said, ‘It will not benefit a man tomorrow to have entered Paradise if he enters the Fire, nor will it harm him to have entered the Fire tomorrow if he enters Paradise.’ He said, ‘You are right. By God, the one who enters Paradise will not benefit you if you enter the Fire, and the one who enters the Fire will not harm you if you enter Paradise.’ I saw ʿUmar weep until some of the embers in the brazier went out…”

…that were in the brazier.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān related to us: ʿAbd Allāh related to us: Muḥammad ibn Abī Ḥumayd al-Madanī related to us, from Ibrāhīm ibn ʿUbayd ibn Rifāʿah, who said: “I was present when Muḥammad ibn Qays was speaking to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. I saw ʿUmar weep until his ribs moved against one another.”

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān related to us, saying: ʿAbd Allāh related to us: Abū al-Ṣabbāḥ related to us: Sahl ibn Ṣadaqah, the client of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Marwān, told me: “One of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz’s close family members told me that, when the caliphate passed to him, they heard loud weeping in his house. They asked about the weeping and were told that ʿUmar had given his slave girls a choice. He said, ‘A matter has come upon me that has occupied me to the exclusion of you. Whoever wishes me to set her free, I shall set her free; whoever I keep, she will have no claim against me.’ They wept in despair of him.”

Ibn ʿUthmān related to us, saying: ʿAbd Allāh related to us: Ibrāhīm ibn Nashīṭ informed us: Sulaym ibn Ḥumayd al-Muzanī related to us, from Abū ʿUbaydah ibn ʿUqbah ibn Nāfiʿ al-Qurashī, that he visited Fāṭimah daughter of ʿAbd al-Malik, along with an uncle of hers, and said, “Will you not tell me about ʿUmar?” She replied:

“I do not know that he ever bathed after major ritual impurity or a wet dream from the time God appointed him caliph until He took him.”

Ibn ʿUthmān related to us: ʿAbd Allāh related to us, from Maymūn ibn Mihrān, that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz was brought chard and round loaves. He ate, then lay down on his bed, covered his face with the edge of his cloak, and began to weep and say: “A sluggish, gluttonous servant drags his feet and aspires to the ranks of the righteous through God.”

Muḥammad ibn Ramḥ told me: al-Layth ibn Saʿd told me that it had reached him that, when Maslamah ibn ʿAbd al-Malik saw ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz’s illness grow severe and thought he was dying, he said, “Commander of the Faithful, you have left your sons dependents, with nothing of their own, and they will inevitably need what they must have. If you were to entrust them to me and to my peers among my people, would we not spare you the burden of providing for them?” He replied:

“Sit me up.” They sat him up, and he said, “As for the poverty and need of my children that you mentioned, by God, I have not withheld from them any right that belongs to them, nor would I give them anyone else’s right. As for your offer to appoint you and your peers as guardians over them, to spare me the burden of providing for them, their guardian is the One who sent down the Book and who takes care of the righteous.” (7:196) “Call them to me.” He said: “I called them, and there were twelve of them. His eyes filled with tears, and he said, ‘How can I leave them as dependents?’ They are only one of two kinds of men: either a man who fears God and is mindful of Him, in which case God will provide for him; or a man who falls into something other than that. I would not wish to have strengthened him in disobedience to God’s command. I have left them in a good position: they will meet no Muslim or member of the protected communities without that person recognizing your rights. Go; may God protect you and provide you with a good guardian in my place.’”—may God have mercy on ʿUmar.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān related to us: Muḥammad ibn Marwān related to us: ʿUmārah ibn Abī Ḥafṣah related to us, that Maslamah ibn ʿAbd al-Malik visited ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz during the illness in which he died and asked, “To whose care are you entrusting your family?” He said, “If you forget God, remind me.”

He returned to the question and said, “To whose care are you entrusting your family?” ʿUmar replied, “If I entrust them to anyone, it is to God, who sent down the Book and takes care of the righteous.”

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān related to us: ʿAbd Allāh informed us that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said to his client Muzāḥim, who was a man of merit: “These people”—meaning his family—“have assigned to me property that I had no right to take, and that they had no right to give me. I have been considering returning it to its owners.” Muzāḥim said, “What will you do about your children?” ʿUmar’s tears fell onto his cheeks. He wiped them with his middle finger and said, “I leave them in God’s care.” ʿAbd Allāh said: “It is known that he felt for his children what people feel for their own.” ʿAbd Allāh said: “It seems that Muzāḥim, despite his merit, was not satisfied with what ʿUmar had said. He went out and visited ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿUmar. He said, ‘The Commander of the Faithful has considered something that will harm you and your father’s children more than such-and-such: he has considered returning al-Basīṭah.’” ʿAbd Allāh said: “It is in al-Yamāmah, and it is a great estate.” He said: “His children’s livelihood came from it.” ʿAbd al-Malik said, “What did you say to him?” He replied, “Such-and-such.” ʿAbd al-Malik said, “By God, how wretched a vizier of the caliph you are!” Then he rose to go in to ʿUmar, who had settled down for his midday rest.

He asked permission to enter. The doorkeeper said, “He has settled down for his midday rest.” ʿAbd al-Malik said, “There is no avoiding it.” The doorkeeper said, “Glory be to God! Have you no pity for him? It is his hour of rest.” ʿUmar heard his voice and said, “Is that ʿAbd al-Malik?” He said, “Yes.” ʿUmar said, “Let him in.” He entered. ʿUmar asked, “What brings you here?” He said, “Muzāḥim told me such-and-such,” then asked, “What do you think? I intend to carry it out this evening.” ʿAbd al-Malik said, “I think you should do it at once. You cannot be sure that something will not happen to you, or that something will not happen in your heart.” ʿUmar raised his hands and said, “Praise be to God, who…”

“[He] made for me, from my descendants, someone who would help me in my religion.” He said: Then, at once, he rose, gathered the people, and ordered that it be returned.

[Hishām ibn ʿAmmār related to us: Yaḥyā ibn Ḥamzah related to us: Sulaymān related to me: ʿUmar examined his estates and tore up their registers, except for the two estates of Khaybar and al-Suwaydāʾ.

ʿUmar asked: “How had Khaybar come to belong to his father?” They replied: “It had been fayʾ for the Messenger of God ﷺ—and the Messenger of God ﷺ—left it as fayʾ for the Muslims. Then, in the time of ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, he gave it to Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam; Marwān gave it to ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, ʿUmar’s father; and ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz gave it to ʿUmar.” So he tore up its register and said:

“I shall leave it as the Messenger of God ﷺ—left it.” “I have been told that it was Fadak.”]

Hishām ibn ʿAmmār related to us: Yaḥyā ibn Ḥamzah related to us: Sulaymān ibn Dāwūd al-Khawlānī related to us: A man pledged allegiance to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. He held out his hand to him, then said: “Pledge allegiance to me without any covenant or pact: you shall obey me so long as I obey God; but if I disobey God, then I have no claim to your obedience.” He pledged allegiance to him.

Hishām related to me: Yaḥyā related to us, from Sulaymān ibn Dāwūd: ʿAbdah ibn Abī Lubābah sent with me the one hundred and fifty, for me to distribute among the poor of the provincial capitals. I went to al-Mājishūn and asked him. He said: “I know of no one among them who is in need today. ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz has made them self-sufficient.” So I handed it over to them; he left none of them out except the soldiers.

Hishām related to us: Yaḥyā related to us: Sulaymān related to us: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz often repeated these words: “What would my own self gain from another self if I killed it? The Book of God says only, ‘A life for a life.’ Whoever kills a person has forfeited his pledge. If I had two lives, I could make amends with one of them and keep the other.”

Hishām related to me: ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd ibn Abī al-ʿIshrīn said to us: Muḥammad ibn Kathīr related to me: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said one day—while reproaching himself:

“Are you awake today, or are you asleep? How can one bewildered and wandering endure sleep?

“If you were awake this morning, the pouring tears would scorch your eyes.

“Your day, deluded one, is frivolity and heedlessness; your night is sleep, while death is ever near you.

“You busy yourself with what will bring you a bitter end. Such is how beasts live in this world.”

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān related to us: ʿAbd Allāh informed us: Hishām ibn al-Ghāz informed us: We stopped at a station on our return from Dābiq. When we set out, Makḥūl went on ahead without telling us where he was going. We traveled a long way before we saw him. I said: “Where did you go?” He replied: “I went to the grave of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz—it is five miles from the station—and prayed for him.” Then he said:

“If I were to swear an oath, I would make no exception: in his time there was no one more fearful of God than ʿUmar. And if I were to swear an oath, I would make no exception: in his time there was no one more ascetic toward this world than ʿUmar.”

Ibn ʿUthmān related to us: ʿAbd Allāh informed us: ʿUmar ibn Saʿīd ibn Abī Ḥusayn related to us, from Mujāhid: He witnessed the death of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. He passed by an ʿIbādī or a Nabataean—who was plowing with two oxen of his—and the man stood up when I passed him. The ʿIbādī or Nabataean said to him:

“Where have you come from? Were you present when this man died?” I replied: “Yes.” His eyes brimmed with tears, and he prayed for God’s mercy upon him. I said: “You pray for God’s mercy upon him, though he was not of your religion?” He replied: “I am not weeping for your king; I am weeping for a light that was on earth and has been extinguished.”

Muḥammad ibn Abī Zukayr related to me: Ibn Wahb informed us: Mālik related to me, from Ibn Abī Ṣaʿṣaʿah: He used to tell ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz about the campaigns against Constantinople. ʿUmar wept bitterly. Mālik said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said one night, when Muẓāḥim and a man called Ibn Māfinah were with him:

ʿUmar entered his house, then said to Muẓāḥim: “Admit Ibn Māfinah.” He admitted him. I entered and saw a dining table with a dish on it, covered by a napkin, while ʿUmar stood praying. He performed two units of prayer, then came over and sat down. He drew the table toward him with his hand and said to me: “Eat. How far our living today is from our living when we were in Egypt!” I said: “Why, Commander of the Faithful?” ʿUmar replied: “I remember when, if the people of a village had hosted me, I would have had enough to feed them all.” Then he said: “How far this living of ours is from our living in Medina!”

Then he made himself weep. Muẓāḥim called out to him: “Get up.” I got up. The next day he told me that when something like this happened to ʿUmar, he would not return to his food. Mālik said: “I find this admirable in ʿUmar: that a person should serve himself.”]

Muḥammad related to us: Ibn Wahb related to us: Mālik related to me: ʿUthmān ibn Ḥayyān was governor of Medina during the caliphate of al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik. Ibn Ḥazm was judge at that time. ʿUthmān ibn Ḥayyān was later dismissed, and Abū Bakr ibn Ḥazm was appointed in his place. After that, Riyāḥ ibn Ḥayyān governed Medina. Mālik said: Riyāḥ related to me: “No courier ever came to us in Syria from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz except with a revival of a Sunna, a distribution of wealth, or an instruction that brought good.”

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān related to us: ʿAbd Allāh informed us: Ḥarmalah ibn ʿImrān informed us: Sulaymān ibn Ḥumayd related to me: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz wrote to ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿUmar: “There is no one whose sound judgment and good conduct are dearer to me than yours, unless he is in charge of a group of Muslims or protected people, for whose well-being his sound judgment and good conduct can achieve what no one else can, or whose corruption can harm them in a way no one else can.”

Ibn ʿUthmān related to us: ʿAbd Allāh related to us: Jarīr ibn Ḥāzim related to us: al-Mughīrah ibn Ḥakīm related to us: Fāṭimah said to me: “During the illness in which ʿUmar died, I used to hear him say: ‘O God, conceal my death from them for even one hour of the day.’” She said: “One day I said to him: ‘Commander of the Faithful, shall I leave you, so that perhaps you may doze a little? You have not slept.’”

She said: “I left him and went to a room beside the one he was in. I heard him saying, ‘That abode of the Hereafter We assign to those who seek neither exaltation on earth nor corruption; and the outcome is for the God-fearing’ (28:83), repeating it again and again. Then he fell silent and remained so…”

…for a long time, and I could hear no sound from him. I said to a young attendant of his who served him: “Woe to you, go in and see.” When he entered, he cried out. I went in to him and found him dead, his face turned toward the qibla, one of his hands placed over his mouth and the other over his eyes.

[Ibn ʿUthmān related to us: ʿAbd Allāh said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: “I considered my own affairs and the affairs of the people, and saw nothing better than death”—ʿAbd Allāh said: “meaning, because of the people’s corruption and what had come upon them.” He said to his preacher, Muḥammad ibn Qays: “Pray for me to die.” I refused, and he insisted. He said: “So I prayed for him, while ʿUmar raised his hands, saying ‘Amen’ to my prayer and weeping. His young son was present, and when he saw ʿUmar weeping, he wept too. ʿUmar said: ‘And this one is with us.’ So I prayed for that too. Muḥammad ibn Qays says: ‘I felt embarrassed, and prayed for myself along with them as well.’ God recognized ʿUmar’s sincerity, and before long he died, and that son of his died; Muḥammad ibn Qays, however, lived on.”]

[Yūnus ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us: Ashhab informed me, from Mālik, who said: The pages of Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik and the pages of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz fought, and Sulaymān’s pages struck [them]. Sulaymān was incensed, and it was said to him: “This is what his conduct has brought about and done to him.” ʿUmar went in to him, and Sulaymān said: “What is this? Your pages have beaten my pages.”
