ʿUmar said: “I knew nothing of this until you told me just now.” Sulaymān said to him: “You lie.” ʿUmar said to him: “You say to me, ‘You lie’! I have not lied since I first girded my waist-cloth. And there is ample room in the land away from this gathering of yours.” Then he left him and did not return. He made preparations to leave for Egypt. Sulaymān asked about him [when he had been away too long, and they said: …]

“‘He intends to leave for Egypt, and has made preparations.’ So Sulaymān sent to him]: ‘Come back and enter to see me.’ He told the messenger: ‘When I come to him, let him not reproach me, for reproach breeds [resentment]’. ʿUmar came, and Sulaymān said to him: ‘Whenever I have had an important matter, you have always come to mind.’”] It is said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz rose from his gathering and went to his place of prayer. He mentioned Sahl ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, ʿAbd al-Malik, and Muẓāḥim, and said: “O God, You know how they supported me and assisted me; repay them accordingly. Let nothing from that increase in me except love for them, and longing for what is with You.” Then he returned to his gathering.

Yūnus ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us: Ashhab informed me, from Mālik, who said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz asked a man about the people’s affairs and about the judge. Then he said: “The subjects ought to render to the ruler his due, and the ruler ought to render to the subjects the due they have against him, without being coerced into doing so or taking pleasure in it.”

Yūnus related to me: Ashhab related to us, from Mālik, who said: When ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz was appointed caliph, one of his governors wrote to him: “When the people heard of your appointment, they hastened to pay the zakāt al-fiṭr. A considerable sum has accumulated, and I did not wish to make any decision about it until you wrote to me with your view.” ʿUmar wrote back acknowledging receipt of his letter, saying: “By my life, I do not care what they thought of us. Why have you kept it back until today? Disburse it as soon as you read my letter.”

Ibrāhīm ibn Muḥammad al-Shāfiʿī related to me: I heard my grandfather, Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Shāfiʿ, say: “I hope that God will admit Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik to Paradise for appointing ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz.”

Ibrāhīm ibn Muḥammad related to us: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ḥasan al-Zuraqī related to us, from his father—who served under al-Jarrāḥ ibn ʿAbd Allāh, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz’s governor over all of Khurāsān, in its warfare, prayers, and revenues—who said: ʿUmar wrote to Ibn al-Jarrāḥ: “I have been told that you appointed ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ahtam, though God has not yet blessed ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ahtam in his office, and has enriched him; he is also a kinsman of the Commander of the Faithful. I have been told that you appointed ʿUmārah. I have no need of ʿUmārah, of striking ʿUmārah, or of a man who has stained his hand with the blood of Muslims. Dismiss him.”

Ibrāhīm ibn Muḥammad related to me: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ḥasan related to us, from his father:

Al-Jarrāḥ wrote to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz: “To proceed, Commander of the Faithful: You wrote to me in the mandate you gave me, ordering me not to inflict punishment on any of God’s creatures, nor to bind any of God’s creatures in such a way as to prevent prayer.” This was in a letter of reproach addressed to him.

Ibrāhīm related to me: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ḥasan related to us: My father related to me: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz wrote to his governor in Yemen, ʿUrwah ibn Muḥammad al-Saʿdī:

“I am writing to you, ordering you to restore to the Muslims what was wrongfully taken from them. You write back to me, arguing with me, though you do not know the distance between us, nor do you know the sudden assaults of death. If I wrote to you to restore to a man the wrongful taking of a sheep, you would write to ask whether I should restore a white one or a black one. So restore to the Muslims what was wrongfully taken from them, and do not argue with me. Peace.”

Ibrāhīm related to me: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ḥasan related to us: My father informed me: I have been told that al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik appointed ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz over the Ḥijāz—Medina, Mecca, and al-Ṭāʾif—but ʿUmar was slow to set out. Al-Walīd said to his chamberlain: “Woe to you! Why has ʿUmar not set out for his post?” He replied: “He says he has three requests to make of you.” Al-Walīd said:

“Bring him to me at once.” He brought him to al-Walīd. ʿUmar said to him: “You appointed the men who came before me. I do not wish you to hold me to the practices of hostility, oppression, and injustice.” Al-Walīd said to him: “Act justly, even if you send us not a single dirham.” ʿUmar said: “As for the pilgrimage, you see how old and infirm I have become.” I am uncertain about the stipend: perhaps he asked al-Walīd for it, and al-Walīd distributed it among the people.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān related to us: ʿAwn informed us, from Maʿmar, who said: Ismāʿīl ibn related to me: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz wrote to some of the people of Syria—he said:

“None memorized it other than Makḥūl and al-Awzāʿī”: “To proceed: Whoever often remembers death will find little sufficient for him, and whoever knows that his speech is an action will speak little except about what benefits him.”

Ibn ʿUthmān related to us: ʿAwn informed us, from Maʿmar, who said: al-Ḥasan wrote to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz: “To proceed: Whoever’s final illness is death has died.” ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz wrote back to him: “To proceed: It is as though this world had never existed, and the Hereafter had always been. Peace be upon you.”

Ibn ʿUthmān related to us: ʿUmar ibn ʿAlī related to us: ʿAbd Rabb ibn Hilāl ibn Abī Hilāl informed us: Maymūn ibn Mihrān informed me: I was with ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz when he began to speak eloquently, until his companions were moved. He noticed one of them wiping away a tear, and broke off his speech. Maymūn said: I said, “Continue your speech, Commander of the Faithful, for I hope that through you God will benefit those who hear it and those to whom it reaches.” He gestured with his hand: “Leave me be! There is temptation in speech, and action is more fitting for a person than speech.”

[Ibn Bukayr and Abū Zayd related to us: Yaʿqūb related to us: I heard my father relate: Thirty thousand dirhams from the revenues of Bahrain came to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. The man who managed his household’s food came to him and said: “Commander of the Faithful, God has provided you with an allowance.” He asked: “From where?” The man said: “Thirty thousand from your property in Bahrain have come to you.” ʿUmar said the prayer of return to God and said: “Call Muẓāḥim for me.” When Muẓāḥim came, he said: “Muẓāḥim, did you add that money that came to us from Bahrain to the property of God, as I suppose?”—Ibn Bukayr was unsure. Muẓāḥim said: “It slipped my mind, Commander of the Faithful.” He said: “Then return it, and add this money to the treasury of the Muslims.”

The steward of that property came in to him and said: “Commander of the Faithful, free me from slavery—may God free you from the Fire.” ʿUmar looked at him and said: “You and that property both belong to the property of God, so there is no way for me to free you.” The man said: “Commander of the Faithful, I had a jar of preserved ginger that I used to bring you every year as a gift, and I have brought it now.” ʿUmar said: “Bring it.” The man took out a piece and placed it on his lips. Then ʿUmar said: “Stop. When you have doubts about something, leave it. I have no need of your jar.”]

ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to me: Ibn Wahb related to us: Yaʿqūb related to me—I think from his father—who said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz admitted Ziyād ibn Abī Ziyād, while the Umayyads were there waiting to enter his presence. Hishām said: “Was Ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz not satisfied with what he had done, that he admitted ʿAbd [ʿAbd] Allāh ibn ʿAyyāsh, letting him step over our necks?” He said to al-Farazdaq: “Who is this?”

He replied: “A man from Medina, one of the Qurʾān reciters; a slave.” Al-Farazdaq said:

“O reciter whose need has been fulfilled, this is your time; my time has passed.”

ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to us: Ibn Wahb related to us: Yaʿqūb related to me, from his father, who said:

An eminent elderly man from Syria came in to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz and said: “Commander of the Faithful, I entered Egypt with Marwān, and I fought at Dayr al-Jamājim and in such-and-such a campaign. Will you grant me something?” He said: “Sit down, old man.” The old man was there. Then a young man from the Anṣār spoke to him: “Commander of the Faithful, I am so-and-so son of so-and-so. My father was among those who witnessed al-ʿAqabah, Badr, and Uḥud”—and he went on to list campaigns.

ʿUmar said: “Old man, what did you mention?” The old man knelt down—or stood up—and said: “Here it is, Commander of the Faithful.” ʿUmar said: “These are the noble deeds, not what you have been listing since today, old man.”

“Those noble deeds—not two bowls of milk, mixed with water, which afterward became urine.”

“See to the young man’s need.”

Muḥammad ibn Abī Zukayr related to us: Ibn Wahb informed us; Mālik related to us, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿīd, from Marthad, who said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to me that he would sometimes go out with a small warrant, about this size—and Mālik indicated with some of his fingers—on which was written a grant of forty thousand dinars for ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. No one knew where he directed it.

Muḥammad and Zayd ibn Bishr related to me. They said: Ibn Wahb informed us; he said: Mālik related to me that when ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz was appointed, people came to him, but he accepted only a man who possessed goodness or piety. When someone interceded with him for a friend of his, he said: “We have left him behind, just as we left behind brocade and embroidered cloth.”

Muḥammad related to us: Ibn Wahb informed us. He said: I heard Mālik relate that when Ṣāliḥ ibn ʿAlī arrived in Syria, he asked about the grave of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, but could find no one to tell him, until he was directed to a monk. He went to him and asked about it. The monk said: “Are you looking for the grave of the upright man? It is in that field.”

“Ibn Wahb said: Mālik related to me that one day ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz mentioned…” what had passed of justice and injustice, while Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik was with him. Hishām said: “By God, we do not find fault with our forefathers, nor do we lower our standing among our people.” ʿUmar replied: “And what fault could be greater than that of one whom the Qurʾān has censured?”

Ibn Wahb said: Mālik related to me that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, while caliph, stood before the people on the pulpit on a Friday and said: “People, I forget you here, but I remember you in your lands. Whoever has suffered an injustice at the hands of his governor has no need of permission to come to me; whoever has not, let me not see him. By God, if I were to withhold this wealth from myself and my household and keep it from you, I would indeed be miserly. Were it not that I might revive a sunna or act according to what is right, I would not wish to live even for a moment.”

Muḥammad related to me. He said: Mālik informed me, from Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd and Rabīʿa ibn Abī ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, who said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz used to say: “No lump of clay is easier for me to break up, and no document easier for me to revoke, than a document I have issued a ruling upon, then come to see that the truth lies elsewhere: I break it up.”

“Muḥammad related to me. He said: Ibn Wahb informed us; Mālik related to me that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz was with Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik at his residence. Sulaymān used to say: ‘If this man were ever away from me, I would find no one who understood me.’ ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said to him: ‘Why do you not give this woman her due?’ He said:

‘Which woman?’ He replied: ‘Fāṭima daughter of ʿAbd al-Malik.’ Sulaymān said: ‘Did you not know…’” the testament of the Commander of the Faithful, ʿAbd al-Malik? Get up, so-and-so, and bring me the letter of the Commander of the Faithful”—he had written that daughters were entitled to nothing. ʿUmar said to him: “You have referred it to the Qurʾān.” One of Sulaymān’s sons, who was there, said: “There are always men who find fault with the caliphs’ and their commander’s letters, until their faces are beaten.” ʿUmar said: “If this matter were left to you and your likes, the harm that would befall the common people would be greater than the harm that would befall that man from having his face beaten.” Sulaymān grew angry at that and rebuked that son of his. He said:

“Would you confront Abū Ḥafṣ with this?” ʿUmar said: “If he was hasty with us, we have had our due.”

Zayd ibn Bishr related to us: Ibn Wahb related to us; he said: Ibn Zayd related to me, from ʿUmar ibn Asīl ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, who said: “ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz governed for only two and a half years—thirty months. By God, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz did not die before a man would come to us with a great sum of money and say: ‘Give this to whichever poor people you think best.’ He would not leave until he came back with his money, having considered who among them he should give it to and found no one. So he returned with his money. ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz had made the people well-off.”

Abū Isḥāq Ibrāhīm ibn Hishām ibn Yaḥyā al-Ghassānī related to me: My father related to me, from my grandfather, who said: Jaʿūna ibn al-Ḥārith came in to see ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. He said: “Jaʿūna, I have come to love you, so beware lest I come to hate you. Do you know what your family love about you?” He said: “Yes: they love my virtue.” ʿUmar said: “No. They love that your dark complexion provides for them, that they eat from your provisions, and that they travel with supplies on your back. So fear God, and give them nothing but what is wholesome.”

Ibrāhīm ibn Hishām related to me: My father related to me, from my grandfather, who said: One night we sat up talking with ʿUmar. He took a white, quilted cap from his head and said: “How much do you think this is worth?” We said: “A dirham, Commander of the Faithful.” He said: “By God, I do not think it was acquired lawfully.”

“Ibrāhīm related to me: My father related to me, from my grandfather, from Maymūn ibn Mihrān, who said:

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said to me: ‘Tell me a report.’ I told him a report that made him weep bitterly. I said: ‘Commander of the Faithful, had I known you would weep like this, I would have told you a gentler report.’ He said: ‘Maymūn, we eat this lentil plant, which, as you know, is a broth that softens the heart, brings on tears, and weakens the body.’”

“From my grandfather, from Maslama ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, who said: I visited ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz during his illness. He was wearing a dirty shirt, so I said to his wife Fāṭima: ‘Wash the Commander of the Faithful’s shirt.’ She said: ‘We will do so, God willing.’ Then I visited him again, and the shirt he was wearing was still as it had been. I said: ‘Fāṭima, did I not ask you to wash the Commander of the Faithful’s shirt?’ She said: ‘By God, he has no shirt other than this one.’”

Ibrāhīm related to me: My father related to me, from my grandfather, who said: Ibn Abī Zakariyyā and I were at the houses of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz when we heard weeping in his house. We asked about it, and they said: “The Commander of the Faithful gave his wife the choice either to remain in her home as she was, knowing that he was occupied with the burden upon his shoulders and had no time for women, or to return to her father’s home.” She wept, and her serving women wept because she was weeping.

Ḥarmala related to me: Ibn Wahb informed us; he said: al-Layth related to me, from one of his brothers, from Ḥarī ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, that Rayyān ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz: “Commander of the Faithful, why not ride out and refresh yourself?” ʿUmar said: “Who will make up the work of that day?” He replied: “You can make it up the following day.” ʿUmar said: “The work of one day has weighed heavily upon me; what, then, if the work of two days were piled upon me in a single day?” Ziyād said: “Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik used to ride out, enjoy himself, and make up his work.” ʿUmar said: “Sulaymān did not make up even a single day of this world.”

“Ibrāhīm ibn Hishām ibn Yaḥyā related to me. He said: My father related to me, from my grandfather, who said: Fāṭima daughter of ʿAbd al-Malik had a serving girl whom ʿUmar admired. When he came into the position he came to hold, Fāṭima adorned and perfumed her and sent her to ʿUmar, saying: ‘I know that you admire her, and I have given her to you, so that you may satisfy your desire with her.’ When she came in to him, ʿUmar said to her: ‘Sit down, girl. By God, nothing in this world was more desirable to me to possess than you. Tell me your story: how did you become a captive?’ She said: ‘I was a Berber girl. My father committed a crime and fled from Mūsā ibn Nuṣayr, ʿAbd al-Malik’s governor over Ifrīqiya. Mūsā ibn Nuṣayr captured me and sent me to ʿAbd al-Malik, who gave me to Fāṭima; then Fāṭima sent me to you.’ He said: ‘We nearly brought ourselves to disgrace.’ He prepared her for the journey and sent her back to her family.”

Ibrāhīm related to me: My father related to me, from my grandfather, who said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz used to forbid Sulaymān to kill the Ḥarūriyya, saying: “Keep them confined until…” they repent.” A Ḥarūrī who was bent on death was brought before Sulaymān and said to him: “Ah, your beard has been plucked out, you wicked son of a wicked man!” Sulaymān said: “Bring me ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz.” When ʿUmar came to him, Sulaymān again addressed the Ḥarūrī and said to him:

“What do you say?” He replied: “What should I say, you wicked son of a wicked man?” Sulaymān said to ʿUmar:

“Abū Ḥafṣ, what do you think should be done to him?” ʿUmar was silent. Sulaymān said: “I charge you to tell me what you think should be done to him.” He replied: “I think you should insult him as he insulted you.” Sulaymān said: “Is that all?” Then he ordered the man beheaded. Sulaymān stood up and ʿUmar left. Khālid ibn al-Rayyān, Sulaymān’s chief of guards, followed him and said: “Abū Ḥafṣ, you told the Commander of the Faithful, ‘I think you should insult him as he insulted you.’ By God, I expected him to order me to behead you.” ʿUmar said: “If he had ordered you, would you have done it?” He replied: “Yes, by God, if he had ordered me, I would have done it.

“When the caliphate passed to ʿUmar, Khālid ibn al-Rayyān came and took up his position with the guards—before that he had been in charge of the guards of al-Walīd and ʿAbd al-Malik. ʿUmar looked at him and said: ‘Khālid, put down that sword. O God, I have put Khālid ibn al-Rayyān down for Your sake; O God, never raise him up again.’ Then ʿUmar looked over the faces of the guards and summoned ʿAmr ibn al-Muhājir al-Anṣārī. He said: ‘By God, ʿAmr, you know there is no kinship between us except Islam. But I have heard you recite the Qurʾān often, and I have seen you pray in a place where you think no one can see you. I saw that you prayed well. Take this sword; I appoint you…” over my guards.”

Ḥarmala related to me: Ibn Wahb informed us; al-Layth related to me, from ʿUqayl, from Ibn Shihāb, that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz told him that al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik sent for him at midday, at an hour when he did not usually summon him. He found him in a small chamber with two doors: one through which people entered to see him, and another behind him through which he would turn aside to go to his family. He said: “I entered and found him frowning, his brow knitted. He gestured for me to sit, and I sat before him in the place of a litigant. No one was with him except Ibn al-Rayyān, standing with his sword.

“He said: ‘What do you think of someone who reviles the caliphs? Do you think he should be killed?’ I was silent.

“He said: ‘Why are you not speaking?’ I was silent. He repeated the question. I said: ‘Should he be killed, Commander of the Faithful?’ He said: ‘No, but he reviled the caliphs.’ I said: ‘I think he should be punished [for it] for what he has done against the caliphs.’ He raised his head toward Ibn al-Rayyān. I thought he was saying, ‘Strike off his head.’ Then he said: ‘He is surely bewildered among them.’ He turned on his hip and went in to his family. Ibn al-Rayyān gestured to me with his hand to leave.

“Ibn al-Rayyān was ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz’s protector. I went away, and every gust of wind from behind me made me think it was a messenger coming to summon me back to him.”

Ḥarmala related to me: Ibn Wahb informed us; al-Layth related to me that when ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz became caliph, he removed Khālid ibn al-Rayyān from the post he had held—he had been an executioner, standing over the heads of the caliphs. ʿUmar said: “I remember his arrogance and his bearing. O God, I dismiss him for Your sake; never raise him up again.” Nufayl ibn al-Furāt related to me: “I have never seen a nobleman’s name fade away so completely that he was no longer mentioned, until people would ask: ‘What has become of Khālid? Is he alive, or has he died?’”

Ibrāhīm ibn Hishām ibn Yaḥyā al-Ghassānī related to me: My father related to me, from my grandfather:

“ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz wrote to one of his governors, asking him to buy honey for him, and said: ‘Do not incur any loss over it.’ The governor loaded it onto his mount from the postal service. When he came to ʿUmar, ʿUmar asked: ‘Did a servant carry it?’ He replied: ‘It was carried by the postal service.’ ʿUmar ordered the honey to be sold, put its price into the Muslims’ treasury, and said: ‘You have spoiled your honey for us.’”

My grandfather said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz wrote to me: “The cold weather has set in, so put the whip away.”

My grandfather said: I was sitting with Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik when a man came to him and said: “Commander of the Faithful, ʿAbd al-Malik granted my grandfather a fief, and al-Walīd and Sulaymān confirmed it. Then, when ʿUmar became caliph—may God have mercy on ʿUmar—he took it away.” Hishām said to him: “Repeat what you said.” He said: “Commander of the Faithful, ʿAbd al-Malik granted my grandfather a fief, and al-Walīd and Sulaymān confirmed it. Then, when ʿUmar became caliph—may God have mercy on ʿUmar—he took it away.” Hishām said: “By God, there is something astonishing about you: you mention the one who granted your grandfather the fief and the ones who confirmed it…

and kept it in his possession, but you do not pray for mercy upon him; yet you mention the one who took it away and pray for mercy upon him. I have upheld what ʿUmar did—may God have mercy on ʿUmar. Get up.”

“Ibrāhīm related to me: My father related to me, from ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, who said: Abū Jaʿfar summoned me and asked: ‘How much income did ʿUmar have when the caliphate came to him?’

“I said: ‘He kept giving it away until his income was one hundred dinars.’” Had he lived longer, he would have given that away too.

“Ibrāhīm related to me. He said: My father related to me, from my grandfather, who said: While ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz was at ʿArafāt with Sulaymān, lightning flashed and thunder boomed so violently that Sulaymān was frightened. He looked at ʿUmar, who was laughing, and said: ‘ʿUmar, how can you laugh when you hear what you hear?’ ʿUmar replied: ‘Commander of the Faithful, this is God’s mercy, yet it has frightened you. What, then, if His punishment came?’”

Abū ʿUmar related to me: Ḍamra related to us, from Ibn Abī Ḥamla, from ʿAmr ibn Muhājir, who said: A Jew met me and said: “Your companion will take charge of this affair and rule justly.” When ʿUmar took office, I met him, and he said: “Did I not tell you once? Let him take care of himself, for he has been poisoned.” I said to him: “Commander of the Faithful, the Jew who told me that you would take office and rule justly also told me that you had been poisoned.” He said: “May God curse him—how well he knows! I know the very hour at which I was poisoned. Even if my cure lay in reaching my earlobe with my hand, I would not do it; nor, if a perfume were brought to me, would I lift it to my nose.”

Saʿīd ibn Asad related to me: Ḍamra related to us, from Ibn Shawdhab, who said: Ṣāliḥ ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and his associate wrote to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, hinting to him about the bloodshed of Muslims. They were his governors over part of Iraq, and they wrote: “The people can be set right only by the sword.” ʿUmar wrote back to them: “You two vile men, among the vilest of the vile, you two low fellows among the low, hinting to me about the bloodshed of Muslims! There is no Muslim whose blood is not less dear to me than yours.”

He said: Al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik wanted ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz to depose Sulaymān. ʿUmar said: “Commander of the Faithful, we pledged allegiance to both of you in a single compact; how can we depose him and leave you in place?”

He said: “Slave girls were presented to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, with al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik in his company. Whenever a girl passed whom al-ʿAbbās liked, he would say: ‘Commander of the Faithful, take this one.’ When he had done this repeatedly, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said to him: ‘Are you ordering me to commit fornication?’ Al-ʿAbbās went out and passed some members of his family. He said: ‘Why are you sitting at the door of a man who claims your forefathers were fornicators?’”

Abū Saʿīd ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ibrāhīm related to me: al-Walīd related to us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd ibn Abī Muslim al-Thaqafī related to us that his father set out on the summer campaign, in charge of its administrative register. He said: “I went out with him. When we were at Marj al-Lāj, a letter from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz reached him: ‘Turn back from wherever the Commander of the Faithful’s letter reaches you, for…’”

May God not grant victory to an army in which you are present. Al-Walīd said: I mentioned this to Ibn al-Mubārak, and he related to me, from Maʿmar or someone else, that ʿUmar wrote to the commander of the summer expedition: “I have learned that Ibn Abī Muslim has enlisted in one of the summer expeditions. Send him back in disgrace, for I dislike praying for the people in any undertaking when Ibn Abī Muslim is among them.” He said: So he sent him back from the mountain pass.

Qabīṣah ibn ʿUqbah related to us: Sufyān related to us, from ʿAmr ibn Maymūn, who said:

The scholars in ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz’s company were like pupils.

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz al-Ramlī related to us: Ḍamrah related to us, from Kurayz ibn Sulaym, who said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz wrote to ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAwf al-Qārī: “Ride to the building at Rafah called Bayt al-Maks [the House of the Poll Tax], demolish it, then carry it to the sea and scatter it completely.”

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to us: al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr al-Ramlī related to us. He said:

Zakari ibn Shaddād related to me: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz wrote to ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAwf al-Qārī: “When this letter of mine reaches you, ride with those who are with you to the polluted building at Rafah, uproot it from its foundations, then scatter it into the sea.”

“Abū al-Nuʿmān related to us: Ḥammād ibn Zayd related to us, from Ayyūb, who said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz was asked, ‘Commander of the Faithful, why not go to Medina? If God decrees your death, you would be buried in the fourth place beside the grave of the Messenger of God ﷺ—and those of Abū Bakr and ʿUmar.’

“He said: ‘By God, for God to punish me with every punishment except the Fire—for there is no endurance of it—is dearer to me than for God to know that I believe myself worthy of that place.’”

Muslim ibn Ibrāhīm related to us: Jarīr related to us: Ziyād ibn Mikhraq related to us. He said:

I heard ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz preaching to the people. He said: “Were it not for a practice that I might revive or an innovation that I might extinguish, I would not care to live even for a moment.”

Muslim related to us: ʿAlī ibn Saʿd related to us: Rabāḥ ibn ʿUbaydah related to us. He said: Musk was brought out from the treasuries and placed before ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. He held his nose, for fear of smelling it. One of his companions said to him, “Commander of the Faithful, what harm would it do you if you smelled it?” He replied, “Can one benefit from this except by its fragrance?”

Saʿīd ibn Asad related to me: Ḍamrah related to us, from Rajāʾ, who said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz appointed a man to office. Then he learned that the man had been an official of al-Ḥajjāj, so he dismissed him. The man came to apologize to him and explain what he had done. ʿUmar said to him: “Your association with him is enough evil and ill omen—a day or part of a day.

Saʿīd related to me: Ḍamrah related to us, from Rajāʾ, who said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz asked about Yazīd ibn Abī Muslim, al-Ḥajjāj’s deputy: “What has become of him?” They replied, “Commander of the Faithful, he has gone on the summer expedition.” So ʿUmar wrote ordering that he be sent back, and said: “I will not seek victory through an army in which he is present.”

He said: So they sent him back from the mountain pass.

From Rajāʾ, who said: Two men were disputing before ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, and a man was sitting with him. He said to one of the disputants, “The Commander of the Faithful has spoken the truth.” ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz grew angry and said, “Falsehood is being fabricated in my presence! Get up. I have repudiated this, and this”—he pointed to his beard—“has not yet grown in.”

Through the same chain, from Rajāʾ, who said: ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥasan—at that time a young man—came to Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik. He used to call on ʿUmar to seek his help with Sulaymān in his affairs. ʿUmar said to him, “If you would, do not wait at my door except at a time when you think you will be admitted to see me, for I dislike your waiting at my door and not being admitted.” One day he came to him, and ʿUmar said, “The Commander of the Faithful has learned that someone in the army has the plague. Go back to your family, for I am anxious to spare you.”

“Saʿīd related to us: Ḍamrah related to us, from Ibn Shawdhab, who said: ʿUmar ibn ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: ‘Al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik is in Syria, al-Ḥajjāj in Iraq, Muḥammad ibn Yūsuf in Yemen, ʿUthmān ibn Ḥayyān in the Ḥijāz, and Qurrah ibn Sharīk in Egypt.

By God, the earth was filled with injustice.”

Al-Rabīʿ ibn Rawḥ related to us: Ḥanẓalah ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Rabīʿ ibn Sabrah ibn Maʿbad al-Juhanī related to us. He said: My father related to me, from his father, who said: I said to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz—after his son, brother, and client Muzāḥim had died within a few days—“[O] Commander of the Faithful, I have never seen a man struck, on successive days, by a greater calamity than yours. I have never seen a son like your son, a brother like your brother, or a client like your [client].” He was silent for a while, then said to me, “How did you put it, Rabīʿ?” I repeated it to him. He said, “No, by Him who decreed death for them, I would not wish that any of it had not happened, in view of what I hope from God through them.”

Al-Rabīʿ ibn Rawḥ related to us: Ḥanẓalah ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Rabīʿ ibn Sabrah related to us, from his father, from a son of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said, when he fell ill with the illness from which he died: “Buy from the monk the place for my grave.” They bought the place for his grave from him for six dinars. The poet said, mentioning ʿUmar:

The people left behind, in the tomb where they were buried
at Dayr Simʿān, the weighing of the scales, I say, when a bearer of news announced ʿUmar’s death to me: May the decree of justice and religion never be far away.

Al-Rabīʿ ibn Rawḥ related to us: ʿUthmān ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to us, from Yaʿqūb ibn Jaʿdah, from Ḥammād al-ʿAdawī, who said: I heard a voice at the death of Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik saying:

Today it has settled, and its resting place is secure;ʿUmar, the Guided One, has raised its pillar.

Al-Musayyab ibn Wāḍiḥ related to us. He said: Baqiyyah related to us, from Saʿīd ibn ʿAlī, who said:

A young son of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz died, and ʿUmar fainted. When he came to, we said to him, “Over something like this?” He replied, “It is not that I am grieving for myself; rather, he is a part of me, and I may soon follow him.”

Abū al-Naḍr Isḥāq ibn Ibrāhīm ibn Yazīd al-Dimashqī related to us: Muʿāwiyah ibn Yaḥyā related to us. He said: Arṭāh related to us. He said: I said to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, “If you appointed someone trustworthy over your food, you would not be assassinated; and if you had guards when you prayed, you would not be assassinated. Keep away from the plague.” He said, “O God, if You know that I fear any day other than the Day of Resurrection, then do not make me safe from my fear.”

Saʿīd ibn Asad related to me: “Ḍamrah related to us, from ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd ibn ʿAbd Allāh Abū al-Akhtam, from Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, who said: I spent the night at my sister Fāṭimah’s, the wife of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. When evening came, he entered the house. There was a chest in the room. He opened it, took out two garments of haircloth, set aside his clothes, then put on the haircloth garments and stood to pray.”

Abū Zayd ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī al-Ghamr related to me: Yaʿqūb ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to us, from his father, who said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz delivered this sermon—and it was the last sermon he delivered—and praised and glorified God, then said:

He praised and glorified God, then said: “You were not created in vain, nor will you be left neglected. You have a return, when God will come to judge among you and decide between you. Ruined and lost is the one who departs from God’s mercy and is denied a Garden as wide as the heavens and the earth. Do you not know that tomorrow only those will be secure who feared God today, were in awe of Him, exchanged what passes away for what endures, little for much, and fear for safety? Do you not see that you are in the loins of those who have perished, and that after you, you will become the forebears of those who remain, and so it will continue until you are returned to the Best of heirs? Each day you escort to God someone departing and returning, whose appointed term has ended and whose lifespan is over, until you conceal him in a cleft in the earth, in a fissure. Then you leave him unprepared and without a pillow; he has parted from loved ones, lain upon the dust, and been turned toward the Reckoning, held in pledge for what he did, [independent] of what he left behind, and in need of what he sent ahead. So fear God before you meet Him and death comes upon you. By God, I say this, though I know of no one whose sins exceed my own; so I ask God’s forgiveness. Whenever one of you brings us a need that what we have cannot meet, we strive to fulfill as much of it as we can. Whenever one of you is burdened by a need that what we have cannot meet, I wish that he would begin with me and my household, so that our livelihood and his might be one and the same. By God, if I wanted a life of ease other than this, my tongue could readily speak of it, and I knew its means. But a decree from God has already gone forth, a speaking Book and a just practice, in which He has shown the way to obedience to Him and forbidden disobedience to Him.” Then he raised the edge of his robe and wept, moving those around him to tears.

Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb related to us: ʿUmar ibn ʿAlī ibn Muqaddam related to us, from ʿAbd Rabbih, from Maymūn ibn Mihrān, who said: One night I was at ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz’s evening gathering. He gave an exhortation and noticed a man whose tears had overflowed. He fell silent. I said, “Commander of the Faithful, resume speaking; perhaps God will benefit through it those who hear it and those to whom it is conveyed.” He replied, “Maymūn, speech is a trial, and deeds are more fitting for a person than words.”

Salamah related to me: Aḥmad related to us: ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us. He said: My father informed me:

Wahb said: “If there is a Guided One in this community, it is ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz.”

Saʿīd ibn Asad related to me: Ḍamrah related to us, from Rajāʾ ibn Abī Salamah, who said:

When ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz cut off the stipends of his associates, ʿAnbasah ibn Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ said to him, “Commander of the Faithful, I see a matter that can be put right only by attending to one’s estate.” He replied, “That is the right course, Abū Khālid. But remember death often: you will not bring it into something abundant without making that abundant thing little, nor into something little without making it abundant. That is the right course, Abū Khālid.”

“Abū Bishr related to me: Saʿīd ibn ʿĀmir related to us. He said: I heard my grandfather Asmāʾ ibn ʿUbayd, who said: ʿAnbasah ibn Saʿīd came to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz and said, “Commander of the Faithful, the caliphs before you used to give us gifts, but you have withheld them from us. I have dependents and an estate, and I would like to look after my estate and provide for my dependents.” ʿUmar replied, “The dearest of you to us is the one who does that.” When he took office, ʿUmar said:

“Abū Khālid! Abū Khālid!” He came over, and ʿUmar said, “Remember death often. Whenever you remember it while your life is constricted, it will make it spacious for you; and whenever you remember it while your life is spacious, it will make it constricted for you.”

Abū Bishr related to us. He said: Saʿīd ibn ʿĀmir related to me. He said: Juwayriyah ibn Asmāʾ related to me that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz learned that Yazīd ibn Abī Muslim was with one of the Muslim armies. He wrote to the army’s commander ordering him to send Yazīd back, and said: “I would dislike seeking victory through an army in which he is present.”

From Juwayriyah ibn Asmāʾ, from Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Ḥakīm, who said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz seldom failed to read from the codex in the morning, though he did not read for long.

Juwayriyah said: I do not know whether it was Ismāʿīl or someone else who related this: ʿUmar said to Muzāḥim, “Find me a stand for my codex.” He brought him a stand that pleased him. ʿUmar asked, “Where did you get it?” He replied, “Commander of the Faithful, I went into one of the treasuries and found this piece of wood, so I made a stand from it.” ʿUmar said, “Shame on you! Go and have it appraised in the market.”

He said: The man took it to the market, where they appraised it at half a dinar. He returned and said, “Commander of the Faithful, they appraised it at half a dinar.” ʿUmar said, “Do you think that if you put one dinar in the public treasury, you will be clear of it?” Muzāḥim said, “They appraised it at only half a dinar.” He said, “Put two dinars in the public treasury.”

“From Juwayriyah ibn Asmāʾ, from Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Ḥakīm—as far as I know—who said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said to his doorkeeper, ‘Let no one enter to see me today except a Marwānid.’

“When they had gathered before him, he spoke, praised and glorified God, then said: ‘To proceed: Banū Marwān, you have been given a share, honor, and wealth in this world. I reckon that half—or two-thirds—of this community’s wealth is in your hands. Return what you hold of this wealth.’ They fell silent. He said, ‘Will you not answer me?’ They fell silent. He said, ‘Will you not answer me?’

“One of the men spoke and said, ‘No, by God! That will never happen until our heads are separated from our bodies. By God, we will not disown our fathers and impoverish our sons.’ ʿUmar said, ‘Were it not for the fact that you would enlist against me those from whom I seek this right, I would press your faces to the ground. Get up and leave me.’”

Abū Bishr related to me: Saʿīd related to us, from Juwayriyah ibn Asmāʾ, from Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Ḥakīm, who said: We were with ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz until the people dispersed and his household went in for the midday rest. Suddenly a herald called, “The communal prayer!” We were badly alarmed, fearing that some breach had arisen on some front or that some event had occurred.

Juwayriyah said: What had happened was that ʿUmar had summoned Muzāḥim and said, “Muzāḥim, these people have given us gifts. By God, it was not right for us to accept them. Now they have come into my possession, and I have no one to answer for them before God but me.” Muzāḥim said to him, “Commander of the Faithful, do you know how many children you have? They are so many.” His eyes brimmed with tears; he began to weep and say, “I entrust them to God.” Then Muzāḥim went straight from there to ʿAbd al-Malik.

ʿAbd al-Malik gave him permission to enter, though he had lain down for his midday rest. ʿAbd al-Malik asked, “What brings you here at this hour, Muzāḥim?

“Has something happened?” He replied, “Yes—the gravest thing that could happen to you and your father.” He asked, “What is it?” Muzāḥim said, “The Commander of the Faithful summoned me,” and told him what ʿUmar had said.

ʿAbd al-Malik asked, “What did you say to him?” He replied, “I said, ‘Commander of the Faithful, do you know how many children you have? They are so many.’” He asked, “What did he say to you?” Muzāḥim replied, “He began to weep and say:

“‘I entrust them to God. I entrust them to God.’” ʿAbd al-Malik said, “You are a wretched adviser in matters of religion, Muzāḥim!” Then he sprang up and went to ʿUmar’s door and asked permission to enter. The doorkeeper said:

“The Commander of the Faithful has laid his head down for his midday rest.” He said, “Ask permission for me.” The doorkeeper said:

“Have you no pity for him? This is his only respite in the night and day.” ʿAbd al-Malik said:

“Ask permission for me, you motherless man!” ʿUmar heard the exchange and said, “Who is that?” The doorkeeper replied, “It is ʿAbd al-Malik.” He said, “Let him in.” He entered while ʿUmar was lying down for his midday rest.

ʿUmar said, “What do you need, coming at this hour?” He replied, “Muzāḥim told me something.” ʿUmar asked:

“And what was your judgment about it?” He said, “My judgment was that it should be carried out.” ʿUmar raised his hand and said, “Praise be to God, who has given me among my descendants someone to help me in the affairs of my religion. Yes, my son, I will pray the noon prayer, then climb the pulpit and return it openly before the people.” ʿAbd al-Malik said, “Commander of the Faithful, who can guarantee that you will reach the noon prayer? And if you live until noon, who can guarantee that your resolve will remain intact until then?” ʿUmar said:

“The people have dispersed and gone back for their midday rest.” ʿAbd al-Malik said, “Order your herald to call, ‘The communal prayer!’ Then the people will gather.” Ismāʿīl said: I went out and came to the mosque. ʿUmar arrived and climbed the pulpit. He praised and glorified God, then said:

“To proceed: These people had given us gifts. By God, they had no right to give them to us, and we had no right to accept them. I see that what has come into my possession is something for which I alone am answerable before God. Behold, I have returned it, beginning with myself and my household, …”

“Read, Muzāḥim.” He said: A small chest had been brought earlier—or he said, a jawna—containing those documents. He said: Muzāḥim read one of them. When he had finished reading it, ʿUmar handed it to him, while seated on the pulpit and holding a bowl in his hand. He said: ʿUmar began cutting it with the bowl. Muzāḥim then took up another document and began reading it. When he had finished, he handed it to ʿUmar, who cut it. Then he took up another document. He went on like that until the call to the noon prayer was made.

Abū Bishr related to me; Saʿīd related to us; Juwayriya ibn Asmāʾ informed us: ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿUmar said: “Commander of the Faithful, what prevents you from putting your judgment into effect in this matter? By God, I would not mind if the cooking pots boiled because of you and me as this matter was carried out.”

He said: ʿUmar replied to him: “My son, I am training the people as one trains a difficult beast. If God lets me live, I shall proceed according to my intention and judgment. If I am hastened to my appointed end, God knows my intention. I fear that, if I confront the people all at once with what you propose, they will force me to take up the sword. There is no good in a good that comes only by the sword.” He kept repeating this several times.

Abū Bishr related to us; Saʿīd related to us; Juwayriya informed us, from Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Ḥakīm, who said: When Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik died, the people of Syria clapped their hands. He said: Muzāḥim and I went to some provisions of ʿUmar’s that were among his baggage, and I carried them. Then I set out for the mosque. A man met me and said: “Your companion is addressing the people.” I said: “As caliph?” He said: “As caliph.” I came to him while he was on the pulpit. The first thing I heard him say was: “People, by God, I have never asked God for it, either privately or openly. Whoever among you dislikes it, the matter is his to decide.” A man from the Anṣār said:

“Commander of the Faithful, by God, that is swifter than what we dislike. Hold out your hand, and let us pledge allegiance to you.” He said: That Anṣārī was the first to pledge allegiance to him. I do not know whether this is from Ismāʿīl or someone else. He said: I think it is from Ismāʿīl. He said: ʿUmar walked in Sulaymān’s funeral procession. He entered Sulaymān’s grave. When he had finished burying him, the caliphs’ mounts were brought, but he did not ride any of them. He said: “My mule.” A man ran to the camp, and ʿUmar waited until his mule was brought. He said:

The caliphs’ pavilions had been set up. I think that he did not take shelter in any of them before his mule was brought. He mounted it and then returned.

He said: Sulaymān had ordered the people of his realm to bring horses for a race, with a prize for the winner. Every contingent of Muslims had been taken up with bringing horses back to him, but he died before the race could be held.

He said: When ʿUmar took office, he refused to hold it. He was told: “Commander of the Faithful, you are imposing great expenses on the people. They have brought the horses from distant lands, and that will anger the enemy.” They kept speaking to him until he held the race. He rewarded those who came first, and did not disappoint those who did not: he gave them a lesser amount. He said: The people had suffered severe hardship at Constantinople from hunger. The people returned, and he sent them food.

Saʿīd ibn Asad related to us, saying: Ḍamrah related to us, from al-Rayyān ibn Muslim, who said:

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz sent the family of Abū ʿAqīl—the household of al-Ḥajjāj—to the governor of Yemen, and wrote to him: “To proceed: I have sent you the family of Abū ʿAqīl. They are the worst household among the Arabs.

Disperse them among your districts according to the extent of their inclination toward God. Peace be upon us and you”—for he had only exiled them.

Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb related to us; ʿUmar ibn ʿAlī related to us, from ʿAbd Rabbih, from Maymūn ibn Mihrān, who said: One night I was at ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz’s evening gathering and said: “Commander of the Faithful, how do you endure what I see? By day you are occupied with people’s needs, and at night you are here with us; then God knows what you do in private.” He turned away from answering me, then said: “Leave me, Maymūn. I have found that meeting with men sharpens their minds.”

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ibrāhīm related to us; Ayyūb—meaning Ibn Suwayd—related to us, from ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz: “My father would not put anyone on a par with ʿArāk ibn Mālik.”

Abū Hāshim Ziyād ibn Ayyūb related to me; Saʿīd ibn ʿĀmir related to us, from Aḥmad ibn al-Ashʿath, from Saʿīd ibn Abī ʿArūbah, who said: A man said to him: “I saw so-and-so; he did not kiss the Black Stone.” He replied: “I have seen someone better than him kiss it.” He was asked: “Who, Abū al-Naḍr? Qatādah?” He said: “Someone better than him.” He was asked: “Al-Ḥasan?” He said: “Someone better than him.”

He said: “I saw ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz kiss the Stone”.

Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmar related to us: “Sufyān related to us, saying: I asked ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, ‘What was the last thing your father said when he was dying?’ He said:

He had these sons: ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, ʿAbd Allāh, ʿĀṣim, and Ibrāhīm. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said:

“We were young boys, and we came to him as if to greet him and bid him farewell. The one who attended to him then was a client of his. He was asked: ‘You have left these sons of yours with no money, and you have not entrusted them to anyone.’ He said: ‘I would not give them anything that was not theirs, nor would I take from them any right of theirs. I have entrusted them to the One who takes care of the righteous. These two are only one of two kinds of men: a man who obeys God, Mighty and Majestic, and a man who abandons God’s command and neglects it’”.

THE FINAL REPORTS ABOUT ʿUMAR IBN ʿABD AL-ʿAZĪZ

[THE FIRST REPORTS ABOUT AL-ZUHRĪ]

Ibn Shihāb—whose name was Muḥammad ibn Muslim ibn ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Shihāb al-Zuhrī:

Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmar related to us, saying: Sufyān said: “I saw al-Zuhrī with red hair and beard, and the redness had faded a little, as if he had applied katam.” Sufyān said: “Al-Zuhrī was somewhat small-eyed, and he had a short forelock.”

Sufyān said: “I saw Ibn Judʿān sitting with al-Zuhrī. Ibn Judʿān liked perfume, and said: ‘Abū Bakr, why did you not have these two garments of yours fumigated with incense?’”

Al-Zuhrī had washed the garments, and Ibn Judʿān smelled the odor of the wash water—or perhaps he said, the odor of the basin. Sufyān said: “I heard al-Zuhrī, when relating from a man, say: ‘So-and-so related to me, and he was a vessel [of knowledge],’ and ‘So-and-so related to me, and he was one of the vessels of knowledge’—he would not say, ‘He was a scholar’”.

Al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAẓīm related to me, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us, saying: Mālik said: “Ibn Shihāb passed us on a mule. I went over to him and asked him about some reports, and he related them to me. He said to me: ‘I have related them to you, if you have retained them.’ I said: ‘Shall I repeat them back to you?’ He said: ‘Go ahead.’ So I repeated them to him. Then I said to him: ‘Abū Bakr, you pursued knowledge until you became one of its vessels, and then you left Medina and went away from it.’ He said: ‘I used to live in Medina when the people were still truly people.’”

ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī said: “These six were among those on whom people relied for ḥadīth: al-Zuhrī for the people of Medina; ʿAmr ibn Dīnār for the people of Mecca; Abū Isḥāq and al-Aʿmash for the people of Kūfah; and Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr and Qatādah for the people of Baṣrah.”

ʿAlī related from Ibn ʿUyaynah, who said: Ayyūb said: “After al-Zuhrī ibn Shihāb, I know no one more learned in the ḥadīth of Medina and the people of the Ḥijāz than Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr.” He said: Yaḥyā was from Baṣrah and settled in al-Yamāmah.

Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmar related to us; Sufyān related to us, from al-Hudhalī, who said: “I sat with al-Ḥasan and Ibn Sīrīn, but I have never seen anyone like this man, as al-Zuhrī would say.” Al-Hudhalī said: “Knowledge will remain in Medina as long as this man remains”—meaning Ibn Isḥāq, the author of the Sīrah.

“Ibn Abī ʿUmar related to us, saying: Sufyān said: They used to think that, on the day al-Zuhrī died, no one was more knowledgeable than he in the Sunnah”.

“ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Uwaysī related to me; Mālik related to us, saying: Ibn Shihāb related a lengthy report to me while I was holding the reins of his mount. I said to him, ‘Repeat it—’”

“to me.’ He said: ‘No.’ I said to him: ‘What do you think? Would you not have liked it to be repeated to you?’ He said: ‘No.’ I said to him: ‘Did you write it down?’ He said: ‘No’”.

Muḥammad ibn Abī Zukayr related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, from Mālik, who said:

“I took hold of Ibn Shihāb’s mule’s reins while he was mounted on it and asked him about a report. What amazed me about him was that he said: ‘I have already related it to you.’ I said: ‘Yes.’” Mālik said: “What he said amazed me”. I said to him: “Then repeat it to me.” He said: “No.” I said—I wanted to get the better of him—: “Did you not write it down?” He said: “No.” I said: “And you do not ask for the report to be repeated to you?” He said: “No.” So I let go of the metal”.

“Ibn Bukayr and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṣāliḥ, Abū Ṣāliḥ, related to us. They said: Al-Layth related to us, from Jaʿfar ibn Rabīʿah, who said: I asked ʿArāk ibn Mālik: ‘Who is the most learned in jurisprudence among the people of Medina?’ He said: ‘As for the one most knowledgeable about the judgments of the Messenger of God ﷺ and the judgments of Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, and ʿUthmān; the most learned in jurisprudence; and the most knowledgeable about the past affairs of the people, it is Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib. As for the one with the greatest store of ḥadīth, it is ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr. And if you wish, you can make a sea burst forth from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh.’” He said: Then ʿArāk ibn Mālik would say to me: “The most knowledgeable of them all, in my view, is—”

“—Ibn Shihāb, for he gathered all of their knowledge together with his own”.

“Ibn Bukayr related to us, saying: Al-Layth related to us, saying: Ibn Shihāb said: ‘No one endured the pursuit of knowledge as patiently as I did, and no one spread it as widely as I did’”.

Abū Ṣāliḥ ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṣāliḥ said: I heard al-Layth ibn Saʿd say:

“I have never seen a scholar more comprehensive than Ibn Shihāb, nor anyone with more knowledge than he. If you heard Ibn Shihāb relate about exhortation [and warning, you would say, ‘He knows nothing but this’; and if he related about the Arabs] and genealogies, you would say, ‘He knows nothing but this.’ If he related about the prophets and the People of the Book, you would say, ‘He knows nothing but this.’” He said: “If he related about the Qurʾān and the Sunnah, his report would be followed by a comprehensive supplication, in which he would say: ‘O God, I ask You for every good encompassed by Your knowledge in this world and the Hereafter, and I seek refuge in You from every evil encompassed by Your knowledge in this world and the Hereafter.’”

Al-Layth said: “Ibn Shihāb was among the most generous people I have ever seen. He would give to everyone who came and asked him, until he had nothing left with him. Then he would borrow from his servants, saying to one of them: ‘So-and-so, lend me some, as you know; I will repay you double, as you know.’ They would lend it to him, and he saw no harm in doing so. He said: Sometimes a petitioner came and he had nothing to give him. His face would change then, and he would say to the petitioner: ‘Be glad; God will bring something good.’ God provided Ibn Shihāb, in accordance with his patience and endurance, with either someone who would give him enough for his household, or someone who would sell to him on credit. He would feed people tharīd in times of plenty and otherwise, and give them honey to drink. Ibn Shihāb would stay up over the honey just as drinking companions stayed up over their drink, saying: ‘Give us drink, and tell us reports.’ If he saw one of his companions growing drowsy, he would say to him: ‘You are not one of the late-night companions of Quraysh, of whom God said, “In idle talk they would pass the night”’ (Qurʾān 23:67). He had a saffron-dyed pavilion, wore a saffron-dyed cloak, and sat on a saffron-dyed cushion.”

He said: “I heard him lamenting aloud over the loss of knowledge and saying: ‘Knowledge is going away, along with many of those who used to act upon it.’ I said to him: ‘Have you entrusted any of your knowledge to someone whom you hope will succeed you among the people?’ He said: ‘By God, no one has spread knowledge as widely as I have, or endured it as patiently as I have. We used to sit with Ibn al-Musayyib, and none of us could ask him about anything unless he began the report, or a man came and asked him about some matter that had—’”

“befallen him. Our time sitting with him had grown so long that we heard nothing from him except the answer.”

Al-Layth said: “I heard him say: ‘I have never entrusted anything to my heart and then forgotten it’”.

He said: “He disliked apples and the dregs of fire, saying that they cause forgetfulness. He used to drink honey and say that it strengthens memory”.

Ibn Bukayr related to us, saying: Al-Layth related to me, saying: “One day I came to Ibn Shihāb with something based on personal opinion. He drew his face tight and said: ‘Opinion!’—as if disliking it. Then another day I came to him with reports from the Sunnah. His face brightened, and he said: ‘When you come to me, bring me something like this.’”

“ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿImrān related to us; Ibn Wahb related to us; al-Layth related to me, from Ibn Shihāb, who used to say: ‘I have never entrusted anything to my heart and then forgotten it.’ He said: He disliked apples and the dregs of fire, saying that they cause forgetfulness. He used to drink honey and say that it strengthens memory”.

“Al-Layth related to me, saying: One day I came to Ibn Shihāb with something based on personal opinion. He drew his face tight and said: ‘Opinion!’—as if disliking it. Then another day I came to him with reports from the Sunnah. His face brightened, and he said: ‘When you come to me, bring me something like this’”.

“Ibn Bukayr related to us; al-Layth related to me; ʿUqayl ibn Khālid related to me, from Ibn Shihāb, who said: He would be with me on a journey. He said: He would give to whoever came and asked him, until nothing was left with him. [Then he would borrow from his companions, and they would keep lending to him until they had nothing left. They would swear that they had nothing left, so he would borrow from his servants,] saying: ‘So-and-so, lend me some, and I will repay you double, as you know.’ They would lend it to him, and he saw no harm in doing so. Sometimes a petitioner came and he had nothing to give him; his face would change then, and he would say to the petitioner: ‘Be glad; God will bring something good.’ God would provide Ibn Shihāb with one of two men: either someone who would give him enough for his household, or someone who would sell to him and grant him time to pay.

He said: He would feed them tharīd and give them honey to drink as well. He said: Ibn Shihāb would stay up over the honey just as people who drink wine stay up.

He said: He would relate reports to us, then say: “Give us drink; tell us reports.”

ʿUqayl said: When he saw me growing drowsy, he would say: “You are not one of the late-night companions of Quraysh, of whom God said, ‘In idle talk they would pass the night’” (Qurʾān 23:67). He had a saffron-dyed pavilion, wore a saffron-dyed cloak, and sat on a saffron-dyed cushion.

Ibn Bukayr related to us, saying: Al-Layth said: Ibn Shihāb said: “Those two young men corrupted the people of that highland”—meaning the people of Medina—as if he meant those who accepted personal opinion.

“Saʿīd ibn ʿUfayr related to me, saying: ʿAṭṭāf ibn Khālid related to me, from ʿAbd al-Aʿlā ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Farwah, from Ibn Shihāb, who said: The people of Medina suffered a period of need during the time of the civil strife of ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān, and it affected the whole city. I thought that we, the members of the household, had been struck by it more than anyone else in the city, because I knew my family’s circumstances. I wondered whether there was anyone to whom I was connected by kinship or affection, and from whom I might hope to obtain something if I went to him. I could think of no one to whom I could go. Then I said:

‘Provision is only in God’s hands.’ Then I set out and arrived in Damascus. I put down my baggage, then went in the morning to the mosque and made my way toward the largest gathering I saw in the mosque, and the most crowded—”

[They were] welcoming, so I sat with them. While we were thus, a man came out from ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān. He was the most dignified and handsomest of men, and the finest in appearance. He came toward the gathering where I was, and they shifted about for him until they made room. He sat down and said:

“Today the Commander of the Faithful received a letter unlike any he has received since God appointed him caliph.” They asked, “What is it?” He replied: “His governor in Medina, Hishām ibn Ismāʿīl, wrote to him, reporting that a son of Muṣʿab ibn al-Zubayr, born to a concubine, had died. The boy’s mother wanted to take her inheritance from him, but ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr prevented her and claimed she had no inheritance. The Commander of the Faithful recalled a report he had heard from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, said to have been related from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb concerning mothers of children. The Commander of the Faithful did not remember that report.” Ibn Shihāb said: “I said:

‘I shall relate it to you.’” Qabīṣa rose and took me by the hand, then led me out with him until he brought me into the house to ʿAbd al-Malik. Then he came to the room where ʿAbd al-Malik was and said:

“Peace be upon you.” ʿAbd al-Malik replied, “And upon you be peace.” He asked, “May I enter?”

“Enter,” he said. Qabīṣa entered, still holding my hand, and said: “[This man], Commander of the Faithful, will relate to you the report you heard from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab concerning mothers of children.” He said, “Yes?” I said: “I heard Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab relate that— “ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ordered that mothers of children be assessed at a fair value against their sons’ property and then set free. He continued this practice for some time during his caliphate. Then a Qurashī man who had a son by a concubine died. ʿUmar had been fond of that boy. A few nights after his father’s death, the boy passed ʿUmar in the mosque. ʿUmar asked him, ‘How have you dealt with your mother, my nephew?’ He replied, ‘I have done what is best, Commander of the Faithful. My brothers gave me the choice of letting them enslave my mother or of surrendering my inheritance from my father. My inheritance from my father was easier for me to give up than to have my mother enslaved.’

“ʿUmar said, ‘Did I not order that she be assessed at a fair value? Whenever I form an opinion or order something, you accept it.’ Then he rose and sat on the pulpit. The people gathered around him, and when he was satisfied that they were assembled, he said: ‘People, I had once issued an order concerning mothers of children, which you know. Then I came to a different opinion. Any man who has a child’s mother in his possession may retain her as his property for as long as he lives; when he dies, she is free, and he has no claim over her.’

“Then he said, ‘Who are you?’ I said:

“‘I am Abū Muḥammad ibn Muslim ibn ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Shihāb.’ He said, ‘By God, your father was a man who stirred up trouble during the civil strife and caused us harm in it.’ I said, ‘Commander of the Faithful, say what the righteous servant said.’ He replied, ‘Yes: “No reproach shall be upon you today” (Qurʾān 12:92).’

“I said, ‘Commander of the Faithful, assign me a stipend, for I have been left off the register.’ He said, ‘Your town is a place where I have assigned no one a stipend since the matter began.’ Then he looked at Qabīṣa. The two of us were standing before him, and it was as if he signaled to Qabīṣa to assign me one. Qabīṣa said, ‘The Commander of the Faithful has assigned you one.’”

“I said, ‘And a gift, Commander of the Faithful—may God sustain you, and may you sustain us with it. By God, I left my family in a state of need known only to God, and need has afflicted the people of the town.’ He said, ‘The Commander of the Faithful has already given you a gift.’

“I said, ‘And a servant, Commander of the Faithful, to serve us. By God, I left my family with no servant except my sister; she is the one who kneads, bakes, and cooks for them.’ He said, ‘The Commander of the Faithful has provided you with a servant.’

“Then he wrote to Hishām ibn Ismāʿīl: ‘Send for Ibn al-Musayyab and ask him about the report he heard and relates concerning mothers of children, from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.’ Hishām wrote back to him with a report identical to mine, without adding or omitting a single letter.”

“Aḥmad ibn Shabīb ibn Saʿīd, an Egyptian, related to us: My father related to us, from Yūnus, who said: Ibn Shihāb said: ‘I came to Damascus during the time of Ibn al-Ashʿath’s movement.’ He said:

“‘At that time ʿAbd al-Malik was occupied with his own affairs. I sat in a gathering whose members I did not know,’” and he mentioned something like the account of the child’s mother. “ʿAbd al-Malik said, ‘No man has died leaving behind anyone like you.’”

“Saʿīd ibn ʿUfayr related to me: Ḥafṣ ibn ʿImrān ibn al-Wassām related to us, from al-Sarī ibn Yaḥyā, from Ibn Shihāb, who said: ‘I came to Damascus intending to go on campaign. I went to— “ʿAbd al-Malik to greet him. I found him in a domed pavilion, on bedding raised high above the standing height of a man, while the people below him sat in two rows. I greeted him and sat down. He said, ‘Ibn Shihāb, do you know what happened in Jerusalem on the morning that Ibn Abī Ṭālib was killed?’ I said, ‘Yes.’ He said, ‘Come here.’ I rose and passed behind the people until I came behind the pavilion and around to his face. He leaned toward me and said:

“‘What happened?’ I said, ‘No stone was lifted in Jerusalem without blood being found beneath it.’

“He said, ‘No one alive knows this except you and me. Do not let it be heard from you.’ I did not speak of it until he died.”

“ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Uwaysī related to me: Ibrāhīm ibn Saʿd related to us, from his father:

“Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik paid Ibn Shihāb’s debt of eighty thousand dirhams. I heard my father reproach Ibn Shihāb about the debt, saying, ‘Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik has paid eighty thousand on your behalf, and you know what the Messenger of God ﷺ—said about debt.’ Ibn Shihāb said to my father, ‘I rely upon the wealth of God. If this upper room of mine were to remain for me and its lower part were filled with gold or silver’—Ibrāhīm said, ‘I am unsure which of the two he said’—‘I would not regard it as compensation for my wealth.’” Ibrāhīm said: At that time, he was in an upper room.

“Muḥammad ibn Abī Usāma al-Ḥalabī related to me: Ḍamra related to us, from Rajāʾ ibn Abī Salama, who said: Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik paid four thousand dinars on al-Zuhrī’s behalf. Then he said:

“‘Perhaps you will incur debt again, Ibn Shihāb?’ He replied, ‘No, Commander of the Faithful. I heard Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab say: “A believer is not stung from the same hole twice.”’ Rajāʾ said: Yūnus related to me from al-Zuhrī that he did incur debt again, but he had a provision for paying it— “—off.”

“Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir related to us: Dāwūd ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī al-Karām al-Jaʿfarī related to us. He said: I heard Mālik ibn Anas say: ‘Ibn Shihāb was among the most generous of people. When he acquired that wealth, a client of his admonished him, saying, “You have seen the hardship and distress that have passed over you. Consider how you will live, and hold on to your wealth.”

“Ibn Shihāb replied, “Woe to you! I have never seen generosity ruled by experience.”’

“Muḥammad ibn Abī Zukayr related to us: Ibn Wahb informed us: Mālik related to me from Ibn Shihāb that he used to slit open the skin bag containing honey so that people could lick it.

“Mālik said: ‘Neither Ibn al-Musayyab nor anyone else would do such a thing.’”

“Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Ḥasan al-Marwazī related to us: Saʿīd ibn ʿĀmir related to us, from Sallām ibn Abī Muṭīʿ, who said: I heard Ayyūb say: ‘If I were to write down [reports] from anyone, I would write them down from Ibn Shihāb.’”

“Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Ḥasan related to us: ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us: Maʿmar informed us, from al-Zuhrī, who said: ‘My knee touched Ibn al-Musayyab’s knee for eight years.’

“Yaḥyā ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bukayr related to us: al-Layth related to me, saying: Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd said: ‘No one has retained as much knowledge as Ibn Shihāb has.’”

“ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Uwaysī related to us: Ibrāhīm ibn Saʿd related to us. He said:

“I heard Ibn Shihāb relate to my father: ‘Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik sent for me, asking me to write some of my reports for his sons. I said, “If you asked me about two reports, I would not be able to put them together. But if you want them, summon a scribe. When people gather around me to ask questions, I will write for them what you want.” He sent a scribe, who stayed for a year; not a day passed without my filling it [with writing].’ He said: ‘One of Hishām’s sons met me and said, “Abū Bakr, I think we have taken too little from you.” Ibn Shihāb said: “I was only on the rough, hard ground; today I have descended into the valley bottoms.”’”

“Abū ʿUmayr related to us: Ḍamra related to us, from Ibn Abī Salama. He said: Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik paid four thousand dinars on al-Zuhrī’s behalf, then said to him, ‘Woe to you, Ibn Shihāb! Do you think you will incur debt again?’ He replied, ‘No, Commander of the Faithful. I heard Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab say, “A believer is not stung from the same hole twice.”’

“Rajāʾ said: Yūnus related to me that al-Zuhrī did incur debt again. He said: ‘His estates were sufficient to pay his debt.’ Ḍamra said: ‘He used to buy the dates set aside for alms, then invite the Bedouins and divide them among them.’ Ḍamra said: ‘I accompanied Hishām for four years, and Ibn Shihāb for—’”

“—four years.”

“ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Uwaysī related to me: Ibrāhīm ibn Saʿd related to us, from ʿIkrima, who said: ‘We used to visit al-Aʿraj, and Ibn Shihāb used to visit him too. We would write, but Ibn Shihāb would not write. Sometimes a report was long. Ibn Shihāb would take a sheet from al-Aʿraj’s papers—al-Aʿraj used to copy Qurʾāns—and write that report on the piece of paper. Then he would read it and erase it from the page. Sometimes he would take it with him and read it, then erase it.’”

“Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir related to us: Maʿn related to me, from Ibn Shihāb’s nephew, who said:

“Ibn Shihāb compiled the Qurʾān in eighty days.

“Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir related to us, saying: Ibn Shihāb said: ‘We used to regard writing as nothing, but the rulers compelled us to do it, so we wanted to make it equally available to everyone.’

“ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿAbd Allāh related to me: Ibrāhīm ibn Saʿd related to us, saying: ‘The first person to set down these reports for people was Ibn Shihāb.’

“Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir related to us: ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Abī Thābit related to me, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, who said: I heard Ibn Shihāb say: ‘I have eaten neither apples nor vinegar since I began training my memory.’

“ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿImrān related to me: Ibn Wahb related to us: Yaʿqūb ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to me, who said: ‘I saw Ibn Shihāb: he was a poor man, with a sparse beard, a few long hairs, and scant hair on his cheeks.’

“Muḥammad ibn Abī Zukayr related to us: Ibn Wahb related to us: Mālik related to me from Ibn Shihāb— “—who said: ‘We used to visit him at his house in Banū al-Dayl, and he suffered from his eyes. People would bring him kohl in shells, and tell him about those kohl preparations. He longed for reports and was preoccupied with them, and that caused him difficulty.’

“Zayd ibn Bishr and ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿImrān related to me. The two of them said: Ibn Wahb related to us, from Mūsā ibn ʿAlī: He asked Ibn Shihāb about something. Ibn Shihāb said, ‘I have heard nothing about it, and it has not arisen among us.’ I said, ‘It has arisen among some of your brethren.’ He replied:

“‘I have heard nothing about it, and it has not arisen among us, and I am not going to say anything about it.’”

“Muḥammad ibn Abī Zukayr related to us: Ibn Wahb informed us: Mālik related to me, saying: Rabīʿa said to me, ‘I told Ibn Shihāb: “Sit with the people in the mosque”—as if he meant, “to give them legal opinions.”’ Rabīʿa also said to Ibn Shihāb: ‘When you tell people something that is your own opinion, tell them that it is your opinion.’”

“Zayd ibn Bishr and ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿImrān related to me. The two of them said: Ibn Wahb informed us: Yūnus related to me from Ibn Shihāb, who said: ‘This knowledge is storehouses, and questions are what open them.’”

“Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us: Sufyān related to us: ʿAmr related to us, saying: ‘I have never seen anyone more at ease with reports than Ibn Shihāb, and I have never seen the dinar and the dirham— “—as more insignificant to Ibn Shihāb than it was.”

“Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā related to me, from Sufyān, who said: Near the end of his life, Rabīʿa said to al-Zuhrī, ‘If only you would settle in Medina, sit in the mosque of the Messenger of God ﷺ—and give legal opinions to the people.’ He replied, ‘If I did that, people would tread on my heels. I ought not do it until I have renounced this world and turned toward the Hereafter.’”

“He said: Sufyān also said: ‘Al-Zuhrī died on the day he died, and no one knew the Sunna better than he did.’” He said: Al-Zuhrī was asked about renouncing this world. He replied: “It is when the lawful does not deprive a person of gratitude, and the unlawful does not overcome his patience.”

“He said: Sufyān also said: They once said to al-Zuhrī, about a report he had related, ‘Repeat it for us.’

“He said, ‘Repeating a report is harder than moving a rock.’

“Zayd ibn Bishr related to us: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: I heard al-Layth relate:

“‘Ibn Shihāb used to say, “I have never entrusted anything to my heart and then forgotten it.”’”

“He said: He disliked eating apples and drinking what a mouse had left behind, and used to say that it caused forgetfulness. He used to drink honey and say that it aided memory.

“Al-Layth informed me, from al-Jumaḥī, who said: ‘I have never seen anyone closer to Ibn Shihāb in anything than Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd. Were it not for Ibn Shihāb, many of the Sunnas would have been lost.’

“Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb related to us: Ḥammād related to us, from a man, from al-Zuhrī, who said:

“He used to say to his companions: ‘Bring me some of your poetry; bring me some of your reports, for the ear has grown weary and the heart has turned sour.’

“Ḥaywa ibn Shurayḥ related to me: Baqiyya related to us, from Shuʿayb ibn Abī Ḥamza, who said:

“Makḥūl was asked, ‘Who is the most learned person you have met, Abū ʿAbd Allāh?’ He replied, ‘Ibn Shihāb.’ He was asked, ‘And then who?’ He replied, ‘Ibn Shihāb.’ He was asked, ‘And then who?’ He said, ‘Ibn Shihāb.’”

“Ḥaywa related to us: My father related to us, from Shuʿayb, from al-Zuhrī, who said: ‘For forty-five years I traveled back and forth from the Ḥijāz to Syria and from Syria to the Ḥijāz, and I never heard a report that I found novel.’”

“He said: I heard al-Ḥajjāj ibn Abī Manīʿ al-Ruṣāfī say: ‘Al-Zuhrī lived at al-Ruṣāfa for twenty years minus four months, throughout the caliphate of Hishām, except when he may have gone on pilgrimage; they had access to him.’

“Salama ibn Shabīb related to me: ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us, from Maʿmar, who said: ‘I said to al-Zuhrī, “They say that you have not related reports from any of the clients.” He replied, “Indeed, I have related from them.” Then he mentioned Sulaymān ibn Yasār, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Aʿraj, and Abū ʿUbayda, the client of— [He mentioned] ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf, Nudbah, a client-woman of Maymūnah, and ʿAṭāʾ, the client of Sibāʿ. Then he said: “I did not narrate from them, though I found the sons of the Emigrants and the Helpers, and could lean on whichever of them I wished. What need had I of anyone else?”

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmmār related to us; ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mundhir related to us, from Wuhayb, who said: I heard Ayyūb say, “I have seen no one more learned than al-Zuhrī.” He said:

Ṣakhr ibn Juwayriyah said, “Abū Bakr, not even al-Ḥasan?” He replied, “I have seen no one more learned than al-Zuhrī.”

Salamah related to me; ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to me; Maʿmar related to us, from Ṣāliḥ ibn Kaysān, who said: I and al-Zuhrī met while we were seeking knowledge. We said, “Let us write down the Sunan.” I wrote down what had come from the Prophet ﷺ—then he said, “Let us write down what has come from his Companions, for it is Sunna.” I said, “It is not Sunna, so let us not write it down.” He wrote it down, and I did not. He succeeded, and I lost out.

Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Malik related to us; ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us, from Maʿmar, who said: I have seen no one like al-Zuhrī in the field in which he excelled—I mean, in ḥadīth—and I have seen no one like Ḥammād ibn Abī Sulaymān in his field—I mean, in issuing legal opinions.

Al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAẓīm related to me; Abū Ayyūb Sulaymān al-Hāshimī related to us, from Ibrāhīm ibn Saʿd, from al-Zuhrī’s brother’s son, who said: I heard him—I mean al-Zuhrī—say: “Were it not for reports reaching us from the East that we reject and do not recognize, I would not have written a single letter, nor would I have permitted it to be written.”

Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Malik related to me; ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us, who said: Maʿmar said: We used to think that much had been transmitted from al-Zuhrī until al-Walīd was killed; then al-Zuhrī’s notebooks were brought out, loaded onto pack animals.

Salamah related to me; ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us and said: I heard ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿUmar say to him: “When I came of age, I wanted to seek knowledge. I began visiting the elder men of the family of ʿUmar one by one and asking, ‘What have you heard from Sālim?’ Whenever I visited one of them, he would say, ‘You should go to Ibn Shihāb, for Ibn Shihāb used to stay with him.’ Ibn Shihāb was in Syria at the time, so I stayed with Nāfiʿ, and God placed much good in that for me.”

Salamah ibn Shabīb related to me; ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us; Maʿmar informed us, from al-Zuhrī, who said: “I would come to ʿUrwah’s door and then turn back, out of reverence for him. Had I wished to enter upon him, I could have done so.”

Salamah related to me; Aḥmad related to us; Yaʿqūb related to us and said—and he meant his father—: My father said to me: “Ibn Shihāb did not surpass us in knowledge [except] that we used to come to the gathering and he would face us, fasten his garment at his chest, and ask about whatever he wanted, whereas our youth held us back.”

“Al-Zuhrī among his companions was like al-Ḥakam ibn ʿUtaybah among his companions: he would transmit the ḥadīth of some of them to others.” Maʿmar also said: I came to al-Zuhrī at al-Ruṣāfah. There was no one asking him about ḥadīth, so he would dictate it to me.

Abū Bishr related to us; ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us, from Maʿmar, from a man of Quraysh, who said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said to us, “Do you go to al-Zuhrī?” We said, “Yes.” He said:

“Then go to him, for I know no one more learned than he in an established Sunna.” Maʿmar said: “Al-Ḥasan and his contemporaries were alive at that time.”

Salamah related to us, from Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal; Abū al-Qāsim ibn Abī al-Zinād related to us and said: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī al-Zinād came here to us. My father informed me: “I used to circumambulate with Ibn Shihāb, and Ibn Shihāb had writing boards and sheets with him.” He said: “We used to laugh at him for it.”
