Abū Saʿīd ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ibrāhīm related to us; Ayyūb ibn Suwayd related to us and said: I heard al-Awzāʿī say: “Ibn Shihāb never put on perfume for a king before entering his presence. And no Successor who lived through Hishām’s caliphate was more learned in jurisprudence than he.”

Abū Saʿīd related to me; ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Bashīr related to us, from Ibn Isḥāq, from al-Zuhrī, who said: “Hishām told us the Prophet’s ḥadīth, ‘May God brighten the face of a man,’ and by it he spared me a hundred thousand. By God, I am not the one meant by it.”

Hishām ibn Khālid al-Sulāmī related to us and said: I heard al-Walīd ibn Muslim relate, from Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, who said: “Ibn Shihāb is nothing but an ocean.”

Saʿīd said: I heard Makḥūl say: “Ibn Shihāb is the most learned of people in an established Sunna—”

—

Hishām related to us and said: I heard Marwān ibn Muḥammad relate, from Saʿīd, that Makḥūl was more learned in jurisprudence than al-Zuhrī. I heard him say: “Makḥūl was the most learned in jurisprudence among the people of Syria.”

Hishām related to us; al-Walīd ibn Muslim related to us, from Saʿīd: Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik asked al-Zuhrī to dictate to one of his sons. He summoned a scribe and dictated four hundred ḥadīths to him. Then al-Zuhrī left Hishām and said, “Where are you, people of ḥadīth?” He then related those four hundred ḥadīths to them. Hishām stayed for a month or so, then said to al-Zuhrī, “That book you dictated for us has been lost.” He replied, “No harm; call for a scribe.” Hishām summoned a scribe, and al-Zuhrī dictated the four hundred ḥadīths to him. Hishām then compared it with the first book and found that it did not differ by a single letter.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ibrāhīm related to us; Abū Ḥafṣ related to us, from Saʿīd ibn Bashīr, from Qatādah, who said: “No one remains more learned in the Sunna than al-Zuhrī and another man”—meaning himself.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ibrāhīm related to us; al-Walīd related to us; al-Qāsim ibn Hazzān related to us and said: I heard al-Zuhrī say: “People cannot trust the deed of a person who does not know, nor be content with the words of a learned person who does not act.”

Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Malik related to us; ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us, from Maʿmar, who said: I heard al-Zuhrī say: “We used to dislike writing things down until the rulers compelled us to do so. Then I decided not to withhold it from any Muslim.”

Ṣāliḥ ibn Kaysān informed me and said: Al-Zuhrī and I used to seek knowledge. He said to me, “Come, let us write down the Sunan.” We wrote down everything that had come from the Prophet ﷺ. Then he said, “Come, let us write down everything that has come from the Companions.” He wrote it down, but I did not. He succeeded, and I lost out.

Abū Bakr related to us; ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us, from Maʿmar, who said: I heard al-Zuhrī, when he was told, “They say that you have not related from the clients,” reply: “What am I to do with the clients when I find the sons of the Emigrants and the Helpers, and can lean on whichever of them I wish?”

Maʿmar said: He related from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Abī Rāfiʿ, from Abū ʿUbayd, the client of Abū Qatādah, from Nāfiʿ, the client of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb’s son, from ʿAṭāʾ, the client of Ibn Sibāʿ, from al-Aʿraj, from Ḥabīb, the client of ʿUrwah, from Kathīr ibn Aflaḥ, Nabḥān, and Nudbah.

Al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Walīd ibn Ṣubḥ related to us; Abū Mushir related to us; Yazīd ibn al-Samṭ related to me and said: I heard Qurrah ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ḥaywaʾīl say: “Al-Zuhrī had no book except one containing the genealogy of his people.”

Yazīd ibn al-Samṭ said: Al-Awzāʿī used to say: “No one knew al-Zuhrī better than Ibn Ḥaywaʾīl.”

Al-ʿAbbās related to us; Marwān related to us; Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to us and said:

I heard Makḥūl say: “No one remains more learned in an established Sunna than Ibn Shihāb al-Zuhrī—”

— Marwān said: I related it to Saʿīd ibn Bashīr, and Saʿīd said: I heard Qatādah say: “No one remains more learned in an established Sunna than Ibn Shihāb al-Zuhrī and another man.” Saʿīd said: “We used to think he meant himself.”

Al-ʿAbbās related to us; Zayd ibn Yaḥyā related to us; ʿAlī ibn Ḥawshab al-Fazārī related to us and said: I heard Makḥūl mention al-Zuhrī and say, “Every night”—he had a quip about him. Yazīd said, “A little [something]—what a man he is! Were it not that he ruined himself by keeping company with kings.”31

ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Saʿd related to us and said: I heard my uncle mention, from his father, who said: Ṣāliḥ ibn Kaysān was Ibn Shihāb’s tutor. Ṣāliḥ would sometimes mention something, and Ibn Shihāb would correct him without saying, “So-and-so related to us,” or, “So-and-so related to us,” even when what they related contradicted what Ṣāliḥ had said. He said:

Ṣāliḥ would say to him, “You speak to me, when I was the one who straightened your tongue’s crookedness.”

Aḥmad ibn Ḥafṣ related to us; my father related to me; Ibrāhīm ibn Ṭahmān related to me, from Maṭar, from Qatādah, who said: “The most learned of those who remain in the Qurʾān is Mujāhid”—meaning in its exegesis.

Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir related to us; Sufyān related to us and said: Al-Zuhrī was told, “If you were not now at the end of your life, you would stay in Medina, remain in the Mosque of the Messenger of God ﷺ—sit beside one of its columns, and teach the people.” Ibn Shihāb said: “I will not do that until I have renounced this world and become desirous of the next. If I did that, people would tread in my footsteps.”

Al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAẓīm related to us and said: I heard ʿAbd al-Razzāq say:

[Ziyād ibn Saʿd] said to al-Zuhrī: “I like your ḥadīth, but I have no provisions to follow you.” He replied, “Follow me; I will relate to you and provide for you.”

Al-ʿAbbās related to us; ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī related to me and said: I heard Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah say: Ibn Saʿd informed me; he said: I heard al-Zuhrī say: “I have thirty ḥadīths concerning khulʿ, but I have not related them, nor has anyone asked me about any of them.”

He said: I heard ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān mention, from Ibn al-Mubārak, from Yūnus, who said:

To al-Zuhrī: “Bring out your books for me.” He said, “Girl, bring that basket.” She brought a basket, and in it was some genealogy of his people and poetry. He said, “I have nothing written down,” or words to that effect.

[Reports about Abū Bakr ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr ibn Ḥazm]

Muḥammad ibn Abī Zukayr related to me; Ibn Wahb informed us; Mālik related to me and said:

No one in Medina had as much knowledge of judicial matters as Abū Bakr. Abū Bakr ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr ibn Ḥazm used to learn judicial matters from Abān ibn ʿUthmān.

Mālik said: Abān ibn ʿUthmān had learned some judicial matters from his father, ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān.

He said: Abū Bakr [ibn Muḥammad] ibn ʿAmr ibn Ḥazm was a judge for ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz when ʿUmar was governor of Medina during the caliphate of Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. He said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz had appointed Ibn Mujammiʿ al-Anṣārī as judge. When two men brought a dispute before him and he ruled that one of them must swear an oath, if that man refused to swear, Ibn Mujammiʿ made him pay the claim on his behalf. ʿUmar therefore removed him from the judgeship.

Ibrāhīm ibn Muḥammad related to me; Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī related to me and said: They said to ʿUmar:

“You appointed Abū Bakr ibn Ḥazm: upright through his prayers, complete [in devotion]. If worshippers do not take him as their model, then whom should they follow?” He said: The marks of his prostration had worn into his forehead and nose.

Muḥammad ibn Abī Zukayr related to me; Ibn Wahb informed us; Mālik related to us: Muḥammad ibn Hishām appointed Muḥammad ibn Abī Bakr ibn ʿAmr ibn Ḥazm as judge; he was an excellent, righteous judge.

Yūnus ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to me; Shihāb informed us, from Mālik; Ibn Ghaziyyah informed me and said: Ibn Shihāb said to me, “Who is in Medina?” He replied, “Ḥabīb.”

Ibn Shihāb said: “There is no one there like ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Bakr, but what prevents his reputation from rising is that his father is still alive.”

Muḥammad ibn Abī Zukayr related to me; Ibn Wahb informed us; Mālik related to me: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz wrote to Abū Bakr ibn ʿAmr ibn Ḥazm. ʿUmar had appointed him governor of Medina after he had been a judge. Mālik said: Abū Bakr ibn Ḥazm held authority in Medina twice as governor. ʿUmar wrote to him, instructing him to write down for him the knowledge held by ʿAmrah bint ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad. I asked Mālik, “The Sunan?” He said, “Yes.”

He wrote them down for him. Mālik said: I asked his son ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Bakr about those books, and he said, “They were lost.” Abū Bakr had been removed from office in a disgraceful manner.

Ḥarmalah related to me; Ibn Wahb informed us, from Ibn Lahīʿah, who reported to him that ʿUmārah ibn Ghaziyyah related to him: Ibn Shihāb said: Al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad said, “If you want the ḥadīth of ʿĀʾishah, you should go to ʿAmrah bint ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, for she is among the most learned people in the ḥadīth of ʿĀʾishah; ʿĀʾishah had raised her in her care.”

Zayd ibn Bishr and ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿImrān related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us and said: I heard Mālik say: “No Anṣārī other than Abū Bakr ibn ʿAmr ibn Ḥazm was governor of Medina,” and he was a judge.

[Reports about Nāfiʿ, the client of Ibn ʿUmar]

Aṣbagh ibn al-Faraj related to us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rajāʾ informed me, from Yūnus ibn Yazīd, who said: Nāfiʿ said: “Who will excuse me from this Zuhrī of yours”—meaning Ibn Shihāb—“who comes to me and I relate from Ibn ʿUmar to him, then goes to Sālim ibn ʿAbd Allāh and asks, ‘Did you hear this from Ibn ʿUmar?’ Sālim says, ‘Yes.’ Then he relates it from Sālim and leaves me out, though the wording is mine.”

ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿImrān related to me; Ibn Wahb related to us; Usāmah ibn Zayd informed me that Abū Bakr ibn Ḥafṣ ibn Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ related to him: He asked Sālim ibn ʿAbd Allāh, “From which side did Ibn ʿUmar mark the sacrificial camels?” He replied, “From the right side.”

Then I asked Nāfiʿ, and he said, “From the left side.” I said to Nāfiʿ, “Sālim informed me that he used to mark them from the right side.” He said, “But did Sālim—? He only once saw Ibn ʿUmar brought two camels, bare and lanced, and he could not stand between them, so he marked this one on the right side and that one on the left.” I went back to Sālim and told him. He said, “Nāfiʿ is right; it is as he said.” He said: “And he said, ‘Ask him, for he knows the ḥadīth of Ibn ʿUmar better than any of us.’”

Muḥammad ibn Abī Zukayr related to me; Ibn Wahb informed us; Mālik related to me and said:

I was told that ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar visited ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar, and Nāfiʿ, his client, was with Ibn ʿUmar. He said to him, “I mean this one.”32 After that, whenever Ibn ʿUmar went to visit him, he would say to Nāfiʿ, “Do not come with me.” Mālik said: He feared that ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar would tempt Nāfiʿ with what he offered him and buy him from him.

Mālik said: I used to visit Nāfiʿ, the client of Ibn ʿUmar, when I was then a young boy, and I had a boy with me. Nāfiʿ would come down to me, sit with me, and relate ḥadīths to me. He used to sit in the mosque after the dawn prayer, and hardly anyone would come to him. He wore his cloak, and sometimes, he said, he would place it over his mouth and speak to no one. He would sit until the sun rose, then leave before performing a rakʿah.

He said: Nāfiʿ only began relating ḥadīths after Sālim ibn ʿAbd Allāh died. While Sālim was alive, Nāfiʿ would not give anyone a legal opinion about anything. Ibn Wahb said: I heard Mālik say: “He was—”

Saʿīd ibn Abī Hind, Nāfiʿ, the client of Ibn ʿUmar, and Mūsā ibn Maysarah would sit after the dawn prayer until the day had grown bright. Then they would disperse without speaking to one another. We asked him, “Was this because they were occupied in remembering God?” He replied, “All of that.”

He said: I heard Mālik say: “After the dawn prayer I used to see Nāfiʿ wrap himself in a black cloak, place it over his mouth, and speak to no one. He was young.”

He said: Ibn Abī Uways said, reporting from his father: “We used to go to him”—meaning Nāfiʿ—“and he was ill-tempered.” I said, “What am I to do with this slave?” So I left him, and [someone else] stayed close to him and benefited from him.

[Reports about Ziyād ibn Saʿd al-Khurāsānī]

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us: Sufyān said: “Ziyād ibn Saʿd said to me:

‘This one has a better memory than Nāfiʿ’”—meaning ʿUmar ibn Nāfiʿ.

He said: Ziyād ibn Saʿd al-Khurāsānī had gone to Medina before I did.

Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb related to us: Ḥammād ibn Zayd related to us, from Ayyūb, who said: “I wrote to Nāfiʿ asking him about ʿAbd Allāh’s position regarding wounds. He wrote back to me: ‘I heard nothing from ʿAbd Allāh about it.’”

Our companions related to us, from ʿAlī, who said: I heard Sufyān say: “Ziyād ibn Saʿd would accept nothing as satisfactory unless it was a short report that could be memorized or a report dictated to him.”

He said: ʿAlī said: ʿAbd al-Razzāq said: “I saw Zamʿah presenting Ziyād’s books to Maʿmar for a fee.”

ʿAlī said: I heard Sufyān say: “Ziyād ibn Saʿd related from Hilāl ibn Abī—”

Maymūnah. Ayyūb said to him, “I would not have thought you had sat with this man. Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr narrates from him.” He replied, “Abū Bakr, I did sit with him.”

[Reports about Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Anṣārī]

ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿImrān related to me: Ibn Wahb related to us: al-Layth related to me.

He said: I heard Ibn Bukayr relate from al-Layth, from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, who said:

“Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd would relate to us, and [his words] would flow over us like pearls”—and ʿUbayd Allāh gestured with one hand over the other.

ʿUbayd Allāh said: “When Rabīʿah appeared, Yaḥyā would stop his account out of deference to Rabīʿah and reverence for him.”

ʿAbd Allāh said: One day Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd recited this verse: “There is nothing whose treasuries are not with Us, and We do not send it down except in a known measure” (Qurʾān 15:21). Jamīl ibn Nubātah al-ʿIrāqī said, “Abū Saʿīd, what do you think? Is magic among the treasuries of God that He sends down?” Yaḥyā replied:

“Enough! This is not among the questions Muslims discuss.” And he silenced the group. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Ḥabībah said:

“Abū Saʿīd is not one of those who engage in disputation; he is one of the imams of the Muslims. But turn to me. I say that magic can cause harm only by God’s permission. Do you say otherwise?” He fell silent and said nothing. ʿUbayd Allāh said: “It was as if a mountain had been lifted from us.” Ibn Bukayr added more to this account, but I did not—”

—master its wording.33

Abū Ṣāliḥ and Ibn Bukayr related to us: al-Layth ibn Saʿd related to us, from Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd, who said: “I found people criticizing the use of books, even if they contained a report. Had we written things down then, we would have written down a great deal of Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab’s knowledge and opinions.”

Abū Ṣāliḥ said: al-Layth related to me, saying: “When Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd was first brought the books containing his knowledge for review, he thought there were too many of them, because he had no book of his own, and he denied having them. Then he was told, ‘We will present them to you: whatever you recognize, you may approve; whatever you do not recognize, you may reject.’ He recognized all of it.”

Zayd ibn Bishr and ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿImrān related to me: Ibn Wahb related to us, who said:

Mālik said: “I heard Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd say, ‘I would rather have written down what I heard than possess wealth equal to all my own.’”

Ibn Bukayr related to me: I heard al-Layth say: “Rabīʿah wrote things down. A man came to him and said, ‘Abū ʿUthmān, some men from the people of Ifrīqiyah have instructed me to ask you, Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd, and Abū al-Zinād.’ He said, ‘Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd is just now coming out of ʿUmar’s small door.’ The man said, ‘Here is Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd; go ahead and ask him whatever you wish. As for Abū al-Zinād, he is neither well-regarded nor a jurist.’ Al-Layth said: I thought he was hinting at him only so that I would not go to him. Ibn Bukayr said: He did not say much about him.”

[Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb related to us: Ḥammād ibn Zayd related to us, who said: “Ayyūb came to us—”

—once from Medina. We asked him, ‘Abū Bakr, whom did you leave there as the most learned?’ He said, ‘I left no one there more learned than Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd.’]

[I heard our companions say: ʿAbd al-Wahhāb ibn ʿAbd al-Majīd had written from Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd, but his books were lost. He then set out to visit him and wrote from him again.

ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī said: “There is no book in the world from Yaḥyā more sound than ʿAbd al-Wahhāb’s book. Every book from Yaḥyā is a burden upon it”—meaning ʿAbd al-Wahhāb’s book.]

Abū al-Nuʿmān related to us: Ḥammād ibn Zayd related to us, from Hishām ibn ʿUrwah, who said: “The upright, trustworthy man”—as Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd described him—“related to me from my father, though I did not hear it from my father: ‘The hand of one who steals from a trust is to be cut off.’”

[ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAmr ibn Ḥafṣ]

Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir related to us: Abū Ḍamrah related to us, who said: “Ziyād ibn ʿUbayd Allāh, of Banū ʿAbd al-Dār—whom Abū al-ʿAbbās had appointed over Medina—sent to ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿUmar ibn Ḥafṣ, appointing him to one of his administrative posts. ʿUbayd Allāh refused, but Ziyād persisted until he compelled him. ʿUbayd Allāh said, ‘Since you have compelled me to take up your post, let me choose.’

“He said, ‘Choose.’ ʿUbayd Allāh chose al-Rāghibah. He was told, ‘Abū ʿUthmān, you have chosen the worst of his posts, and the least sound.’34 He replied, ‘He is the governor, and he compelled me, so I chose the least onerous and least burdensome one.’”

Abū Ḍamrah said: ʿUbayd Allāh said: “I set out and stopped at Qudayd. I instructed a caller to proclaim, ‘Whoever has a claim upon us for God’s sake, let him come forward with it.’ An elderly man from Khuzāʿah said, ‘What is this man saying?’ They told him, ‘This is the governor’s envoy. He is saying, “Whoever has a claim upon us for God’s sake, let him come forward with it.”’ The old man said, ‘I have not heard such words since the Messenger whom ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān sent to us, until this day.’”

[Reports about ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd ibn Hurmuz]

Muḥammad ibn Abī Zukayr related to me: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: I heard Mālik relate that Muḥammad ibn ʿAjlān asked about something, but the answer did not satisfy him. Ibn Hurmuz kept explaining it to him until he understood. Ibn ʿAjlān then stood up and kissed his head.

Mālik said: “I was told that Ibn Shihāb said to Ibn Hurmuz while speaking with him, ‘I adjure you by God: do you know that in the past people used to pray without washing themselves with water after relieving themselves?’ Ibn Hurmuz fell silent and gave him no answer.”

I said to Mālik, “Why did he fall silent?” He said, “He did not want to say yes to him, since that practice had been abandoned; so he left it and did not answer him.”

Zayd ibn Bishr, ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿImrān, and Yūnus related to us. They said: Ibn Wahb related to us, who said: Bakr ibn Muḍar said: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd ibn Hurmuz said: “I learned knowledge only for myself.”

Yūnus and Ḥarmalah related to us: Ibn Wahb informed us: Muḥammad ibn Dīnār related to me that ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd ibn Hurmuz used to say: “I would like a man not to guard his own opinion as carefully as he guards the Sunnah.”

[Muḥammad ibn Abī Zukayr related to us: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Mālik said: “I knew Ibn Hurmuz as a man whom I wanted to emulate. He spoke little, gave few legal opinions, and was extremely cautious. Often he would give a man a legal opinion, then send someone after him to bring him back, so that he could tell him something different from what he had ruled.” He said: “He was well versed in dialectical theology. He refuted the people of heretical doctrines and was among the most knowledgeable of people about the differences among these doctrines.”]

Ibn Wahb said: Mālik related to us that one day he went to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd ibn Hurmuz and found him sitting alone on his bed, with no one else there. He was speaking of the ordinances of Islam, what had been undone of them, and what he feared might be lost; his tears were streaming.

He said: “His father was killed on the Day of al-Ḥarrah, and Ibn Shihāb used to relate from his father.”

Zayd ibn Bishr related to me: Ibn Wahb informed me: Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm ibn Dīnār related to me that ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd ibn Hurmuz used to say: “I dislike a man guarding his own opinion as carefully as the Sunnah is guarded.”

Zayd ibn Bishr and ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to me: they said, Ibn Wahb informed us: Mālik related to me, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd ibn Hurmuz, that when he was asked about something, he would say:

“There is consideration and reflection involved in this.” They would say, “Yes, so I will do it.” He would reply, “It requires time and reflection”—ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said, “And I do not like to occupy myself with that”—they both said:

“When, then, am I to pray? When am I to remember [God]?”

Ibn Wahb said: Mālik related to me, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd ibn Hurmuz, who said:

“I would like one of the things a scholar leaves behind after him to be ‘I do not know,’ so that those who come after him may follow that example.”

[Muḥammad ibn Abī Zukayr related to me: Ibn Wahb informed us: Mālik related to me, from Ibn Hurmuz, that a man would come to him and ask him about something. He would give him an answer, then send someone after him to bring him back and say, “I was hasty. Do not accept anything I told you until you come back to me.” He said: Few of the people of Medina gave legal opinions. Mālik said: “One who fears God is not like one who does not fear Him.”]

Muḥammad ibn Abī Zukayr related to us: Ibn Wahb informed us: Mālik related to me, from Ibn Hurmuz, that when a man came to him and asked whether he should seek knowledge, he would say to him, “If you consider yourself suited to it, then seek it.” He said: When a man came to Ibn Hurmuz and asked him about a matter, he would say, “Have you asked anyone?” The man would say, “Yes.”

He would ask, “Who?” If the man named someone whom Ibn Hurmuz did not approve of, he would say, “I do not know him,” and would not ask what that person had said. If the man told him the name of someone he approved of, he would ask what that person had said, and the man would tell him.

Ibn Wahb said: Mālik related to me: “There was no one in Medina, of Quraysh or any other people, who had standing and faced a difficult matter without turning to Ibn Yazīd ibn Hurmuz.”

Ibn Wahb said: Mālik related to me: “When the sheep and camels collected as alms arrived in Medina, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd ibn Hurmuz would abstain from the meat: he would neither buy nor eat it. He was asked, ‘Why?’ He said, ‘Because they used to bring them to the governors, who did not distribute them as they should.’” He said: I heard Mālik relate, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd ibn Hurmuz, that he used to say: “I marvel at a person who is provided with lawful sustenance, yet, desiring profit, lets a small amount of unlawful gain into it and thereby corrupts all his wealth.”]

Muḥammad related to me: Ibn Wahb informed us: Mālik related to me, from Ibn Hurmuz, who said:

“I have not pursued this matter as fully as it deserves”—when he was asked for a legal opinion. Mālik said: “This man gives legal opinions without knowledge; he has not pursued it as fully as it deserves, nor sought this matter from those who know it. I condemn people like these for giving legal opinions.”

Ibn Zayd ibn Bishr related to us: Ibn Wahb informed me: Zayd related to us, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Hurmuz, that he said—when he stopped engaging in dialectical theology: “We were nothing but judges, but we did not understand the matter in which we were engaged. People’s sexual relations were declared lawful by our words, and property was taken by our words. We were nothing but judges.”

Ibn Hurmuz said: “We encountered the people of knowledge who came before us. When they were asked about something, some of them would say to the others, ‘Consider what your companion says.’ They would say, ‘It seems we are comparing this matter with one that occurred in the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ; as though it were like the matter of so-and-so in the time of Abū Bakr, or something similar in the time of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.’ Then they would give the same ruling. [And] they would say, ‘No, we have nothing else to go by.’ Then he said: ‘Rabīʿah, Abū al-Zinād, and I met together and said, “What is it that confuses people?” It seemed as though he was drawing an analogy to it!’ He said: ‘We ventured to do so, while the others held back. We said, “It is like it.”’

“We were asked about certain things and said, ‘We disapprove of them.’ Then others came who had been with us and ranked below us, and said, ‘No—why should we disapprove of them?’ Then others came, who had been with us and ranked below us, and said, ‘Why should we disapprove of them? They are nothing but lawful and unlawful.’ So they dared to do what my companions and I had held back from, just as—”

—we dared to do what those before us had held back from.

[Zayd ibn Bishr related to us: Ibn Wahb informed us: Mālik ibn Anas informed me that he heard ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd ibn Hurmuz say: “A scholar should bequeath to those who sit with him after his death the words ‘I do not know,’ so that they may have them as a principle to turn to whenever one of them is asked about something he does not know, and say, ‘I do not know.’”]

Abū al-Ḥasan Aḥmad ibn Abī al-Ḥawārī related to us, who said: I heard Marwān relate from Mālik, who said: “I studied with Ibn Hurmuz for thirteen years. In winter, I had made myself padded trousers. We used to sit with him in the courtyard during the winter.”

He said: “He made me swear not to mention his name in the account.”

Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir related to us: Muṭarrif related to me, from Mālik, who said: Yazīd ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Hurmuz said: “Mālik, do not hold on to any of this opinion that you took from me. By God, Rabīʿah and I were the ones who started it.”

Ibn Abī Salamah said to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd ibn Hurmuz: “A man asks me for a legal opinion, and I give him my opinion and say, ‘This is my opinion.’ Is that permissible for me?” He replied, “No, by God—not until you know. If this were permissible for you, it would be permissible for the water-carriers who carry waterskins on their backs.”

[Reports about Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir]

Ibrāhīm ibn Muḥammad related to me, who said: I heard Sufyān say: Ibn al-Munkadir was asked, “What is the best of things?” He replied, “Bringing joy to a believer.” He was asked:

“What remains of the things one takes pleasure in?” He replied, “Generosity toward one’s brothers.”

Zayd ibn Bishr related to me: Ibn Wahb informed us: Ibn Zayd related to me, who said: Ṣafwān came to Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir while he was dying. He kept comforting him and easing his distress until it was as though lamps shone in his face. Then Muḥammad said to him, “If you could see what I am experiencing, your eyes would be gladdened.” Then he died.

Zayd related to us: Ibn Wahb informed us: Ibn Zayd related to us—and mentioned Muḥammad and Abū Bakr, the two sons of al-Munkadir—who said: “When one of them was close to death, he wept. He was asked, ‘What makes you weep? We used to envy you for this day.’ He said, ‘By God, I do not weep because I knowingly committed anything I had abandoned of disobedience to God, brazenly defying Him. Rather, I fear that I may have done something I thought insignificant, though it is great in God’s sight.’”

He said: “The other brother wept at the time of death, and was asked the same. He replied, ‘I heard God, Mighty and Majestic, say:

“And there will appear to them from God what they had never reckoned with” (Qurʾān 39:47). I await what you see; by God, I do not know what will appear to me.’”

It used to be said: “Muḥammad, their brother, was the least devoted of them in worship—and what a man Muḥammad was in his time!”

[Zayd ibn Bishr related to us: Ibn Wahb informed us: Ibn Zayd related to me, who said: “He went out—”

A group of men were on a campaign, among them Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir, on the summer expedition. While they were marching in the rear guard, a man from the group said, “I crave fresh cheese.” Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir said:

“Ask God to provide it for you, for God is able to feed it to you.” The men prayed, and they had gone only a short way when they found a stitched-up basket, as though it had been brought from al-Sayyālah or al-Rawḥāʾ. It contained fresh cheese. One of the men said, “If only we had honey to go with it.” He replied, “The One who fed it to you is able to feed you honey. Ask Him to provide it, and He will feed you honey.” They prayed to God, and after traveling a little they found a qāqirah35 of honey by the road. They dismounted and ate the cheese and honey, then mounted again.”

Ibn Zayd related to us: Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir related to us: “A man entrusted me with one hundred dinars. I said, ‘My brother, if we need them, may we spend them and repay you later?’ He said, ‘Yes.’ We needed them, so we spent them. Then his messenger came: ‘We need the money now.’ I said, ‘There is nothing in my house.’ That day I kept praying, ‘O God, do not ruin my trust; restore it.’ I went out, then came back to go in, and there was a man I did not know taking me by the shoulder. He handed me a purse, and it contained one hundred dinars. The people had no idea where they had come from. They did not learn their source until ʿĀmir and Ibn al-Munkadir had both died. Then a man came and told him, ‘ʿĀmir sent me with them. Give them to him, and do not mention me until either I die or Ibn al-Munkadir dies.’”

He said: He did not mention them until they had both died.

Zayd related to us; Ibn Wahb informed us; Ibn Zayd related to me: Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir was asked, “What remains of the pleasures of this world?” He said, “Supporting one’s brothers and showing them generosity.”

Zayd related to us; Ibn Wahb informed me; Ibn Zayd related to me: “The accursed wolf used to appear to Ibn al-Munkadir in the mosque, between him and the pulpit, and terrify him.” He said:

“One morning he came to my father and said, ‘Abū Usāmah, shall I tell you something? I saw the accursed one come to me in a dream and fight me, so I fought him. Then I seized36 it, and God split it into two halves. I threw one half here and the other there, and I hope God has helped me against it.’” He said: Ibn al-Munkadir did not see it after that.

Zayd related to us; Ibn Wahb informed us; Ibn Zayd related to me: “A woman fell unconscious and began speaking while unconscious. She was told, ‘Zayd ibn Muslim, Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir, Abū Ḥāzim, and Rabīʿah ibn Abī ʿAbd al-Raḥmān are among the people of Paradise, and they will abide there forever, in their companionship.’”

Zayd related to us; Ibn Wahb informed me; Ibn Zayd related to me, from Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir, who said: “My Lord, show me what this world is like in Your sight, so that I may know it.” He said: Someone came to him in his dream and said, “Ibn al-Munkadir, you asked God to show you what this world is like in His sight. That is something that can never happen.”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us; Sufyān related to us; ʿAmr related to us, from Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir, who said: “ʿUthmān passed by a storyteller who was telling stories after the evening prayer. ʿUthmān said to him:

‘Woe to you! Do not keep these people from their evening meal.’”

Sufyān related to us; ʿAmr related to us, who said: “I saw Ibn al-Munkadir as a boy in Medina, with white patches on him.”

Abū Bishr related to me; Saʿīd ibn ʿĀmir related to us, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak, who said:

“Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir said: ‘ʿUmar—his brother—spent the night in prayer, while I spent the night rubbing my mother’s feet. I would not wish to trade my night for his.’”

Abū Bishr related to me; Saʿīd ibn ʿĀmir related to me, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak, who said:

“Abū Ḥāzim gathered some people from the mosque and took them to Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir to ask him to ease the burden of worship he had placed upon himself. When they spoke to him, he said, ‘I face the night and it overwhelms me. But when I enter the prayer and recite the Qurʾān, the night passes before I have reached what I need.’”

Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā and Ḥarmalah related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us; Mālik related to us— [from] Ibn Ḥayyān al-Murrī, when he was governor of Medina: Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir and his companions admonished some people about something they had heard concerning the bathhouses. Among them was a client of Ibn Ḥayyān, who reported it to him. Ibn Ḥayyān sent for Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir and his companions and had them flogged because they had spoken in support of what was right and forbidden what was reprehensible. He said:

“You speak out about such things!” I said to Mālik, “Was Ibn al-Munkadir flogged?” He replied, “By God, yes. Rabīʿah too. He was one of the qannitīn37. He was flogged, and his head and beard were shaved, but for something other than this.” He said: Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab was flogged one hundred times and put in a pair of drawers.

Mālik said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said, “I do not envy a man who has suffered no harm in this matter.”

I heard Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir say: “The reason Rabīʿah was flogged was Abū al-Zinād’s informing against him. After so-and-so al-Taymī, [the new governor] was appointed. He sent for Abū al-Zinād, put him in a room, and sealed the door, intending to kill him by hunger and thirst. When Rabīʿah heard of this, he went to the governor, spoke to him, and condemned what he had done. The governor said, ‘Did I do this to him for any reason other than what he did to you? Leave him to die.’ Rabīʿah refused to let him be, until he had him released. He said, ‘I will bring him to account before God, mighty and glorious’—or words to that effect.”

[Reports about Ṣafwān ibn Sulaym]

I heard al-Ḥumaydī relate from Sufyān, who said: “Ṣafwān ibn Sulaym made the pilgrimage. I went38 and asked about him. I was told, ‘When you enter the Mosque of al-Khayf, go to the minaret—the minaret—and look a little in front of it for an old man. When you see him, you will know that he fears God. That is Ṣafwān.’

“I did not ask anyone else about him. I went as I had been told, and there I saw an old man. When I saw him, I knew he feared God. I sat down beside him and said, ‘Are you Ṣafwān?’ He said, ‘Yes.’ So I asked him.”

Abū Bakr related to us; Sufyān related to us, who said: “Ṣafwān ibn Sulaym made the pilgrimage with only seven dinars. He bought a sacrificial camel with them. He was questioned about this, and he said, ‘I heard God say, “The sacrificial camels We have appointed for you are among the symbols of God; in them there is good for you” (Qurʾān 22:36).’”

[Muslim ibn Abī Maryam]

I heard Ibn Qaʿnab say: Mālik ibn Anas mentioned Sulaym ibn Abī Maryam and praised him highly.

[Yaʿqūb ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Ashajj, Bukayr ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Ashajj, and Makhramah ibn Bukayr]

Zayd ibn Bishr related to us; Shuʿayb ibn Yaḥyā related to us, who said: Yaʿqūb ibn al-Ashajj arrived and went in to ʿĪsā ibn Abī ʿAṭāʾ and greeted him. ʿĪsā was governor of Egypt and was from the people of Medina. ʿĪsā ibn Abī ʿAṭāʾ said to him, “How fortunate you are: you go on campaign and guard the frontier, while we are unable to campaign or guard the frontier.” Yaʿqūb ibn al-Ashajj said to him:

“You are in a good state.” When he left, he said, “What have I done? I have uttered a word that, I think, nothing but martyrdom can expiate.” He made preparations and went out to fight the enemy. A man was assigned to his detachment. The man put on his armor, bound his waist, and sat waiting for the troops to set out. He asked them, “Who has been appointed over us?” They said, “So-and-so al-Barrī.” He said, “Al-Barrī flies off and does not return”—as though he had taken his name as a bad omen. He said, “It makes no difference to me who is appointed over us.” He fell asleep while sitting and waiting for them. Then he woke and said to those around him, “By God, just now I saw as though I had entered Paradise and drunk milk there.” They said, “We adjure you to induce vomiting.” So he induced vomiting and brought up milk. Then he set out with the detachment. The detachment was struck at a place called Buḥayrat al-Ṭayr. After him, Bukayr ibn al-Ashajj arrived, and he was asked, “Won’t you come in so we can greet ʿĪsā ibn Abī ʿAṭāʾ?” He replied, “He is a man whose face I hope never to see again. I fear I will slip as my brother did.”

Zayd ibn Bishr related to me; Ibn Wahb informed me; al-Layth related to us, from Yazīd ibn Abī Ḥabīb, who said: “One of those who met the Companions and the Successors said, ‘Bukayr left nothing of the Messenger of God’s way and bearing ﷺ.’” Al-Layth said, “That was because of his composure and his moderation.” He said: Bukayr resembled them in the excellence of his bearing and his character.

Zayd ibn Bishr related to me; Ibn Wahb informed me, who said: Ibn Zayd said to me: Usāmah ibn Zayd said, “One night, Yaʿqūb ibn ʿAbd Allāh returned with us, then fell behind us to give a beggar his garment alone—” and there he was, having been asked for his waistcloth. He gave it to him, wrapped himself in his cloak, and returned to his family wrapped in his cloak.

Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir related to me; ʿĪsā ibn al-Mughīrah ibn al-Ḍaḥḥāk al-Judhāmī related to me, who said: I heard Makhramah ibn Bukayr say: “My paternal uncle, Yaʿqūb ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ashajj, was killed in a sea campaign.” ʿĪsā said: “He was a man of merit and worship, and he was the brother of Bukayr ibn ʿAbd Allāh. He had a daughter called Umm ʿAmr who suffered seizures. When he was killed, Umm ʿAmr said, ‘In a dream, I saw my father come to me and say, “My daughter, what is happening to you?” I told him.’

“He said, ‘Would you recognize it if I brought it to you?’ I said, ‘Yes.’ A black dog came, and he said, ‘Is this it?’

“‘I said, “Yes.” He seized it and slaughtered it.’”

ʿĪsā said: “I saw Umm ʿAmr, daughter of Yaʿqūb, when she was an old woman of more than ninety years: one of the wisest and most eloquent of women.”

Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir said: Ibn Abī Uways related to me, who said: “I read in Mālik ibn Anas’s own handwriting in his book: ‘I made my way through the rows until I stood beside Makhramah ibn Bukayr in the Rawḍah. I said to him, “People say that you did not hear these traditions that we transmit from your father directly from your father.” He said, “By the Lord of this pulpit and this grave, I heard them from my father; by the Lord of this pulpit and this grave, I heard them from my father”—three times.’”

Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir said: Ibn Abī Uways related to me, who said: “I read in Mālik ibn Anas’s book: ‘Jaʿfar ibn Sulaymān came to see Makhramah ibn Bukayr.’ He said:

“‘Makhramah was the same age as my grandfather. He was our neighbor and my grandfather’s friend. Jaʿfar ibn Sulaymān came in to see him and asked him to take up an official post. When Jaʿfar left, he stopped by my grandfather and my father—my father was Jaʿfar’s friend—and said, “This old man must take office for us.” Then he went on.’”

Makhramah came and stood before my grandfather and my father. He said, “Munḏir, you know what is between you and this man. By God, if he does not excuse me from his post and insists that I take it, I will not speak to your father again for as long as I live.” My grandfather said to my father, “This man is mad; get me out of this.” My father went to Jaʿfar and said, “Makhramah is our neighbor, and he thought I was the one who spoke to you about him. He said such-and-such to my father, and I would like you to excuse him.” He said:

Jaʿfar laughed and said, “We have excused him.”

Ibrāhīm said: Our shaykhs related this to us.

[Sālim Abū al-Naḍr]

Muḥammad ibn Abī Zukayr related to me; Ibn Wahb informed us; Mālik related to me, who said:

“The people of earlier times liked solitude and being apart from others. Sālim Abū al-Naḍr used to do this. He would come to Rabīʿah’s gathering and sit there, and they liked that about him. When talk became abundant there—that is, when many people gathered—Abū al-Naḍr would leave them.” Mālik said: “People used to be given to solitude.”

He said: “Ibn al-Aswad, Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, the orphan of ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, was devoted to solitude, campaigning, and pilgrimage.”

[ʿUmar ibn Ḥusayn]

Yaḥyā ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bukayr related to me, who said: I heard Mālik say: “When death came to ʿUmar ibn Ḥusayn, he said, ‘For the like of this, let the workers strive.’”

Muḥammad ibn Abī Zukayr related to me; Ibn Wahb informed us; Mālik related to me, from ʿUmar ibn Ḥusayn, that he was a man of merit, chastity, sound counsel in public affairs, and devotion.

He said: “He was very unpretentious. He would go to the market carrying a garment, either to sell it or one he had bought.” He said: “The judges used to consult him.” Mālik said: “Someone who was present at his death told me that he heard him say, ‘For the like of this, let the workers strive.’”

I said to Mālik, “Do you think he said this because he had witnessed something?” He said, “Yes, in my opinion.”

Mālik was asked, “A man who completes the Qurʾān in one night?” He said, “How excellent that is! The Qurʾān is a guide to every good.”

Mālik said: “Someone who used to pray beside ʿUmar ibn Ḥusayn during Ramadan told me, ‘I would hear him begin the Qurʾān every night.’” I said to Mālik:

“Every night?” He said, “Rather, we would hear him reciting through the night until, when the next night came, he would begin at the start of the Qurʾān.” Mālik said: “He would complete it in a night and a day.”

Mālik said: “Every night, ʿUmar ibn Ḥusayn would perform the ʿishāʾ prayer, then return home. But on the night of the twenty-third, after performing the ʿishāʾ prayer, he would stand in prayer with the people, then spend the rest of the night in prayer.”

[Reports about ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr]

Muḥammad ibn Abī Zukayr related to me; Ibn Wahb informed us; Mālik related to me, from ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr: “He prayed for his father for a year.”

He said: “In winter, I would see him come to the mosque wearing a man’s cloak and a waistcloth. He would pray until the cloak fell from his back.”

He said: “During Ramadan, ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Allāh would fast continuously through the night of the seventh, the night of the seventeenth, and the night of the twenty-seventh.” I said to Mālik, “Did he fast continuously for two days and one night?” He replied, “Yes.” He said: “When Rabīʿah and others woke in the mornings after those nights, they would go to him and ask how he was and how he had awakened. He would tell them.”

He said: “His daughter had prepared almond gruel for him. He drank it and liked it, but afterward he gave it up. He said, ‘I found that it stirred up my urine.’”

He said: “It had run out for him.” He said: “He neither asked for it nor sent anyone to get it; he waited until God brought it to him. He would not interrupt his voluntary prayer for anyone who sat with him until he had finished the prayer he intended to perform. Once a man came to ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr [carrying] a letter and some dirhams. He sat with him to hand them over, but ʿĀmir prolonged his supplication. When ʿĀmir saw this, he took them from the man, put them beneath his foot or thigh, and continued with his prayer as before. When he had finished, the man said to him, ‘If you had turned to me and finished with me, then resumed your supplication…’ ʿĀmir said to him, ‘I have learned from experience that this is the devil’s final trick: a man comes to another while he is supplicating and talks to him until he interrupts what he is doing. If I had done that with you, someone else would have come’—or words to that effect. He was asked, ‘Is it recommended for a man to do this?’ He said, ‘Yes, unless someone comes to him with a small request that he can make, then leaves; or someone asks him about a matter that has arisen for him. In such cases, and the like, I think he should turn to him. But otherwise, this is not like someone who draws it out.’”

Muḥammad b. Abī Zukayr related to me: Sufyān said: “ʿĀmir b. ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr bought himself from God six times.” He also said: “For a year after my father’s death, I asked God for only one thing and asked Him for nothing else: that He forgive my father.”

Reports about Ziyād, the client of Ibn ʿAyyāsh

Muḥammad b. Abī Zukayr related to me: Ibn Wahb reported to us; Mālik related to us:

“Ziyād, the client of Ibn ʿAyyāsh, would pass by me while I was sitting. Sometimes the sound of him behind me would startle me. He would put his hand between my shoulders and say: ‘You must be cautious. If what these companions of yours say about dispensations is true, it will do no harm; but if the matter is otherwise, you will have taken precautions.’ By this he meant what Rabīʿa and Zayd b. Aslam used to say.”

Mālik said: “People helped Ziyād buy his freedom, and they hastened to do so. After the amount agreed upon had been paid, a great deal of money remained. Ziyād returned it to those who had helped him, in proportion to their shares. He kept their names with him and continued to pray for them until he died.”

He said: “Ziyād was a man who kept apart. Almost no one would sit with him; he would always withdraw by himself after the afternoon prayer and after the dawn prayer.”

Mālik related to me that Ziyād, the client of Ibn ʿAyyāsh, came to ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz when he was caliph. I said to Mālik: “Was Ziyād still enslaved then?” He said: “Yes.” ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz offered to buy him with funds from the public treasury and set him free, but Ziyād refused. Mālik said:

Mālik said: “I do not know why Ziyād, the client of Ibn ʿAyyāsh, left that offer.”

[ʿArāk b. Mālik]

Saʿīd b. Anas related to me: Ḍamrah related to us, from Rajāʾ b. Abī Salamah, who said:

ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: “I know no one who prays more than ʿArāk b. Mālik. That is because he bows and prostrates every ten.”39

Ibrāhīm b. al-Mundhir related to us: Muḥammad b. Maʿn related to me; my father reported to me, from his mother, from her uncle, Maʿn b. Naḍlah, who said: “She said to me: ‘How wondrous are Mālik’s sons! Whenever I looked toward a circle in the mosque where there were elders, I saw him among the oldest of them.’”

Ibrāhīm said: Muḥammad b. Maʿn said to me: “He meant ʿArāk b. Mālik.”

Reports about Rabīʿa b. Abī ʿAbd al-Raḥmān

Yaḥyā b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Bukayr related to us: al-Layth related to me, from Yaḥyā b. Saʿīd, who said: “He said to me: ‘I have seen no one more perceptive than Rabīʿa b. Abī ʿAbd al-Raḥmān.’”

Al-Layth said: ʿUbayd Allāh b. ʿUmar said to me about Rabīʿa: “He is the one we turn to for our difficult questions, and the best of us.”

Muḥammad b. Abī Zukayr related to me: Ibn Wahb reported to us; Mālik related to me:

“Yaḥyā b. Saʿīd knew best what was due to Rabīʿa. Rabīʿa would sometimes joke with him about a point of legal opinion—and Yaḥyā b. Saʿīd heard him say this—‘This is better for you than what you acquire of this world.’”

Zayd b. Bishr related to us: Ibn Wahb reported to me; Ibn Zayd related to me, who said: “Rabīʿa b. Abī ʿAbd al-Raḥmān spent a long time as a devout worshipper, praying night and day. He was devoted to worship. Then he turned to sitting with people, and sat with al-Qāsim, speaking with sound judgment and intelligence. When al-Qāsim was asked about something, he would say: ‘Ask this man’—meaning Rabīʿa.”

He said: “If it was something addressed in God’s Book, al-Qāsim would inform them of it; or if it was in the practice of His Prophet ﷺ. Otherwise, he would say: ‘Ask this man’—meaning Rabīʿa—or Sālim. Rabīʿa attained learning, excellence, and continence. There was not a single man in Medina more generous with what he had to a friend, a friend’s son, or someone who came seeking it from him. People would ask him to travel with them, but he would refuse to accompany anyone unless that person would not take provisions along, and Rabīʿa had nothing with which to carry them.”

Muḥammad b. Abī Zukayr related to me: Ibn Wahb reported to me; Mālik related to me, from Rabīʿa, who said: “He used to say: ‘People are with their scholars like children in the laps of those who raise them.’” He said: “He meant their fathers.”

Mālik said: “When Rabīʿa b. Abī ʿAbd al-Raḥmān came before the Commander of the Faithful, Abū al-ʿAbbās, he ordered a gift for him, but Rabīʿa refused to accept it. When he refused, the caliph gave him five thousand dirhams to buy a slave girl with, but Rabīʿa refused to accept them.”

Ibn Wahb said: Mālik related to me, from Rabīʿa, who said: “When he intended to set out for Iraq, he said to me: ‘If you hear that I have related anything to them or given them a legal opinion, do not count me as anything.’” He said: “It happened as he said. When he arrived there, he stayed at home. He did not go out to them or relate anything to them until he returned.”

Ibn Wahb said: Mālik related to me that Rabīʿa said to Ibn Shihāb—when he spoke with him about a matter of knowledge: “Ibn Shihāb, you relate things to people from the Messenger of God ﷺ while I tell them my own opinion. If they wish, they can accept it, and if they wish, they can leave it. So consider what you relate to people.”

Zayd b. Bishr and ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb reported to us; Bakr b. Muḍar related to me, who said: al-Walīd b. Yazīd said to Rabīʿa: “Why have you abandoned transmitting reports?” He replied:

“Commander of the Faithful, time has grown old, and the people of contentment have become few.”

Muḥammad b. Abī Zukayr related to me: Ibn Wahb reported to us; Mālik related to me: A man informed me that he went to Rabīʿa and found him weeping. He asked: “What makes you weep?”—and was alarmed by his weeping—and said to him: “Has some calamity befallen you?” He replied: “No. But people seek legal opinions from those who have no knowledge, and a grave matter has appeared in Islam.”

He said: “I heard Mālik say: ‘We would sit with Rabīʿa and others. When a man of age and distinction arrived, they would say to him, “Here,” so that he would sit near them. Sometimes a man who was not of such age would come to Rabīʿa, and we would say to him, “Here.” Rabīʿa would not be satisfied until he seated him beside himself, as though he did that because of the man’s distinction in his eyes.’”

Ibn Wahb said: Mālik related to me, saying: “Ibn Khaldah al-Anṣārī was a judge, and Rabīʿa would sit with him among a group of scholars. Litigants would come to him to bring their disputes before him. They would say to him: ‘These litigants of yours are troubling us.’ He would say to them:

“‘Let me talk with you; when a litigant comes to me, I will turn my face toward him.’” Mālik said: “When a litigant came to him while he was with them in the gathering, he would turn his face away from them until the litigant had finished. Mālik said: ‘People were more at ease in their affairs in those days.’ Mālik said: ‘Whoever was in Rabīʿa’s gathering then, and whoever was around him!’—as though he were praising him and those who sat in his gathering.”

Abū Ṣāliḥ related to us: al-Layth related to me, from Yaḥyā b. Saʿīd, who said: “I have seen no one sounder in judgment than Rabīʿa.” Al-Layth said: “He was the one the people of Medina turned to with their difficult questions, and their leading authority in legal opinions.”

Ibn Bukayr reported to me, from al-Layth b. Saʿd, who said: Mālik b. Anas wrote:

“I was present with them in Medina and elsewhere. Their leading authorities in legal opinions at that time were Ibn Shihāb and Rabīʿa b. Abī ʿAbd al-Raḥmān.”

Saʿīd b. Anas related to me: Ḍamrah related to us, from Rajāʾ b. Abī Salamah, from Ibn ʿAwn, who said: “I sat with al-Qāsim b. Muḥammad. Anyone who did not know al-Qāsim would think that Rabīʿa was the master of the gathering, since he dominated the conversation. One day he came and said:”

“‘To me’”—I said to him, meaning Qatādah—“and al-Qāsim said: ‘It is enough for you to stop where God has stopped.’”

Ibrāhīm b. al-Mundhir related to us: Muṭarrif related to me, from the nephew of Yazīd b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Hurmuz, who said: “I saw Rabīʿa flogged, and his head and beard shaved. His beard grew back unevenly, with one side longer than the other. He was told: ‘Abū ʿUthmān, why not even it out?’ He said:

“‘No, not until I meet them before God, Mighty and Majestic.’”

Ibrāhīm related to us: Muṭarrif related to us: the nephew of Yazīd b. Hurmuz related to me, who said:

“A man came to Ibn Hurmuz to ask him about donkey urine. Ibn Hurmuz said: ‘It is impure.’

“The man said: ‘But Rabīʿa does not consider it objectionable’—or, ‘That is what I heard from Rabīʿa.’40 He replied: ‘You need not mention Rabīʿa’s faults.’ For sometimes we would discuss a question and disagree with Rabīʿa about it, then perhaps return to his opinion a year later.”

Ibrāhīm related to us: Ibn Wahb related to me: ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. Abī Salamah related to me, who said: “When I came to Iraq, the people of Iraq came to me and said: ‘Relate to us from Rabīʿa of opinion.’

“I said: ‘People of Iraq, you call him Rabīʿa of opinion! No, by God, I have seen no one more scrupulous about a practice of the Prophet than he.’”

ʿAlī said: Sufyān said: Rabīʿa b. Abī ʿAbd al-Raḥmān said: “When analogy becomes repugnant, abandon it”—that is, when it becomes objectionable.

Wakīʿ said: “Our companions said: ‘I read to Sufyān: Rabīʿa b. Abī ʿAbd al-Raḥmān said: “When analogy becomes repugnant, abandon it”—that is, when it becomes objectionable.’”

Wakīʿ said: Abū Ḥanīfah said: “Some analogical reasoning is uglier than urinating in a mosque.”

[Ibn Abī Hardah]

Muḥammad b. Abī Zukayr related to us: Ibn Wahb reported to us; Mālik related to me that Ibn Abī Hardah told him that his father was a man who fasted continuously. A small dish of pre-dawn meal would be brought to him. His wife would sometimes speak to him about it, and he would say: “O God, give me relief from her.” He said: “He meant that he wanted relief from this world”—and he meant death. He was one of the devout worshippers.

Reports about ʿAbd al-Wahhāb b. Bakht

Muḥammad b. Abī Zukayr related to us: Ibn Wahb reported to us; Mālik related to me, from ʿAbd al-Wahhāb b. Bakht, that on a journey he did not consider himself more entitled than his travelling companions to what was in his baggage. He said: “He performed the pilgrimage, the lesser pilgrimage, and military campaigns often, until he was martyred.”

Muḥammad b. Abī Zukayr related to me: Ibn Wahb reported to us; Mālik related to me, from ʿAbd al-Wahhāb b. Bakht, who said: “He had married among us in Medina and settled there. Then he set out for Iraq. When he mounted his camel at al-Siqāyah and al-Ḥarb, he turned toward his destination and said:

“‘Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the right path.’”

Mālik said: “I think he took that only from Moses, when he set out toward Midian and said, ‘Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the right path’” (Qurʾān 28:22).

“‘…the right path’” (Qurʾān 28:22). Mālik also said that ʿAbd al-Wahhāb b. Bakht passed through al-Saʿyā while intending to go on campaign. He saw spears with their iron points. He raised his hand and said: “Praise be to God, who did not make you mine.”

Zayd b. Bishr related to us: Ibn Wahb reported to me, who said: al-Layth said: Abū Hārūn al-Miskīn related to me, from ʿAbd al-Wahhāb b. Bakht, that he would outdo the people of the mosque in remembrance of God, Mighty and Majestic.

[ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Maʿmar al-Anṣārī]

Muḥammad b. Abī Zukayr related to me: Ibn Wahb reported to us [Mālik related to me, from him, saying: “He was a judge”] and he would fast continuously and relate fine reports.

Muḥammad related to us: Ibn Wahb reported to us; Mālik related to me, from ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Anṣārī. He was a righteous man who would visit the governor, speak with him about affairs, and advise him when consulted. He would not be accommodating toward him or withhold any truth when speaking to him. Mālik said: “Other people are afraid of being beaten.”

[Zayd b. Aslam]

Muḥammad b. Abī Zukayr related to me: Ibn Wahb reported to us; Mālik related to me, who said:

“I heard him asked: ‘Would you engage in disputation by analogy in the gatherings of Rabīʿa and Yaḥyā b. Saʿīd, with some people trying to outdo others?’ He said: ‘No, by God.’”

Mālik said: “As for the gathering of Zayd b. Aslam, none of this took place there, unless he himself began by mentioning something.”

Ibn Wahb said: Mālik related to me, who said: “[Zayd b. Aslam] said to Muḥammad b. ʿAjlān: ‘Go and learn how to ask questions, then come back.’” He said: “I never feared anyone as I feared Zayd b. Aslam.”

Ibn Wahb said: Mālik related to me, who said: “In this town I met men who were a hundred years old or thereabouts, relating reports that were not accepted from them; they were not authorities.” I said to Mālik: “Were such reports accepted from others who were younger than them?” He said: “Yes.”

Reports about Abū Jaʿfar the Reciter

Zayd related to us: Ibn Wahb reported to me; Ibn Zayd related to me that Abū Jaʿfar the Reciter was with his patron, Ibn ʿAyyāsh, on the frontier road. When some people came to Abū Jaʿfar, they would go to his patron and apologize to him for doing so. He said: “He will not be satisfied until our Lord and Master is satisfied with that.”

With the same chain of transmission, Ibn Zayd said: Ṣafwān used to say: “O God, my Lord, I have longed to meet You, so long for my meeting.”41

“‘…Your meeting, so love my meeting.’”

Zayd related to us, from Ibn Wahb: Ibn Zayd related to me, from Sulaymān b. Sulaymān al-ʿAṣrī, who said: “I saw Abū Jaʿfar the Reciter at the Kaʿbah. I said to him: ‘Abū Jaʿfar?’ He said: ‘Yes. Convey my greetings to my brothers, and tell them that God has placed me among the living martyrs, who are provided for. Convey my greetings to Abū Ḥāzim, and tell him that Abū Jaʿfar says to him: “Be vigilant, be vigilant, for God and His angels look upon your gathering in the evenings.”’”

Abū Ḥāzim and his reports

Saʿīd b. Manṣūr related to us: Yaʿqūb b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to us, from his father, who said:

“I heard ʿAwn b. ʿAbd Allāh say: ‘I have never seen anyone make so much of this world as this lame man does’”—meaning Abū Ḥāzim.

Saʿīd b. Manṣūr related to us: Yaʿqūb b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to us, from Abū Ḥāzim, who said: “Any deed on account of which you would dislike death—leave it. Then it will not matter to you when you die.”

Zayd b. Bishr related to us: Ibn Wahb reported to me; Ibn Zayd related to me, who said: Abū Ḥāzim said to me: “I saw us in your father’s gathering: forty learned jurists. The least of our virtues was that we would help one another with what we had. No two among us were ever seen persisting in dispute or contending over a report…”

They will never benefit either of them. Abū Ḥāzim said: “How different are the people who used to open me when I was closed from the people who close me when I am open!”

Zayd related to us; Ibn Wahb informed us; Ibn Zayd related to me, saying: A man said:

“I saw people in narrow lanes and dust, and I saw a palace with water sprinkled all around it. None of the servants, few or many, came near it. I said: ‘What prevents the people from passing along that road?’ I was told: ‘It is not theirs.’ I said: ‘Whose is it?’ They said: ‘It belongs to that man who is praying beside the palace.’ I said: ‘Who is that?’ They said: ‘Zayd ibn Aslam.’

“I said: ‘By what means was he granted that?’ They said: ‘Because people were safe from him, and he was safe from them.’”

Zayd related to me; Ibn Wahb informed me; Ibn Zayd related to me, saying: Abū Ḥāzim used to say to them: “May God not show me the day of Zayd, and may He take me before Zayd [ibn] Aslam. O God, there is no one left whom I would prefer for my own sake and my religion.” He said: Then Zayd came to him and was struck down, but he did not rise and was not among those who attended him. He said: Abū Ḥāzim used to say: “O God, You know that when I look at Zayd, looking at him reminds me of the strength to worship You. So what would it be like to meet him and converse with him?”

Zayd related to us; Ibn Wahb informed me; Ibn Zayd related to me, saying: My father had companions who sat with him, and sometimes he would send me to one of them. He said: The man would kiss my head, stroke it, and say:

“By God, your father is dearer to me than my children and my family. By God, if God were to give me the choice between taking him or taking them, I would choose for Him to take them and leave Zayd to me.”

Zayd related to us; Ibn Wahb informed me; Ibn Zayd related to me, saying: Abū Ḥāzim said:

A man came to me and said: “I saw the Prophet ﷺ—Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar come out through this door. They were asked: ‘Where are you going, Messenger of God?’ He replied: ‘We are going to Abū Ḥāzim, to take him with us.’” Then Abū Ḥāzim would say: “O God, bring it to pass, and hasten it.”

Zayd related to us; Ibn Wahb informed me; Ibn Zayd related to us that Abū Ḥāzim had related to him, saying: “By God, there were forty learned jurists in your father’s gathering, each of them a person of note. By God, the least of our qualities was sharing what we had. If a man learned something at night, he would surely set out with it in the morning; and if he learned it in the morning, he would surely bring it around in the evening.”

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr related to us; Yaʿqūb ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to us, saying: I heard Abū Ḥāzim say: “A little of this world distracts one from much of the Hereafter.” He also said: “You will find a man so concerned about another man’s worry that he is more worried about it than the one who has the worry is about his own.”

He also said: “Whatever you would like to have with you in the Hereafter, send it ahead today; and whatever you would dislike having with you in the Hereafter, leave it today.” He also said: “Leave every deed on account of which you would dislike to die; then it will not matter to you when you die”. That is because you will find a man committing sins; when he is asked, “Would you like to die?” he says, “And how could I, when I have what I have?” He is asked, “Then why do you not leave the sins you commit?” He says, “I do not want to leave them, and I do not want to die until I have left them”. He also said: “There are two things which, if you do them, will bring you the good of this world and the Hereafter. I will not prolong this for you.” He was asked: “And what are they, Abū Ḥāzim?” He said: “Do what you dislike when God loves it, and leave what you love when God dislikes it”.

Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmar related to us, saying: Sufyān said: Abū Ḥāzim said: “I preach, yet I see no place for it; I intend it only for myself”. He also said: “Conceal your good deeds; profit from concealing your bad deeds.”

Sufyān said: Abū Ḥāzim was asked, “What is your wealth?” He said:

“The best of my wealth is my trust in God, and my despair of what is in people’s hands.”

Sufyān said: Abū Ḥāzim said: “Having a righteous enemy is dearer to me than having a corrupt friend.”

Sufyān said: Abū Ḥāzim said to some people: “Being kept from supplication frightens me more than being kept from its answer”.

Sufyān said: Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik said to Abū Ḥāzim: “Abū Ḥāzim, how can one be saved from this affair?” He said: “It is simple.” He asked: “What is that?” He said:

“Take nothing except from what is lawful, and place nothing except where it is due.” He asked: “Who can manage that, Abū Ḥāzim?” He said: “The one who seeks Paradise and flees from the Fire.”

Ibn Abī ʿUmar related to us, saying: Sufyān said: One of the emirs said to Abū Ḥāzim:

“Present your need to me.” He said: “Far from it, far from it! I have presented it to the One before whom no needs are withheld. Whatever of it He gives me, I am content with; whatever of it He withholds from me, I accept.”

He said: Ibn Shihāb said: “He is my neighbor, yet I did not know this was in him”. Abū Ḥāzim said: “I said to myself: ‘If I were wealthy, he would have known me.’ Then I said to myself: ‘He will not escape me.’ I said: ‘In former times, the rulers sought out the scholars, while the scholars fled from them. Today, the scholars seek knowledge until they have gathered all of it, then they bring it to the doors of the rulers; the rulers flee from them, while the scholars seek them out.’”

Sufyān said:

Abū Ḥāzim said: “I found that the world consists of two things: one thing that is mine, and one thing that belongs to someone else. As for what is mine, even if I sought it before it was lawful to me, using the stratagems of the heavens and the earth, I could not obtain it.”

“As for what belongs to someone else, I have not obtained it in the past, nor do I hope to obtain it in what remains. My provision is kept from others just as the provision of others is kept from me. So which of these two things should I spend my life pursuing?!”

[ʿUmārah ibn Ukaymah al-Laythī]

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us, from Sufyān, from al-Zuhrī, from Ibn Ukaymah.

He said: I heard al-Ḥumaydī—or was informed about him—say: When ʿAbd al-Razzāq came to us, he related to us from Maʿmar, from al-Zuhrī, from Ibn Ukaymah, saying “from Ibn Ukaymah”.

ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Muʿādh related to us; my father related to us; Muḥammad ibn ʿUmar related to us; ʿUmar ibn Muslim ibn ʿUmārah ibn Ukaymah al-Laythī related to us, saying: I heard Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab say:

I heard Umm Salamah, the wife of the Prophet ﷺ—say: The Messenger of God ﷺ—said: “Whoever has an animal he is to slaughter, when the crescent of Dhū al-Ḥijjah appears, let him not take anything from his hair or his nails until he has offered his sacrifice.”

Abū Ṣāliḥ related to me; al-Layth related to me; Khālid ibn Yazīd related to me, from Saʿīd ibn Abī Hilāl, from ʿUmar ibn Muslim al-Jundaʿī: Ibn al-Musayyab informed me that Umm Salamah related to him from the Messenger of God ﷺ—who said: “Whoever intends to offer a sacrifice, let him not trim his nails or remove any of his hair during the first ten days of Dhū al-Ḥijjah.”

[Abū Ṣāliḥ]

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Numayr and Aḥmad ibn Ishkāb related to us; they said: related to us— Yaḥyā ibn al-Yamān related to us; al-Aʿmash related to us, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, who said: “Of this world, I wished for nothing but two white garments in which I could sit with Abū Hurayrah.”

[Saʿd ibn Ibrāhīm]

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us; Sufyān related to us; al-Zuhrī related to us, saying: I heard Abū al-Aḥwaṣ. Sufyān said: Saʿd ibn Ibrāhīm then asked: “Who is Abū al-Aḥwaṣ?”

Al-Zuhrī said: “Have you not seen that shaykh?” Al-Zuhrī began describing him, while Saʿd did not recognize him. Sufyān gave another version: Saʿd asked, “Who is Abū al-Aḥwaṣ?”—as though angry that al-Zuhrī had related from a man unknown to us—and al-Zuhrī said: “Have you not seen the shaykh who used to pray in the Rawḍah, the client of Banū Ghifār?” Al-Zuhrī began describing him to Saʿd. He said: “I never saw Saʿd affirm it.”

Abū Bakr related to us; Sufyān related to us; Misʿar related to us, saying: Saʿd ibn Ibrāhīm said: “Only trustworthy men should relate from the Messenger of God ﷺ.” Then Sufyān said: Saʿd was very strict in what he accepted, and in those who accepted from him. I was once with al-Zuhrī when Ibn Jurayj came to him and said: “Abū Bakr, I would like to read a book to you.” Al-Zuhrī said: “Saʿd has spoken to me about his two sons”—and Saʿd was there—or Sufyān sometimes said: “Saʿd ibn Saʿd”. When I left al-Zuhrī, Ibn Jurayj said: “Did you not see how afraid he is of Saʿd?”

Sufyān said: Saʿd’s two sons were with him that day. Sufyān said: When I met— Ibrāhīm ibn Saʿd, I said to him: “I saw you and a brother of yours with al-Zuhrī, and I told him what al-Zuhrī had said to Ibn Jurayj.” He said: “That brother of mine, the one who was with me, has died.”

Sufyān said: I went to al-Zuhrī one day while Saʿd was with him. I asked him, but it was as though he—

Saʿd said to him: “Answer the young man.” Saʿd was afraid that al-Zuhrī had slighted me by not answering. Al-Zuhrī said: “I shall give him his due.” He said: “Indeed.” Al-Zuhrī then wished to do so.

Reports about Mālik

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥīm related to me; ʿAlī related to us, from al-Aṣmaʿī, from Shuʿbah, who said: “I came to Medina a year after Nāfiʿ’s death, and the teaching circle belonged to Mālik.” Al-Aṣmaʿī said:

“I asked the people of Medina, and they said: ‘It belonged to Nāfiʿ, then after him to ʿUbayd Allāh, then after him to Mālik.’”

ʿAlī said: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān had related to us from al-Aṣmaʿī, from Shuʿbah. When I asked al-Aṣmaʿī about it, I said: “Did you hear it from Shuʿbah?” He said: “I do not know.”

Yaḥyā ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bukayr related to me; Ibrāhīm ibn Ṣāliḥ—who was trustworthy—related to me, from Ibn Lahīʿah, who said: Abū al-Aswad Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Nawfal came to us in a year—Ibn Bukayr said, “I think it was”—134 or thereabouts. We said to him: “Here is Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd in Iraq. Whom do they count on for legal opinions after Rabīʿah?” They said:

“A young man from Dhū Aṣbaḥ called Mālik ibn Anas”.

ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAẓīm related to me, saying: Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Qaṭṭān was asked:

“Was Mālik more retentive, or Sufyān?” He said: “Mālik. I never asked Mālik about a hadith and had him say, ‘I shall look into it.’” He said: “I used to ask Sufyān, and he would say, ‘Wait until I look into it.’”

Muḥammad ibn Abī Zakīr related to me; Ibn Wahb informed us; Mālik related to me, saying:

Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd said to me: “Write me one hundred of the finest hadiths of Ibn Shihāb.” He gave me an old sheet of parchment that had yellowed. He said: I think he had it from when he was a young man. He said: I wrote those hadiths for him until I filled it and set them out clearly for him. Mālik said:

“He was a man from whom I learned, and he did not die before he began coming to me to ask for legal opinions.”

Ibn Bukayr related to me, saying: Mālik said: “There were four students of this discipline in our town. Kathīr ibn Farqad was taken early by death; ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAṭāʾ risked his own well-being; another fell into errors”—Ibn Bukayr said, meaning al-Mājishūn—“and he said nothing about himself”.

I heard one of our shaykhs, a man of contentment, acceptance, virtue, knowledge, and the utmost reliability, relate from Ibn al-Mājishūn, ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Abī Salamah, who said:

“We used to sit with Rabīʿah. When Mālik withdrew and stayed at home, I heard that he was putting together some books. Whenever I met him, I would joke with him and say: ‘Now the field is clear for you.’”

He said: “By God, day after day his standing and reputation kept rising and rising until he became preeminent and a leader.” Then he would say: “And who was he preeminent over, and whose leader was he?”—meaning that he became preeminent among the people of Medina, the descendants of Qurashī emigrants and others, and the Anṣār.

Ibn Bukayr related to me, saying: I asked al-Darāwardī about Mālik ibn Anas’s jurisprudence.

He said: Abū Suhayl ibn Mālik informed me: “We are a people from Dhū Aṣbaḥ. Our grandfather came to Medina in modest circumstances and married a client woman of the Taymīs. He was under their protection and lived among them, so we were affiliated with them, though they have no claim upon us by way of favor or anything else.”

“”Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir related to us; Maʿn ibn ʿĪsā related to me: Mālik ibn Anas used to say: ‘Do not take knowledge from four; take it from others. Do not take it from a foolish man who openly displays his foolishness, even if he is the most prolific transmitter of people; nor from a liar who lies in people’s reports, once he has been found to do so, even if he is not suspected of lying about the Messenger of God ﷺ; nor from a man of passion who calls people to his own desire; nor from a shaykh who has virtue and devotion if he does not know what he is relating.’

“Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir said: I mentioned this report to Muṭarrif ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Yasārī”, the client of Zayd ibn Aslam, “and he said: ‘I do not know what this is, but I bear witness that I heard Mālik ibn Anas say: “I encountered in this town”—meaning Medina—“elders possessed of virtue, righteousness, and devotion, who used to relate reports; yet I never heard a single hadith from any one of them.”’ He was asked: ‘Why, Abū ʿAbd Allāh?’ He said: ‘They did not know what they were relating’”.

Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAbd Allāh said: Mālik ibn Anas ibn Abī ʿĀmir al-Aṣbaḥī.

Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir related to me, saying: Muḥammad ibn Fulayḥ said: Mālik left Rabīʿah’s teaching circle, and my father ordered me to leave with him.

Ibrāhīm related to me; Yaḥyā ibn al-Zubayr ibn ʿAbbād ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr related to me, saying: Mālik said to me: “You and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz have withdrawn.” He said:

I replied: “Yes.” He said: “You have hastened; this is not its time.” He said: Then, twenty years later, I met Mālik, and he said: “Abū Muḥammad, have you withdrawn?” I replied: “Yes.” He said: “Now is its time.” He said:

So Mālik stayed at home and withdrew.

Ibrāhīm related to us; Muṭarrif related to us, saying: Ibn Abī Ḥāzim was one of Ibn Abī Salamah’s companions and was devoted to him. He said: When he sent to Ibn Abī Salamah, he set out for Iraq. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Abī Ḥāzim said: I said to ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Abī Salamah: “You know my affection for you and my devotion to your side. I would like you to direct me to a man from whom I can learn and whom I can stay with while you are away, having left Medina.” He said to me: “I know no one I can direct you to for learning except this Aṣbaḥī, Mālik ibn Anas.” I said: “How can you direct me to him, when you know how distant we are from one another, and that this was only so before?” Ibn Abī Salamah said: “If you are staying with him only for his own sake, then no, and there is no honor in that. But if you are staying with him for your own sake, so that you may benefit from him in your religion and learn from him, then stay with him.”

Ibn Abī Ḥāzim said: When Ibn Abī Salamah departed, I bade him farewell, [and] attended the dawn prayer and prayed beside Mālik. When it grew light—and I was on his right—he looked at my face, saw me, and said: “Has your companion left?” I said: “Yes, Abū ʿAbd Allāh.” He fell silent and said no more to me.

“”Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir related to us; Maʿn related to me, from Mālik, who said: When I met Abū Jaʿfar, he said to me: ‘Mālik, who among the elders remains in Medina?’ I said: ‘Commander of the Faithful, Ibn Abī Dhiʾb, Ibn Abī Salamah, and Ibn Abī Sabrah’””.

Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir related to us; Muṭarrif related to me, from Mālik, who said: We used to visit ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd ibn Hurmuz. Some of us would speak over others, and we would talk. Rabīʿah and Ibn Abī Salamah were with us. One day we came, and we talked at length—while Dāwūd ibn Qays al-Farrāʾ sat silent and did not speak. I said to Ibn Hurmuz: “Abū Bakr, what do you think?” He said: “I do not know what they are saying but I would like to be like this man”—and he pointed to Dāwūd ibn Qays, as though his silence had pleased him.

“”Ibn al-Madīnī said: I heard Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd say: ‘Mālik’s mursal report is dearer to me than Sufyān’s mursal report’”.

“”I heard Jaʿfar ibn ʿAbd al-Wāḥid al-Hāshimī say to Aḥmad ibn Ṣāliḥ: ‘Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd said: “Al-Zuhrī’s mursal report resembles nothing.”’ Aḥmad became angry and said:

‘What does Yaḥyā know of al-Zuhrī’s scholarship? It is not as Yaḥyā said’”.

Al-Faḍl ibn Ziyād related to me, from Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, who said: Ibn Abī Dhiʾb heard that Mālik had not followed the hadith “The two parties to a sale have the option [to rescind].” He said: “He should be asked to repent, or else his neck should be struck.” Mālik had not rejected the hadith, however, but interpreted it differently. Someone said to him: “Who knows more, Mālik or Ibn Abī Dhiʾb?” He said: “Ibn Abī Dhiʾb knows more than Mālik in this matter. Ibn Abī Dhiʾb was sounder in his person, more scrupulous in piety, and more steadfast in upholding the truth before rulers than Mālik. Ibn Abī Dhiʾb once went in to Abū Jaʿfar, and he was not intimidated from telling him the truth. He said: ‘Injustice is rampant at your door—and you are Abū Jaʿfar!’”

Ḥammād ibn Khālid said: Ibn Abī Dhiʾb resembled Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab in his time. Whenever Ibn Abī Dhiʾb and Mālik were together before a ruler, Ibn Abī Dhiʾb would speak the truth, command what is right, and forbid what is wrong, while Mālik remained silent. It was only said: “Ibn— Ibn Abī Dhʾib and Saʿd ibn Ibrāhīm were men who enjoined right and forbade wrong.” He was asked, “What do you say about his hadith?” He replied, “He was reliable in his hadith, truthful, a righteous and devout man.”

Abū Yūsuf said: “Ibn Abī Dhʾib was Qurashī, while Mālik was ʿUmānī.”

Volume One

The Letter of al-Layth ibn Saʿd to Mālik ibn Anas ﵏

Abū Yūsuf related to us: Yaḥyā ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bukayr al-Makhzūmī told me:

This is the letter of al-Layth ibn Saʿd to Mālik ibn Anas.

“Peace be upon you. I praise God to you—there is no deity but Him. To proceed: May God keep us and you safe, and grant us a good outcome in this world and the next. Your letter has reached me, in which you mention the sound state of your affairs, which gladdens me. May God make that endure for you and bring it to completion by helping you give thanks to Him and by increasing His kindness to you.

You mentioned your examination of the books I sent you, your setting them in order, and your sealing them with your seal. They have reached us. May God reward you well for what you did with them: they were books that had come to us from you, and I wanted to ascertain their contents by having you examine them.

You mentioned that what I wrote to you about correcting what had reached me from you had prompted you to begin offering me advice, and you hoped it would find a place,”

“and that what had prevented you from doing so previously was only your favorable opinion of us, and that the reason was simply that I had not discussed anything of this kind with you. You also mentioned that you had heard I issue legal opinions on matters that differ from the practice followed by the people as a whole among you, and that I ought to fear for myself because those around me rely on what I have told them in my legal opinions. You said that people follow the people of Medina, to which the Emigration was made and where the Qurʾān was revealed. What you wrote to me about this was right, God willing, and had the effect on me that you wished. I do not consider anyone to whom knowledge may be ascribed more averse to anomalous legal opinions, more inclined to honor the scholars of Medina who have passed away, or more committed than I am to their legal opinions on matters on which they agreed—praise be to God, Lord of the worlds; He has no partner.

“As for what you mentioned about the Messenger of God ﷺ—residing in Medina, and the Qurʾān being revealed to him there among his Companions, and what God taught them from it, and that people consequently followed them in this: it is as you said.
