As for your mention of the words of God, Mighty and Glorious: ‘The first forerunners among the Emigrants and the Helpers, and those who followed them in goodness: God is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him, and He has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow…’ (9:100)”

“‘…beneath which rivers flow, abiding there forever. That is the great triumph’ (9:100).

“Many of those first forerunners went forth to strive in God’s path, seeking God’s good pleasure. They raised armies, and people gathered around them. They made the Book of God and the Sunna of their Prophet known among them and concealed nothing they knew from them. In every army there was a group who taught—[for God]—the Book of God and the Sunna of His Prophet, and exercised their own judgment on matters that the Qurʾān and Sunna had not explained to them. Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, and ʿUthmān, whom the Muslims had chosen for themselves, directed them in this. Those three did not neglect the Muslim armies or remain unaware of them. Rather, they wrote to them even about minor matters, to uphold the religion and guard against disagreement, by reference to the Book of God and the Sunna of His Prophet ﷺ. They left no matter explained by the Qurʾān, practiced by the Prophet ﷺ—or enjoined after his time without informing them of it.

“When a matter arose, the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ—in Egypt, Syria, and Iraq acted upon it during the time of Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, and ʿUthmān, and continued to do so until they died; they were not instructed to do otherwise. Therefore, we do not consider it permissible for the Muslim armies today to introduce a practice that their predecessors among the Companions of the Messenger of God and their Successors did not follow, now that the scholars have departed and those who remain among them are unlike those who came before.

“Moreover, the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ—disagreed after his death on many matters of legal opinion. Were I not aware that you already know them, I would write them to you. Then the Successors disagreed on matters after the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ”

“ ﷺ. Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib and his peers differed even more. Then those who came after them disagreed. I was present with them in Medina and elsewhere, and their leading authorities on legal opinion at that time were Ibn Shihāb and Rabīʿa ibn Abī ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. You know and witnessed Rabīʿa’s disagreement with some of the earlier practice, and I heard your view of it, as well as that of the people of independent judgment among the Medinans: Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd, ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, Kathīr ibn Farqad, and many others older than he. Your dislike of this led you to leave his circle.

“You and ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿAbd Allāh discussed with me some of the things we criticized Rabīʿa for in this regard. You both agreed with me about what I objected to, and disliked in him what I disliked. Yet, praise be to God, Rabīʿa had much good in him: sound judgment, eloquent speech, manifest excellence, a good way in Islam, and sincere affection for his brothers in general and for us in particular. ﵀ forgive him, and reward him with better than his deeds.

“Ibn Shihāb would often differ in his views when we met him. When one of us wrote to him, he might write back on a single matter in three different ways, despite the excellence of his judgment and knowledge; the answers contradicted one another, and he was unaware of what he had previously held on that matter. This is what makes me abandon what I objected to, and leave it aside.

“You know, from what you criticized, that I object to anyone among the Muslim armies joining the two prayers on a rainy night. The rain in Syria is far heavier than the rain in Medina—only God knows by how much.”

“No leader among them ever joined the prayers on a rainy night, though they included Abū ʿUbayda ibn al-Jarrāḥ, Khālid ibn al-Walīd, Yazīd ibn Abī Sufyān, ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, and Muʿādh ibn Jabal. We have been told that the Messenger of God ﷺ—said, ‘The most knowledgeable among them about what is lawful and unlawful is Muʿādh ibn Jabal.’ He also said, ‘On the Day of Resurrection, Muʿādh will come a bowshot ahead of the scholars.’

“Also among them were Shuraḥbīl ibn Ḥasana, Abū al-Dardāʾ, and Bilāl ibn Rabāḥ. Abū Dharr was in Egypt, as were al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwām and Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ. In Ḥimṣ were seventy men of the people of Badr. And throughout all the Muslim armies and in Iraq were Ibn Masʿūd, Ḥudhayfa ibn al-Yamān, and ʿImrān ibn al-Ḥuṣayn. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib lived there for years with the Companions of the Messenger of God who were with him, yet they never joined the Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ prayers.

“Another example is judgment on the basis of one witness’s testimony together with the oath of the claimant. You know that judgment on this basis has continued to be given in Medina, but the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ—did not give judgment on this basis in Syria, Ḥimṣ, Egypt, or Iraq. The Rightly Guided Caliphs, Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, and ʿAlī, did not write to them instructing them to do so. Then ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz was appointed, and he was as you know in reviving the Sunna, and in cutting off the hand, and in the grandfather’s…”

“in upholding the religion, soundness of judgment, and knowledge of what had previously been the people’s practice. Zurayq ibn al-Ḥakam wrote to him: ‘You used to give judgment in Medina on the basis of one witness’s testimony and the oath of the claimant.’ ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz wrote back to him: ‘We used to give judgment on that basis in Medina, but found the people of Syria following a different practice. So we give judgment only on the testimony of two upright men, or of one man and two women.’ He never joined the Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ prayers on a rainy night, even when rain poured down upon him at his residence in Khunāṣira.

“Another example is that the people of Medina rule, in the case of women’s dowries, that whenever a woman wishes to claim her deferred dowry, she may do so, and it must be paid to her. The people of Iraq agreed with the people of Medina on this, as did the people of Syria and Egypt. None of the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ—or those who came after them gave a woman judgment for her dowry unless death or divorce separated the couple, whereupon she could assert her right.

“Another example is their view of a man who swears to abstain from his wife: divorce does not take effect against him until he is summoned to return, even if four months have passed. Nāfiʿ told me, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar—and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar is the one from whom that ruling, requiring the man to be summoned after the months have passed, was transmitted—that he used to say about the abstention mentioned by God in His Book: ‘When the term has been reached, it is not lawful for the man who has sworn abstention except to return to his wife, as God commanded him, or to resolve upon divorce.’

“You say that if he remains beyond the four months specified in God’s Book and is not summoned, no divorce takes effect against him. We have been told that ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, Zayd ibn Thābit, Qabīṣa ibn Dhuʾayb, and Abū Salama ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf said of such abstention: ‘When the four months have passed, it is a second divorce.’ Saʿīd ibn…”

“al-Musayyib, Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Hishām, and Ibn Shihāb said: ‘When the four months have passed, it is a divorce, and he may take her back during the waiting period.’

“Another example: Zayd ibn Thābit used to say that when a man gives his wife the choice, and she chooses her husband, it is one divorce; and if she divorces herself three times, it is one divorce. ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān gave judgment according to this, and Rabīʿa ibn Abī ʿAbd al-Raḥmān used to say it. People had almost come to agree that if she chose her husband, no divorce had occurred; if she chose herself once or twice, he could take her back; and if she divorced herself three times, she was irrevocably separated from him and could not be lawful for him again until she married another husband, who consummated the marriage with her, and then died or divorced her—unless he took back his words in the same sitting and said, ‘I gave you the choice of one divorce only.’ In that case, he would be required to swear an oath, and he and his wife would be left together.

“Another example: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd used to say: ‘If a man marries a slave woman and then her husband buys her, his purchase of her counts as three divorces.’ Rabīʿa used to say the same. And if a free woman married a slave and bought him, the same applied.

“We have heard of some legal opinions of yours that are objectionable. I had written to you about some of them, but you did not answer me in your letter. I feared you had found this burdensome, so I stopped writing to you about matters I objected to and about those on which I had challenged your opinion.

“One such matter is that I heard you instructed Zufar ibn ʿĀṣim al-Hilālī, when he wished to pray for rain, to perform the prayer before the sermon. I found this astonishing, because the sermon and the prayer for rain are like those on Friday, except that when the imām is nearing the end of his sermon, he turns to face the qibla and supplicates, turns his cloak inside out, then comes down and prays. [And] ʿUmar ibn…”

“ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, Abū Bakr ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr ibn Ḥazm, and others prayed for rain. All of them put the sermon and supplication before the prayer. Zufar ibn ʿĀṣim was the first person to do this, and people disapproved of it.

“Another example: I heard that you say of two partners who jointly own property that no alms are due from them until each of them individually owns the amount on which alms become due. But ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb’s letter states that alms are due from them both, and that they should settle the difference equally. This was practiced during the governorship before yours of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz and others. The one who told us of this was Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd. He was no lesser than the outstanding scholars of his time. ﵀ forgive him, and make Paradise his abode.

“Another example: I heard that you say that if a man becomes insolvent after another man has sold him a commodity, and the seller has collected part of its price or the buyer has spent part of it, the seller may take back whatever of his goods he finds. But people held that if the seller has collected any of its price, or the buyer has spent any part of it, it is no longer the same commodity.

“Another example: you say that the Prophet ﷺ—gave al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwām compensation for only one horse. Everyone relates that he gave him four shares for two horses and denied him a share for the third horse. The whole community follows this hadith—the people of Syria, Egypt, Iraq, and Ifrīqiya—and no two people disagree about it. It was not fitting for you—even if you had heard it from a reliable man—to oppose the entire community.

“I have left aside many other matters like this. I wish God would grant you success and prolong your life, because I hope people will benefit from it, and I fear the loss that would come if a ruler were gone, along with the comfort I take in your presence, even though our lands are far apart. This is your standing with me and my opinion of you; be certain of it. Do not stop writing to me with news of yourself, your circumstances, your son and your family, or any need of yours or of anyone who can reach you through you. That would make me glad.

“I wrote to you while we are well and in good health, praise be to God. We ask God to grant us and you gratitude for what He has bestowed upon us, and to complete the blessings He has given us. Peace be upon you and God’s mercy.

Volume One

Mālik’s Letter

In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful. Abū Yūsuf related to us; Yaḥyā ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bukayr related to us, saying: This is the letter of Mālik ibn Anas to al-Layth ibn Saʿd:

“Peace be upon you. I praise God to you—there is no deity but Him. To proceed: May God preserve us and you through obedience to Him, in private and in public, and keep us and you safe from everything unwelcome.

“I wrote to you while those with me—children and family—are in the state you would wish, and God is praised.

“Your letter came to me, in which you speak of your circumstances and the blessings God has bestowed upon you, at which I rejoice. I ask God to let the good He has bestowed upon us and you endure, and to make us grateful to Him. I understood what you said about books you had sent for me to review and return to you. I have done so, and made changes to them until they were in order as you wished. I sealed each of their bundles with my seal, whose inscription reads: ‘God is sufficient for me, and He is the best guardian.’

“I was glad to look after you and meet your needs, as you deserve. I put myself out for you at times when I would not otherwise have gone out, because the pilgrimage was underway, so you would receive what had come to me…”

“with it, where I delivered it to him. In this I did what I considered incumbent upon me on account of your rights and your standing. What I learned from my side of this matter prompted me to begin offering you advice, and I hoped it would find a place with you. Before today, the only reason I had not done this was that my opinion of you had always been favorable, but you had never discussed any of this matter with me or written to me about it.

“Know—may God have mercy on you—that I have heard you issue legal opinions on matters contrary to the practice followed by the people as a whole among us, in the land where we are. Given your integrity, merit, standing among the people of your land, the people there’s need for you, and their reliance on what comes from you, you have good reason to fear for yourself and to follow what you hope will bring you salvation. For God, Mighty and Glorious, says in His Book: ‘The first forerunners among the Emigrants and the Helpers, and those who followed them in goodness: God is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him, and He has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding there forever. That is the great triumph’ (9:100).

“God, Mighty and Glorious, also says: ‘Those who listen to the word and follow the best of it: they are the ones God has guided, and they are people of understanding’ (39:18).

“People follow the people of Medina: the Emigration was made to it, the Qurʾān was revealed there, and what is lawful was permitted and what is unlawful was forbidden there, while the Messenger of God ﷺ—was among them. They witnessed the revelation and its descent; he commanded them and they obeyed him, and he made things clear to them and they followed him, until God took him to Himself and chose for him what is with Him. May blessings and peace be upon him…”

“with it, where I delivered it to him. In this I did what I considered incumbent upon me on account of your rights and your standing. What I learned from my side of this matter prompted me to begin offering you advice, and I hoped it would find a place with you. Before today, the only reason I had not done this was that my opinion of you had always been favorable, but you had never discussed any of this matter with me or written to me about it.

“Know—may God have mercy on you—that I have heard you issue legal opinions on matters contrary to the practice followed by the people as a whole among us, in the land where we are. Given your integrity, merit, standing among the people of your land, the people there’s need for you, and their reliance on what comes from you, you have good reason to fear for yourself and to follow what you hope will bring you salvation. For God, Mighty and Glorious, says in His Book: ‘The first forerunners among the Emigrants and the Helpers, and those who followed them in goodness: God is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him, and He has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding there forever. That is the great triumph’ (9:100).

“God, Mighty and Glorious, also says: ‘Those who listen to the word and follow the best of it: they are the ones God has guided, and they are people of understanding’ (39:18).

“People follow the people of Medina: the Emigration was made to it, the Qurʾān was revealed there, and what is lawful was permitted and what is unlawful was forbidden there, while the Messenger of God ﷺ—was among them. They witnessed the revelation and its descent; he commanded them and they obeyed him, and he made things clear to them and they followed him, until God took him to Himself and chose for him what is with Him. May blessings and peace be upon him…” upon him, and His mercy and blessings. Then those who came after him, the people of his community who followed him most closely, took their place. Whenever something befell them about which they had knowledge, they carried it out; whatever they did not know, they asked about. Then they adopted, in their independent judgment and because their time was so near to his, the strongest view they found on the matter. If someone opposed them, or a man stated another view that was stronger and more fitting, his view was set aside and the other view was acted upon.

Then the Successors after them followed that path and adhered to those practices. When a matter was established and acted upon in Medina, I saw no one opposing it, because they possessed that inherited tradition, which cannot rightly be appropriated or claimed falsely. Even if all the people of the provincial centers were to say, “This is the practice in our town, and it is what those who came before us followed,” they would have no sound basis for that claim, and would have no right to it as the people of Medina did.

So consider, may God have mercy on you, what I have written to you for your own good. Know that I hope nothing prompted me to write to you but sincere counsel for God alone, concern for you, and care for your well-being. Give my letter the consideration it deserves from you. If you do so, you will know that I spared no effort in advising you. May God grant us and you success in obeying Him and His Messenger in every matter and in every circumstance. Peace be upon you, and the mercy of God.

Written on Sunday, seven days having passed of Ṣafar.

[ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿUmar]

Yaḥyā ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bukayr related to us: al-Layth ibn Saʿd said: “When Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd was taken from Medina to Abū al-ʿAbbās, I wrote to ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar to ask him.”

He said: “ʿUbayd Allāh wrote back to me: ‘You have written to ask me about something beyond the reach of my judgment and beyond what my understanding can encompass.’” He said: “So I stopped asking him about it.”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us: Sufyān said: “I saw ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿUmar and Mālik ibn Anas come to al-Zuhrī in Mecca and speak with him. He said, ‘I intend to go to Medina, and my route passes by the two of you. Come to me in Medina, God willing.’” Sufyān said: “ʿUbayd Allāh was the one who spoke, and Mālik was with him. The two of them had heard nothing from him in Mecca.”

Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir related to us: Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah related to us: “ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿUmar said to us”—we had come to him seeking ḥadīth from him—“You have scattered ḥadīth about and taken away its light. If ʿUmar saw you and me, he would beat us with the whip.”

Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā related to us: Sufyān related to us: “Muḥammad ibn ʿAjlān was trustworthy, reliable, and knowledgeable in ḥadīth.”

Saʿīd ibn Asad related to me: Ḍamrah related to us: Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, the nephew of Ruzayq ibn Ḥakīm al-Aylī, said: “Rabīʿah, Abū al-Zinād, Ṣafwān ibn Sulaym, Zayd ibn Aslam, and Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir passed by us, along with elders from among the people of Medina. Al-Walīd ibn Yazīd sent for them to ask them about an oath he had sworn.”

Saʿīd related to me: Ḍamrah related to us: Thābit ibn Kathīr al-Aylī said: “The first time I became acquainted with Abū Ḥāzim, I saw Rajāʾ ibn Ḥaywah rise to him. I said, ‘Who is this man to whom Rajāʾ ibn Ḥaywah rose—’”

“—and then sat beside him?” They said, “This is Abū Ḥāzim.”

Saʿīd related to us; Ḍamrah related to us; ʿUmar ibn Saʿīd al-Aylī related to us: I heard Ḥusayn ibn Rustum say: “This community has drawn near to its end, its first joined to its last, and the call to depart has been given among them.”

Report about Ibn Samʿān, Yazīd ibn ʿIyāḍ, and other liars

“ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿImrān related to us; Abū Zayd ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd ibn al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah related to us; Ibn al-Qāsim related to me: He said: I asked Mālik about Ibn Samʿān.

“He said, ‘A liar.’ I asked, ‘And Yazīd ibn ʿIyāḍ?’ He said, ‘Even more of a liar, and still more of a liar.’”

“Ibn Bukayr related to us; Ibn Wahb related to me; Mālik related to me: ‘I visited ʿĀʾishah, daughter of Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, and asked her about some ḥadīth, but I was not satisfied to take anything from her because of her weakness.

“Mālik said: ‘I met many men, some of whom had met the Companions, but I did not ask them about anything.’” It was as though he considered them unreliable.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ibrāhīm related to us. He said: I heard al-Muʾammal ibn Ismāʿīl say:

“I heard Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Qaṭṭān say: ‘I testify that Ibrāhīm ibn Abī Yaḥyā—’”

“—was a liar.”

He said: “I heard Ḥammād ibn Ḥafṣ say: ‘I was present when Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd was visited by an elder from among the people of Baṣra, and they discussed ḥadīth. The elder said to Yaḥyā, “Ibn Abī Rawwād related to us such-and-such.” Yaḥyā said, “Recognize him as a liar.”’

“After a while, he asked, ‘Was it the father or the son who related it to you?’ He said, ‘The father, rather.’ Yaḥyā said, ‘The father is unobjectionable. I only thought you meant the son.’”

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ibrāhīm related to us: Khālid ibn Yazīd al-Azraq related to us, having heard Muḥammad ibn Saʿīd say: “I hear a fine saying, and see no harm in giving it a chain of transmission.”

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmmār al-Mawṣilī related to us: al-Qāsim related to us, from Isrāʾīl, from ʿAmr ibn Khālid, the client of ʿAqīl ibn Abī Ṭālib. Muḥammad ibn ʿAmmār said: “I asked Wakīʿ about him. He said: ‘He was a liar. When we recognized his lying, he moved to another place. He related’”—that is, he claimed to relate—“from Ḥabīb ibn Abī Thābit, from ʿĀṣim ibn Ḍamrah, from ʿAlī, that ʿAlī led them in prayer while not in a state of purity, then repeated the prayer and ordered them to repeat it.”

Muḥammad related to us; ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī related to us, from Sufyān al-Thawrī, who said:

“I heard him say: ‘Ḥabīb ibn Abī Thābit never narrated anything at all from ʿĀṣim ibn Ḍamrah.’”

“Al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Walīd ibn Ṣubḥ related to us; Yaḥyā ibn Ṣāliḥ related to us; ʿUfayr ibn Maʿdān al-Kalāʿī related to us: ‘ʿUmar ibn Mūsā came to Ḥimṣ. We gathered around him in the mosque, and he kept saying, “Your righteous elder related to us; your righteous elder related to us.”

“When he had said it many times, I asked, ‘Who is this righteous elder of ours? Name him for us so that we may know him.’ He said:

“‘Khālid ibn Maʿdān.’ I asked him, ‘In what year did you meet him?’ He said, ‘I met him in the year 108.’ I asked, ‘And where did you meet him?’ He said, ‘I met him on the campaign in Armenia.’ I said to him—”

“Fear God, elder, and do not lie. Khālid ibn Maʿdān died in the year 104, yet you claim to have met him four years after his death. And I will tell you another thing: he never campaigned in Armenia. He used to campaign against the Byzantines.”

Al-ʿAbbās related to us; Ibn Mushhir related to us; ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Wāḥid related to us: “I said to Mālik ibn Anas, ‘Abū ʿAbd Allāh, do you know Samʿān?’ He said, ‘Yes, I know him. He was a liar.’”

[Al-Walīd ibn Kathīr]

Aḥmad ibn al-Khalīl related to me; Isḥāq ibn Ibrāhīm related to us; ʿĪsā ibn Yūnus related to us: al-Walīd ibn Kathīr related to us; he was considered reliable in ḥadīth.

[ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ]

Aḥmad ibn al-Khalīl related to me; Yaḥyā ibn Abī Bukayr related to us; Ayyūb ibn Thābit related to us: “I saw ʿAṭāʾ; he had a withered limb and was humpbacked.”

Al-Faḍl ibn Ziyād related to us: “I heard Abū ʿAbd Allāh say: ‘Knowledge is a treasure store, and God apportions it to whomever He loves. If He were to single anyone out for knowledge, the Prophet’s household would have the strongest claim to it. ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ—whose father’s name was Aslam—was an Abyssinian; Yazīd ibn Abī Ḥabīb was a black Nubian; al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī was a client of the Anṣār; and Ibn Sīrīn was a client of the Anṣār.’”

Aḥmad related to us; ʿAbd al-Ṣamad related to us; Sallām related to us: “I heard Qatādah say: ‘The most knowledgeable of people about what is lawful and unlawful is al-Ḥasan; the most knowledgeable of them about the rites of pilgrimage is ʿAṭāʾ ibn—’”

“—Abī Rabāḥ; and the most knowledgeable of them in Qurʾānic exegesis is ʿIkrimah.”

Salamah ibn Shabīb related to us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ibrāhīm ibn ʿUmar ibn Kaysān related to us; my father informed me: “I remember that, in the time of the Umayyads, they would appoint someone to call out among the pilgrims: ‘Let no one give people legal opinions except ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ—and if ʿAṭāʾ is not there, then ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Najīḥ.’”

Salamah related to us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ibrāhīm related to us; my uncle Wahb ibn ʿUmar related to me. He said:

“I remember a cushion being laid out for Ibn Abī Najīḥ in the Sacred Mosque, where he would give people legal opinions. That was an order from the governor.”

Yūsuf ibn Muḥammad al-Makkī related to us: “Our companions related to us that the muftī of Mecca after ʿAṭāʾ was Ibn Abī Najīḥ.” Yūsuf said: “He was the most learned in jurisprudence among our companions in his time. Ibn Jurayj’s practical knowledge of jurisprudence did not match the extent of his books.”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us; ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Abī Ḥāzim related to us: “I heard my father say: ‘I met no one more knowledgeable about the pilgrimage than ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ.’”

Abū Saʿīd ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ibrāhīm related to me; Abū Masʿūd related to us. He said:

“I heard al-Awzāʿī say: ‘When ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ died, he was, at the time of his death, the person most pleasing to the people on earth; yet most of them did not make their way to him.’”

Abū Nuʿaym related to us; Sufyān related to us, from Salamah ibn Kuhayl, who said: “I saw no one who sought God’s pleasure through this knowledge except these three: ʿAṭāʾ, Ṭāwūs, and Mujāhid.”

Qabīṣah ibn ʿUqbah related to us; Sufyān related to us, from Aslam al-Minqārī, from Abū Jaʿfar, who said: “No one more knowledgeable about the pilgrimage than ʿAṭāʾ remains.”

Qabīṣah related to us; Sufyān related to us, from ʿUmar ibn Saʿīd, from his mother, who said: “Ibn ʿUmar came to Mecca and people asked him questions. He said, ‘People of Mecca, are you gathering questions for me when Ibn Abī Rabāḥ is among you?’”

Qabīṣah related to us; Sufyān related to us, from Aslam al-Minqārī, who said: “A Bedouin came and asked a question. They pointed him toward Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, but the Bedouin kept asking, ‘Where is Abū Muḥammad?’ Saʿīd said to him, ‘We have nothing to offer here when ʿAṭāʾ is present.’”

Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā related to us, from Sufyān, who said: “Ibn Abī Najīḥ used to give people legal opinions.”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us; Sufyān related to us: “Ibn Abī Najīḥ and Ibn Shubrumah met at the court of one of the governors. He asked them about a legal question. Ibn Abī Najīḥ gave his view on it, and Ibn Shubrumah gave his. Ibn Shubrumah said to Ibn Abī Najīḥ:

“‘Lead with your view, Abū Bashshār.’ Ibn Abī Najīḥ replied, ‘I neither lead nor drive.’”

Salamah related to us; Aḥmad related to us; ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: “After ʿAṭāʾ had grown old and weak, he would stand for prayer and recite two hundred verses from Sūrat al-Baqarah while standing. He would not sway or move.”

[ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Najīḥ]

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Qāsim ibn Abī Burdah related to me. He said:

“I heard my grandmother, my father’s mother, Umm Yaʿlā, daughter of Muṭahhar ibn ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bādhān, say:”

“I heard my father, Muṭahhar ibn ʿAlī, say to my mother, Qasamah, daughter of Yaʿlā ibn Mūsā ibn Bādhān—who was the paternal cousin of ʿUthmān ibn al-Aswad ibn Mūsā ibn Bādhān—: ‘I saw ʿAmr ibn Dīnār with ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Najīḥ. I met him and said, “Abū ʿAmr, have you joined the Shīʿah?” He said to me, “No, by God.” I said to him, “Did I not see you with Ibn Abī Najīḥ?” He said, “Yes. He and I were discussing something, but I no longer sit with him.” Then he said, “My father said: By God, ʿAmr was far removed from the Qadarī position”—meaning ʿAmr—“for he had been a friend of Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī.”’”

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad related to me; my father informed me: “Abū Barzah—whose name was Ibn Bashshār”—my father said, “Some of our people have said: ‘He was Bashshār, the client of ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Sāʾib ibn Ṣayfī ibn [Abī] Rifāʿah al-Makhzūmī. His son Nāfiʿ ibn Abī Barzah was the client of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Surāqah ibn Mālik ibn Juʿshum ibn Marāḥ ibn Murrah ibn ʿAbd Manāf ibn Kinānah. He bought him from Fāṭimah, daughter of ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Sāʾib, and freed him during the pilgrimage. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān went to Egypt, where the dwellings of Banū Mudlij were.’” Aḥmad said: “ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Sāʾib had freed Abū Barzah before he sold Nāfiʿ. Aḥmad said:

“‘Bādhān’s clientage belonged among Banū Jumah.’ He said: ‘The mother of ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Qāsim was Fāṭimah, daughter of Abī Najīḥ. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Najīḥ,’ ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Qāsim said, ‘was a client of Thaqīf, and lived at al-Ṣafā. My grandfather, ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Qāsim, inherited his mother’s share of her father Abū Najīḥ’s estate, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Najīḥ gave him his remaining share. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Najīḥ died leaving only young children, who later died. His dwelling thus passed to ʿAbd Allāh and Nāfiʿ, the sons of—’”

“—al-Qāsim ibn Nāfiʿ, his sister’s sons. They were under the guardianship of ʿUthmān ibn al-Aswad as orphans in the care of al-Qāsim.”

Reports about Ṭāwūs

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr related to us; Sufyān related to us, from Ibrāhīm ibn Maysarah, who said: “I saw no one for whom noble and lowly people were of equal standing except Ṭāwūs.”

Muḥammad al-Makkī related to us; ʿAbd Allāh informed us, from Maʿmar, whom al-Zuhrī informed: Ṭāwūs related to us that Ibn ʿUmar used to rule that if a woman menstruated after having performed the visitation, she need not depart until her final encounter was with the House. I heard him say—one or two years before he died, when he was asked about this—“As for women, they have been granted a dispensation.”

Al-Zuhrī said: “I told Sālim about it. He said, ‘We did not know that.’”

Al-Zuhrī said: “Had I seen Ṭāwūs, I would have known that he was not lying.”

Muḥammad ibn Abī Zakīr related to us; Ibn Wahb informed us, who said: Mālik said: “I was told that Ṭāwūs appointed a collector and was given dinars for expenses so that he could prepare for his departure. It was customary to give those sent out to collect alms what they needed to equip themselves. Ṭāwūs took the money and put it in a niche of his, then went out and distributed everything he collected there, without keeping anything for himself. When he returned, they asked him what he had brought back. He said, ‘I distributed it among them.’ It seems they disapproved of what he had done, and said to him, ‘Return to us the dinars we gave you—’”

“He said, ‘They are in the niche; I took none of them.’ They found them and took them.”

Qabīṣah related to us; Sufyān related to us, from Layth, from Ṭāwūs, who said: “Learn what you learn for your own sake, for people have lost their trustworthiness.” He said: “How carefully he used to count out the ḥadīth, letter by letter!”

Abū ʿUmayr ʿĪsā ibn Muḥammad al-Ramlī related to us; Ḍamrah related to us, from Ibn Shawdhab, who said: “I attended Ṭāwūs’s funeral in Mecca in the year 106, and heard them say:

“‘May God have mercy on you, Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. You performed forty pilgrimages.’”

Qabīṣah related to us; Sufyān related to us, from Ḥabīb ibn Abī Thābit, who said: “Ṭāwūs said to me, ‘When I have related a ḥadīth to you and established it for you, do not ask anyone else about it.’”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us. He said: “Sufyān was told, ‘ʿAbd al-Razzāq relates from you, from ʿAmr, from Ṭāwūs, that he said, “When I relate something to you, seal it.”’ Sufyān said:

“‘This does not sound like Ṭāwūs’s way of speaking.’”

ʿAmr related to us: “Ṭāwūs said to me, ‘When I relate something to you, hold fast to it with both hands.’”

Abū Bakr related to us; Sufyān related to us; ʿAmr related to us, who said: “I saw no one more scrupulous about what was in other people’s hands than Ṭāwūs.”

Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā related to me; Sufyān related to us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, who said: “Ṭāwūs said: ‘I saw the Prophet ﷺ at the door of the Kaʿbah, while I was inside the Kaʿbah. He said:

“‘Uncover your face and make your recitation clear.’” He said: “Ṭāwūs said, ‘Leave this, this—’”

“A dream.” He said: “It seemed to us that he had become more expansive in his speech, though he would very often veil his face.”

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Sufyān related to us, from Muḥammad ibn Saʿīd—or Saʿīd ibn Muḥammad; Abū Nuʿaym said, “That is how he said it”—who said: Among Ṭāwūs’s supplications was: “O God, keep wealth and children from me, and grant me faith and righteous action.”

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Sufyān related to us, from Abū Umayya, from Dāwūd ibn Sābūr, who said: Ṭāwūs was asked, “Supplicate for us with some supplications.” He said: “I find no reverent fear in my heart just now.”

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān related to us: ʿAbd Allāh related to us; Wuhayb ibn al-Ward informed us: Dāwūd ibn Sābūr related to me, saying: We said to Ṭāwūs—or Ṭāwūs was asked—“Supplicate for us with some supplications.” He said: “I find no expectation of reward in that.”

Salama related to me: Aḥmad related to us: ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us; Maʿmar informed us, saying: I heard Ayyūb say to al-Layth: “Consider what you have heard from these two men and hold fast to it”—meaning Ṭāwūs and Mujāhid.

Salama related to us, from Aḥmad: ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us, from his father, who said: Wahb said: “There will continue to be forbearance in Ṣanʿāʾ as long as Simāk ibn al-Faḍl is there.”

Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Malik related to us: ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us, saying: I heard al-Nuʿmān ibn— Al-Zubayr related that Muḥammad ibn Yūsuf—or Ayyūb ibn Yaḥyā—sent Ṭāwūs five hundred dinars and told the messenger: “If he accepts them from you, the governor will clothe you and treat you well.” The messenger set out with them and came to al-Jund, where Ṭāwūs was. He said: “Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, this is an allowance the governor has sent you.” Ṭāwūs said: “I have no need of it.” The messenger tried to get him to take it, but he refused. Ṭāwūs was distracted, so the messenger threw the money into a niche in the house and then left. He told them: “He accepted it.” They waited a while, then word reached them of something Ṭāwūs had done that displeased them. He said: “Send to him and have him send our money back to us.”

The messenger came to Ṭāwūs and said: “The money the governor sent you.” Ṭāwūs said: “I accepted none of it.” The messenger returned and told them, and they realized that Ṭāwūs was telling the truth. It was said: “[Look for] the man who took it there and send him to him.” [He came to him] and said: “The money I brought you, Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān?” Ṭāwūs said: “Did I accept anything from you?” He said: “No.” Ṭāwūs said: “Do you know where you put it?” He said: “Yes, in that niche.” Ṭāwūs said: “Then look for it where you put it.” The man reached in, and there it was, in al-Baṣra, with a spider’s web grown over it. He said:

“He took it and went with it to them.”

ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī said: Among the companions of Ibn ʿAbbās, Sufyān did not consider anyone equal to Ṭāwūs.

Anyone.

Salama related to us, from Aḥmad: ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us; my father informed me, saying: Ṭāwūs was praying on a cold, dark morning when Muḥammad ibn Yūsuf, the brother of al-Ḥajjāj—or Ayyūb ibn Yaḥyā—passed by in his retinue while Ṭāwūs was prostrating. He ordered that a sāǧ—or a ṭaylasān—be placed over him. Ṭāwūs did not raise his head until he had finished what he was doing. When he had said the salutation, he looked and saw the sāǧ on him, so he shook it off [and cast it away] without looking at it, then went on to his house.

Salama related to us: Aḥmad related to us: ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us, from Maʿmar, who said: Ṭāwūs stayed with a sick companion of his until he missed the pilgrimage. Another time he said: “with a man.”

Salama related to us, from Aḥmad: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī related to us: Ḥammād ibn Zayd related to us, from Saʿīd ibn Abī Ṣadaqa, who said: I heard Qays ibn Saʿd say: “Ṭāwūs among us was like Ibn Sīrīn among you.”

Abū Bishr related to us: al-Muʿtamir related to us, from Hishām, from Qays ibn Saʿd, who said: “I do not consider any of my companions superior to him”—meaning Ṭāwūs.

Reports about ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṭāwūs

Salama related to us, from Aḥmad: ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĪsā ibn Jubayr Raysān informed us, saying: I asked ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṭāwūs: “What people are you from? I have heard that your lineage goes back to Hamdān.” He said: “No, rather, it goes back to Khawlān.”

ʿAbd al-Razzāq said, from Maʿmar, who said: Ibn Ṭāwūs was told, concerning his father’s debt: “You should secure the creditors’ claims.” He said: “Should I secure their claims while Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān is detained in his house?” He said: “So he sold property worth one thousand five hundred.”

He was detained. He said: “So he sold property worth one thousand five hundred.”

Salama related to us, from Aḥmad: ʿAbd al-Razzāq ibn Hammām ibn Nāfiʿ related to us, from Maʿmar, who said: Ayyūb said: “If you are going to travel to anyone, then go to Ibn Ṭāwūs.”

Salama related to us: Aḥmad related to us: ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us, from Nuʿmān, who said: “I have never seen the son of a jurist like Ibn Ṭāwūs.” I said: “What about Hishām ibn ʿUrwa?” He said:

“How excellent he was! But he was not his equal.”

Salama related to me, from Aḥmad: ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Dhimārī related to us, saying: Ṭāwūs ibn Kaysān used to live in al-Jund. He said: Hishām ibn Yūsuf informed me; the son of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṭāwūs informed me that he said: “We are a people from Persia, and no one holds a bond of clientage over us—except that Kaysān’s clientage belonged to the family of Hūd al-Ḥimyarī, and so it belongs to Ṭāwūs’s mother.”

Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Malik related to me: ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us; Maʿmar informed us, saying: Ayyūb said to me: “If you are going to travel to anyone, travel to Ibn Ṭāwūs; otherwise, stick to your trade.”

Abū Bishr related to me: al-Muʿtamir related to us, from Hishām, from Qays ibn Saʿd, who said:

“I do not consider any of my companions superior to him”—meaning Ṭāwūs.

He said: Ibn al-Madīnī said: “Among the sons, there is no one like Ibn Ṭāwūs.”

Sufyān said to us: Ibn Jurayj used to unsettle us, saying: “When he comes to you, you will find that our shaykh is a rough man.” He said: So he came to us, and I went to him while he was sitting with Ibrāhīm ibn Maysara, and I began asking him questions. He said: “What is this?” Ibrāhīm ibn Maysara said to him:

“This man will be harder on you than Yūsuf ibn ʿImrān; he will stick with you.” He said: I followed him to Minā. He alighted at Qarn al-Thaʿālib and pitched his ropes. I marked his location by a rock on the mountain, then went to him early the next morning. Sufyān ibn Saʿīd was with him, having asked him about the report of Abū Dharr and ʿUthmān—a lengthy story that had occurred42 He had not retained it accurately. Sufyān said: “Repeat it to me.” He said: “By God, I will never repeat it.”

Salama related to us: Aḥmad related to us: ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us, from Umayya ibn Shibl, who said: Ibn Ṭāwūs came to us and sat down. Someone said to him: “Will you not relate something to us?” He said:

“If you ask me about something, I will mention it; otherwise, I will give it to you as a gift.”

Reports about Mujāhid ibn Jabr

Ibn Numayr related to us: Yūnus ibn Bukayr related to us, from al-Aʿmash, who said: Mujāhid took part in the battle of al-Jamājim. They asked him about it, and he said: “43 I stayed away from it for the sake of good.”

Ibn Numayr related to us: My father related to us: al-Aʿmash related to us, saying: When I saw Mujāhid, I would think he was a kharbandaj who had lost his donkey and was worried.

Abū Bakr ibn Abī Shayba related to us: Abū Usāma related to us: al-Aʿmash related to us, saying:

“When I saw Mujāhid, I thought little of him: he was shabby, and looked—as I recall—as though he were a kharbandaj. But when an Arab man spoke…”

Abū Saʿīd ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿīd al-Ashajj related to me: ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ajlāḥ al-Kindī related to us, from his father, from Mujāhid, who said: “We pursued this knowledge without having any intention for it; then afterward God granted us the intention.”

He said: Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī said: “Mujāhid ibn Jabr was the client of Qays ibn al-Sāʾib al-Makhzūmī.”

Saʿīd ibn Asad related to me: Ḍamra ibn Rabīʿa related to us: Rajāʾ ibn Abī Salama related to us, from Yazīd ibn Yazīd, who said: I said to Mujāhid: “Abū al-Ḥajjāj…”

Muḥammad ibn al-Muṣaffā related to us: Baqiyya related to us, from Ḥabīb ibn Ṣāliḥ, who said:

“I heard Mujāhid say: ‘The Qurʾān exhausted my knowledge.’”

The report of Saʿīd and al-Ḥajjāj

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: ʿAbd al-Wāḥid ibn Ayman related to us, saying: I said to Saʿīd ibn Jubayr: “You are coming before al-Ḥajjāj, so consider what you will say to him. Do not say anything that would make him deem your blood lawful.” He said: “If he asks me, ‘Are you an unbeliever or a believer?’ then, by God, I will not testify that I am an unbeliever when I do not know whether I will be saved from it or not.”

Qabīṣa related to us: Sufyān related to us, from ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib, who said: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: “No one comes to me to ask me…”

Abū Bishr related to me: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to us, from Sufyān, from ʿAmr ibn Maymūn ibn Mihrān, from his father, who said: “Saʿīd ibn Jubayr died, and there was no one on earth except that he was in need of his knowledge.” He said: “I think this refers to Qurʾānic exegesis.”

Abū ʿĀṣim al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Makhlad related to us, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muslim, who said:

“When Saʿīd ibn Jubayr stood in prayer, he was like a stake.”

Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb related to us: Ḥammād ibn Zayd related to us: al-Faḍl ibn Suwayd al-Ḍabbī related to us, saying: My father died and appointed al-Ḥajjāj as my guardian. I was in his care. Then Saʿīd ibn Jubayr was brought in—and I was present—and al-Ḥajjāj began reproaching him as a man reproaches his son. He said: “Did I not make you a partner in my trust? Did I not do this for you? Did I not do that for you?” Then a word slipped out from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr. He said: “He imposed his will upon me.” Al-Ḥajjāj became angry and said: “You regarded the command of God’s enemy over you as binding, but you did not regard the Commander of the Faithful—or me—as having any claim upon you? Strike off his head!”

Salama related to us, from Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal: Yaḥyā ibn Ādam related to us: Mufaḍḍal related to us, from Mughīra, who said: “Before al-Jamājim, no one in Kūfa gave legal opinions to the people except Saʿīd ibn Jubayr; that was before Ibrāhīm.”

Zayd and Ibn Ḥisāb related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Maʿmar, from Ayyūb and Kathīr ibn Kathīr ibn al-Muṭṭalib ibn Abī Wadāʿa, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, who said: “Ask me, young people, for I am soon to depart from among you.”

[Sufyān al-Thawrī]

He said: ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī said: The companions of Ibn ʿAbbās were six: ʿAṭāʾ Ṭāwūs, Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Jābir ibn Zayd, and ʿIkrima. The person most knowledgeable about these men was ʿAmr ibn Dīnār, who met them all; and the people most knowledgeable about ʿAmr and these men were Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna and Ibn Jurayj. Among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ there were only three who had followers who preserved what they learned from them and upheld their positions in jurisprudence: Zayd ibn Thābit, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, and Ibn ʿAbbās. The most knowledgeable about Zayd ibn Thābit and his views was the group of ten: Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, Abū Salama ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUtba, ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr, and Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān.

ʿAlī said: Maʿn ibn ʿĪsā related from ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Sumayy, who said: “Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān’s name was Abū Bakr, and his teknonym was Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān.” ʿAlī said: Khārija ibn Zayd, Sulaymān ibn Yasār, Abān ibn ʿUthmān, and Qabīṣa ibn Dhūʾayb—and Marwān mentioned another—were [also among them]. The person most knowledgeable about their views and reports was Ibn Shihāb, followed by Mālik, then after Mālik, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī. He said: The people most knowledgeable about ʿAbd Allāh were ʿAlqama, al-Aswad, ʿAbīda, al-Ḥārith ibn Qays, ʿAmr ibn Shuraḥbīl, and another whom he mentioned. The knowledge and reports of these men came down to Sufyān ibn Saʿīd. Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd ibn Sufyān admired this line of transmission and followed it.

ʿAlī said: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān said: “What do you remember about drinking during the circumambulation?”

—during the circumambulation?” I said to him: “ʿAbd al-Muʾmin, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.” He said: “There is nothing to that.” I said to him: “Rather, a trustworthy person related it to me.” He said: “Who is he?” I was reluctant to tell him. When I returned home, I looked and found a report about this question before it, followed by ʿAbd al-Muʾmin. I saw that Saʿīd had spoken about circumambulation.

ʿAlī said: One day, Rawḥ ibn ʿUbāda related to us two reports from Hishām ibn Ḥassān, from Muḥammad, from Shurayḥ: one about a wound exposing the bone and another about something else. We challenged Rawḥ about them and discussed them, then I went to ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and mentioned them to him. He said to someone: “Is it the touch of a feverish man?” He said: “There is nothing to that.” When I returned to Rawḥ, he said: “Strike out the two reports I related to you; they are mistaken. They are actually from al-Ḥasan and Muḥammad.” When we returned from Jarīr, I said to him: “Is no one going to give us anything from al-Aʿmash?” He said: “Do not say that.” He leaned back and related thirty reports to me, none of which I knew;44

ʿAlī said: One day, while I was with him, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related from Sufyān, from Manṣūr, from Abū al-Ḍuḥā: “You are only a warner, and every people has a guide” (Qurʾān 13:7). I said to the man who related it:

“It is only from Umayya.” ʿAbd al-Raḥmān heard and said: “What is he saying?” I told him.

He said: “Who related it to you?” I said: “Yaḥyā related it to us from Sufyān, from Umayya, from Abū al-Ḍuḥā.” He said: “God is our help.” I said: “And Wakīʿ too.” He said: “There is nothing to that.” ʿAlī said: I returned home and brought out Yaḥyā’s report, and it was from his father, from Abū al-Ḍuḥā. I brought out Wakīʿ’s report, and it was from Manṣūr, from Abū al-Ḍuḥā; and, as though beneath it, there was another report from Sufyān, from his father, from Abū al-Ḍuḥā.

“hastening toward the caller” (Qurʾān 54:8). My mind went to it, so I went to Yaḥyā and mentioned that to him. He said: “If it were not evening, I would bring out the book; but come in the morning.” I went to him early the next day, and he brought out the original. He said: “The man has caught us out.” It is from Manṣūr, from Abū al-Ḍuḥā.

I heard Ḥusayn ibn Ḥasan al-Marwazī say: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān said: I went out to a funeral at which ʿUbayd Allāh ibn al-Ḥasan was present. I sat with him—he was judge at the time—and asked him about a question. He got it wrong. I said: “That is wrong. I did not mean that; I only wanted to lead you on to what comes next.” He was silent for a while, then said: “What is it?” I said: “Such-and-such.” He was silent again, then raised his head and said: “You are right. I was mistaken; the correct answer is what you said.”

He said: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān said: “Had he wanted to persist in his error and declare me wrong, he could have done so, and those around him would have helped him by endorsing his answer and declaring me wrong.”

ʿAlī said: Sufyān al-Thawrī’s companions were Yaḥyā, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, Wakīʿ, Abū Nuʿaym, al-Ashjaʿī, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak.

He said: It reached me from Ibn Maʿīn, who said: I heard Wakīʿ say: “I never wrote down from—”

I never heard a single hadith from al-Thawrī without memorizing it; when I returned home, I would write it down.

He said: It reached me from Ibn Maʿīn that he said: “No one in his transmission of Sufyān al-Thawrī’s hadith resembles him except Ibn al-Mubārak, Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Qaṭṭān, Wakīʿ, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī, and Abū Nuʿaym.” He was asked, “What about al-Ashjaʿī?” He replied: “Al-Ashjaʿī is reliable and trustworthy, but bring me someone who narrates from him.”

Yaḥyā said: After these men, among those who transmitted from Sufyān were Yaḥyā ibn Ādam, ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Mūsā, Abū Aḥmad al-Zubayrī, Abū Ḥudhayfa, Qabīṣa, Muʿāwiya al-Qaṣṣār, and al-Firyābī.

Yaḥyā was asked: “What about Abū Dāwūd al-Ḥaffarī?” He replied: “Abū Dāwūd al-Ḥaffarī is a righteous man.”

[Yaḥyā said: Qabīṣa was two months older than Yaḥyā ibn Ādam.

He said: I heard Qabīṣa say: “I gave testimony before Sharīk, and he tested me about my testimony. I mentioned that to Sufyān, and he objected to what Sharīk had done, saying that he had no right to test him. He said: I prayed one of the obligatory prayers with Sufyān—he mentioned which prayer it was, but ʿAlī forgot it.”]

[He said: I heard Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb al-Thaqafī, a man of considered opinion, say: “Abū Ḥanīfa was a follower of my father. He heard from Sufyān along with my father, and he obtained his hearing notes from me after my father’s death.”]

“[…after my father’s death.]” He said: It reached me from Yaḥyā ibn Maʿīn that he said: “Sufyān did not dictate hadith. He dictated only two hadiths to them: the hadith of the Antichrist and the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd’s sermon.” He was asked: “What about the people of Yemen?” He replied: “He did dictate to the people of Yemen. They were weak—or he said, infirm—when they were with him, so he dictated to them.”

He said: I heard Bakr ibn Khalaf say: “ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Walīd al-ʿAdanī did not write that down in that way. Rather, he wrote from Sufyān, who dictated it to him. I do not know whether Abū Bishr was recounting what he heard from al-ʿAdanī or speaking in his own words.”

Sufyān had stayed in Mecca as a fugitive; the concealment had made him gray-haired. Al-Makhzūmī lodged him in one of his houses, which yielded much income, without charging him rent. He asked Sufyān to teach him hadith, explaining that he could not retain and accurately record it unless it were dictated. Sufyān told him: “Find someone nimble-handed; I will dictate to him, then read it back to you.” Al-ʿAdanī was a teacher in Mecca, with excellent handwriting and a quick hand. Al-Makhzūmī enlisted him and took him to Sufyān. Sufyān dictated to him these hadiths, which they call al-Jāmiʿ. Then Sufyān read it aloud to al-Makhzūmī and a group who had attended the reading and heard it. Among them was ʿUthmān ibn al-Yamān, originally from Basra, who had moved with his family to Mecca. They say that Muḥammad ibn Kathīr al-ʿAbdī al-Baṣrī attended the reading of some of it and heard from Sufyān in Mecca; likewise Yazīd ibn Abī Ḥakīm al-ʿAdanī.

Abū Bishr related to me from Bishr ibn al-Sarī, who said: “ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī came to Mecca and asked me what I had heard from Sufyān. He was among those who attended Sufyān’s reading to al-Makhzūmī. I was reluctant to let him see my books, so I borrowed ʿUbayd Allāh ibn al-Walīd’s books and handed them to him. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān then told me: ‘I looked through them…’”

“…and I saw no record of hearing from Sufyān with fewer errors and omissions than this one.”

He said: I heard ʿĪsā ibn Muḥammad say: Al-Firyābī said: “I was in Mecca and went to Sufyān to consult him about my affairs—he was concerned about my situation because of our bond of allegiance. Mecca had become too difficult for me, and I had resolved to return to Faryāb.” He said: “Woe to you! Do not do that. Come, let us buy you a basket and two saddle-packs, and set out for the regions of Syria.” I said: “Abū ʿAbd Allāh, I would prefer to go with you to Kūfa, if you would teach me hadith.” He said: “Then come along.” So I went with him and lodged with him or near him. He would dictate to me. Sometimes he would say: “I want to go to a shaykh; come with me.” I would say to him: “Go and listen, and when you return, tell me what you heard from him.” He would do that.

ʿĪsā said to me: Al-Firyābī considered his transmission to be more accurate than that of Sufyān’s other companions.

ʿĪsā also said: “I arrived to see him during the days of the upheavals, before ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṭāhir set out for Syria and Egypt. When I came to him, he began to marvel and say: ‘You have put yourself at risk.’ I saw that his appearance did not resemble that of the hadith scholars, and I regretted having set out to see him. But when I got to know him, spent time with him, and spoke openly with him, I found that reality differed from appearances.”

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥīm Ṣāʿiqa related to me: I heard ʿAlī say: Yaḥyā told me: “When I set out for Kūfa, Shuʿba wrote a letter for me to Sufyān. I waited about a month or more and did not go to him until some time after I arrived. When he read it, he said: ‘You have been here for such and such a time.’ He had written to him: ‘Write to me the hadith of ʿAmr ibn Murra about supplication.’ He dictated it to me. When he later came to Basra, he paused at a word in it, so I asked him about it. He said: ‘Did I not dictate it to you?’” Yaḥyā said: “When he arrived, he lodged next to me and sent for me. When he saw me, before greeting me, he said: ‘You hoped you would see me here?’”

He said: “He asked me about the shaykhs Ibn al-Ashhab, Sulaymān ibn al-Mughīra, and others. Then he moved elsewhere, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān used to visit him.”

He said: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān never saw Yaḥyā with him except on one occasion. After Yaḥyā, he was barred from entering and did not visit him again until he died.

He said: Yaḥyā brought Muʿādh ibn Muʿādh and Khālid ibn al-Ḥārith in to see him.

He said: ʿAlī said that ʿAbd al-Raḥmān said: “I met Sufyān ten times before he came to Basra.”

Abū Sufyān Muḥammad, one of our companions, related to me from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī, who said: “He moved and lodged near us with an old woman. I would visit him while he was lying down, discuss matters with him, and he would relate hadith to me. I would say to him: ‘Abū ʿAbd Allāh, you differ from us in this hadith.’ He would sit up in alarm and say: ‘Who differs from me?’ I would name so-and-so. He would say: ‘Yaḥyā…’ I said this to him several times. One day he said to me: ‘Look at what Misʿar or Shuʿba disagrees with me about and tell me; as for anyone else, do not tell me.’” He said: “He would often say: ‘I wish I could review a great deal.’”

Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb related to us: Ḥammād ibn Zayd related to us, saying: “I went in to see Sufyān and said to him: ‘Are you not afraid that you will die without having an imam over you? Are you not afraid that an ignorant person will look at you and follow your example?’ He replied: ‘I have had no one to advise me. Prepare me so I can leave.’”

Abū Nuʿaym and Qabīṣa related to us, saying: Sufyān related to us from Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh, who said: “I went in to see al-Ḥajjāj and did not greet him.”

ʿĪsā related to me from al-Firyābī, from Sufyān, with this hadith, adding: “I went in to see al-Mahdī”—or he named him—“and did not greet him.”

Al-Firyābī said: Sufyān said: “A young woman came and stood at my head. I thought they wanted us to be beguiled by her. Muḥammad, if only you had seen her! If only you had seen her!”

Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Faḍl ibn Ziyād related to us, saying: I heard Abū ʿAbd Allāh say:

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī said: “I performed the pilgrimage in the year fifty-one, in fifty-two, and in fifty-three. I married in fifty-four, and performed the pilgrimage in fifty-five, fifty-six, fifty-seven, fifty-eight, and fifty-nine. In every one of those years I met Sufyān.”

He said: I heard Abū ʿAbd Allāh say: “In Kūfa, Sufyān would relate three hundred hadiths a day from memory. He had no book. The memorizers would memorize them, then get up and write them down. Yaḥyā ibn Yamān would retain them by memory; whenever Sufyān related a hadith, he would tie a knot in a thread. When he left Sufyān, he would untie a knot and write down a hadith, then untie another knot and write down another hadith. Abū Nuʿaym would write on tablets, and he would transmit from Sufyān whatever had been recorded on his tablets. Al-Ashjaʿī would transmit from him only if he had written it in a book; that was the most accurate form.”

[Al-Faḍl ibn Ziyād related to us, saying: I heard Abū ʿAbd Allāh say: ʿAbd al-Razzāq said: “When Sufyān came to us, he said: ‘Bring me someone who writes quickly.’ We brought him Hishām ibn Yūsuf. He would write while we checked the book, and when he finished, we would seal the book until we could copy it.”]

Zayd ibn al-Mubārak related to me, saying: Abū Thawr was asked: “Ibn Hammām says: ‘We used to seal up Sufyān’s dictation until we had copied it.’” He replied: “Ibrāhīm said: ‘I never saw him with Sufyān. I did see him after Sufyān had left, and saw that his head was shaved.’ I said: ‘Why was Ibn Hammām’s head shaved?’”

They replied: “He had been ill and was recovering from his illness, so he shaved his head. The people of that region do this: when a man falls ill, they shave his head, then he goes out.”

[I asked Ibn Numayr to bring out for me the hadith of Yaḥyā ibn al-Yamān. He brought out some booklets, but then I saw him hesitating, so I asked: “What is this?” He said: “Let it go. His hadith is unlike that of our companions. He would suppose something and then relate it as a hadith, especially after he suffered paralysis. He refused to bring out for me the rest of what he had heard from him.

He said: It reached me from Yaḥyā ibn Maʿīn that he said: Wakīʿ said to me: ‘If the Sufyān from whom Yaḥyā ibn Yamān relates is the one we met, then he is not that one.’]

He said: I heard Qabīṣa say: Ibn Abī Dhīb said of Mālik and Sufyān: “No one comes to us from the East without our comparing him to Mālik and Sufyān.”

Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Faḍl ibn Ziyād related to me: Abū Ṭālib related to us from Abū ʿAbd Allāh, who said: Mālik was told: “Sufyān gives legal opinions.” He said: “Does he, indeed?” When Ibn Abī Dhīb heard Mālik’s remark, he said: “What business is it of his? By God, no man from the East has ever come to us better than Sufyān.”

He said: Sufyān was his friend. He said: Sufyān and al-Awzāʿī went in to see Mālik. When they left, Mālik said: “One of them knows more than his companion but is not fit to be an imam; the other is fit to be an imam”—meaning al-Awzāʿī was fit to be an imam, whereas Sufyān was not.

He said: Mālik had no favorable opinion of Sufyān.

Salama ibn Shabīb related to us: Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal related to me: Shuʿayb ibn Ḥarb related to us, saying: Mālik said: “I bade Sufyān farewell, and he said: ‘He has indeed left me resolved not to drink nabīdh.’”

I heard al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Ḥasan say: I heard ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī say: “People say that Sufyān permitted drinking nabīdh. I bear witness that I saw him [not] take it. A medicine was prescribed for him, and he was told: ‘We can prepare nabīdh for you.’ He said:

‘No; bring me honey.’

And what ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī said was: “I would ask Sufyān, and he would say: ‘Put this off, put this off. I have not reviewed my books for four years. Prepare me to leave.’ I prepared him, hoping he would let me have access to his books, but he died.”

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān said: “If someone saw Sufyān relating hadith and said, ‘This man is not a scholar: he puts things forward and back and makes them sound correct,’ then even if he tried his utmost to distort the meaning, he would not succeed.”

He said: “I went with Sufyān to ʿIkrima ibn ʿAmmār, and found that his writing was cumbersome and poor. He said: ‘Shall I write it for you, Abū ʿAbd Allāh?’ Sufyān replied: ‘No. I want it to be in my own handwriting.’”

I heard ʿAbd al-Raḥmān say: “People say Sufyān liked to delay the ʿAṣr prayer. I bear witness that I saw him delay it among us until after the mosque where they hasten the ʿAṣr prayer.”

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān said: “He used to wish for death, and I asked him about it. He said: ‘I want to die safe from these people.’ When he fell ill, however, he came to dislike what he had wished for. He would say to me: ‘How do you find me today?’ and I would reply: ‘Well.’”

On the day he died, I went out to perform the ʿAṣr prayer. He said: “You are leaving me in this state and going out?” So I prayed at his bedside. He said to me: “Read Sūrat Yā Sīn to me, for it is said that it brings relief to the sick.” I read it to him, and had not finished when he breathed his last.

Ḥusayn ibn al-Ḥasan related to me, saying: I heard al-Haytham ibn Jamīl say: I heard Muhalhil say: “I went out with Sufyān to Mecca.” He said: “Al-Awzāʿī made the pilgrimage, and we shared a house. One day, as we sat there, a eunuch came in and said: ‘The emir has come to you,’ and ʿAbd al-Ṣamad was in charge of the people. As for al-Awzāʿī and me, we stayed where we were; Sufyān, however, went inside… It was not long before ʿAbd al-Ṣamad arrived and came in. Al-Awzāʿī greeted him, and he asked: ‘Where is ʿAbd Allāh?’” Muhalhil said:

“We said: ‘He went in to attend to a need.’ I got up and said to him: ‘The man will not leave before you come out.’ He threw off his cloak and came out wearing only a waist-wrapper, with neither cloak nor shirt.

“He had a large belly. He greeted him and flung himself down in the middle of the room. ʿAbd al-Ṣamad said:

“‘Abū ʿAbd Allāh, you are the leading man and scholar of the East. I heard of your arrival and wanted to follow your example.’ Sufyān lowered his head, then said: ‘Shall I direct you to something better than what you came for?’ He asked: ‘What is that?’ Sufyān replied: ‘Give up the position you hold.’ I said: ‘Surely we belong to God and to Him we return’ (Qurʾān 2:156). ‘You greet ʿAbd al-Ṣamad with that?’ His complexion changed, and he said: ‘Abū ʿAbd Allāh, Abū Jaʿfar would not be satisfied even with this.’ He stood up and left in anger. We said: ‘Now he will send someone to bind us together in shackles.’ But nothing happened.”

Ḥusayn related to us, saying: I heard Muʾammal ibn Ismāʿīl say: “We were with Sufyān when Bishr ibn al-Sarī arrived. Sufyān said: ‘If he sits with us, I will get up.’ Some of those who were with us got up and informed him. He sat off to one side. Muʾammal said: ‘Before that, Sufyān used to honor him and draw him close.’ When Sufyān got up, I went to him, and he asked me, so I said: ‘Yes.’

“He said: ‘If he sits with us, I will get up.’ I said: ‘If you would like me to go with you to see him, I will.’

“So I went to him, and we entered. He turned toward me and away from Bishr, and began speaking to me while turning away from him. Bishr said to him: ‘Abū ʿAbd Allāh, what have you seen me do? What have you heard about me?’ He replied without speaking to him directly: ‘Tell him: “Did I not pass by you yesterday while you were sitting with al-Qaddāḥ?”’ Bishr said to him: ‘Abū ʿAbd Allāh, by God, I did not sit with him to ask him anything, to learn from him, or to hear anything from him. A man had a need to discuss with me, and I sat with him to speak about that man’s need.’”

Al-Muʾammal said: “What do you think of a man who says: ‘I bear witness that God has a House toward which He has commanded people to pray, but I do not know whether it is in Mecca or somewhere else’?” Sufyān replied: “He is a believer.”

Ibn Abī ʿUmar related to us, saying: Sufyān said: “Do you know which people are most eager for knowledge?” They were silent. He said: “The most knowledgeable among them.” Then he said: “I have seen no one more eager for knowledge than Sufyān. If people were asked, ‘Who is the most knowledgeable?’ they would say: ‘Sufyān al-Thawrī.’”

Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna said: Sufyān al-Thawrī said: “We have acquired something of this matter”—meaning knowledge—“and wish we could find someone who would come in so we could throw it to him.”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to me from Sufyān, who said: “Al-Thawrī came to Mecca, and I met him. He said to me: ‘Ibn ʿUyayna, ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Abī Rawwād is giving legal opinions!’”

ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī said: Sufyān al-Thawrī remained in hiding in Basra for a year or thereabouts. Yaḥyā said: “I arranged for al-Muʿtamir to reach him. Sufyān said to me: ‘Yaḥyā, your companion is a Muslim’”—that is, for this reason. He said: It reached me from someone other than ʿAlī that Yaḥyā said:

“Al-Muʿtamir asked me to speak to Sufyān on his behalf, asking him to teach him hadith. I did so, and found that al-Muʿtamir had brought out hadiths of al-Layth ibn Abī Sulaym to ask Sufyān about them. Sufyān found fault with him for his transmission; al-Muʿtamir had better command of al-Layth’s hadith than Sufyān did. That is why Sufyān said to Yaḥyā, ‘Your companion is a Muslim’”—that is, for this reason.

Al-Muʿtamir had better command of al-Layth’s hadith than Sufyān did; that is why Sufyān said to Yaḥyā, “Your companion is a Muslim”—that is, for this reason.

ʿAlī said: I heard ʿAbd al-Razzāq say: “Sufyān stayed dictating to us for forty-eight days.”45

Ḥusayn ibn Ḥasan related to me from al-Haytham ibn Jamīl, from Sufyān’s nephew, who said: “When Sufyān devoted himself to worship, he fell ill. We would take him to physicians, but they could not identify what was wrong with him. At last we went to a monk from the region of al-Ḥīra. When he looked at his contortion, he said: ‘Your companion has no illness. What afflicts him is due to the fear that has entered him,’ or something to that effect.”

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Makhzūmī related to me: Abū al-Sarī related to me, saying: I was told by ʿĀmir ibn Ṣāliḥ ibn Rustum, who said: “I was with Yūnus ibn ʿUbayd when Sufyān al-Thawrī came to him and asked him about some hadiths. Then Sufyān got up, and Yūnus said: ‘I have never seen a Kūfan better than him.’”

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥīm related to me from Zakariyyā, from Ḥafṣ ibn Ghiyāth, who said:

“I asked Sufyān: ‘What do you say about the Mahdī? People are talking about him a great deal.’ He replied: ‘If he passes your door, do not take any position about him until the people unite behind him.’”

ʿAlī was asked: “Would you rank anyone above Sufyān, Manṣūr, and al-Aʿmash?” He replied: “No.”

He said: Aḥmad said: “Sufyān and al-Awzāʿī went in to see Mālik. When they left, Mālik said: ‘One of them knows more than his companion but is not fit to be an imam’”—meaning al-Awzāʿī—“‘and Sufyān is not fit for it. Mālik had no favorable opinion of Sufyān.’”

Al-Faḍl ibn Ziyād, the companion of Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, related from Abū Ṭālib: Aḥmad said: “Sufyān met Ḥammād ibn Salamah during the pilgrimage season and said to him, ‘Abū Salamah, have you written anything from Salamah ibn Kuhayl?’ He said, ‘Yes.’ He said, ‘An astute shaykh.’ I said, ‘Did Ḥammād say, “An astute shaykh”?’ He said, ‘No, that was not Ḥammād’s wording. Ḥammād was too dignified to say something like that. Rather, Sufyān said to Ḥammād, “He is an astute shaykh.”’”

[Abū Saʿīd al-Ashajj related to me: Ibn Yamān related to us, saying: I heard Sufyān say:

“The trial of ḥadīth is more severe than the trial of gold and silver.”]

[Abū Saʿīd al-Ashajj related to me: Abū Khālid related to us, saying: Sufyān ate one night until he was full, then said, “When a donkey is given more fodder, it does more work.” He then stood in prayer until morning.]

Aḥmad ibn al-Khalīl related to me: Al-Faḍl said: I heard al-Thawrī say, more than once: “I wish I could come away from this ḥadīth with neither gain nor liability.”

Aḥmad ibn al-Khalīl related to me: Masʿūd ibn Khalaf related to me: Ḥajjāj ibn Muḥammad related to me: Fuḍayl ibn Marzūq related to me, saying: I heard Abū Isḥāq say to al-Shaʿbī:

“I wish I could come away from my deeds with neither gain nor liability.”

Aḥmad related to me: Masʿūd ibn Khalaf related to me, saying: I heard Yūsuf ibn Asbāṭ say: Shuʿbah said to me, “What brings you here?” I said, “I have come seeking knowledge.” He said:

“Sit down so I can tell you what is better for you.” He swore solemn oaths, exerting himself in them, that what I sought was a drink, and that it distracts one from the remembrance of God and from prayer.

I was told that Ibn Maʿīn was once asked: “They rank ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī above Wakīʿ.” Ibn Maʿīn said: “May God, the angels, and all people curse whoever ranks ʿAbd al-Raḥmān above Wakīʿ.”

Abū Yūsuf said: “Something other than this would be more in keeping with the speech of the people of knowledge. Whoever takes account of himself and knows that his speech is part of his deeds would not say the like of this. Wakīʿ is a fine, virtuous, learned man.”

[Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal was asked: “When Wakīʿ and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī disagree, whose opinion do you follow?” He replied: “ʿAbd al-Raḥmān is more often in agreement, especially with Sufyān. He was especially devoted to Sufyān’s ḥadīth. The early authorities approve of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, and he avoids drinking intoxicants.”] He also held that crops should not be grown in the land of the Euphrates.

[Aḥmad ibn al-Khalīl related to us: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿUthmān related to us, saying: Abū Qaṭan related to us, saying: Shuʿbah said to me, “Abū Qaṭan, Sufyān al-Thawrī has become the foremost of people in scrupulous piety and knowledge.”]

Aḥmad ibn al-Khalīl related to us: Al-Faḍl ibn Dukayn said: “I kept company with Sufyān al-Thawrī from the year 147. I kept company with him for eight years, until he left Kūfah in the year 155. By God, he never returned to Kūfah before he died. I never heard him say anything good or bad about ʿUthmān.”

[Aḥmad ibn al-Khalīl related to me, saying: I heard Abū Nūḥ Qarāḍ say: Shuʿbah said, “Sufyān is an excellent man, were it not that he gathers things up”—meaning, he takes from everyone …]

“… all of them.”]

Volume Two

[Volume Two]

[Continuation of the Biographical Entries]

[Continuation: The People of Medina]

[Continuation of the Third Generation]

[ʿIKRIMAH, THE CLIENT OF IBN ʿABBĀS]

Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb related to us: Ḥammād related to us, from al-Zubayr ibn al-Khirrīt, from ʿIkrimah, who said: “Ibn ʿAbbās used to put a shackle on my leg while teaching me the Qurʾān and the Sunna.”

Saʿīd ibn Asad related to us: Ḍamrah related to us, from Rajāʾ, who said: I heard Ibn ʿAwn say: “They did not leave Ayyūb alone until they drew out of him what he had not intended”—that is, ḥadīth from ʿIkrimah.

ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Uwaysī related to us: Ibrāhīm ibn Saʿd related to us, from his father, from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, who used to say to his client Burd: “Burd, do not lie about me as ʿIkrimah lied about Ibn ʿAbbās.”

Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā related to me: Sufyān related to us, from Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī, who said:

“On the very first occasion that we sat with ʿIkrimah, he said to us, ‘Can your Ḥasan do something like this?’”

Abū Bakr related to us: Sufyān related to us: ʿAmr related to us, saying: “Whenever I heard…”

“… ʿIkrimah relating traditions about them as though he were looking down on them, watching them.”

Salamah related to me: Ibrāhīm ibn Khālid related to us, from Umayyah ibn Shibl, who related to me: “A man from the people of Medina said: ‘ʿIkrimah and Kuthayyir ʿAzzah died on the same day, and their funeral biers were brought out on one day. The people—that is, the people of Medina—said, “The most learned man and the most eloquent poet have died.”’”

(Folio 2a) [ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī said: “ʿIkrimah died in the year 104. No one bore him in his funeral procession; they made four men carry him—as I was told. He died in Medina.”]

[I heard Ibn Bukayr say: “ʿIkrimah came to Egypt intending to go to the Maghrib, and left this house”—he gestured toward a house beside Ibn Bukayr’s house—“then he set out for the Maghrib. The Khārijites who are in the Maghrib took their knowledge from him.”]

ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī said: “ʿIkrimah held the views of Najdah al-Ḥarūrī.”

Al-Muʿallā ibn Asad related to us: Ḥātim ibn Wardān related to us: Ayyūb related to us, saying:

“The traditionists of Ibn ʿAbbās gathered together—among them Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Ṭāwūs, and ʿAṭāʾ—around ʿIkrimah and seated him. They began asking him about traditions of Ibn ʿAbbās. Whenever he related a tradition to them, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr would make this gesture with his hand”—he counted to thirty—“until they asked him about the fish.” ʿIkrimah said: “It was accompanying the two of them in shallow water.” Saʿīd said: “I bear witness that Ibn ʿAbbās said: ‘The two of them were carrying it in a basket.’”

Ayyūb said: “He used to state both versions.”

Salamah related to me: Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal related to us: Ibrāhīm ibn Khālid al-Ṣanʿānī, the muezzin, related to us, from Umayyah ibn Shibl, from Maʿmar, from Ayyūb, who said: “ʿIkrimah came to us, and the people gathered around him until he was lifted onto the roof of the house.”

Salamah related to us: Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal related to us: Ibrāhīm ibn Khālid related to us, from Umayyah ibn Shibl, from ʿAmr ibn Muslim, who said: “ʿIkrimah came to Ṭāwūs, who had him ride on a fine camel worth sixty dinars. He said, ‘Shall I not buy this man’s knowledge for sixty dinars?’”

Al-Walīd ibn ʿUtbah related to us: Abū Mis-har related to us: Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to us (2b), saying: Khālid ibn Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiyah said of ʿIkrimah, the client of Ibn ʿAbbās: “A learned man is an excellent companion, and an ignorant man is a wretched companion. The learned man takes what he knows; the ignorant man takes everything he hears.” Saʿīd said: “ʿIkrimah would relate a tradition, then say to himself, ‘If it was indeed so.’”

Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb related to us: Ḥammād ibn Zayd related to us, saying: Ayyūb was asked:

“Did you—or did they—regard ʿIkrimah with suspicion?” He said: “As for me, I did not regard him with suspicion.”

Abū ʿUmayr related to us: Ḍamrah related to us, saying: Dāwūd ibn Abī Hind was asked:

“Do you transmit from ʿIkrimah?” He said, “That is Ayyūb’s practice.” He said, “ʿIkrimah,” and we said, “ʿIkrimah.”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us: Sufyān related to us: ʿAmr related to us, saying: “Jābir ibn Zayd handed me a sheet containing questions for me to ask ʿIkrimah. I seemed to hesitate, so he took it from me.” ʿAmr said: “[Jābir] said, ‘This is ʿIkrimah, the client of Ibn ʿAbbās; this is the most learned man among people.’”

Salamah related to me, from Aḥmad: ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us, saying: I heard Maʿmar say: I heard Ayyūb say: “I had intended to travel to ʿIkrimah, to some distant region.” He said: “I was in the market in Baṣrah when suddenly there was a man on a donkey.” He said:

“They said, ‘It is ʿIkrimah.’ The people gathered around him. I went over to him, but I could not think of anything to ask him; the questions had slipped from my mind. So I stood beside his donkey. The people began asking him questions, and I memorized [the answers].”

Salamah related to us: Aḥmad related to us: Ḥajjāj related to us, saying: I heard Shuʿbah relate from …

Khālid al-Ḥadhdhāʾ said: “ʿIkrimah said to a man who was asking him, ‘What is the matter with you? Have you run dry?’”

Shuʿbah said: “Then Ayyūb related to me: Khālid al-Ḥadhdhāʾ was asking ʿIkrimah, and Khālid fell silent. ʿIkrimah said, ‘What is the matter with you? Have you run dry?’—that is, ‘Have you run out?’”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us: Sufyān related to us: ʿAmr related to us, from Abū al-Shaʿthāʾ, who said: “A certain person related to me from Ibn ʿAbbās: ‘If a Muslim slaughters an animal and forgets to invoke God’s name, let him eat it, for the word “Muslim” contains one of God’s names.’” (That is, by “a certain person,” he meant ʿIkrimah.) (3a) Abū Bakr related to us: Sufyān related to us: ʿAmr related to us, saying: “I saw Abū al-Shaʿthāʾ asking ʿIkrimah and saying, ‘This is the client of Ibn ʿAbbās; this is the most learned man among people.’” ʿAmr said: “He handed me a sheet, and I began asking him questions. I seemed to hesitate, so he snatched the sheet from my hand and began asking him.”

Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb related to me: Ḥammād related to us, from Ayyūb, who said: ʿIkrimah said:

“I have given my own opinion only on two matters. I was asked about a chicken that fell into a pot and died. I said, ‘Pour out the broth and eat the meat.’ And I gave my opinion about a man who completed the rites except for the circumambulation, then had intercourse with his wife. I said, ‘All that remains is for him to circumambulate the House. He should leave the Sacred Precinct, enter the state of consecration for an ʿumrah, then return, so that one circumambulation takes the place of another circumambulation, and one consecration takes the place of another consecration.’”

“… the Sacred Precinct and enter the state of consecration for an ʿumrah; then he can return, so that one circumambulation takes the place of another circumambulation, and one consecration takes the place of another consecration.”

Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb related to us: Ḥammād ibn Zayd related to us, from Ayyūb, from someone who went between Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib and ʿIkrimah regarding a man who had made a vow to commit an act of disobedience to God. Saʿīd said:

“He must fulfill it.” ʿIkrimah said: “He must not fulfill it.” The man came to Saʿīd and told him what ʿIkrimah had said. Saʿīd said: “The client of Ibn ʿAbbās will not stop until a rope is put around his neck and he is led about.” The man then came to ʿIkrimah and told him what Saʿīd had said. ʿIkrimah replied: “You are a wicked man. Since you reported his words to me, report mine to him: ‘Is this vow to God or to Satan?’ By God, if he says, ‘To God,’ he will be lying; and if he says, ‘To Satan,’ he will be an unbeliever.”

Salamah related to us, from Aḥmad: ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us, saying: “I heard my father mention that when ʿIkrimah came, the grandfather, Ṭāwūs, had him ride on a fine camel. He was asked, ‘You gave him a camel, when a small thing would have sufficed for him.’ He replied, ‘I bought the knowledge of this man with this camel.’”

Muḥammad said: “I heard ʿAlī,” and he related from Yaʿqūb al-Ḥaḍramī, from …

His grandfather said: “ʿIkrima stood at the door of the mosque and said: ‘There is no one in it but an unbeliever.’” He said:

“ʿIkrima held the view of the Ibāḍiyya.”

He said: Qatāda said: “Ask the servant only about the Qurʾān.” (3b)

[Jābir ibn Zayd]

Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb related to us: Ḥammād ibn Zayd related to us, from Ayyūb, who said: Jābir ibn Zayd was mentioned, and he began to marvel at his legal knowledge.

Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb related to us: Ḥammād ibn Zayd related to us, who said: Ayyūb was asked, “Did you see Jābir ibn Zayd?” He said: “Yes, by God! He was intelligent, intelligent.”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us: Sufyān related to us: ʿAmr related to us, who said: I heard Ibn ʿAbbās say: “If the people of Baṣra were left to follow the opinion of Jābir ibn Zayd, he would give them ample knowledge from the Book of God.”
