Abū Bishr related to me from Yazīd ibn Zurayʿ. He said: ʿUbayd Allāh ibn al-Ḥasan and Ismāʿīl ibn ʿUlayya came to me. Ismāʿīl said: “We have come to greet you, Abū Muʿāwiya.” [ʿUbayd Allāh said: “We] did not come for that, but we heard a ḥadīth from you and have come to hear it from you.”

“ʿAlī said: ‘ʿAbd al-Raḥmān crossed out al-Mubārak’s ḥadīth.’”

Al-Faḍl related to me. He said: I heard Abū ʿAbd Allāh being asked by Abū Jaʿfar: “Do you prefer Mubārak or al-Rabīʿ?” He replied: “Al-Rabīʿ.” “As for ʿAffān and those men, they prefer Mubārak to him. But al-Rabīʿ was a man of military campaigns and merit.”

He was asked: “Did ʿAbd al-Raḥmān transmit from al-Rabīʿ ibn Ṣubayḥ?” He replied:

“Yes.”

He said: I heard Abū ʿAbd Allāh say: “I used to leave aside Wakīʿ’s ḥadīth—the ḥadīth of al-Rabīʿ—and I regretted it.” He was asked: “So did you write down Mubārak’s ḥadīth?” He replied: “Yes.”

ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī said: Abū al-ʿAlāniya’s name was Muslim.

“ʿAlī said: ‘When I took leave of Sufyān, he said: “You will be tested with this responsibility, and people will need you. So fear God, and keep your intention in it good.”’”

He said: I heard ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yaʿqūb ibn Abī ʿAbbād al-Qulzumī—and he was…

“one of ʿAlī’s companions—said: ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī came to us one day and said: ‘Last night I saw, as though I had stretched out my hand and taken one of the stars of the Pleiades.’ We went with him to one of the interpreters of dreams, and he recounted the dream to him. The interpreter said: ‘You will attain knowledge, so take care how you conduct yourself.’

“One of our companions said to him: ‘Perhaps you should study something of jurisprudence’—as though he meant the use of personal opinion. He replied: ‘If I occupy myself with that, I will withdraw from what I am engaged in.’”

“Abū Bishr ibn Khalaf related to me. He said: I came to Mecca, where there was a young man with a strong and extensive memory. He used to review the Musnad and its transmission routes. I asked him: ‘How did you come by this?’ He replied: ‘I will tell you. In Sufyān’s time, I asked him to transmit the Musnad to me. He said: “I know that what you want in asking is to review it together. If you guarantee that you will review it with me and not name me, I will do so.” I guaranteed it, and kept going to him. He began transmitting to me this material which, when [repeated?], he had committed to memory.’”53

Abū Yūsuf said: I mentioned this to one of Juwayriya’s descendants who used to keep company with ʿAlī. He said: “I heard ʿAlī say: ‘I was away from Baṣra [on] my journey to Yemen—I think he mentioned three years—and my mother was alive. When I returned to her, she began saying: “So-and-so is a friend of yours, and so-and-so is an enemy of yours.” I asked her: “How did you know, Mother?” [She said:] “So-and-so and so-and-so”—among them she mentioned Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd—“would come and greet me, saying, ‘Be patient. When he returns, God will gladden you through what you see.’ So I knew that these men loved you and were your friends. But so-and-so and so-and-so, when they came, would say, ‘Write to him, put pressure on him, and make things difficult for him so he will come back to you.’”’ This, and the like of it.”

Al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAẓīm—or that man descended from Juwayriya—related to me. He said: ʿAlī said: “I had compiled the Musnad, exhaustively arranging it by transmission routes. I wrote it on sheets and placed it in a large book-chest, leaving it at home while I was away on this journey. When I returned, I went one day to review what I had written. I moved the book-chest and found it heavy and weighty, unlike before. I opened it and found that the termites had gotten into the books and turned them to mud. After that, I no longer had the energy to compile it.”

“I heard ʿAlī while people were coming to him regularly to study chapters he had compiled. I saw him reciting the chapters on prostration to them from memory. He had written down the beginning of a ḥadīth, and would pass over the page and sheet. When he faltered over something, they would prompt him with the word or portion he needed. Then he would continue over the sheets and pages. When he faltered and needed to be prompted with a word or a portion, he would say: ‘God is our help! In the days when we pursued these chapters, we used to meet the shaykhs and review them with them, benefiting from what we had forgotten. We used to memorize them. Now we have come to need prompting in some of them.’”

He said: I heard Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb rank Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī above everyone who transmitted from Nāfiʿ. He was asked: “But ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ranks Mālik higher.” He replied: “He says that only because he heard from him and wants to stand level with Ḥammād. Mālik is certainly worthy of that rank, but Ayyūb transmits the ḥadīth in full, just as he hears it, whereas Mālik abbreviates and omits from a ḥadīth what he does not affirm. Ayyūb is therefore superior to the others.”

They said to Sulaymān:

“But Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd used to say that it was ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿUmar.” Sulaymān replied: “He wrote down and heard from ʿUbayd Allāh; he was only trying to stand level with Ḥammād. ʿUbayd Allāh is trustworthy and precise, as is Mālik, but Ayyūb stands above them.”

“Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥīm Ṣāʿiqa related to me. He said: I heard ʿAlī say: ‘The people with the strongest retention from al-Zuhrī were Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna and Ziyād ibn Saʿd, then Mālik, Maʿmar, and Yūnus, who took from his book.’” He also said: “Al-Awzāʿī’s ḥadīth is close [in quality].” And he said:

“Al-Layth ibn Saʿd only took from his book.” ʿAlī said: “Among al-Zuhrī’s students was Ṣāliḥ ibn Kaysān; most of them only read their material to him.”

ʿAlī said: Yaḥyā used to say: “Al-Zuhrī’s students are Mālik, Sufyān, and Maʿmar.” ʿAbd al-Raḥmān would rank no one above Mālik.

ʿAlī said: Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd told me: “When Ibn al-Mubārak returned from Maʿmar, I asked him: ‘Write down the account of the Slander for me.’ He said to me: ‘What will you do with it? Maʿmar only read it to al-Zuhrī. I will write down Yūnus’s version of the ḥadīth for you.’ I said: ‘I do not want it.’”

ʿAlī said: Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd related to me from Khālid ibn al-Ḥārith. He said: I heard Ibn Abī Dhiʾb say: “I read [my material] to al-Zuhrī.”

He said: Al-Aṣmaʿī related from ʿAbd Allāh al-ʿUmarī. He said: “I saw Mālik reading [his material] to al-Zuhrī.”

He said: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān stopped Mālik and said: “Reduce the reading.”

“ʿAlī said: ‘Ibn Jurayj heard nothing from Ibn Shihāb; rather, [Ibn Shihāb’s material] was read to him.’” Yaḥyā said: Sufyān ibn Ḥabīb said to me: “Indeed, he heard such-and-such from him.” I went to Ibn Jurayj and asked him about it. He replied: “I do not know whether I heard it or read it.”

I went to him and asked him about it. He replied: “I do not know whether I heard it or read it.”

(40b) “Al-Faḍl said: Aḥmad said: ‘Al-Layth ibn Saʿd had extensive knowledge and sound ḥadīth.’” He also said: “Yūnus transmitted more from al-Zuhrī than ʿUqayl, though the two were close in standing.”

“He said: I asked Aḥmad: ‘Where did Hushaym write from al-Zuhrī?’ He replied: ‘In Mecca.’

“Then al-Zuhrī returned and died shortly afterward.”

Aḥmad said: “How precise and retentive Yazīd ibn Zurayʿ was! How sound his ḥadīth was! He was truthful and precise. He used to make palm-leaf baskets and eat [from their sale]. His father…”

“Zurayʿ was governor of Baṣra, but Yazīd did not eat anything from his wealth. He used to recite the number of [his reports] as a memory aid. However, he was hasty and spoke at length. One day he became unsure about a ḥadīth of his, and someone asked him: ‘Have you become uncertain?’ He replied: ‘If I become uncertain, I will keep going back to its source again and again until I have mastered it!’ Any report he transmitted from Saʿīd—you need not worry whether he heard it from someone else; his hearing from Saʿīd was early. He used to acquire ḥadīth with care.”

“Al-Faḍl ibn Ziyād said: I heard Abū ʿAbd Allāh mention Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Qaṭṭān and say: ‘By God, we have never known anyone like him.’” “Then he said: I heard ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī mention Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Qaṭṭān and say: ‘Your eyes have never seen anyone like him.’”

Al-Faḍl said: I heard Abū ʿAbd Allāh say: “When Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd came across a difficult word, he would mark its vowels; otherwise, he would not.”

He said: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Bishr—he was uncertain about it—said to me: “Ask Bahz.”

Abū ʿAbd Allāh said: “Bahz’s writing was sound.”

“Muḥammad related to me. He said: I heard ʿAlī say: ‘The three leading transmitters from Qatāda are…’”

“Saʿīd, Hishām, and Shuʿba. Of them, Saʿīd was the most precise, Hishām transmitted the most, and Shuʿba knew best what he had heard.” He also said: “After these men, no one is like Hammām when transmitting from his book.”

Al-Faḍl related to us. He said: Abū ʿAbd Allāh Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal said: “How sound Hammām’s ḥadīth is, in my view.”

He said: ʿAffān ibn Muslim related to us; Ḥammād ibn Zayd related to us. He said: “When strangers arrived, we would go to them, and Hishām al-Dastawāʾī would say: ‘Bring out what you have while it is still fresh.’” He said:

“Jarīr ibn Ḥāzim was the one among us with the strongest memory. (41a)

“Qatāda heard nothing from Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar, nor anything from Abū Qilāba. He had heard that [a drink] was being prepared for him in a jar of his, and said: ‘That is a Bedouin from Jarm.’ He did not hear from Abū Qilāba; rather, reports reached him later, and because he was eager for ḥadīth, he transmitted them. He did not hear from Abū Rāfiʿ. He did hear some reports from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ and Sālim ibn Abī al-Jaʿd, which Ḥassān transmitted with a chain of transmission. ‘If you remove Abū Nuʿaym from ḥadīth, nothing remains.’”

Aḥmad ibn al-Khalīl related to me; Muḥammad ibn Kathīr al-Ṣanʿānī related to us. He said:

“I heard Maʿmar say: ‘I kept company with Qatāda when I was fourteen years old. There was nothing…’”

I heard it in those years as though it were written in my breast.

Muḥammad related to me: I heard ʿAlī say: “The most reliable people regarding Nāfiʿ are Ayyūb, then ʿUbayd Allāh.” I asked him: “Ṣakhr?” He said: Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd said:

“His book was lost, so he sent for it from him in Medina. There is nothing wrong with him; he is dearer to me than anyone else.”

ʿAlī said: “It was only Layth ibn Saʿd who read it to Nāfiʿ.”

He said: I heard Ibn Bukayr say: “Layth ibn Saʿd made the pilgrimage in the year thirteen, and heard from Ibn Shihāb in Mecca. He also heard from Abū Mulayka, ʿAṭāʾ, Abū al-Zubayr, Nāfiʿ, ʿImrān ibn Abī Anas, and a number of shaykhs.”

“Ibn Bukayr said: Ḥubaysh ibn Saʿīd informed me, from al-Layth, who said: ‘I came to Abū al-Zubayr, and he brought out some books for me. I asked: “Did you hear this from Jābir?” He said: “And from others.” I said: “Did you hear it from Jābir?” He brought this sheet out to me.’” Al-Layth said:

“I had visited Nāfiʿ, and he asked me, ‘Who are you?’ I said, ‘I am a man from Egypt.’ He asked, ‘From which people?’ I said, ‘From Qays.’ He asked, ‘The son of Rifāʿa?’ I said, ‘Or a man from his people.’

“Al-Layth said: Nāfiʿ read to me and said, ‘Like the one about whom I circulated a story concerning his father.’ He meant: ‘Like the one who drinks from silver vessels.’”

ʿAlī said: I heard ʿAbd Allāh ibn Dāwūd say: “We were at al-Aʿmash’s gathering when a man came and said, ‘Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna held a session today.’ I asked, ‘What is he relating?’ He said: ‘From ʿAmr ibn Dīnār (41b), from Ibn ʿUmayr: “The wayfarers are those who fast.”’

“He said: Sufyān said, ‘I entered Aden, and no one asked me about anything.’ I said, ‘These people are ignorant; they do not need to ask about anything.’”

“ʿAlī said: Sufyān said: ‘Wāʾil ibn Dāwūd did not hear anything from his father. He only consulted his book for the report about the wedding feast.’”

ʿAlī said: Shuʿba said: “I asked Mushāsh, ‘Did al-Ḍaḥḥāk hear from Ibn ʿAbbās?’ He said, ‘No, and he never even saw him.’”

ʿAlī said: “Al-Ṣaqʿab ibn Zuhayr and al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Zuhayr were brothers. Abū al-Muʿallā was Yaḥyā ibn Maymūn, and Abū Qatāda al-ʿAdawī was Muslim ibn Yazīd.”

ʿAlī said: “I have been unable to find anyone who identifies Abū al-Ashʿath or Abū Asmāʾ al-Raḥabī.”

He said: I heard ʿAlī say: “The name of Abū Sawwār al-ʿAdawī was Ḥassān ibn Ḥurayth.”

I heard ʿAlī say: Yaḥyā said: “I came to Kūfa once, when al-Aʿmash had sworn that he would not relate traditions. I thought, ‘If only you would go by him.’ So I went by him while he was sitting at the entrance to the alley. I thought, ‘Who would dare speak to this man?’ I came up, and Abū Muʿāwiya arrived and sat down. I saw no one ask him anything except Abū Muʿāwiya. He sat with him and asked, ‘Where have you come from?’ He replied, ‘I have come from Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid.’ He asked, ‘What did he relate to you?’ So he began relating to him, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, about Qurʾānic commentary. He asked him, ‘What else did he relate to you?’ So he began relating to him. He said, ‘Indeed, he used to seek out the shaykhs.’ Al-Aʿmash said, ‘It passes right into my breast.’ Then Yaḥyā said to his son, ‘Was I not having you verify it?’ He said, ‘Yes.’

“[He related:] ‘Shaqīq, from ʿAbd Allāh.’ He related two traditions that day, and I wrote them down.”

“The name of Abū Qays ibn Abī Ḥāzim was ʿAwf ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥārith.”

Yaḥyā said: “Al-Aʿmash resembled the ascetics.” He said: “He was a man of merit and a man of the Qurʾān.”

ʿAlī said: I heard Yaḥyā say: “I never transmitted anything from Saʿīd concerning Qatāda’s opinions.”

Yaḥyā said: “When I first began seeking traditions, I saw ʿImrān ibn Ḥudayr. They were all Abū Mijlaz’s opinions, and I wrote none of them down.”

ʿAlī was asked about Sayyār, who relates traditions (42a) of Jaʿfar ibn Sulaymān on asceticism. He said: “Not everyone is to be taken from. I would never have thought anyone would relate from this man.”

A man said to ʿAbd al-Raḥmān: “Abū Saʿīd, no one is falling away.” He said: “You speak truly.” Yaḥyā said: “Nothing harms anyone, because every people will find someone to transmit from them.”

ʿAlī said: I heard Ibn Mahdī say: “More than once, when Hishām ibn Abī ʿAbd Allāh related a tradition, I heard him say, ‘How many a man who related this tradition has had the earth eat his tongue.’”

ʿAlī said: “I was told that he never slept without a lamp beside him. He was asked about it, and said, ‘When I remember the darkness of the grave, sleep does not come to me.’”

ʿAlī said: “Khālid ibn al-Ḥārith brought out for us the book of Hishām al-Dastawāʾī. He said, ‘He brought out for us Shuʿba’s book,’ and began to mention his merits.” He said: “Hishām al-Dastawāʾī’s kunya was Abū Bakr, and his father’s name was Sanbar.”

ʿAlī said: “I said to ʿAbd al-Raḥmān: ‘Abū ʿĀmir related to us, from Hishām, from Qatāda, from Saʿīd: “If a pilgrim in consecration kisses, he owes a sacrificial offering.”’ He rejected it and dismissed it. He said: ‘There is nothing of this sort. But when Muslim, al-Ḥawḍī, and these younger men brought it, it was just as Abū ʿĀmir had said.’”

ʿAlī said: “I said to Muʿādh ibn Hishām, concerning the tradition of Rifāʿa al-Juhanī, that he was ʿUrāba.

“He said: ‘No, in my father’s book it is ʿUrāda.’ He brought out the book, and I saw it; people say ʿUrāba al-Juhanī.”

ʿAlī said: “Al-Ḥusayn al-Juʿfī related to us, from Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ, who said: ‘I asked Sufyān about Abū Mālik.’ He said, ‘He was one of the jurists.’”

ʿAlī said: “The kunya of Sulaymān ibn Dīnār was Abū Ayyūb.”

ʿAlī said: “Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd said: ‘ʿAwf was uncertain about the tradition of Abū al-ʿĀliya, from Ibn ʿAbbās. He said, “I do not know whether it was ʿUbayd Allāh, al-Faḍl, or ʿAbd Allāh.”’”

ʿAlī said: “Ḥujr ibn Qays al-Madarī; and Abū Mawḍūd, from whom Sufyān al-Thawrī related, from al-Ḥasan, in Qurʾānic commentary, was Baḥr ibn Mūsā.”

He also said: “Khālid al-Ḥadhdhāʾ, from Abū Yaḥyā, who was ʿUmayr (42b) ibn Saʿīd al-Nakhaʿī. I asked him, ‘Did he meet him?’ He said, ‘Yes, he related more than one tradition from him.’”

ʿAlī said: “Among the companions of Ibn ʿAbbās, there is none like Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.” He was asked, “Nor Ṭāwūs?” He said, “Nor Ṭāwūs, nor anyone.”

ʿAlī said: “The name of Abū al-Zinbāʿ, from whom Abū Ḥayyān al-Taymī related, was Ṣadaqa ibn Ṣāliḥ; and Abū Sulayṭ al-Badrī was Asīra ibn ʿAmr. The Abū Ḥayyān who related from ʿAbd Allāh was named Mundhir al-Ashjaʿī. The name of Abū Khālid al-Wālibī was Hurmuz; Abū al-ʿAnbas was Saʿīd ibn Kathīr ibn ʿUbayd; and ʿUbayd, Abū Saʿīd, who was nursed by ʿĀʾisha, was related from by Ibn ʿAwn and Shuʿayb ibn al-Ḥabḥāb.”

ʿAlī said: “The name of Abū al-Jawzāʾ was Aws ibn ʿAbd Allāh, and the name of Abū al-ʿAjfāʾ al-Sulamī was Haram ibn Nasīb.” ʿAlī said: “ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī called him Haram and attributed him to a man from his people. Yaḥyā ibn al-Walīd ibn al-Musayyib al-Ṭāʾī was given the kunya Abū al-Zaʿrāʾ.”

“The name of Abū Miskīn, from whom Sufyān related, was al-Ḥurr. The name of Abū Bukayr was Marzūq al-Taymī. Abū Jaʿfar, from whom Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr relates, is the same man from whom ʿUthmān al-Barrī related. He is not Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī; he is an Anṣārī. The one who—”

“Thābit ibn ʿUbayd related from him, from Abū Jaʿfar, a man of the Anṣār. He is not the companion of Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr; he is someone else. This man saw Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq. The name of Abū Qays ibn Abī Ḥāzim was ʿAwf ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥārith.”

ʿAlī said: Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd related from Sufyān, from Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid, who said: “I saw Qays ibn Abī Ḥāzim asking for rain at the end of the prayer.”

ʿAlī said: “Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd said: Shuʿba said: ‘Qatāda heard only three traditions from Abū al-ʿĀliya.’ He mentioned the tradition about the thorn trees, the tradition of Ibn ʿAbbās, ‘Men of sound judgment bore witness to me,’ and the tradition of Ibn ʿAbbās, ‘No one should say, “I am better than Yūnus.”’”

ʿAlī said: “The name of Abū Thaʿlaba al-Khushanī was Jurhum ibn Nāshim.”

ʿAlī said: “Those who issued legal opinions were al-Ḥakam and Ḥammād. Among them, in the case of al-Zuhrī, Qatāda was the most learned in my view.”

ʿAlī said: “Abū Qutayba related from Shuʿba (43a), who said: ‘I asked Mushāsh, “Did al-Ḍaḥḥāk hear from Ibn ʿAbbās?” He said, “No, nor did he see him.”’”

Abū Qutayba said: “I said to Shuʿba: ‘Al-Barrī says, “Abū Isḥāq related to us; he said—”’”

“‘I heard Abū ʿUbayda; I heard ʿAbd Allāh.’ He said, ‘Oh! He was six years old!’”

ʿAlī said: “Shuʿba said: ‘Of all those who heard from ʿAlqama, only Abū Qays heard from him.’”

ʿAlī said: “Abū Isḥāq did not hear from ʿAlqama. He only saw him praying while wearing a mustaqa.”

“ʿAlī said: Yaḥyā used to complete the Qurʾān every day and night, between the sunset and night prayers.”

ʿAlī said: “The name of Abū al-Aswad was Ẓālim ibn ʿAmr, and Abū Ḥarb was his son.”

“ʿAlī said: I asked Yaḥyā, ‘Is Sufyān more reliable in the case of ʿAmr ibn Dīnār than Ibn Jurayj?’ He said, ‘Rather, Ibn Jurayj is more reliable.’

“ʿAlī said: I discussed Ibn Jurayj’s case in relation to ʿAmr with Sufyān, and he said: ‘He would pass by me and say, “You have certainly beaten us to ʿAmr’s cushion.”’”

“He said: ‘I never saw him ask him anything at all; he had finished before me.’”

ʿAlī said: “Yaḥyā said: ‘Hishām ibn ʿUrwa would not dictate, and he allowed me to write down only two traditions from him: the tradition about the pilgrimage, from his father, from ʿĀʾisha; and the tradition of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar: “God does not take knowledge away.”’

“Yaḥyā said: ‘There was a disagreement between Mālik and me about a tradition of Nāfiʿ, and this reached Hishām ibn ʿUrwa. When I came, he said, “Well now, Iraqi! What was the matter between you and Mālik?” What was between them was nothing much, so I said, “Nothing happened between me and him.”’”

ʿAlī said: “He said to me, ‘Do you mean by it—’ He said: ‘The dogs have had their fill of the lawful, while we have not had our fill of it this year.’”54

ʿAlī said: “He washed his clothes, put on the felt cloak of the door, and sat behind the door.”

ʿAlī said: “The name of Abū al-Jawzāʾ was Aws ibn ʿAbd Allāh, and Abū Ḥabra was Shayḥa ibn ʿAbd Allāh.”

ʿAlī said: “Yaḥyā said: ‘Among the scattered notes I had, from Saʿīd, from Qatāda, from Naṣr ibn ʿImrān, from Hilāl ibn Ḥiṣn, was the tradition of Abū Saʿīd.’”

(43b) I said to him: “Did Qatāda not hear it from Hilāl ibn Ḥiṣn?” He said: “No; Shuʿba heard it from Abū Jamra.”

ʿAlī said: “Ayyūb, from al-Qāsim al-Taymī ibn ʿĀṣim, from Zahdam ibn Muḍarrib al-Jarmī.”

ʿAlī said: “The name of Abū Rajāʾ al-ʿUṭāridī was ʿImrān ibn Taym. They also said: Milḥān.”

ʿAlī said: “Yaḥyā said: ‘Among the scattered notes I had was the tradition of ʿUbayd Allāh, from ʿUmar, ascribed to Nāfiʿ, the tradition of Dhū al-Yadayn.’”

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥīm related to me: “I asked ʿAlī, ‘Did Nāfiʿ hear from ʿĀʾisha?’ He said, ‘Not by any sound chain.’”

He said: “I asked ʿAlī about the name of Abū al-Malīḥ. He said: ‘ʿĀmir ibn Usāma ibn ʿUmayr al-Hudhalī.’”

ʿAlī said: “Ṭalḥa ibn Yaḥyā and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz were of the same age. He was born in the days when al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib was killed, in the time of Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya.”

“Al-Aʿmash and Hishām ibn ʿUrwa were born in the year sixty-one or sixty-two.”

He said: “I asked ʿAlī about the name of Abū Tamīma. He said: ‘Ṭarīf ibn Mujālid.’ The name of Abū Bakra was Nufayʿ ibn al-Ḥārith.”

ʿAlī said: “Nāfiʿ, Nufayʿ, and Ziyād were sons of Sumayya; they were brothers.”

ʿAlī said: “The name of Abū al-ʿAsharāʾ was Usāmah ibn Mālik ibn Qaḥṭam.” They said: “ʿUṭārid ibn Barz”. They also said: “Sayyār,” or “Abū Sayyār ibn Bilz.”

Ghālib, Abū al-Hudhayl, is the son of Hudhayl.

ʿAlī said: Sufyān said: “Ibn Ṭāwūs never narrated to us except from his father. So I wrote ‘from his father’ at the beginning of the book. Later I wrote ‘and he said,’ and: ‘The Messenger of God ﷺ said: “The maternal uncle inherits when there is no heir.”’” Maʿmar said: “This is Ibn Ṭāwūs, from a man of Medina.”

ʿAlī said: Yaḥyā said: “Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid told me, concerning the story of Ayman ibn Muḥayrīḍ, that my father and my uncle witnessed Badr with the Prophet ﷺ. I did not hear al-Shaʿbī from ʿĀmir.”

ʿAlī said: Misʿar was older than Shuʿbah, and al-Shaʿbī did not hear from ʿĀʾishah.

ʿAlī said: Shuʿbah said: “From ʿAmr ibn Murrah, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salamah”.

ʿAmr said: “Whenever I saw ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salamah, you would recognize and disapprove [of him]”. Shuʿbah would say: “I will throw him off my neck and put him on yours.”

ʿAlī said: Sufyān said: “Al-Aʿmash did not hear from Ibrāhīm the report of —the blind man who fell into the well, whereupon the Prophet ﷺ ordered whoever had laughed to perform ablution. He said: “I said to ʿAbd al-Raḥmān: ‘Hishām narrated it from al-Ḥasan.’ He said:

‘Ḥammād ibn Zayd narrated it to us from Hishām.’ Ḥammād said: ‘I mentioned that to Ḥafṣ, and he said: “I narrated it to al-Ḥasan from Ḥafṣah.”’ I said to ʿAbd al-Raḥmān: ‘Al-Zuhrī narrated it, too.’ He said: ‘I saw it in some books from Sulaymān ibn Arqam, from al-Ḥasan’. They know this report only through Abū al-ʿĀliyah.”

ʿAlī said: Sharīk said: “Abū Hāshim said: ‘I narrated it to Ibrāhīm from Abū al-ʿĀliyah.’”

ʿAlī said: Sufyān said: “Ibn Jurayj did not leave out anyone who narrated from ʿAṭāʾ except ʿAmrah.”

ʿAlī said: ʿAṭāʾ became confused in his later years, so Ibn Jurayj left him.

Regarding Qays ibn Saʿd, ʿAlī said: “Ḥammād ibn Salamah’s book from Qays ibn Saʿd was lost on the road to Mecca, and he wrote it down from memory.”

ʿAlī said: “I never heard Yaḥyā disclose to anyone that he had memorized something except three men: Ashʿath, Misʿar, and another whom he named.” Muḥammad Ṣāʿiqah said: “I have forgotten him.”

ʿAlī said: Muʿādh ibn Muʿādh narrated to us from Abū Ḥurrah, who said: “We used to visit al-Ḥasan. Ashʿath would come and sit close to him, and al-Ḥasan would say: ‘Bring your alms —and your possessions and your inheritance.’ Then he would ask him about matters he did not understand.”

ʿAlī said: “Furāt ibn al-Aḥnaf al-Hilālī. Aḥnaf was given the byname Abū Baḥr”.

ʿAlī said: “A Jarmī narrated from Shuʿbah, from Abū Isḥāq, from al-Sāʾib ibn Mālik. He said: Shuʿbah said: ‘He is Abū ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib.’”

ʿAlī was asked: “Did Ibn Abī Najīḥ hear the tafsīr from Mujāhid?” He said: “No.” Sufyān said: “No one heard it from Mujāhid except al-Qāsim ibn Abī Bazzah; Mujāhid dictated it to him. Al-Ḥakam, Layth, and Ibn Abī Najīḥ took his book.”

ʿAlī said: Sufyān said: “So-and-so ibn Muslim”—he named him—“said to me: ‘Tell Layth ibn Abī Sulaym to fear God and return al-Qāsim ibn Abī Bazzah’s book of Mujāhid’s tafsīr, for he does not sleep’.” I said to him: “Did Ibn Abī Najīḥ not hear the tafsīr?” He said:

“Yes. Mujāhid’s tafsīr is transmitted through al-Qāsim ibn Abī Bazzah.” (44b)

ʿAlī said: “Ibn Abī Najīḥ was a Muʿtazilī. Ayyūb said to me: ‘What a man they corrupted!’ He said he used to utter a vile, reprehensible statement.”

“ʿAlī said: ʿAbd al-Wahhāb ibn Hammām—the brother of ʿAbd al-Razzāq—narrated to us from Ibn Jurayj, who said: ‘I came to ʿAṭāʾ intending to pursue this field of knowledge. ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr was with him. ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUbayd said to me: “Have you read the Qurʾān?” I said: “No.” He said:

“Go and read the Qurʾān, then seek knowledge.” He said: “So I went away and stayed for a time, until I had read the Qurʾān. Then I came to ʿAṭāʾ, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUbayd was with him. He said: ‘Have you learned the Qurʾān?’ I said: ‘Yes.’ He said: ‘Have you learned the laws of inheritance?’ I said: ‘No.’ He said: ‘Then learn the laws of inheritance, and after that seek knowledge.’ So I studied the laws of inheritance, then came back. He said: ‘Have you learned the laws of inheritance?’ I said: ‘Yes.’ He said: ‘Now seek knowledge.’ So I stayed close to ʿAṭāʾ for seventeen years.’”

ʿAlī said: “Ibn Jurayj related that ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUbayd had heard nothing from his father and did not mention him. He said: ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr died before Ibn ʿUmar.”

Bishr ibn al-Mufaḍḍal said: Abū al-Muʿallā al-ʿAṭṭār said: “My age and that of al-Ḥasan al-ʿAranī are the same.”

ʿAlī said: “Zakariyyā ibn Abī Zāʾidah did not hear from Dāwūd ibn Abī Hind anything except a report from his father, from Dāwūd ibn Abī Hind: ‘There is no inheritance until a dower has preceded it.’”

ʿAlī said: Yaḥyā said: “Zakariyyā brought out three sheets for me: one sheet from his teachers, Saʿd ibn Ibrāhīm and others; one sheet from Jābir; and one sheet from ʿĀmir. I returned them to him and said: ‘Narrate to me what you have memorized.’ Regarding the report ‘A pledged animal may be ridden’, he said: ‘ʿĀmir narrated to us.’”

ʿAlī said: “I heard ʿAbd al-Raḥmān say: ‘When I first came to Shuʿbah, I was with him as he narrated a report. Ghundar leaned forward. Shuʿbah looked at him and said: “I missed you—you have heard all my hadith, and yet you lean forward for this one.”’”

He said: “I heard one of the hadith scholars say to Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb:

‘In a report of Shuʿbah over which they disagreed, what did Ghundar say?’

“Sulaymān said: ‘You fool! ʿAbd al-Raḥmān was too discerning to say that. He only said, “How?” in Ghundar’s book.’ Sulaymān said: ‘Ghundar used to say: “I heard—”’” (45a)

“—Shuʿbah’s hadith, and I read it to him.’ Sulaymān said: ‘The written version of his hadith was sound. As for him, it was as though he indicated it with a gesture; he did not understand this matter.’”

I said to Muḥammad ibn al-Muthannā: “Why did you not write down Ghundar’s books from Shuʿbah accurately?” He said: “Abū Yūsuf, Ghundar was forgetful. I would ask him for the book, and he would say to me: ‘You have heard this book, but you do not know it.’ I disliked arguing with him, out of regard for the hadith scholars, fearing that afterward I would be told: ‘Ghundar said you do not understand.’ So I missed it for that reason.”

ʿAlī said: “They are three brothers: ʿUbayd Allāh, ʿAwn, and Nājiya, sons of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUtbah ibn Masʿūd.”

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥīm said: “I asked ʿAlī about Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.” He said:

“It was said that he was forty-two years old.”

ʿAlī said: “Sufyān al-Thawrī and Ibn Jurayj met and discussed touching the penis. Ibn Jurayj said: ‘One must perform ablution because of it.’ Sufyān said: ‘One need not perform ablution because of it.’ Sufyān said to him: ‘What do you think a man must do if he holds semen in his hand?’ Ibn Jurayj said:

‘He must wash his hand.’ He said: ‘Which is greater, semen or touching the penis?’ Ibn Jurayj said: ‘Satan is the only one who put that on your tongue.’”

I said to ʿAlī: “Did al-Musayyib ibn Dārim hear from ʿUmar?” He said: “Yes.”

ʿAlī said: “The first to whom it was presented were Nāfiʿ and al-Zuhrī.”

ʿAlī said: “When something was presented to Sufyān, he would not change anything, because he did not consider it anything.”

ʿAlī said: “When Sufyān was asked about something, he would say: ‘I do not know.’”

He would be asked: “Whom should we ask?” He would say: “Ask the scholars, and ask God for success.”

ʿAlī said: “Al-Ṣabbāḥ ibn Mujāhid is reliable, the brother of ʿAbd al-Wahhāb ibn Mujāhid.”

ʿAlī said: “As for ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ, Abū Rabāḥ’s name was Aslam. He was the freedman of Ḥabībah bint Maysarah ibn Khaytham.”

ʿAlī said: Sufyān related from al-Hajarī, who said: “I used to see Mujāhid frequenting Abū ʿIyāḍ while he was a young man, learning from him.” (45b) “Then I later learned that he—that is, Abū ʿIyāḍ—had been a companion of ʿUmar.”

ʿAlī said: Muḥammad ibn ʿUyaynah said: “We were as prosperous as could be. We had camels that we used for watering, until people said, ‘This one’—meaning Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah.”

I heard Ḥammād ibn Ḥafṣ say: “ʿImrān was a money changer called ʿImrān al-Khāqānī. In the early period he was known for the Khāqānī dinars.”

“Al-Faḍl related to me, saying: I heard Abū ʿAbd Allāh Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal mention Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah. He said: ‘His father took him to Mecca when he was young, and he heard from people such as ʿAmr ibn Dīnār and Ibn Abī Najīḥ in jurisprudence. You cannot place him alongside anyone—meaning his peers—without finding him ahead of them.’”

“Al-Faḍl related to us: I heard Abū ʿAbd Allāh, and he was asked: ‘Does Yazīd ibn Hārūn have jurisprudence?’ He said: ‘Yes! How perceptive, intelligent, and understanding he was!’ He was asked: ‘And Ibn ʿUlayyah?’ He said:

‘He had jurisprudence, though I did not tell him my view of Yazīd ibn Hārūn. How comprehensive Yazīd’s qualities were! He was devoted to prayer, a memorizer, exacting in hadith, resolute, and sound in his method.’”

He was asked: “If only he had remained where he was.” He said: “Not everyone has everything brought together in him; inevitably, there is something [lacking]. He misread two words in a report of Hammām, from Maṭar, from Dukhayl. He said: ‘Dufayl.’ And in a report of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, he said: ‘ḥanṭan,’ whereas it is ‘ḥabṭan.’”

Abū Yaʿfūr the elder was Waqdān al-Kūfī. His son, Yūnus ibn Abī Yaʿfūr, heard from Ibn Abī Awfā.

Al-Thawrī, Shuʿbah, and Ibn ʿUyaynah heard from Muṣʿab ibn Saʿd.

Abū Yaʿfūr the younger was ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿUbayd ibn Nisṭās, an ʿĀmirī of Kūfah.

Saʿīd ibn Abī Ṣadaqah was Abū Qurrah.

“Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb and Ādam related to us. They said: Ḥammād ibn Salamah related to us from ʿĀṣim ibn Bahdalah, from Ḥabīb ibn Abī Jubayrah, from Yaʿlā ibn Sayyābah—who is Yaʿlā ibn Umayyah al-Thaqafī, Abū al-Marāzim. They say that Sayyābah was his mother.”

“He said: I heard Ibn Qaʿnab say: I heard Mālik ibn Anas say:

‘Yaʿlā ibn Umayyah is Yaʿlā ibn Munyah: Umayyah was his father and Munyah his mother.’”

Abū Nuʿaym and Qabīṣah related to us. They said: Sufyān related to us from Manṣūr (46a), from al-Shaʿbī, from al-Miqdād—Abū Nuʿaym said: “from Abī Karīmah al-Shāmī”—who said: “The Messenger of God ﷺ said: ‘A guest’s overnight stay is an obligatory right upon every Muslim. If the guest is still at his courtyard in the morning, it is a debt he owes; if he wishes, he may repay it, and if he wishes, he may leave it.’”

Ādam related to us: Shaybān related to us from Manṣūr, from al-Shaʿbī, from al-Miqdād Abū Karīmah al-Shāmī.

ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Muʿādh related to us: My father related to us: Shuʿbah related to us from Manṣūr. Al-Shaʿbī heard from al-Miqdām Abū Karīmah, a man from among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ibrāhīm related to us: Marwān al-Fazārī related to us: Yazīd—meaning Ibn Sinān Abū Farwah al-Jazarī—related to us: Abū Yaḥyā Sulaym al-Kalāʿī related to me: al-Miqdām ibn Maʿdīkarib said: We said to him, “Abū Karīmah, people claim that you did not see the Messenger of God ﷺ?” He said: “Indeed, by God, I saw him. He took hold of my earlobe while I was walking with my uncle.” He then said to my uncle:

“Do you think he remembers him?” We said: “Then tell us something you heard from the Messenger of God ﷺ.” He said: “I heard him say: ‘On the Day of Resurrection, the water of the miscarried fetus will be gathered to the aged man, at the age of thirty-three. The believers among them will be in Adam’s form, Joseph’s beauty, and Job’s heart: beardless, with kohl-rimmed eyes, and possessing afāfī’”. We said: “And what of the unbeliever, O Prophet of God?” He said: “He will be made to grow for the Fire until his skin is forty cubits [long], and until one of his teeth is like Mount Uḥud.”

The sound reading is al-Miqdām. As for Sufyān’s report, Abū Nuʿaym and Qabīṣah said “al-Miqdād.”

Abū Yūsuf said: Khallād ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Sufyān, from al-Miqdām ibn Maʿdīkarib al-Kindī. As for al-Miqdād, he is Ibn ʿAmr, the horseman of the Messenger of God ﷺ. He was [from] Bahra, an ally of Banū Zuhrah, and was under the guardianship of al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghūth. That is why those who said “al-Miqdād ibn al-Aswad” said so.

Muḥammad ibn Ṣāliḥ related to me: al-Walīd ibn Kāmil related to us from al-Muhallab ibn Ḥajar al-Bahrānī (46b), from Ḍubāʿah bint al-Miqdād, from her father, who said: “I saw the Messenger God’s Messenger ﷺ when he prayed toward a screen, placed it to his right or left, and did not stand in line with it. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yūsuf related to us: Muḥammad ibn Ḥumayd related to us: al-Walīd ibn Kāmil informed me, from al-Muhallab ibn Ḥajar, from Ḍubāʿah daughter of al-Miqdād ibn al-Aswad al-Bahrānī, from her father, that she heard him say: “I never saw the Messenger of God ﷺ”—and he mentioned something similar.

Muḥammad ibn al-Muṣaffā related to me: Baqiyyah related to us: al-Walīd ibn Kāmil related to us, from al-Muhallab ibn Ḥajar, from Ḍubāʿah daughter of al-Miqdād, from her father, something similar.

[Abū Nuʿaym al-Dārī and Abū Hind al-Dārī are said to have been brothers. Tamīm was given the kunya Abū Ruqayyah.

Abū ʿUmayr al-Ramlī informed me. He said: “Tamīm had no mention [of a son]; rather, he had a daughter named Ruqayyah, and he was given his kunya from her.”]

Khallād ibn Aslam related to me: al-Naḍr informed us: Shuʿbah related to us: Salamah related to us. He said: “I heard Abū Juḥayfah relate from the Prophet ﷺ that a man slaughtered before the prayer, so the Messenger of God ﷺ ordered him to replace it.”

[Al-Faḍl related to me. He said: Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal was asked, “Which do you prefer in hadith, Shuʿbah or Sufyān?” He replied: “Shuʿbah is nobler in his transmitters and more consistent in his hadith.”]

[He was asked: “Do you prefer al-Masʿūdī or Abū ʿUmays?” He replied: “Each of them is trustworthy.” Al-Haytham ibn Khārijah said to him: “Which of the two has more [hadith] in your view?” He replied: “Al-Masʿūdī had more hadith of the two.”]

[He was asked: “Do you prefer Ibn ʿAjlān or Ibn Abī Dhʾib?” He replied: “Both men are trustworthy; each of them is trustworthy.”]

Al-Haytham ibn Khārijah asked him: “Do you prefer Abū Dāwūd or Abū ʿUbaydah al-Ḥaddād?” He replied: “Abū Dāwūd had the better memory of the two, while Abū ʿUbaydah made few mistakes and had many written notes.”] [He was asked: “Was Sufyān al-Thawrī or Ibn ʿUyaynah the one with the better memory?” He replied:

“Al-Thawrī had the better memory and made fewer mistakes than anyone. As for Ibn ʿUyaynah, he had a good memory, except that when he dealt with the hadith of the Kūfans (74a), he made many mistakes; he also made mistakes in some matters concerning the hadith of the Ḥijāzīs.” He was asked: “So-and-so claims that Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah—”

“—had the better memory of the two.” He laughed, then said: “So-and-so thinks well of Ibn ʿUyaynah—and that is why!”]

He was asked about Jābir al-Juʿfī and Layth ibn Abī Sulaym. He replied: “Jābir was stronger in hadith of the two, and Layth had the better judgment of the two. People abandoned Jābir’s hadith only because of his poor judgment; he held bad opinions. As for Layth, his hadith is inconsistent, but he has sound judgment.”

It was said: “Al-Ḥajjāj?” He replied: “Ḥajjāj is the strongest of them in hadith, and in my view his hadith is acceptable.” He was asked: “Did Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd narrate from him?” He replied: “He did not narrate from any one of them. Al-Ḥajjāj ibn Arṭāʾah had seen him.” He was asked: “Did he see Layth?”

He replied: “No, but he did not narrate from Sufyān or anyone else from him.”

He was asked about Jābir and Ḥajjāj: “Which of the two do you prefer?” He lowered his head, then said: “I do not know [what] to tell you.” Abū Jaʿfar said to him: “Then what of Layth ibn Abī Sulaym?”

He replied: “He is below them, except that his hadith is inconsistent.” Then he said: “Shuʿbah narrated about seventy hadiths from Jābir, and Jābir’s hadith among them contains few reports attributed to the Prophet. He held bad opinions.” It was said: “Did ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī not omit Jābir’s hadith from his book?” He replied: “Rather, he narrated from him later. At first, about fifty reports reached us [from him], then he abandoned him.”

He was asked: “When the views of al-Zuhrī and Qatādah come together, which do you prefer?” He replied:

“Al-Zuhrī’s view is more pleasing to me.”

He mentioned al-Muthannā ibn al-Ṣabāḥ and said: “He heard from ʿAṭāʾ and Ṭāwūs, but he is not like Ibn Jurayj.”

He was asked about Ibn Abī Fudayk. He replied: “There is no harm in him.” He was asked: “Do you prefer him or Abū Ḍamrah?” He replied: “I do not know.”

He said: “Ashʿath ibn ʿAbd al-Malik is more firmly established than Ashʿath ibn Sawwār. He was a man of the Sunnah”—meaning Ashʿath ibn ʿAbd al-Malik.

He said: “Among al-Ḥasan’s companions, no one is more firmly established than Yūnus, and no one has a stronger chain of transmission from al-Ḥasan than Qatādah.” He said: “ʿAwf had been attending al-Ḥasan’s gatherings for longer than Yūnus.”

[He said: “No one transmitted more hadith from the Syrians than Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAyyāsh and al-Walīd ibn Muslim.”]

He was asked: “Whom do you rank highest among al-Shaʿbī’s companions?” He replied: “There is no one among them like Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid, then Muṭarrif—except for what concerns Mujālid, for he used to transmit often—”

—and was inconsistent.

He was asked: “Who transmitted more from Abū ʿUthmān al-Nahdī: al-Taymī or ʿĀṣim?”

He replied: “Muʿtamir had one hundred reports from his father, from Abū ʿUthmān, and I wrote down fifty of them from Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd.”

He was asked: “Which has more accurate hadith, Ḥammād or Abū Maʿshar?” He replied: “Ḥammād’s hadith is more accurate than Abū Maʿshar’s.”

I heard Abū ʿAbd Allāh say: “So-and-so related from Yaḥyā that Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr was more to his liking than Suhayl.” Abū ʿAbd Allāh said: “That is not how I see it.”

He was asked about what Maʿmar narrated from Thābit. He replied: “How excellent his hadith is!”

Then he said: “Ḥammād ibn Salamah is more to my liking. There is no one with regard to Thābit like Ḥammād ibn Salamah.” He said: “I used to visit him and say, ‘This man is a storyteller,’ then I would turn the hadith around on him and say, ‘How is—’”

“—this?” He would reply: “No, it is from so-and-so.”

He was asked about Hammām and Ḥammād. He replied: “Both are trustworthy.” He was asked: “Which of the two do you prefer?” He replied: “Both.” Then ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī said: “Hammām is like Saʿīd ibn Abī ʿArūbah in truthfulness.”

He was asked about Jarīr ibn Ḥāzim and Abū Hilāl. He replied: “No—Jarīr is a man of the Sunnah and has more hadith. As for Abū Hilāl, he does not retain them.” He said: “Jarīr made mistakes in some of Qatādah’s hadiths.”

[He was asked about Jarīr al-Rāzī and Abū ʿAwānah: “Which of the two do you prefer?” He replied:

“Abū ʿAwānah, when using his book.”]

He was asked about ʿAbdah and Ḥafṣ. He replied: “ʿAbdah is more firmly established. As for Ḥafṣ, he used to confuse his hadith.” He said: “ʿAbdah was a righteous, trustworthy man. He would teach the Qurʾān and transmit hadith. We came to him while a boy was sitting before him, writing as he dictated. Then he would say to the boy:

‘Read.’ The boy could not read well, so he would say, ‘Erase it.’ The boy would erase it, and he would dictate to him. This can only be from someone whom God has guided. He was poor and patient, and he wore a worn-out fur coat that was worth almost nothing.”

He was asked about Zuhayr and Zāʾidah. He replied: “These are trustworthy—”

“—Shuʿbah, Zāʾidah, Sufyān, and Zuhayr.” He said: “I heard Ṣadaqah ibn al-Faḍl say:

‘Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd thought poorly of Zuhayr and used to say: “That man is a hypocrite.”’”

Al-Faḍl said: Abū ʿAbd Allāh was asked about Bishr ibn al-Mufaḍḍal. He replied: “Yes.”

He was asked: “Khālid ibn al-Ḥārith?” He replied: “Khālid is superior.”

He said: “I heard Abū ʿAbd Allāh say: ‘Yaḥyā is several degrees above Ismāʿīl in every respect.’”

[He was asked about Sharīk and Isrāʾīl in relation to Abū Isḥāq: “Which do you prefer?”

He replied: “I prefer Sharīk [because Sharīk heard from Abū Isḥāq earlier]. As for the shaykhs, [I prefer] Isrāʾīl.”] [Abū ʿAwānah was asked: “Is he more firmly established, or Sharīk?” He replied:

“When Abū ʿAwānah transmits from his book, he is more firmly established; when he transmits without his book, he may make mistakes.” ʿAffān said: “Abū ʿAwānah’s book was sound; it had many vowel marks and dots. It was labatan.”] [He was asked: “Then Sharīk or Isrāʾīl?” He replied: “Isrāʾīl transmitted as he had heard it; he was more firmly established than Sharīk. Sharīk cannot be measured by analogy; he would transmit hadith from conjecture.”] [He said: “Sharīk was older than Sufyān.”]

He said: “Abū ʿAwānah has transmitted more from Abū Bishr than Shuʿbah and Hushaym have, across all the hadith. Abū ʿAwānah’s book is sound, and the reports of Yaḥyā are in it; he gives the hadith at its full length, while Hushaym has the better memory and shortens the hadith. Abū ʿAwānah gives it at length, so in every respect his hadith is more accurate in our view than Hushaym’s—except that, toward the end of his life, he used to read from other people’s books and read errors. When he used his own book, he was reliable.”]

I heard Abū ʿAbd Allāh, and Abū Jaʿfar asked him: “Which do you prefer, Mūsā ibn ʿUbaydah or Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq?” He replied: “No—Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq.” I asked him: “Did Shuʿbah narrate from Mūsā ibn ʿUbaydah?” He replied: “Yes.” Abū Jaʿfar said: “Shuʿbah says, ‘from Abū ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz al-Rabadhī.’” He replied: “Yes. Shuʿbah did not narrate any rejected hadith from him.” Abū Jaʿfar said: “Did al-Thawrī also narrate from him?” He replied: “Yes.” Abū Jaʿfar said to him: “Al-Fāryābī makes many mistakes. How sound Muḥammad ibn Kathīr’s hadith is!” Al-Fāryābī was a righteous man. He said: “Muḥammad ibn Kathīr heard from him in Mecca.” (48b)

[He said: “I asked Abū ʿAbd Allāh about Abū Shihāb and Ismāʿīl ibn Zakariyyā. He replied: ‘Both are trustworthy. Ismāʿīl had been transmitting earlier than Mughīrah and Abū Farwah, except that Abū Shihāb seemed to be—’”]

I asked Abū ʿAbd Allāh: “When Wakīʿ and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān disagree over a position, whose do you accept?” He replied: “ʿAbd al-Raḥmān is more often in agreement, especially concerning Sufyān; he was particularly attentive to Sufyān’s hadith.”]

He said: “I heard Abū ʿAbd Allāh mention the hadith of Manṣūr, from Mujāhid, that ʿUmar said to his camel driver: ‘Do not allude to women in your singing.’ He said: ‘They differed over it. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and others said it was from Ibn ʿUmar, while Wakīʿ said that ʿUmar had said it to his camel driver.’”

I was told that ʿAbd Allāh ibn Dāwūd agreed with ʿAbd al-Raḥmān.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Sufyān related to us, from Manṣūr, from Mujāhid, who said: “It was—”

ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, when he heard the camel driver. He said: “ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb used to forbid the camel driver from alluding to women in his singing while he was in a state of consecration.”

Ibn Bashshār related to us: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to us: Sufyān related to us, from Manṣūr, from Mujāhid, who said: “Ibn ʿUmar used to forbid the camel driver from alluding to women in his singing while he was in a state of consecration.”

Bunḍār related to us: Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd related to us, from Sufyān, from Manṣūr, from Mujāhid, from Ibn ʿUmar, the same report.

[Al-Faḍl related to me. He said: I asked Abū ʿAbd Allāh: “How was ʿUbaydah?” He replied:

“How excellent his hadith is! He is more to my liking than Ziyād ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Bakkāʾī.”]

[I was told that Ibn Maʿīn said: “Ziyād al-Bakkāʾī is nothing, though I wrote down the Maghāzī from him.”]

Al-Faḍl related to me. He said: I asked Abū ʿAbd Allāh: “Was there anyone in al-Yamāmah ranked above ʿIkrimah ibn ʿAmmār, such as Ayyūb ibn ʿUtbah, Mulāzim ibn ʿAmr, and these men?”

He replied: “ʿIkrimah is above these men”—or something to that effect. Then he said: “Shuʿbah narrated from him—”

“... hadiths.”

Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Ḥasan related to me, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī, who said:

“I went with Sufyān al-Thawrī to ʿIkrima ibn ʿAmmār. I found that his writing was difficult to read and poor, so I said, ‘Shall I write it out for you, Abū ʿAbd Allāh?’ He replied, ‘No. I would like it to be in my own handwriting.’”

Al-Faḍl related to me and said: I asked Abū ʿAbd Allāh, “Al-Aswad ibn ʿĀmir, from Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh, from Hishām, from Ibn Sīrīn, from Abū Hurayra, from the Prophet ﷺ—[reports that] the sun was never held back—or made to return—for anyone except Yūshaʿ ibn Nūn.” He said, “Yes, that is how it is, or something like that.” I asked, “Did anyone besides al-Aswad transmit it from Abū Bakr?” He said, “I have heard it only from al-Aswad.”

Then Abū ʿAbd Allāh said: “Abū Bakr is inconsistent in the hadiths of these younger men. As for his hadiths from those older men, how close he is [in his transmission] from Abū Ḥuṣayn and ʿĀṣim—though he is inconsistent from Abū Isḥāq, or something like that.” Then he said: “He is not like Zāʾida, Zuhayr, and Sufyān. Sufyān was above these men and had the best memory.”

He said: “I asked Abū ʿAbd Allāh, ‘Do you regard Ibn Fuḍayl as on a par with ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Mūsā?’ He said, ‘No. Ibn Fuḍayl was more discreet, while ʿUbayd Allāh was given to confusion and transmitted objectionable hadiths.’ I asked, ‘And is Abū Nuʿaym on a par with them?’ He said:

‘No. Abū Nuʿaym was alert in hadith and took a stand in the affair’—meaning the inquisition.”

Dāwūd ibn Qays was like Ibn ʿAjlān in reliability, and Abū al-Khayr had more [hadiths] than Hishām ibn Saʿd.

He said: “I asked him about Ayyūb ibn Mūsā. He said, ‘Ayyūb was a Meccan Qurashī, a cousin of Ismāʿīl ibn Umayya. Mālik transmitted from Ayyūb, but transmitted nothing from Ismāʿīl.

“‘Ismāʿīl was older than him and more favored by me.’

“He said: ‘Yūnus ibn Abī Isḥāq’s hadith contains additions beyond what others have. I asked him, “They say that the others heard from Abū Isḥāq by heart, while Yūnus, his son, heard from books, so his transmission is more complete.” He said, “How so? Isrāʾīl, his son, heard from Abū Isḥāq and wrote...”’”

“... and he alone [heard and wrote it], so there was no addition in it as there was in Yūnus’s. I asked, ‘Which do you prefer, Yūnus or Isrāʾīl, in [their transmission] from Abū Isḥāq?’ He said, ‘Isrāʾīl.’ I asked, ‘Do you prefer Isrāʾīl to Yūnus?’ He said, ‘Yes. Isrāʾīl is a man of books.’”

He said: “I heard Abū ʿAbd Allāh say: ‘Al-Aʿmash and Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb were clients, whereas Abū Ḥuṣayn was an Arab. Had that not been so, they would not have treated al-Aʿmash as they did. He had few hadiths, and his hadiths were sound.’ He was asked, ‘Which of the two had sounder hadiths, he or Abū Isḥāq?’ He said, ‘Abū Ḥuṣayn had sounder hadiths, because he had few of them. Likewise, Manṣūr had sounder hadiths than al-Aʿmash, because he had few of them.’ He said: ‘Nāfiʿ ibn ʿUmar is more pleasing to me than Ibn Khuthaym, though Ibn Khuthaym is acceptable.’ Of Ibn al-Qaṭṭān and Abū Hilāl he said, ‘How closely matched they are.’ I asked, ‘Which do you prefer, Juwaybir or Kathīr?’ He said, ‘Juwaybir. He transmitted from al-Ḍaḥḥāk some fine hadiths on Qurʾanic exegesis. So long as a report is not ascribed to the Prophet ﷺ—there is no harm in his hadith.’ I asked Abū ʿAbd Allāh, ‘Which do you prefer, Bishr ibn Ḥarb or Abū Hārūn al-ʿAbdī?’ He said, ‘Bishr ibn Ḥarb.’”

Al-Faḍl related to me: Muḥammad ibn Ḥumayd al-Rāzī related to us, saying: I heard Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal say, “ʿAnbasa ibn Saʿīd has sounder hadiths than Abū Jaʿfar al-Rāzī.”

Abū Ṭālib said: Abū ʿAbd Allāh was asked about the hadiths of Khuṣayf. He said: “Among the hadith scholars, ʿAbd al-Karīm is held in higher regard than him, and is more firmly established in hadith than Khuṣayf. Sālim al-Afṭas is stronger in hadith than Khuṣayf. ʿAbd al-Karīm is a man of the Sunna, but he is not above Sālim. Khuṣayf is the weakest of them—and Shanaj between ʿUyayna—weakens him.” He was asked about Fiṭr and Maḥall. He said: “Fiṭr was excessive in his Shiʿism, and Maḥall had few hadiths. Fiṭr had more hadiths, and Maḥall was blind and reliable.”

He said: “Sulaymān ibn Burayda is more reliable than ʿAbd Allāh ibn Burayda.”

He said: “And Wakīʿ said, ‘Sulaymān’s hadiths were considered sounder among them.’”

He said: “I wrote to Abū ʿAbd Allāh asking him about al-Zuhrī and al-Shaʿbī: which of the two he preferred when they differed, and which of the two was more knowledgeable. The reply came to me: ‘Both are learned. If al-Zuhrī heard the hadith from the Prophet ﷺ—then one follows him, and he is the one we prefer. If al-Shaʿbī heard the hadith and al-Zuhrī did not, then he is the one we prefer.’”

Abū Ṭālib said: Abū ʿAbd Allāh said: “I prefer al-Ḥakam transmitting from Ibrāhīm to al-Aʿmash transmitting from Ibrāhīm.” He also said: “Sharīk was earlier than Isrāʾīl and Zuhayr, because he was the oldest of them.”

I heard Abū ʿAbd Allāh say: “ʿAffān would hear in the morning and recite back in the evening.”

I asked Abū ʿAbd Allāh about Muṭarrif, and he said: “They used to give him precedence over Mālik’s companions.”

Abū Yūsuf said: “Muṭarrif had once come to Mecca to perform the lesser pilgrimage. His lodging was near al-Ḥumaydī’s, so I went to him. Al-Ḥumaydī met me and asked, ‘Where are you going?’

“I said, ‘To Muṭarrif, to read the Muwaṭṭaʾ.’ He said, ‘Did you not hear the Muwaṭṭaʾ from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Maslama ibn Qaʿnab?’ I said, ‘Yes, I heard it.’ He said, ‘Go back to circumambulating [the Kaʿba] and do not occupy yourself with it.’ I walked back with him toward the mosque. He said, ‘Ibn Qaʿnab preferred hearing [a text read aloud] to having it read to him. When hearing was not possible or practicable for him, the least he could do was to establish the text by recitation before Mālik. And,’ I said—or he said to me—‘he was the one who read it to Mālik. The people of Medina regard recitation before the teacher as equivalent to hearing, and they are also lenient about recitation.’ I said to him:

“‘I heard from Ibn Abī Uways’s waqf.’ He asked him, ‘When you say, “Mālik related to me,” did you hear it from him?’ He said, ‘No, but it was read to him. Sometimes I would be inside the room while it was being read to Mālik outside the room, and that was considered sufficient.’ Al-Ḥumaydī said, ‘That is the same as what I told you.’ For this reason, he kept me from hearing the Muwaṭṭaʾ from Muṭarrif, as I have related.”

Al-Faḍl related to me, saying: I heard Abū ʿAbd Allāh, and he was asked, “Who is [the leading scholar] in Medina today?”

He said, “Ibn Abī Uways is learned and has much knowledge,” or something to that effect.

He said: I heard Salama say: “I was present when Mālik’s questions were read to Ibn Abī Uways. They were read to him—[there is] doubt about Ibn Wahb—or something like that.” I mentioned this to Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, and he said, “There is no need for this. Ibn Abī Uways is reliable, and he took a praiseworthy stand in the affair of— “... the inquisition; he took a praiseworthy stand in it.”

Salama said: “I said to Aḥmad, ‘I went looking for ʿAffān at your house, and they said he had gone out. I went out to ask the neighbors about him, and they said he had headed in this direction. I said, “I’ll go and ask after him until I’m directed to him.” I went on until I reached a cemetery, and there he was, sitting and reciting over the grave of the daughter of my brother, Dhū al-Riʾāsatayn. I got down to him and said, “Shame on you!”

“He replied, “Man, the bread, the bread!” I said, “May God never let your belly be full.”’ Aḥmad said to me:

“‘There is no need for that. Do not mention it. He took a praiseworthy stand in the inquisition—or something to that effect.’”

Salama said: “I asked Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal about Muḥammad ibn Muʿāwiya al-Naysābūrī. He said to me, ‘Yaḥyā ibn Yaḥyā al-Naysābūrī is an excellent man.’”

He said: “I mentioned Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr to him, and he praised him highly and made much of his standing. I had heard Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb—in Mecca—censure him from time to time over one thing or another. Al-Ḥumaydī did likewise. Relations between him and al-Ḥumaydī were not good, and al-Ḥumaydī would find fault from time to time with the things he transmitted from Sufyān.

“I heard Saʿīd say: ‘Do not ask me about the hadiths of Ḥammād ibn Zayd, for Abū Ayyūb puts us all on the same level. And do not ask me about the hadiths of Sufyān, for this...’”

“... al-Ḥumaydī puts us all on the same level.”

He said: “I heard Saʿīd say: ‘Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna used to say, “You should stick to the earlier hearing—the material you heard from me earlier.”’”

He said: “I heard al-Ḥumaydī say: ‘I was in Egypt, where Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr had a circle in the mosque. The people of Khurāsān and Iraq would gather around him. I sat with them, and they mentioned one of Sufyān’s teachers. They asked, “How many hadiths would he have?” I said, “Such-and-such a number.” Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr drew himself in and objected to that, and Ibn Daysam objected to me even more strongly. I turned to Saʿīd and asked, “How many do you remember from Sufyān, from him?” He named half the number I had given. I turned to Ibn Daysam and asked, “How many do you remember from Sufyān, from him?” He named more than Saʿīd had, about two-thirds of the number I had given. I said to Saʿīd:

“‘Do you remember what you wrote down from Sufyān, from him?’ He said, ‘Yes.’ I said, ‘Then recite it and count it.’ Then I said to Ibn Daysam, ‘Count what you wrote down from Sufyān, from him.’ Saʿīd had some hadiths that were unfamiliar to Ibn Daysam, and Ibn Daysam had many hadiths that were unfamiliar to Saʿīd. So it turned out that hadiths had escaped them both, which they had forgotten. I mentioned the ones they had missed, and I saw embarrassment and shame on their faces.’”

Al-Faḍl related to me, saying: I heard Abū ʿAbd Allāh (51a), and he was asked, “Who is in Mecca?”

He said, “Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr.”

He said: I heard Abū ʿAbd Allāh, and he was asked, “Who is in Kufa from whom one may write down hadith?”

He said, “Their leading scholar today is Ibn Yūnus”—meaning Aḥmad ibn Yūnus.

He said: “I heard Aḥmad, and a man asked him, ‘From whom do you recommend that we write down hadith?’

“He said to him, ‘Go to Aḥmad ibn Yūnus, for he is the shaykh of Islam.’” A man said to him, “Abū al-Walīd and Musaddad send you their greetings.” Abū ʿAbd Allāh said, “May God keep Musaddad well; may God keep Musaddad well.” The man said, “I will convey your greetings to them both.” Abū ʿAbd Allāh said, “Convey my greetings to Musaddad.” The man said to him, “Abū al-Walīd, Abū al-Walīd, Abū ʿAbd Allāh!” Abū ʿAbd Allāh said, “Indeed, by my life, he is the shaykh of Islam, but I want him to hear about it. He had heard that he transmitted to Ibn Riyāḥ, and ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī had written about him.”

He said: “Salama ibn Nubayṭ is reliable. Ibn Shawdhab was from Balkh, settled in Baṣra, where he heard and wrote [hadith], then moved to Syria. He was one of the reliable men.”

He said: “Abū ʿAbd Allāh said: ‘In Baghdad, there were no hadith scholars—and they did not accept transmissions from just anyone—who lacked discernment in hadith and its transmitters. They wrote only from reliable men and did not write from anyone they did not approve of, except Abū Salama al-Khuzāʿī, al-Haytham ibn Jamīl, and Abū Kāmil. Abū Kāmil had discernment...’”

“... in hadith, was careful about people’s suspicions, spoke only when asked, then answered and fell silent. He had sound judgment. Al-Haytham had the best memory among them, and Abū Salama was among the people most knowledgeable about the histories of men. You could ask him about anyone and he would tell you what he knew of him. He was also learned in jurisprudence.”

I heard ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī say: Muḥammad ibn Khāzim said: “I was reading al-Aʿmash’s hadiths from Abū Ṣāliḥ to the Commander of the Faithful, Hārūn. Whenever I said, ‘The Messenger of God ﷺ—said,’ he would say, ‘May God bless my master and lord.’ Then I mentioned the report ‘Adam and Moses met.’ He said—and his uncle—ʿAlī named him, then ʿAlī left—said, ‘Muḥammad, where did they meet?’ Hārūn became angry and said, ‘Who put this into your head?’ He ordered that I be arrested. He appointed one of his retinue to bring me to him in prison. He said, ‘Muḥammad, by God, it was nothing more than something that occurred to me. He swore to me by manumission, by giving away wealth, and by other solemn oaths that he had not heard it from anyone, nor had he discussed it with anyone; it was nothing more than something that had occurred to him.’ When I returned to the Commander of the Faithful, I spoke to him. He said, ‘He must tell me who put these words into his head.’ I said, ‘Commander of the Faithful, he has sworn by manumission and by solemn oaths that it was only something that occurred to him, and that he had not discussed it with anyone.’ He ordered that he be released from prison. He said to me, ‘Muḥammad, woe to you...’”

“I only suspected that some heretics had put into his head this statement that came from him, so that he might point them out to me and I could declare them lawful to kill. Otherwise, I am certain that no Qurashī becomes a heretic.” He said this, or words to this effect.

I heard ʿAlī say: “When I was in Mecca during the time of Sufyān, whenever something came to me that I could not understand, I had no recourse but to Abū Saʿīd, the client of the Banū Hāshim. Whenever I turned to him about something, I found knowledge and an explanation from him.”

Al-Faḍl told me: Abū ʿAbd Allāh said: “Wuhayb was a hadith scholar and a memorizer. He died long ago.”

“He said: ‘Layth ibn Saʿd was very learned and sound in hadith.’”

“He said: ‘I heard Ibn Bukayr say: Layth ibn Saʿd said: “I was in Medina when the pilgrims arrived. The city had a great deal of animal droppings and manure, so I used to wear leather socks. When I reached the mosque door, I would take one off and enter the mosque. Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Anṣārī said: ‘Do not do that, for you are a leading figure whom people observe.’”’”

[ʿAbd Allāh ibn Wahb]

Al-Faḍl told me: Aḥmad said: “ʿAbd Allāh ibn Wahb’s books are sound with respect to the shaykhs from whom he transmitted. He distinguishes direct audition from reading [to a shaykh]. How sound and reliable his hadith is!” He was asked: “Did he not take material poorly?” He said: “He was poor at acquiring material accurately, but when you examine his hadith and what he transmitted from his shaykhs, you find it sound.”

“I heard al-Ḥumaydī say: ‘I used to see Ibn Wahb come to Sufyān. Sufyān lived in a rented house with a long staircase. I would see Ibn Wahb stand at the staircase and say to Sufyān: “Abū Muḥammad, this is what my nephew heard from you; will you authorize me to transmit it?” Sufyān would say: “Yes.”’”

He said: “I saw Ibn Wahb with Jarīr al-Rāzī. Jarīr was reclining, asleep and heavy with sleep, and Ibn Wahb was asleep, heavy with sleep. His scribe, al-Aṣbagh ibn Faraj, was reading to Jarīr, racing through the reading like an arrow, while Jarīr slept and Ibn Wahb slept. Ibn Wahb used to come each year. Al-Ḥuwayṭī said to him: ‘Bring with you the book of Yūnus and that of ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥārith so we can examine them.’ When he arrived, he said to al-Ḥuwayṭī: ‘Qurashī, I have brought the book of Yūnus and the book of ʿAmr.’ He stayed until the time of the ʿumrah. I used to say to al-Ḥuwayṭī: ‘Come with us to him.’ He would say: ‘Spare me this uncomfortable situation,’ and he did not examine them.

“Then he came the following year and said: ‘I have brought the two books.’ He did not examine them until three years had passed…”

“‘He said: “Qurashī, you have kept these two books from me for three years. If you do not examine them and make a copy, I will not let you keep them from me any longer than you already have.” He said: “So we examined them and copied some of them, bit by bit.”’”

[ʿAbd Allāh ibn Lahīʿah]

“He said: ‘I heard Aḥmad ibn Ṣāliḥ say: “I wrote down the hadith of Ibn Lahīʿah from Abū al-Aswad on parchment. He said: ‘I used to write from our companions on sheets of paper and seek God’s guidance about it. I wrote down Ibn Lahīʿah’s hadith from al-Naḍr on parchment, and I asked him about his audition of the hadith. He said: “Ibn Lahīʿah was eager for knowledge and had sound books. Long ago he dictated his hadith to them from his book. Some people who understood hadith wrote it down from him, while others did not retain it accurately. Some attended but did not write it down, then wrote it after hearing it. Thus his knowledge came down to people in this form. Later, his books were no longer available, and he would read from other people’s books; so his hadith came down to people in this form. Whoever wrote from a sound book that had been read to him, wrote it down correctly. Whoever wrote from the book of someone who did not retain it accurately or check his book, got a corrupt original. He had heard from ʿAṭāʾ through one intermediary and through two intermediaries, but people would omit the one or two intermediaries and make it directly from ʿAṭāʾ himself; then he would read it to them as they presented it.” He said: “I thought that Abū al-Aswad had copied from a sound book, so his hadith is sound and resembles the hadith of the scholars…”’”

“‘…of knowledge.’”

I heard Ibn Abī Maryam say: “The books of Ḥaywah ibn Shurayḥ were with a trustee to whom he had entrusted them. Some people would go and copy those books, then bring the copies to Ibn Lahīʿah, and he would read them to them.”

“He said: ‘I was present with Ibn Lahīʿah when a group of our companions, who had made the pilgrimage and returned, came to him to greet him. He said: “Have you written down any unusual hadith?”

“They began reminding him of what they had written until one of them said: ‘Al-Qāsim al-ʿUmarī told us, from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet ﷺ—who said: “When you see a fire, proclaim God’s greatness.”’ Ibn Lahīʿah said: ‘That is an unusual hadith. How did he transmit it to you?’ He told him how. They then inserted it into the hadith of ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, and whenever they came to it they would say: ‘So-and-so, our companion, told us this.’ As this went on, the shaykh forgot. The hadith would be read to him, and he would authorize it and transmit it as part of his hadith from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb.’”

Al-Faḍl told me: “I heard Abū ʿAbd Allāh being asked about Ibn Lahīʿah. He said:

“Whoever wrote from him early on, his audition is sound.”

He said: “I heard that Ibn al-Mubārak said here in Baghdad, in the year seventy-nine: ‘Whoever has been writing from Ibn Lahīʿah for twenty years is worthless.’”

[Rishdīn ibn Saʿd]

He said: “I heard the shaykhs of Egypt say: ‘Among us, Rishdīn ibn Saʿd al-Mahrī was one of the abdāl [spiritual substitutes].’”

He said: “I heard Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr say: ‘I had taken some of his books from him to copy them and hear them from him, but then I grew too lazy to do so.’ He said: ‘He would come to the Qaysāriyyah and say to our companions: “One of you has taken a book of ours and is not returning it to us.”’ He also mentioned that Rishdīn was sound in character and intelligent.”

I discussed Rishdīn ibn Saʿd with Saʿīd ibn Abī Maryam. He said: “Rishdīn ibn Saʿd had merit and diligence”—and he praised him highly—“except that he was lax about shaykhs.” I said to him—or someone else said to him—“You do that too.” He said: “Not in every case. I saw him come to Ibrāhīm ibn Abī Yaḥyā carrying in his cloak sheets in great number and say: ‘Man, authorize me to transmit these, for they are from your hadith.’ Ibn Abī Maryam said: “He replied: ‘Shaykh, how am I to know what is in these sheets?’” Saʿīd said: “I was astonished”—meaning, astonished at Ibn Abī Yaḥyā’s baseness, malice, and contempt in refusing Rishdīn. I said: “What did you see of Ibrāhīm’s baseness and contempt?” He said: “Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Hāshimī told me—and he was a companion of ours and a man of considerable learning—‘I spoke with Ibn Abī Yaḥyā about the superiority of Abū Bakr and ʿUmar.

“He said: ‘Leave me out of this. By God, young man, you are better than Abū Bakr and ʿUmar.’””

Ibn Abī Dhiʾb transmitted from ʿUtbah ibn ʿAmr—who is Ibn ʿAyyāsh ibn Abī Lahab—from Abū Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ: “The dead person is punished because of the living person’s weeping.” Ibn Qaʿnab and Ibn Bukayr transmitted to us from Mālik ibn Anas.

Abū Ṣāliḥ transmitted to us from al-Layth. He said:

Al-Ḥumaydī transmitted to us from al-Darāwardī, from “Yazīd ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Usāmah [ibn] al-Hādī, who was Medinan, reliable, and good in hadith; he transmitted from both younger and older narrators,” who transmitted from Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad and Ibn al-Munkadir, and nine hadiths from Ibrāhīm ibn Saʿd. Saʿd ibn Ibrāhīm has eighteen like them.

[Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid]

Ibn Numayr transmitted to us: Ismāʿīl transmitted to us from al-Nuʿmān, who said: “When ʿAlī was invited to a funeral, he would say: ‘We are indeed standing, but nothing intercedes for a person except his deeds.’”

He said: Abū Khālid transmitted to us from Ismāʿīl, from Ashʿath, from Abū…

ʿUbaydah said: “ʿAbd Allāh said: ‘Whoever among you can put his treasure in heaven, where thieves cannot reach it and moths cannot eat it, even if all his affairs are turned upside down, should do so.’”

Ibn Numayr told me, saying: Muʿāwiyah ibn ʿAmr transmitted to us from Zāʾidah: Ismāʿīl transmitted to us: “My brother Nuʿmān told us: ‘Ḥamzah ibn al-Mughīrah used to pass by us while we were in the ranks and say: “Let your battle cry be ‘They will not be helped’”—a supplication of your Prophet ﷺ.’”

Qabīṣah transmitted to us: Sufyān transmitted to us from Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid, from his father, who said:

“I saw al-Ḥasan—or al-Ḥusayn—come out of the bathhouse and then go in to have the henna stain removed from his nails.”

Ibn Numayr transmitted to us: Muḥammad ibn Bishr transmitted to us: Ismāʿīl transmitted to us: My brother Nuʿmān told me, from Muṣʿab ibn Saʿd, from Ḥafṣah daughter of ʿUmar, who said to her father:

“Commander of the Faithful, what would be wrong with you wearing something softer than this garment of yours, or eating food better than this food of yours? God has opened up the land to you and expanded your provision.” He said: “I will argue with you using your own words. Do you not know what the Messenger of God ﷺ—used to endure of hardship in life?” He began reminding her of what the Prophet ﷺ—used to endure until he made her weep. He said: “I have told you that I had two companions who followed a path. If I follow a path other than theirs, I will be led away from their path. By God, I will share in the harshness of their life, so that perhaps I may attain with them their comfortable life.”

Ismāʿīl said: “By ‘his two companions’ he meant the Prophet ﷺ—and Abū Bakr.”

Al-Ḥumaydī transmitted to us: Sufyān transmitted to us: Ismāʿīl transmitted to us from his brother, from Abū ʿUbaydah, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, who said: “Whoever among you can put his treasure where thieves cannot reach it and moths cannot eat it, let him do so.”

Al-Ḥumaydī said: “Al-Fazārī named his brother al-Ashʿath for us.”

Al-Ḥumaydī transmitted to us: Sufyān transmitted to us: Ismāʿīl transmitted to us: “I used to ask al-Shaʿbī questions and hear from him. When he saw my eagerness, he would say: ‘Wa-yuhīl ibn Abī Khālid, and knowledge has been infused into me.’”

He said: Sufyān transmitted to us: Ismāʿīl transmitted to us from his father, who said: “I came to Medina and stayed with Abū Hurayrah, who was related to his clients. He would lead the people in prayer and make it brief. I said: ‘Abū Hurayrah, was this how the Messenger of God ﷺ—prayed?’

“He said: ‘Yes, and he made it even briefer.’

“From Ismāʿīl, from his father, who said: ‘I heard Abū Hurayrah say that the Messenger of God ﷺ—said: “When one of you has sufficiently provided for his servant…”’ And from his father, who said: ‘I came to al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī to collect a debt from him and found that he had come out of the bathhouse. A servant girl of his was removing the henna stain from his nails with a flask. I came to al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī to collect what he owed me. He said: “Girl, bring it here.” She brought him some dirhams in a bowl, and he said:

“‘Count them.’ I counted until I had received what was owed to me. He said: ‘Eighty dirhams remained in my hand, and he said: “They are yours.” I said: “Pray for blessing for me.” He prayed for blessing for my wealth, my children, and my family.’

“Ibn Abī Khālid said: ‘We still know the effects of that prayer.’”

Al-Ḥumaydī transmitted to us: Sufyān transmitted to us: Ismāʿīl transmitted to us from his mother and sister, who said: “We were with ʿĀʾishah among some women from Kūfah. A woman there was sewing a bedcover. ʿĀʾishah said: ‘Did you invoke God Most High over it?’ She said: ‘No.’ ʿĀʾishah said: ‘Undo it, so that you can pronounce God’s name over it.’”

Through the same chain, from his mother and sister, who said: “We went in to ʿĀʾishah, and a woman asked her about a woman in the state of consecration covering her face with a headcloth. ʿĀʾishah took the edge of her garment from the top of her chest and covered her face with it”—and Sufyān gestured, covering his face down to the ends of his hair.

Through the same chain, from his mother and sister, who said: “We went in to ʿĀʾishah and saw her wearing a rose-colored tunic and a coarse linen headcloth.”

Al-Faḍl told me: “I heard Abū ʿAbd Allāh say: ‘I know no one more reliable than al-Ḥakam, unless it be Manṣūr ibn al-Muʿtamir.’”

He said: “I heard Abū ʿAbd Allāh, when Abū Jaʿfar asked him: ‘Does he transmit from Dāwūd ibn Yazīd al-Awdī?’ He said: ‘Shuʿbah transmitted from him.’ Abū Jaʿfar said: ‘And al-Hajarī?’”

“Does he transmit from him?” He said: “Shuʿbah transmitted from him.”

“He said: ‘I heard Aḥmad ibn Ṣāliḥ mention Maslamah ibn ʿAlī. He said: “A man’s hadith is not abandoned until everyone agrees to abandon his hadith. One may say, ‘So-and-so is weak.’ But as for our saying, ‘So-and-so is abandoned,’ that is not said unless everyone agrees to abandon his hadith.”’”

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Ḥanbal was asked about Muḥammad ibn Ziyād. He said: “He is among the reliable narrators. No one transmitted more from him than Ḥammād ibn Salamah, nor transmitted better hadith; and Shuʿbah transmitted from him.”

Aḥmad said: “ʿAffān told me: ‘Shuʿbah transmitted to us,’ and he told us a hadith from Muḥammad ibn Ziyād.

“Ḥumayd’s sister’s son said: ‘May he be rewarded with good; he used to provide me with information about him.’” Aḥmad said:

“He means Ḥammād ibn Salamah.”

Abū Ṭālib said: “Aḥmad said: ‘Mālik ibn Mighwal is reliable and firm in hadith.’

“He said: ‘Hāshim ibn al-Barīd is unobjectionable.’”

Abū ʿAbd Allāh said: “Abū Nuʿaym said: ‘Misʿar was superior in everything except in…’”

Īmānī, and Misʿar was trustworthy and among the excellent men. (54b)

Abū ʿAbd Allāh said: “The worst thing is that desire has entered his heart.”

Al-Faḍl said: I heard Abū ʿAbd Allāh say: “Al-Muqriʾ’s hadith from Saʿīd ibn Abī Ayyūb and from Ḥaywah ibn Shurayḥ was good. But he used to relate from other people’s books. He had memorized the hadith of Mūsā ibn Ayyūb al-Ghāfiqī, Ḥarملah ibn ʿImrān, and Ḥibbān—and how sound his hadith from Ibn Lahīʿah was!”

I heard Ṣadaqah mention a report from al-Muqriʾ, from Abū Lahīʿah, concerning the hadith of Sahl ibn Saʿd: The Prophet ﷺ ordered a man who had entered on Friday to pray two rakʿahs. Ṣadaqah said: “We copied the hadith of Ibn Lahīʿah from al-Muqriʾ’s own book, and I saw him commend both his hadith and his book.”

Al-Faḍl related to us: Aḥmad related to us: Sufyān said: “I was sitting with Ibn Jurayj when he saw him performing ṭawāf. He said, ‘This shaykh used to come to ʿAṭāʾ and relate hadith to him. Go and ask him.’” Sufyān said: “He came for an ʿumrah, so I went to the ṭawāf and asked. He said, ‘This is Mūsā ibn ʿUqbah.’”

Aḥmad said: Sufyān related to us: Sulaymān ibn Abī al-Mughīrah related to us; he was trustworthy and among the excellent men.

And [he related] from ʿAmr ibn Yaḥyā ibn Qamṭah, who was among the excellent people of Mecca.

Abū Yūsuf said: “He was a Roman, and his mother was Qurashī.”

[Ḥammād ibn Salamah]

“Abū Rabīʿah Fahd ibn ʿAwf related to us. He said: We went to Ḥammād ibn Salamah on a very hot day, and prayed the noon prayer with him. Ḥammād was a man of night worship, and we thought he was fasting. We took pity on him, seeing how exhausted he was, and agreed to leave without asking him anything. We dispersed, though some remained. He performed a rakʿah after the obligatory prayer, then left the mosque and went out onto the road, into the sun. A young boy came up to him and asked him about something he had with him. Ḥammād stood there with him in the sun, questioning him and relating hadith to him. He said:

“Then one of the elders of the mosque said to him, ‘Abū Salamah, our companions left you when they saw how weak you were, yet you stood with this boy in the sun, relating hadith to him.’ He said:

“‘Tonight I saw, as if I were watering a young palm, pouring water at its base. I interpreted my dream as referring to this boy, who had asked me a question.’”

(55a) He said: A dispute had arisen between him and his children’s maternal uncles, so he moved away from them. Some people came to him, and I was among them. They asked him to return to them, so that neither they nor we would be shamed. He said what he said, and they told him, “You are miserly.” What could one expect from a miserly shaykh whose entire capital was three hundred dirhams?

He said: I heard Hadiyyah ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb relate from al-Ḥasan ibn Shaqīq, who said:

Ibn al-Mubārak said: “The hadith of Ḥammād ibn Salamah has exhausted me.” I said to Abū ʿUmar al-Ḍarīr: “Did you memorize from Ḥammād ibn Salamah, from Thābit, the report that says: ‘We went with Anas and he passed by a watering trough, lay on his stomach, and drank from it’?” He said to me: “That is false. Nothing of the sort is from him.” I said: “Indeed, they related it to us from Ibn al-Mubārak, from Ḥammād.” He said: “I don’t know what this is.” Then he said: “Ibn al-Mubārak has certainly worn you out.”

He said: I heard Abū Sharīk ibn Khalaf say: “Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal came to us once and said, ‘Take us to Abū ʿUmar.’ I objected and said, ‘What do you want with Abū ʿUmar?’”

He said: “He transmits from him and relates to us many hadiths from Ḥammād that we do not know and did not write down from Ḥammād’s companions. Take us to him, so we can put them to him; perhaps we will find them with him.” (57a)

Al-Faḍl related to me: I heard Abū ʿAbd Allāh being asked, “What do you say about Ḥammād ibn Salamah?” He replied, “He is one of the excellent men.”

Al-Faḍl said: Abū Ṭālib related to us from Abū ʿAbd Allāh, who said: I asked him about Ḥammād ibn Salamah. He replied: “Ḥammād ibn Salamah was among God’s excellent, righteous servants. What a body of Sunnah he gathered! Ayyūb said, ‘Bring us someone like our young man Ḥammād.’”

He said: I heard Abū ʿAbd Allāh say: “One day a man said, ‘Knowledge is with Shuʿbah, Sufyān, and Ḥammād.’ I objected to his placing Ḥammād alongside Shuʿbah and Sufyān, for I did not know Ḥammād’s hadith. But when I wrote down his hadith, I realized the man had spoken truly: Ḥammād is a scholar.”

Abū Yūsuf related to us: al-Faḍl related to me: Ḥammād related to us from Sufyān, who said:

“Zirzir is a righteous man from among the people of Mecca.” Sufyān said: “Sandal directed me to Zirzir.”

Abū Yūsuf related to us: Abū al-Qāsim al-Makhzūmī related to us: Sufyān related to us from Zirzir. A shaykh from among the people of Mecca said, “Abū Muḥammad, glory be to God! You relate hadith from Zirzir?” He said, “From Zirzir!” Then Sufyān said, “We have related two hadiths from him, so what of it?”

Abū Yūsuf related to us: Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir related to us: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Maymūn related to us— The people said to him: “Abū Isḥāq, glory be to God! You relate hadith from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Maymūn? We seek refuge in God from ulterior motives.”

Abū Yūsuf related to us: Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Sufyān related to us from Abū Ḥayyān, from his father, from al-Ḥārith ibn Suwayd, who said: I heard ʿAbd Allāh say: “Whenever there is something I can say in the presence of a ruler that will spare me two lashes, I say it.”

He said: Sufyān related to us from Abū Ḥayyān, from Abū al-Zinbāʿ, from Abū al-Dahqān, from ʿAbd Allāh: “None shall eat it but the sinners.”

Abū Yūsuf related to us: al-Faḍl related to me: Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal said: “Abū Ḥayyān, Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd ibn Ḥayyān al-Taymī, was among God’s excellent servants. Zinbāʿ had no equal in his time. Abū Yūnus, from whom Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Qaṭṭān related, was called Abū Yūnus al-Ṭawwāf because of how much he circumambulated; he was given the name al-Ṭawwāf and was among God’s excellent servants. Al-Ḥārith ibn ʿUmayr was trustworthy, one of Ayyūb’s companions. ‘There was no one in “‘In Ibn al-Mubārak’s time was anyone more devoted to seeking knowledge than he? He traveled to Yemen, Egypt, Syria, Basra, and Kufa. He was among the transmitters of knowledge and its people. He wrote from both the young and the old; he wrote from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī and from al-Fazārī, and amassed a great deal.’” “‘How few mistakes Ibn al-Mubārak made! He was a man who related from his book, and someone who relates from a book is unlikely to make many mistakes. Wakīʿ, on the other hand, related from memory and did not consult a book; he made mistakes. How much can a man’s memory hold?’” He said: Ibn al-Mubārak likewise said this about Maʿmar: “He was unlike other people in hadith. He was a man devoted to hadith and a ḥāfiẓ. He would review hadith with someone and relate to them.”

I heard Abū ʿAbd Allāh say: “Ibn al-Mubārak came to us in the year 179. I went to him, but did not hear from him.”

He said: “I began seeking hadith in the year 179.”
