Al-Walīd ibn ʿUtba related to me: Baqiyya ibn al-Walīd related to us: Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Aghṭash—Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAyyāsh narrated from him; he is one of the Syrian transmitters and is acceptable—narrated to me, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿĀʾidh al-Azdī, from Muʿādh ibn Jabal, that he asked the Messenger of God ﷺ about what is lawful for a man with his wife while she is menstruating, about praying in a single garment, and about what makes ritual bathing obligatory. The Messenger of God ﷺ said, “What is above the waist-wrapper is lawful for you with a menstruating woman, though abstaining from that is better. As for praying in a single garment, drape it over yourself. When the two circumcised parts pass one another, ritual bathing becomes obligatory.”

He said: Al-Walīd said: Baqiyya related to us: Thawr ibn Yazīd related to me, saying, “The people of Ḥimṣ would take Ibn ʿĀʾidh’s books and, whatever legal rulings they found in them, they would place them at the mosque’s entrance, content with them and satisfied with his report.”

He said: Arṭāh ibn al-Mundhir related to me, saying, “Men from the army divided Ibn ʿĀʾidh’s books among themselves by weight, because they were content with him.”

Saʿīd ibn al-Mundhir related to me: Ḍamra related to us, from al-Saybānī, who said: When the civil strife broke out, the people said, “Let us look at these men; whatever they do, we will follow suit”: Yazīd ibn al-Aswad al-Jurashī, Rabīʿa ibn ʿAmr al-Jurashī, and Ibn Nimrān. He said: These men differed in their views. As for Yazīd ibn al-Aswad, he joined the coastal region; Rabīʿa ibn ʿAmr was with al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Qays al-Fihrī and was killed; and Ibn Nimrān was with Marwān and survived.

Salama related to me: ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us, from Maʿmar, from al-Zuhrī, who said: I was with al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, and it seemed that he had spoken ill of ʿĀʾisha. I said, “Commander of the Faithful, shall I tell you about a man from Syria who had been granted wisdom?” He said, “Who is he?”

(118b) I said, “Abū Muslim al-Khawlānī.”

Saʿīd related to me: Ḍamra related to us, from al-Saybānī, who said: Rajāʾ ibn Ḥaywa said to Ibn Nimrān, “Give me some advice.” He said, “And will you act on it?” He said, “Yes.” He said, “If you can avoid … concerning what they give you, then do so.” This was in the time of ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān.

I said to Yazīd ibn ʿAbd Rabbih al-Zubaydī: Did Baqiyya relate to you, from Ibn Abī Maryam, who said:

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz wrote to the governor of Ḥimṣ: “Look at those men who have devoted themselves to jurisprudence and confined themselves to the mosque, away from seeking worldly gain. Give each of them one hundred dinars, so that they may use it to help them in what they are doing, from the Muslims’ treasury, when this letter of mine reaches you. The best good is that which is done most promptly. Peace.” ʿAmr ibn Qays and Asad ibn Wadāʿa were among those who received it.

Al-Rabīʿ ibn Rūḥ al-Ḥimṣī related to me: Baqiyya related to us: ʿUthmān—I mean Ibn Miqsam—related to us, saying: When Khālid ibn Maʿdān sat down, none of them could bring themselves to mention worldly matters, out of awe of him.

Abū Saʿīd related to us, saying: Abū Mushir related to us, from Saʿīd, who said: Khulayḍ al-Sulāmī said, “So long as these three remain, I do not fear the civil strife”—he meant that people would follow their example—“Rabīʿa ibn ʿAmr al-Jurashī, Yazīd ibn al-Aswad al-Jurashī, and ʿUshūr al-Saksakī.” But when the Day of Rāhiṭ came, these three differed: Rabīʿa was a supporter of al-Zubayr, ʿUshūr was a supporter of Marwān, and Yazīd held back; he was the best of them.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān said: Asad ibn Wadāʿa was the army’s judge in Ḥimṣ.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAmr related to me, saying: ʿAlī ibn ʿAyyāsh informed me, saying:

Khalid ibn Maʿdān ibn Abī Karb was kunya’d Abū ʿAbd Allāh.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to us, saying: Abū Mushir related to us: Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAyyāsh related to us, from Umm ʿAbd Allāh, daughter of Khālid ibn Maʿdān, and Umm al-Ḍaḥḥāk, his freedwoman; the two said: Khālid ibn Maʿdān met seventy of the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ.

Ḥaywa ibn Shurayḥ related to us: Baqiyya related to us, saying: I heard Ṣafwān say, “Rāshid ibn Saʿd lost his eye on the day of Ṣiffīn.”

[Ḥaywa ibn Shurayḥ related to me: al-Walīd ibn Muslim (119a) related to us, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yazīd, from Busr ibn ʿUbayd Allāh al-Ḥaḍramī, who said: “I would indeed travel to one of the provincial centers to hear a hadith.”]

Abū Ṣāliḥ related to us: Muʿāwiya ibn Ṣāliḥ al-Ḥimṣī related to us, from Asad ibn Wadāʿa. Asad had long been held in good regard.

[I heard Aḥmad ibn Ṣāliḥ—and he was mentioning the men of Syria—say: “Al-Awzāʿī”; and he mentioned Ibn Jābir, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yazīd ibn Jābir, and Thawr ibn Yazīd, who is reliable, except that he held the doctrine of free will [qadar];] “and Ṣafwān ibn ʿAmr al-Saksakī, Ḥarīz ibn ʿUthmān al-Raḥabī, Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Maryam al-Ghassānī, ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Zabr, and Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz al-Tanūkhī.”

I asked Abū Saʿīd ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ibrāhīm, “Does Ṣafwān bring his associates close to himself?” He said, “He is reliable.” I said, “And Thawr ibn Yazīd?” He said, “Thawr and Ḥarīz—all of these men are reliable. Thawr was the eldest among them, in people’s estimation.” I said, “Was Abū Bakr Ibn Abī Maryam an exception among these men?” He said, “Yes.”

Muḥammad ibn al-Muṣaffā related to us, saying: Baqiyya related to us, saying: I took Ibn al-Mubārak by the hand and brought him in to Ṣafwān and Abū Bakr. When he came out from them, he said to me, “Baqiyya, keep to these two shaykhs of yours.” He said: Abū Bakr only changed in his later years.

Abū Saʿīd ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ibrāhīm related to us: al-Walīd ibn Muslim related to us: Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to us that Abū Idrīs al-Khawlānī, ʿĀʾidh Allāh, was born during the expedition of Ḥunayn and the defeat of Hawāzin.

(122a) Abū Yūsuf Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān al-Fasawī related to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ibrāhīm related to us, saying: ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn al-Walīd ibn Abī al-Sāʾib related to us, from his father, who heard Makḥūl say, “I have never met anyone like Abū Idrīs al-Khawlānī.”

ʿAlī ibn ʿUthmān ibn Nufayl related to me, saying: Abū Mushir related to us, from Saʿīd, who said:

Abū Idrīs al-Khawlānī was born in the year of Ḥunayn, and he denied having heard from Muʿādh.

Muḥammad ibn Muṣaffā related to us, saying, from Baqiyya, who said: “I testify that I heard from him the hadith of Buḥayr, from Ibn Maʿdān.”

[Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh related to us, saying: I heard one of our associates mention Yarīd ibn Hārūn, who said: Ḥarīz ibn ʿUthmān said, “I do not like anyone who killed two of my grandfathers.”]

[Abū Bishr Bakr ibn Khalaf related to me, saying: Muʿādh ibn Muʿādh related to us, saying: Ḥarīz ibn ʿUthmān al-Raḥabī al-Shāmī related to us—Muʿādh said, “I do not know that I have ever seen a Syrian better than him”—and I heard from ʿAlī ibn ʿAyyāsh, who said: Ḥarīz ibn ʿUthmān related to me, [and I heard him] say to a man, “Woe to you! Do you claim that I curse ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib? By God, I have never cursed ʿAlī.”]

ʿĪsā ibn Muḥammad related to us, saying: Azhar informed us, from [Ibn] ʿAwn, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said, “O God, bless our Syria! O God, bless our Yemen!” They said, “And our Najd?” He said, “O God, bless our Syria! O God, bless our Yemen!” They said, “And our Najd?” He said, “I think that the third time he said: There are earthquakes and civil strife there, and from there the horn of Satan will rise.”

Abū ʿUmayr related to us, saying: I heard Ḍamra, from Ibn Shawdhab, say: When I arrived in Palestine, a man met me and said, “Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, how do you make your living?”

I said, “I have young servants in this market.” He said, “Why don’t you get yourself a key to the treasury?” (122b) I said, “How could I do that?” He said, “And if I told him that it was disapproved of, he would say, ‘You Ḥarūrī! You Kharijite!’”

Ibn Shawdhab said: When I arrived in Palestine and saw al-Saybānī, Ibn Abī ʿAbla, and Ibn Abī Ḥamla, I found myself hoping for a long life.

Ḍamra said: These men were a community apart.

Abū ʿUmayr related to us, saying: I heard Kathīr ibn al-Walīd say: Ibn Abī ʿAbla was heard saying to al-Saybānī and Ibn Abī Ḥamla, “I am older than you two.”

Aḥmad ibn al-Khalīl related to me, saying: Ḥafṣ ibn ʿUmar ibn Abī al-Qāsim related to us, saying: I heard Abū Zurʿa al-Saybānī say, “I used to campaign with al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan to Khurāsān.”

Aḥmad ibn al-Khalīl related to us, saying: Kathīr ibn Hishām related to us, saying: Jaʿfar ibn Burqān related to us, saying: Maymūn ibn Mihrān related to us that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz asked him:

“Who are your patrons?” He replied, “My mother was a client of the Azd, and my father was a mukātab of Banū Naṣr ibn Muʿāwiya. I was born while my father was still a mukātab.” ʿUmar said, “Your patrons are your mother’s patrons.”

Kathīr ibn Hishām said: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr’s daughter was Maymūn’s wife.

Saʿīd ibn Asad related to me, saying: Ḍamra related to us, from Rajāʾ ibn Abī Salama, who said: I heard Yūnus ibn Sufyān say, “Only two Qadarites remain; one of them is Ḥassān ibn ʿAṭiyya.”

[Makḥūl]

Saʿīd related to me, saying: Ḍamra related to us, from Rajāʾ ibn Abī Salama, from Abū ʿUbayd, the client of Sulaymān, who said: “I never heard Rajāʾ ibn Ḥaywa curse anyone except two men:

Yazīd ibn al-Muhallab and Makḥūl.”

Ḍamra related to us, from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ḥamla, who said: We were at a water-channel in Byzantine territory, and people were passing by in the dim light before dawn. Among us was a man who told stories, kunya’d Abū Shayba. He prayed, saying, among other things, “O God, provide us with good things and give us wholesome food.” Makḥūl, who was among the group, said, “God provides only what is wholesome.” Rajāʾ ibn Ḥaywa and ʿAdī ibn ʿAdī were off to one side, where Makḥūl did not know they were. One of them said to his companion, “Did you hear that remark?”

He said, “Yes.” Then Makḥūl was told, “Rajāʾ (123a) and ʿAdī ibn ʿAdī heard what you said.”

That troubled him, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd al-Dimashqī said to him, “I will take care of Rajāʾ for you.”

When the army encamped, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd came and approached Rajāʾ’s tent, as though looking for his companions. Rajāʾ saw him, and knew him, so he turned toward us and said, “Where should I look for my companions?” He replied, “We are your companions.” He came over and sat down, and then brought up Makḥūl.

Rajāʾ said to him, “Leave Makḥūl aside—isn’t he the one who made that remark?” ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd said to him, “What do you say, may God have mercy on you, about a man who killed a Jew, took a thousand dinars from him, and lived off them until he died: was that provision which God had provided him?” Rajāʾ said, “Everything comes from God.”

ʿAlī said: I was there and witnessed the two of them speaking.

[Al-Awzāʿī]

[Saʿīd related to me: Ḍamra related to us, from al-Saybānī, who said: Al-Awzāʿī said to me:

“Abū Zurʿa, our worshippers and our best men have perished over this doctrine”—meaning the doctrine of free will [qadar].]

Al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Walīd ibn Mazyad related to me, saying: My father informed me, from al-Awzāʿī:

He wrote to ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Thābit ibn Thawbān: “To proceed: You know how your father treated me and the special sincerity of his regard. I therefore considered that my way of maintaining my connection with him was to keep giving you sincere counsel, as soon as I first heard that you had stopped attending Friday prayer and the prayers. But you persisted and became obstinate.

“Then I treated you kindly and admonished you, and you answered me with an argument that is neither a proof nor an excuse for you. I wished to join a commitment to my counsel for you, in the hope that God may bring about some good. We have heard that there are five practices upheld by the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ and those who follow them in goodness: following the Sunna, reciting the Qurʾān, adhering to the community, maintaining the mosques, and striving in the path of God.

“Sufyān al-Thawrī related to me that Ḥudhayfa ibn al-Yamān used to say: ‘Whoever wishes to know whether civil strife has befallen him should look: if he now considers lawful something he used to consider forbidden, or considers forbidden something he used to consider lawful, then he should know that it has befallen him.’ Before your father’s death ﵀ you considered abandoning Friday prayer and the congregational prayers forbidden; now you consider it lawful. You used to consider maintaining the mosques among the noblest of deeds, (123b) but now you have forsaken them. You used to consider it a burden to leave your band of guards in the path of God, but now you consider that good.”

Sufyān related to me, with an interrupted chain of transmission, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that he said: “Whoever abandons the Friday prayer four times in succession without an excuse has cast Islam behind his back.”

Al-Zuhrī related to me from Abū Hurayrah: “Whoever abandons the Friday prayer three times without an excuse will have a seal placed upon his heart.”

You have put yourself at great risk on account of these two reports.69 For they are your opinion; it is a secret—what you have adopted—and be content with your forebears. For three years that have passed, while mosques and homes were being burned, blood was being shed, and property was being plundered, you were with your father and did not oppose him in abandoning a Friday prayer or attending a mosque for prayer. You did not turn away from him until he departed this life. Yet you think that, in light of this report, “Stay within your house,” and similar reports, you know better than your father and the people of knowledge whom he met. I seek God’s protection for you, and adjure you by Him, not to cling to your own opinion in isolation from your father and the people of knowledge before him, and not to become a source of strength for the partisans of caprice, or a source of discord for fools who abandon the Friday prayer and cite you as an argument when they are reproached for abandoning it. I ask God not to make your misfortune one that befalls your religion, and not to let wretchedness or the following of desire without guidance from Him prevail over you. Peace be upon you.

Al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Walīd related to us from his father. He said: “In the year when the stars became numerous, we went out at night into the desert with al-Awzāʿī and our companions. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Thābit ibn Thawbān was with us. He drew his sword and said, ‘God has made the matter grave, so be grave yourselves.’ They began to revile and torment him, and to call him weak.” He said:

Al-Awzāʿī said: “I say something better than what you say: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān has been relieved of responsibility”—that is, he is mad.

Al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Walīd ibn Ṣubḥ al-Sulamī al-Dimashqī related to us. He said: Marwān ibn Muḥammad [related to us from Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz], and [Abū Bakr] Ḥassān ibn ʿAṭiyyah used to say: “He is a Qadarī.” Marwān said: Saʿīd’s remarks about Ḥassān ibn ʿAṭiyyah reached al-Awzāʿī, who said: “What misled Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, by God? I have never met anyone more diligent in exertion or more active in good works than he.” Marwān said: “Ḥassān ibn ʿAṭiyyah was born in Baṣrah and grew up here.”

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ibrāhīm related to us. He said: Mus’hir related to us: “When Makḥūl died, they gathered in a circle before Yazīd.” He said: “He was a quiet man. They then moved to Sulaymān ibn Mūsā, who made room for them. When Sulaymān died, they gathered around al-ʿAlāʾ ibn al-Ḥārith. When al-ʿAlāʾ died, Ibn Surāqah was in charge of Damascus. He said, ‘Who is the jurist of this army today?’ They replied, ‘Qays al-Aʿmar.’ He said, ‘Today this army has perished.’”

He said: “He sent for al-Awzāʿī, and brought him from the coast.”

He said: “Numayr ibn Aws wrote to Hishām, asking to be excused from the judgeship. He had grown old and his eyesight had weakened.” He said: “Hishām said, ‘Find me a judge for the people of Damascus.’”

They replied, “Yazīd ibn Yazīd.” He said, “That man is occupied”; Hishām had appointed him to serve with his son Muʿāwiyah. They said, “Yaḥyā ibn Yaḥyā al-Ghassānī.” He said, “That man belongs on the pulpit.”

They said, “Yazīd ibn Abī Mālik.” So he appointed him judge.

I said to ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, “Muḥammad ibn Muhājir?” He said, “Reliable.” I said, “Hishām ibn al-Ghāz?” He said, “How excellent his uprightness in hadith is!” He said, “Al-Walīd used to praise him” and Ibn Jābir. He said: “Ibn Jābir related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said, ‘Attend to your dead with good words.’ Hishām related from Makḥūl that ʿUmar said…” I said, “Ibn Jābir is reliable, and Hishām is reliable, so how did they differ?” He said: “Al-Ghaḍūr related to me: ‘I heard Makḥūl relate from ʿUmar, from the Prophet ﷺ that he said…’ Then I knew that they had not made a mistake.”70 “I asked Abū Saʿīd ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ibrāhīm: ‘Which of Makḥūl’s companions were the most eminent?’” He said: “Sulaymān ibn Mūsā, Yazīd ibn Yazīd ibn Jābir, and al-ʿAlāʾ ibn al-Ḥārith.”

I said to him, “Did al-Awzāʿī spend little time in Makḥūl’s company?” He said, “Yes.”

I said, “And Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz?” He said, “Yes.”

I said to him, “Abū Maʿbad?” He said, “He ranks below these men, though Zayd ibn Wāqid and Burd ibn Sinān were among their leading figures”.

I said to him, “Al-Haytham ibn Ḥumayd—was he the person most knowledgeable about Makḥūl?” He said:

“He was the most knowledgeable of the early and later generations about Makḥūl.”

I said, “And ʿAlī ibn Ḥawshab?”71 “He was a shaykh who kept company with Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, a Fazārī”. He was a blacksmith.

I said to him, “Al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Ḥawshab al-Naṣrī?” He said, “They are a noble family, and they have standing.”

I said to him, “Where does ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yazīd ibn Tamīm stand in relation to his brother ʿAbd Allāh?”

He said: “ʿAbd Allāh was suspected of holding the Qadarī doctrine. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān had a book with him, which he had written for al-Zuhrī. It was with his son, but it was not decreed for us to copy that book from him.”

I said to him, “And al-Waḍīn ibn ʿAṭāʾ?” He said: “He related little from Makḥūl; he used to keep company with other people.”

I said to him, “ʿĪsā ibn Ayyūb al-Qaynī?” He said: “Abū Hāshim al-Qaynī possessed merit, piety, and devotion to Islam.” ʿAbd al-Raḥmān said: Abū Mushir said: “Abū Hāshim’s piety reached such a degree that he did such-and-such,” and he mentioned something I did not understand.

I said to him, “Muḥammad ibn Rāshid?” He said, “He was known for holding the Qadarī doctrine, but he was sound in hadith”.

I said to him, “ʿUmar ibn Yazīd al-Baṣrī?” He said: “He was their secretary, and he was reliable and a jurist. Ibn Shuʿayb used to keep company with him.”

I said to him, “Ibrāhīm ibn Sulaymān al-Afṭas?” He said: “Excellent, excellent! Reliable”.

I asked Hishām ibn ʿAmmār, “Which of Makḥūl’s companions was the most eminent?” He said:

“Sulaymān ibn Mūsā.” I said, “And who came next?” He said, “Al-ʿAlāʾ ibn al-Ḥārith”.

I said to him, “And Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz?” He said, “Yes; these three were the most eminent of Makḥūl’s companions.”

I said to him, “Where does Yazīd ibn Yazīd stand in relation to these men?” He said, “That man ruined himself. He went out with Marwān ibn Muḥammad and helped kill al-Walīd ibn Yazīd, and he took one hundred thousand dinars”.

I said, “And al-Nuʿmān?” He said, “That man holds the Qadarī doctrine.”

I said, “And ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-ʿAlāʾ?” He said, “Excellent! Reliable. He heard from al-Qāsim Abū…”

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, and from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. He was of an earlier generation.”

I said, “And where does ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yazīd ibn Jābir stand?” He said, “He is good”.

He said: Al-Walīd ibn Muslim related to us from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yazīd ibn Jābir, who said: “Makḥūl and I would enter the mosque after the people had prayed. Makḥūl would give the call to prayer and the call to begin it, then step forward and lead the prayer. I would come with Sulaymān ibn Mūsā after they had prayed; he would give the call to prayer and the call to begin it, then I would be brought forward and lead him in prayer.” He said: “He was older than him.”

I asked ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ibrāhīm about ʿAbd Allāh [page marker in source: 125 A] ibn al-ʿAlāʾ, and he declared him reliable. I said to him, “Ibn al-Mubārak did not narrate from him.” He said, “Ibn al-Mubārak only transmitted from the most eminent authorities.”

Hishām ibn ʿAmmār related to us. He said: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥārith al-Salāmī related to us: “I saw Zayd ibn Wāqid and Burd ibn Sinān carrying the head of al-Walīd ibn Yazīd on a shield.”

[ʿAṭiyyah ibn Qays al-Kilābī]

I asked ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ibrāhīm about ʿAṭiyyah ibn Qays. He said: “He was…”

“the oldest of them”. “He had campaigned with Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī, and he and Ismāʿīl ibn ʿUbayd Allāh were the reciters of the army”.

Hishām ibn ʿAmmār related to us. He said: Al-Haytham ibn ʿImrān related to us: “I heard ʿAbd al-Wāḥid ibn Qays al-Sulamī say: ‘People used to correct their codices according to ʿAṭiyyah’s recitation, sitting on the steps of the church in the Mosque of Damascus, before it was demolished.’”

He said: Al-Haytham ibn ʿImrān related to us: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah related to me from his father:

“He used to enter with the elders of the mosque to see Muʿāwiyah.”

Al-Haytham ibn ʿImrān related to us: “I saw ʿAṭiyyah ibn Qays seated in the mosque on a piece of brocade stuffed with feathers.”

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAmr and ʿAlī ibn ʿUthmān ibn Nufayl related to us. They said: Ibn Mus’hir related to us: Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to us from ʿAṭiyyah ibn Qays al-Kilābī, who said: “I campaigned against the Byzantines as a horseman during Muʿāwiyah’s caliphate. ʿUbaydah ibn Qays al-ʿUqaylī was in command of us. We conquered Shamāsah, and my share of the booty amounted to two hundred dinars.”

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ibrāhīm related to us. He said: Abū Mushir related to us:

Saʿīd related to us from ʿAṭiyyah, who said: “I campaigned in the land of the Byzantines during Muʿāwiyah’s caliphate.” He said:

“I went out in a raiding party, and we were a little over forty men, under the command of ʿUbaydah ibn Qays al-ʿUqaylī. We raided a certain [fortress]—Saʿīd named it, but I have forgotten its name. He said: I was a horseman, and my share of the booty amounted to two hundred dinars.”

I asked ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ibrāhīm about the death of Muḥammad ibn Muhājir. He said:

“He lived long enough for Abū Mushir to hear from him,” and he mentioned others. I said to him, “And ʿUmar ibn Muhājir?”

He said, “Suwayd came before him, and narrated from him.”

[Makḥūl]

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAmr al-Dimashqī and ʿAlī ibn ʿUthmān ibn Nufayl related to me. He said: Abū Mushir related to us; Saʿīd related to us from Makḥūl, who said:

“How much knowledge God has bestowed upon this army, though they do not know whence it came to them!”

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to me. He said: Abū Mushir related to us; Saʿīd related to us from Makḥūl:

“He wrote to Muḥammad ibn Hāniʾ, who was in Baʿlabakk: ‘From Makḥūl ibn ʿAbd Allāh to Muḥammad ibn Hāniʾ.’ Then he said, ‘Praise be to God who raised Makḥūl.’”

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to me. Abū Mushir related to us. He said: Saʿīd related to us from Makḥūl: “When he was asked a question, he would not answer until he said, ‘There is no might nor power except through God. This is an opinion; opinion may be right or wrong.’”

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to us, and Abū Mushir related to us. Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to us, saying:

“I was present when Makḥūl and Khālid were being asked questions and discussing them. Khālid disagreed with him, and I saw Makḥūl’s lips trembling.”

Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Malik related to us. He said: ʿAbd al-Razzāq said: “Makḥūl used to say it, as did Ibn Abī Dhiʾb and Bakkār al-Yamāmī”—meaning the doctrine of predestination.

ʿAlī ibn ʿUthmān al-Nufaylī related to us. He said: Abū Mushir related to us; Saʿīd related to us, saying: “In Makḥūl’s time, there was no one more discerning than he in giving legal opinions.” He said: “He would not give a legal opinion until he said, ‘There is no might nor power except through God,’ and he would say, ‘This is an opinion, and opinion may be right or wrong.’”

He said: Abū Mushir related to us; Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to us, saying: “We never met anyone whose bearing in worship was finer than that of Makḥūl, Rabīʿah, and Yazīd.”

Hishām ibn ʿAmmār related to us. He said: Muḥammad ibn Shuʿayb related to us; Ibrāhīm ibn al-Jarrār related to us; Thābit ibn Thawbān related to me: “I arrived in Medina and went to Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, whom people had questioned until they angered him. I asked him, and he answered me. Then he said, ‘Let this be how questions are asked.’ Saʿīd then said, ‘You find the believer between two qualities: like a dove, soft to the touch, whose coo is not forgotten; and like a bee, whose sting is fierce and whose taste is sweet.’”

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAmr related to us. He said: Abū Mushir related to us; Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to us, saying: “In the days of al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, they used to delay the prayer and make people swear that they had not prayed. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Zakariyyā came, and they made him swear that he had not prayed, though he had prayed. Makḥūl came and said, ‘Why have we come, then?’ So he was let go.”

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to us. He said: [Abū] Mushir related to us; Ibrāhīm ibn Abī Shaybān related to me from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ḥamlah—who used to keep company with Ibn Abī Zakariyyā— ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Zakariyyā said to me, “Where are you staying?” I said, “With this man, the governor of Ḥimṣ”—he used to accompany ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Malik. He said, “Alas! You were free, but you made yourself a slave.”

He said: Al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAẓīm related to me: Zayd ibn al-Mubārak wrote to me:

“I brought my mother and my family along. My mother died in Mecca. I intended to settle in Jerusalem; what made me leave was something I heard Abū Nuʿaym say: ‘Ibn Abī Laylā said, “Whoever is known to the ruler in a town is a slave.”’”

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ibrāhīm related to me. Al-Walīd related to us; … from al-Zubayr al-Shajaʿī, who said: “I heard Makḥūl say: ‘I was sitting in the Mosque of Damascus when al-Miqdād entered upon us. He performed a bow of prayer and then went out. I followed him and walked with him until he left through the Bāb al-Jābiyah.’”

Abū al-Yamān al-Ḥakam ibn Nāfiʿ related to us. Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to us from Makḥūl, who said: “I went to Anas in this mosque and asked him about performing ablution after attending a funeral. He said, ‘We had been engaged in prayer, and returned to prayer, so there is no ablution’”.

Aḥmad ibn al-Khalīl related to me. He said: Masʿūd related to us; al-Ḥajjāj related to me from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Shuʿaythī, who said: “I saw Makḥūl hurrying behind his master in the ṣuffah.”

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAmr related to me: “I heard Abū Miskhir identify Ibn Abī Zakariyyā. He said: ‘ʿAbd Allāh ibn Iyās ibn Yazīd: [he is] among the Arabs of Khuzāʿah, and his teknonym is Abū Yaḥyā.’”

ʿAlī ibn ʿUthmān ibn Nufayl related to me: Abū Miskhir related to us; Saʿīd related to us:

“I said to Abū Usayd al-Fazārī, ‘How do you make your living?’ He magnified God and praised God, then said: ‘God provides for the dog and the pig, but does not provide for Abū Usayd.’”

Through the same chain, he said: Saʿīd related to us: “Abū Usayd al-Fazārī passed through the market of heads and recalled this verse: ‘While there they will be grimacing’. He fell down unconscious.”

Abū Saʿīd ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ibrāhīm related to me: al-Walīd ibn Muslim related to us (126b), from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ḥassān al-Kinānī: “Abū ʿUbayd used to attend upon Sulaymān. When ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz became ruler, he said, ‘Where is Abū ʿUbayd?’ He came near him, and ʿUmar said: ‘This is the road to Palestine, and you are one of its people, so go there.’ Later they said, ‘Commander of the Faithful, if only you had seen Abū ʿUbayd and his zeal for good works and worship!’ He said:

‘That makes it more fitting that he not be tempted. He had the prestige of the common people about him.’”

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAmr related to us: Abū Miskhir related to us: Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to us that ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir al-Yaḥṣubī struck Khālid ibn al-Lajlāj and al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Abī al-Zubayr when their voices rose while discussing religious knowledge in the mosque.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān said: Abū Miskhir said: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir al-Yaḥṣubī said:

“Ismāʿīl ibn ʿUbayd Allāh said to me, ‘You studied the Qurʾān with your brother.’ Ismāʿīl said to me—”

“Your brother is five years older than I am.”

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān said: Abū Miskhir related to us that ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir struck ʿAṭiyyah ibn Qays when he raised his hands in prayer.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, Abū Miskhir, related to us: Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to us. He said:

“ʿAṭiyyah ibn Qays said: ‘He rapped me with a stick.’”

Hishām ibn ʿAmmār related to us: “Al-Haytham related to us, from ʿImrān, who said: ‘The head of the mosque in Damascus in the time of al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, and after him, was ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir al-Yaḥṣubī. He claimed to be from Ḥimyar, but his lineage was impugned.’” He attended during Ramaḍān. They said, “Who will lead us in prayer?” They named a man, and they also named al-Muhājir ibn Abī al-Muhājir. He said, “He is a client, and we do not want a client to lead us in prayer.” This reached Sulaymān. When he was appointed caliph, he sent for al-Muhājir and said: “On the first night of the month of Ramaḍān, stand behind the imām. When ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir steps forward, before he says the takbīr, seize his clothes from behind, pull him back, and say, ‘Step back! No man of dubious parentage will lead us in prayer. You lead the people.’” And he did so.

ʿAlī ibn ʿUthmān ibn Nufayl and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAmr related to me. They said: Abū Miskhir related to us: ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Zabr related to us (127a): ʿAmr ibn ibn Muhājir related to us: “ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir came to me, asking me to seek permission for him to see ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. I sought permission for him, and ʿUmar said, ‘The man who flogged his brother for raising his hands! We used to discipline people for that when we were in Medina.’ He did not grant him permission.”

Al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Walīd and ʿAlī ibn ʿUthmān ibn Nufayl related to us. They said: Abū Miskhir related to us— He said: “I heard ʿAbd al-Ḥalīm ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿUbayd Allāh, the son of Ismāʿīl ibn ʿUbayd Allāh’s brother, relate from his uncle Ismāʿīl ibn ʿUbayd Allāh, who said: ‘Umm al-Dardāʾ said, “Ismāʿīl, how can a man sleep with ten thousand beneath his pillow?” I said to her, “Rather, how could he sleep if he did not have ten thousand beneath his head?” She said, “Glory be to God! I can only think that you will be tested with worldly wealth.”’”

Abū Miskhir said: “And he was tested with worldly wealth.”

Al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Walīd and ʿAlī ibn ʿUthmān ibn Nufayl related to us. They said: Abū Miskhir related to us: “I heard Kāmil ibn Salamah say: Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik asked, ‘Who is the leading man among the people of Palestine?’ They said, ‘Rajāʾ ibn Ḥaywah.’ He asked, ‘Who is the leading man among the people of the Jordan region?’ They said:

‘ʿUbādah ibn Nasī.’ He asked, ‘Who is the leading man among the people of Damascus?’ They said, ‘Yaḥyā ibn Yaḥyā al-Ghassānī.’ He asked, ‘Who is the leading man among the people of Ḥimṣ?’ They said, ‘ʿAmr ibn Qays al-Sakūnī.’ He asked, ‘Who is the leading man among the people of al-Jazīrah?’ They said, ‘ʿAdī ibn ʿAdī.’ Hishām said, ‘O people of Kindah!’”

Al-ʿAbbās related to us: Abū Miskhir related to us: Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to me: “These four were the scholars of the community in Hishām’s time.” Sulaymān ibn Mūsā said: “72 If knowledge came to us from the people of the Ḥijāz, from al-Zuhrī, we accepted it; if it came to us from Syria, from Makḥūl, we accepted it; if knowledge came to us from al-Jazīrah, from Maymūn ibn Mihrān, we accepted it; and if it came to us from Iraq, from al-Ḥasan, we accepted it.”

Al-ʿAbbās related to us; Marwān related to us: Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to us: “Whenever ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ came and Sulaymān ibn Mūsā was there, he would say, ‘Stop asking questions. The one who can answer them has come to you.’”

He said: Marwān related to us: “I entered the mosque the first time I sat with Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz (127b).” He said: “The name of Ṣadaqah ibn ʿAbd Allāh was being spoken of throughout the mosque. He had died during Saʿīd’s lifetime. Marwān said: ‘I did not meet him. He had knowledge of Syria; if I had met him, I would have sought it out.’”

“I heard Abū Saʿīd ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ibrāhīm say: ‘Ṣadaqah was one of our shaykhs, and there is no fault in him.’ I said, ‘ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd related munkar reports!’ He said, ‘Ugh! We did not transmit from him or his like about Ṣadaqah’—he alluded to someone else—‘we transmitted from him through Abū Ḥafṣ al-Tinnīsī and our companions.’”

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAmr related to me: Abū Miskhir related to us: Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to us, from Ismāʿīl ibn ʿUbayd Allāh, who said: “If you see a man honoring you, honor him.”

[Bilāl ibn Saʿd]

“I asked ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ibrāhīm about Bilāl ibn Saʿd. He said: ‘He is Bilāl ibn Saʿd ibn Tamīm. He led the people in prayer during Hishām’s caliphate. He left no descendants; he had a daughter.’”

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān related to us: ʿAbd Allāh informed us: al-Awzāʿī informed us— He said: “I heard Bilāl ibn Saʿd say: ‘Do not look at how small the sin is; look at whom you have disobeyed.’” He said: “It is sufficient as a sin that God makes us disdain this world while we long for it.”

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān related to us: ʿAbd Allāh related to us: al-Awzāʿī informed us: “I heard Bilāl ibn Saʿd say: ‘The one among you who renounces the world is desirous of it; the one among you who strives hard falls short; your scholar is ignorant, and your ignorant one is deluded.’”

I heard ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ibrāhīm say: “I heard the report of Bilāl ibn Saʿd from his father: The Prophet ﷺ was asked, ‘What will the caliph after you be entitled to?’ From al-Walīd, in his quarter; but I do not relate it.”

“He said: ‘Sulaymān—meaning ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn [the daughter of] Shuraḥbīl—had sound written material, except that he would transpose things. If anything occurred in it, it was from transmission.’”

Al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Walīd ibn Ṣubḥ related to us: ʿUbayd ibn Abī al-Sāʾib related to us: My father related to me: Rajāʾ ibn Ḥaywah said to me: “When you go to Bilāl ibn Saʿd, tell him— ‘Rajāʾ has sent me to you. He disliked sending you his greetings, and he wants to say to you that (128a) I have heard that you have spoken words like those spoken by people who deny God’s decrees. If that has taken hold in your mind, then evil has taken hold in your mind. If it was a deviation or an error, then turn back soon, so that those who deny God’s decrees may know that you have parted company with them and abandoned what they uphold.’”

“Al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Walīd related to us: Marwān ibn Muḥammad related to us: Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to us: ‘Bilāl ibn Saʿd was accused of holding the doctrine of free will. The next morning, he spoke during his exhortation and said: “How many a person who is pleased is deceived! Woe to the one who is doomed to woe and does not know it: he eats and drinks, though God’s knowledge has already determined that he is one of the people of the Fire”—or something similar.’”

Abū Yūsuf said: “Al-Qāsim ibn Mukhaymirah was a Kufan who settled in Syria, and so too was ʿAbdah ibn Abī Lubābah, a trustworthy Kufan who settled in Syria. I heard al-Ḥumaydī—I think he mentioned it from Sufyān—say: ‘ʿAbdah had a partner who would conduct business on his behalf, and he would settle accounts with him every year and give in charity any profit above the amount. One year, he settled accounts with him while he was on pilgrimage. He said to one of the people of Mecca, “Write down for me the names of some people.” The man wrote them down for him. Word spread among the people, and so many gathered around him that he was overwhelmed by them. They pelted the house where he was staying and stoned him, saying, “Money was entrusted to him to give in charity, but he betrayed that trust and stole it”—or something similar.’”

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān related to us: ʿAbd Allāh related to us: Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAyyāsh informed us, from Usayd ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from Muqbil ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yazīd al-Laythī, who said: “One day, people asked him question after question. He said: ‘You have asked me repeatedly, “What do you think? What do you think?” Do not work for anyone other than God while hoping for reward from God. Let none of you be impressed by his own deeds, however numerous they may be. No servant can attain any measure of God’s greatness—not even the size of a fly’s leg.’”

[Al-Awzāʿī]

Al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Walīd ibn Ṣubḥ related to us: Marwān related to us: “I heard Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAyyāsh say: ‘The people returned from the expedition of al-Nadwah in the year 140. I heard them saying, “Today al-Awzāʿī is the scholar of the community.”’”

Al-ʿAbbās related to me: Abū Miskhir related to us: Muḥammad ibn al-Awzāʿī related to me: My father related to me: “My son, if we accepted from people everything they offered us (128b), we would soon become insignificant in their eyes.”

ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Abī al-Sāʾib related to me: Baqiyyah related to us: “I test people by [asking about] al-Awzāʿī: if someone speaks well of him, we know that he is a follower of the Sunnah; if someone attacks him, we know that he is an adherent of religious innovation.”

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAmr related to us: Abū Miskhir related to us: Haql ibn Ziyād related to us: “Al-Awzāʿī answered seventy thousand questions, or thereabouts.”

Saʿīd ibn Asad related to me: Ḍamrah related to us, from Rajāʾ ibn Abī Salamah from Abū Razīn, who said: “Al-Awzāʿī was first asked about jurisprudence in the year 113.”

“Saʿīd related to me: Ḍamrah related to us, from Rajāʾ ibn Abī Salamah, from ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī, who said: ‘I have never seen a jurist more learned—if I ever met one—than a Syrian.’”

Abū ʿUmayr related to us: “I heard Ḍamrah say: ‘I have never seen anyone more sound in judgment than him’—meaning so-and-so and al-Awzāʿī.”

I heard ʿAbbās ibn al-Walīd ibn Mazyad mention, from their shaykhs, that they said: “Al-Awzāʿī said: ‘My father died when I was young, so I went out to play with the boys. So-and-so passed by us—he mentioned a distinguished elder of the Arabs—and the boys fled when they saw him, but I jumped up. He said, “Whose son are you?” I told him. He said, “My brother’s son! May God have mercy on your father.” He took me to his house, and I stayed with him until I came of age. He enrolled me in the military register, and we were conscripted for a campaign to al-Yamāmah. When I arrived in al-Yamāmah, we entered the congregational mosque. When we came out, one of our companions said to me, “I saw Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr admiring you. He said, ‘I have seen no one in this expedition better turned out than this young man.’” I then sat with him and wrote down fourteen books—or thirteen—from him, but they all burned.’”

Al-Walīd ibn ʿUtbah al-Dimashqī related to me: Abū Miskhir related to us: “I heard Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz say: ‘I never wrote anything.’”

Abū Saʿīd ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ibrāhīm related to me: Abū Miskhir related to us: Saʿīd related to us, from Ismāʿīl ibn ʿUbayd Allāh, from Makhramah ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, that he used to— “remain silent for four months. When he needed something, he would write it down.”

[Makḥūl]

Abū Saʿīd related to me: Abū Miskhir related to us (129a): Saʿīd related to us. He said:

“We used to sit in the mornings with Yazīd ibn Abī Mālik and Sulaymān ibn Mūsā; after noon with Ismāʿīl ibn ʿUbayd Allāh and Rabīʿah ibn Yazīd; and after the afternoon prayer with Makḥūl.”

He said: Saʿīd related to us: “Sulaymān ibn Mūsā used to say: ‘If knowledge came to us from the Ḥijāz, from al-Zuhrī, we accepted it; if it came to us from Iraq, from al-Ḥasan, we accepted it; if it came to us from al-Jazīrah, from Maymūn ibn Mihrān, we accepted it; and if it came to us from Syria, from Makḥūl, we accepted it.’”

Saʿīd said: “These four were the scholars of the people during Hishām’s caliphate.”

Abū Saʿīd related to us: Abū Miskhir related to us: Saʿīd related to us: “Al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Walīd asked Makḥūl about the blood money due for a killing in a sacred month. He said, ‘One and a third blood payments.’ Al-ʿAbbās asked him, ‘Is this ruling applied?’ He said, ‘No.’ He then rebuked him verbally. Yazīd ibn Abī Mālik came in and said, ‘This is what you get from us when you ask us something and we tell you the answer.’ He then sent for Makḥūl and appeased him.”

Through the same chain, he said: Saʿīd related to us that Muʿāwiyah paid on behalf of ʿĀʾishah eighteen thousand dinars.

“Abū Saʿīd related to me: al-Walīd related to us: Saʿīd related to us, from— Sulaymān ibn Mūsā, who said: ‘When I find a man whose knowledge is Ḥijāzī, whose generosity is Iraqi, and whose uprightness is Syrian, then he is a man.’”

“Nuʿaym ibn Ḥammād related to us: Rishdīn related to us, from ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥārith, from Bukayr ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ashajj, who said: ‘ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ was asked about the people of Syria.

“He said: ‘They are the most obedient of people to a created being and the most disobedient to their Creator.’ They asked, ‘And the people of Medina?’ He said:

“‘They are the people most eager for civil strife and least capable of it.’ They asked, ‘And the people of Iraq?’ He said:

“‘The most fertile of people in their tongues and the most barren in their hearts.’ They asked, ‘And the people of Egypt?’ He said: ‘The cleverest of people when young and the most foolish when old.’” I mentioned this report to a shaykh descended from ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, and he added this to what I had heard: “He was asked about the people of Mecca, too. He said: ‘They think most highly of themselves and are held in least esteem by other people.’”

Abū Saʿīd related to me: al-Walīd related to us: Saʿīd related to me, from Sulaymān, who said: “People sought chains of transmission after our companions had died. Had they sought them from us while our companions were alive, then we had sought them from those companions, we would have found those chains intact with them.”

(129b) Abū Saʿīd related to me: ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us— Saʿīd, from Abū ʿAbd Rabb, said: “A man met me and said, ‘Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, do not go away with evil while leaving your family in good circumstances.’”

Saʿīd said: “I think he had gone through one hundred thousand—or twenty thousand—so much so that he would sometimes say to us, ‘We are eight dependents, and we have nothing except ten’”—meaning dependents.

“Abū Saʿīd related to me: al-Walīd and Suwayd related to us, from Saʿīd, from Sulaymān, who said: ‘Do not read the Qurʾān from written copies, and do not take knowledge from people who rely on written pages.’”

He also said: “Al-Walīd related to us: Saʿīd related to us, saying: When al-Zubayr died, Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām met ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr and asked, ‘How much debt did my brother leave?’ He replied, ‘One million dirhams.’ He said, ‘I am responsible for five hundred thousand dirhams.’”

I read in the book of my brother Muḥammad, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak, who said: “Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām reached the age of one hundred and forty while still making the pilgrimage, though he had to be propped up on a litter and carried by men.”

ʿAbd Allāh said: “ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr came to Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām seeking his help in paying al-Zubayr’s debt. Ḥakīm said, ‘Al-Zubayr used to vie with the wind, and I have no power to match that.’ He said, ‘You have one hundred thousand.’ Ḥakīm replied, ‘That would not make a difference to me.’ He said, ‘You have three hundred thousand.’ He replied, ‘That would not make a difference to me.’ He said, ‘I cannot give you four hundred thousand.’ Ḥakīm replied, ‘That is not what I wanted from you. Rather, come with me to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar, and speak to him on my behalf.’ He said, ‘Certainly.’ So he went with him, along with ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar and more than one other person, to intercede for him with ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar.

“When they entered, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar said, ‘Why have you brought these people to intercede with me? It is yours.’ He said, ‘I do not want that.’

“‘Then give me those two sandals of yours in exchange for it, or something like that,’ he said. ‘I do not want that,’ he replied.

“‘Then it is yours to pay until the Day of Resurrection.’ He said, ‘I do not want that.’

“‘Then name your terms.’ He said, ‘I will give you a piece of land in exchange for it.’ ‘Agreed,’ he replied. Then he went out, and afterward ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr kept saying, ‘This is…’ like this, and [he] traded with him. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar said, ‘Do as you wish.’ So he gave him land in exchange for that money. Muʿāwiya later desired it and bought it from him for more than that. ʿAbd Allāh said: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar’s wealth amounted to four hundred thousand.”

Abū al-Nuʿmān and Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb related to us—and this is the wording of Abū al-Nuʿmān—saying: Ḥammād ibn Zayd related to us, saying: Yazīd ibn Ḥāzim related to us, saying:

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Muslim related to me, saying: Qutayba ibn Muslim related to me, saying: “There was a blood-debt—or blood-debts—in Egypt, and the people agreed to gather over it. He issued his order concerning it and ordered them to assemble there.

“My father sent me to Ḍirār ibn al-Qaʿqāʿ and said, ‘Tell him: Your people have assembled at the congregational mosque over so-and-so’s blood.’ He replied, ‘Yes. Wait until I have lunch.’

“He called for his lunch. A cloth was brought and spread out; four loaves and a bowl of marīṣ were brought, then he called for oil and poured it over the dish. He said, ‘Come closer.’ I said, ‘What do you expect from this?’ He replied, ‘I will eat it until I have finished it.’ Some remained, so he lifted the bowl and drank what was in it. Then he said, ‘Praise be to God for the finest wheat, the honey of the bees, the oil of Syria, and the water of the Euphrates. Praise be to God: this, by God, is among the good things.’ Then he wiped his hand and went into the mosque. It was winter, and the people were in rows. He looked toward the sun in the middle of the mosque and sat down. By God, they kept coming to him until they had gathered around him. They continued to clamor until it was nearly noon, while he remained silent.

“A man said, ‘Abū al-Qaʿqāʿ, do you not see your people?’ He said, ‘Have you needed me for this?’ They said, ‘Yes.’ He said, ‘As for you, the accused, you are cleared; and as for you, the claimants, your due is my responsibility.’ He drove some camels of his own forward and paid them what they had asked, without asking anyone for anything.”

Abū Saʿīd related to me, saying: Al-Walīd related to us; Saʿīd—meaning Ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz—related to us, saying: “Al-Zubayr had a thousand workers who paid him the land tax. He would not bring any of it into his house; he gave it all in charity.”

Saʿīd ibn Asad related to me, saying: Ḍamra related to us, from Ibn Shawdhab, from al-Ḥasan, who said: “Ṭalḥa ibn ʿUbayd Allāh sold a piece of land of his for one hundred thousand and gave the proceeds in charity.”

Abū Bishr related to me, saying: ʿUththām ibn ʿAlī al-Kilābī related to us, saying: Hishām ibn ʿUrwa related to us, from his father, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr, who said: “On the Day of the Camel, my father said to me:

“‘My son, look to my debt: one million and two hundred thousand.’”

Abū Bishr related to me, saying: Saʿīd ibn ʿĀmir related to us, from Juwayriya—he said, “I think it is from Nāfiʿ”—who said: “A man from Medina was stranded , and someone said to him, ‘Go to Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām.’ He went to him while he was in the mosque and told him of his need. Ḥakīm got up and went with him to his household. They passed a rubbish heap with a piece of latrine material—or, he said, a rag—on it. Ḥakīm picked it up, shook it out, and took it in his hand. The man thought to himself, ‘I see no good to be had from this man.’

“When he entered his house, he saw some of Ḥakīm’s servants working on camel gear. Ḥakīm tossed the rag to them and said, ‘Make use of this in your work.’ Then he ordered that the man be given a saddled, padded riding camel, bearing young.”

He said: Abū Yūsuf added: Bakr ibn Khalaf related to us, saying: Saʿīd—he is Ibn ʿĀmir—related to us, saying: Juwayriya ibn Asmāʾ related to us, saying: “Al-Zubayr sold a house for six hundred thousand. They said, ‘You have been cheated, Abū ʿAbd Allāh.’ He replied, ‘By God, no. By God—’”

“You know that I have not been cheated; it is for the cause of God.”

Abū Bishr Bakr ibn Khalaf, Saʿīd ibn ʿĀmir, related to us, saying: Juwayriya ibn Asmāʾ related to us, from Muslim ibn Abī Maryam, from a man, who said: “I was a slave owned by ʿUthmān. ʿUthmān sent me on a business journey, and when I returned to him, he was pleased with my service. One day I stood before him and said, ‘Commander of the Faithful, I ask you to make a contract of manumission with me.’ He frowned and said:

“‘Yes. Were it not in God’s Book, I would not do this. I will contract with you for one hundred thousand, on condition that you pay it in two installments. By God, I will not deduct a single dirham from it.’

“I left him, and al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwām met me and said, ‘What is the matter with you?’ I said, ‘The Commander of the Faithful sent me on a business journey, and when I returned, he was pleased with my service. I went to him and said, “Commander of the Faithful, I ask you to make a contract of manumission with me.” He frowned.’ He said, ‘He replied, “Yes. Were it not in God’s Book, I would not do this. I will contract with you for one hundred thousand, on condition that you pay it to me in two installments. By God, I will not deduct a single dirham from it.”’

“He said, ‘Then come along.’ He took me back to ʿUthmān and said in his presence, ‘Commander of the Faithful, did you make a contract with so-and-so?’ ʿUthmān frowned and said, ‘Yes. Were it not in God’s Book, I would not have done this. I contracted with him for one hundred thousand, on condition that he pay it in two installments. By God, I will not withhold a single dirham from it.’

“Al-Zubayr became angry and said, ‘By God, I will not stand before you again! I am only asking you for a favor, and you bar it with an oath.’ He struck me —I do not know whether he said my shoulder or my upper arm—then said, ‘Make a contract with him.’

“So I made the contract. Al-Zubayr took me to his household and gave me one hundred thousand. Then he said, ‘Go and seek God’s bounty with it. If something overcomes you, pay ʿUthmān what he is owed from it.’ I went and sought God’s bounty with it. I paid ʿUthmān what he was owed and al-Zubayr what he was owed, and eighty thousand remained in my hands.”

[Abū ʿAbd Rabb]

ʿAlī ibn ʿUthmān ibn Nufayl related to me, saying: Abū Mushir related to us, saying: Saʿīd related to us, from Abū ʿAbd Rabb, who said: “A man met me and said, ‘Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, do not go away with evil while leaving your family in good circumstances.’” Saʿīd said: “I think he had gone through one hundred thousand, or ten thousand. He would sometimes say to us, ‘We are eight dependents, and we have nothing except what comes from the public treasury.’”

ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān ibn Saʿīd ibn Kathīr ibn Dīnār related to us, saying: Al-Walīd ibn Muslim related to us, saying: Ibn Jābir, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yazīd, related to us that Abū ʿAbd Rabb was among the wealthiest people of Damascus. He said: “He set out on a business journey to Azerbaijan. At evening he came to a place beside a river and a pasture, and camped there.”

Abū ʿAbd Rabb said: “I heard the sound of someone proclaiming God’s greatness and praising God in one part of the meadow. I followed the sound and found a man on a patch of ground, wrapped in a mat. I greeted him and said:

“‘Who are you, servant of God?’ He replied, ‘A man from among the Muslims.’ I said, ‘What is this state you are in?’ He replied:

“‘A state of blessing for which I must praise God.’ I said, ‘How so, when you are only in a mat?’ He said, ‘Why should I not praise God for creating me and fashioning me well, making my birth and upbringing in Islam, clothing my limbs in health, and concealing from me what I would dislike to mention or make known? Who could have a greater blessing than someone who ends the day in the state I am in?’ I said, ‘If you would be willing—may God have mercy on you—to come with me to the encampment, I am camped here by the river.’

“‘Why?’ he asked. I replied, ‘So you can have some food, and we can give you something that will spare you from wearing the mat.’ He said, ‘I have no need of that.’ Al-Walīd said: “I think he said to me, ‘In the ravine I have enough and am well provided for.’” Abū ʿAbd Rabb said: “I tried to persuade him to follow me, but he refused.”

He said: “I turned back , having become small in my own eyes and loathing myself because I had left no man in Damascus who could rival me in wealth, while I was still seeking to increase it. O God, I repent to You of the evil state I am in.” Abū ʿAbd Rabb said: “I repented, though my companions did not know what I had resolved to do. At dawn they set out, as they had done on previous journeys, and brought my mount forward. I turned it toward Damascus and said, ‘We have no… turn, if I go on to anything.’ The group asked me, so I told them; they reproached me for turning back, but I refused.”

Ibn Jābir said: “When he arrived, he gave his cash wealth in charity and equipped [men] for the cause of God.”

Ibn Jābir said: “One of my brothers related to me: ‘I bargained with a man selling cloaks at Dābiq over the purchase of a cloak. I offered him six while he was asking seven. When I kept pressing him, he said to me, “Where are you from?” I said, “From Damascus.” He said, “You do not look like the shaykh who came to me yesterday, a man called Abū ʿAbd Rabb. He bought seven hundred garments from me for seven apiece. He did not ask me to lower the price by even a dirham; he asked me to carry them, so I sent my assistants. He kept distributing them among the poor of the army, and he reached his home with only one garment.”’”

Ibn Jābir said: “Abū ʿAbd Rabb had given his cash wealth in charity and sold his properties, giving their proceeds in charity, except for a house of his in Damascus. He used to say, ‘If this river of yours flowed with gold and silver, and anyone who wished could go out to it and take from it what I went out and took, [that would not suffice]. If it were said, “Whoever touches this column will die,” I would be pleased to draw near to it and die out of longing for God and His Messenger.’”

Ibn Jābir said: “One day I came upon him at the ablution place in Damascus while he was performing ablutions. I greeted him, and he said, ‘O Tall One, do not hurry.’ I waited for him. When he had finished his ablutions, he said, ‘I want to consult you.’ I said, ‘Go ahead.’ He said, ‘I have given away my cash wealth and my properties. Nothing remains except this house of mine, and I have been offered such-and-such thousands for it. What do you think?’ I said, ‘By God, I do not know how much of your life remains, and I fear you may come to need people. Its yield provides the means for your livelihood, and you can live in part of it , so it will shelter you and spare you from other people’s houses.’

“He said, ‘Is that really your advice?’ I said, ‘Yes.’ He said, ‘By God, the proverb has proved right about you.’ I said, ‘What proverb?’ He said, ‘May a long fool not benefit you while his earring is in his saddlebag.’73 ‘Or are you trying to frighten me with poverty?’”

Ibn Jābir said: “He sold it for a great sum and distributed the proceeds. That coincided with his death, and we found of its price only enough to cover the cost of his shroud.”

Ibn Jābir said: “A man who used to associate with him passed by. He said, ‘So-and-so.’ He replied, ‘Yes, may God set you right. What is it?’ The man said, ‘I heard that you own four thousand dirhams.’

“He said, ‘Yes, and forty thousand.’ The man said, ‘Foolishness: neither sense nor wealth.’”

“Saʿīd ibn Asad related to me, saying: Ḍamra related to us, from ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd ibn Yazīd al-Judhāmī, who said: Rajāʾ ibn Ḥaywa said to me, ‘Abū ʿAmr, here is the grave of your brother ʿUbāda ibn al-Ṣāmit, beside the eastern wall.’

“ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd said: ‘I attended a funeral in Bayt al-Maqdis with Rajāʾ ibn Ḥaywa, and he said, “Abū ʿAmr, here is the grave of your brother ʿUbāda ibn al-Ṣāmit.”’”

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAmr related to us, saying: Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: “Among us, no one was more ascetic than Abū ʿAbd Rabb ibn ʿAbbād, a client of Banū ʿUdhrā.”

[Ṣāliḥ ibn Mismār]

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmmār related to us, saying: ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān related to us, saying: My father related to me, from Jaʿfar ibn Burqān, who said that Ṣāliḥ ibn Mismār said: “God does not bless a man with worldly life if it leads him afterward to the Fire.” I said, “You have spoken truly.” He said, “And God has indeed blessed a man with worldly life if it leads him afterward to the Garden.” I said, “You have spoken truly.”

I heard Ṣāliḥ ibn Mismār say: “I marvel at people.” I said, “What about them?”

He said: “They leave this world destitute and leave their treasuries behind.”

I heard Ṣāliḥ ibn Mismār [say]: “God’s blessing upon us in what He has withheld from worldly life is greater than His blessing upon us in what He has bestowed of it.”

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmmār related to us, saying: ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān related to us, saying: Abū al-Malīḥ related to us, saying: “Ṣāliḥ died leaving one dirham and four dāniqs. At the time of his death, he was told:

“‘Entrust your mother and sister to whomever you wish.’ He said, ‘I am ashamed before God to entrust them to anyone other than Him.’”

[Al-Walīd ibn Muslim]

I heard Abū al-Faḍl Ṣadaqa ibn al-Faḍl al-Marwazī—and he was one of the best of men— Abū Yūsuf said: I heard al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAẓīm al-ʿAnbarī say: “We used to say:

“ Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal in Iraq, Ṣadaqa ibn al-Faḍl in Khurāsān, and Zayd ibn al-Mubārak in Yemen.”

He said: “Al-Walīd ibn Muslim made the pilgrimage while I was in Mecca. I had never seen a man better at memorizing long ḥadīths and the ḥadīths about the great battles than he was. At that time, our companions were writing down and seeking legal opinions, so they began asking al-Walīd for his opinions, which he had not memorized.

“Then he made the pilgrimage to us again while I was in Mecca. By then he had memorized the chapter divisions, and the man had become a precise memorizer; he had committed them to memory. Nuʿaym ibn Ḥammād used to disapprove of their seeking legal opinions and abandoning the chains of transmission and the elevated ḥadīths. So the hadith scholars began asking him about chains of transmission and elevated ḥadīths. He said, ‘How strange you are! Whenever you ask us about one kind of knowledge and we study it, you move us on to another kind! If we live and come on pilgrimage, I will bring you what you seek in this area—something like this, or similar to it.’

“He then departed and ﵀ died before he reached Damascus.”

Abū Bishr Bakr ibn Khalaf related to me, saying: Al-Ḥumaydī said: Al-Walīd ibn Muslim said to us: “If you let me, I will relate to you from the reliable shaykhs among ours; but if you refuse, ask, and I will relate whatever you ask for.”

I heard al-Ḥumaydī say: “I came on the day of departure, and al-Walīd was in the mosque of— At Minā there was a great crowd around him. I came at the very end of the people, urging my camel forward, while ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī was answering him. They began asking questions, and he was relating traditions to them, but I could not understand. He said: I gathered a group from among the crowd and said to them, “Make a commotion and disrupt those who are close to him.” They began shouting and making a commotion, saying, “Are we not to hear?” ʿAlī kept saying, “Be quiet, and we will let you hear.” He said: I pushed my way forward and shouted. I had not yet shaved my hair (133a). ʿAlī looked at me but did not recognize me. He said, “If there were any good in you, your hair would not be as I see it.” They dispersed, and he did not relate anything to them.

I heard Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir say: I arrived in Baṣra, and ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī came to me and said, “The first thing I want to do is go out to hear the traditions of al-Walīd ibn Muslim.” I said, “My dear fellow, glory be to God! How can my hearing compare with yours?” I kept refusing, but he persisted. I said:

“Tell me, what is behind this insistence of yours?” He said, “I will tell you. Al-Walīd is a man of Syria, and he has much knowledge. I have not had the opportunity to hear from him, but he related traditions to you in Medina during the pilgrimage seasons. Valuable reports come to you because pilgrims gather in Medina from many different regions, so some of his valuable reports are with one person and some with another.” He said: I took him out to him, and he was astonished by his writing; he almost wrote on the face.

“I asked Hishām ibn ʿAmmār about al-Walīd ibn Muslim. He said, ‘May God have mercy on Abū al-ʿAbbās! He was such-and-such,’ and began recounting his merit, knowledge, scrupulousness, and humility.”

He said: His father, Muslim, had been among the government’s slaves, and they were all declared free. Al-Walīd had an arrogant brother who rode horses, with many servants riding along with him. He was fond of hunting and recreation, and would go out hunting with horsemen and provisions. Al-Walīd paid blood money and deposited it in the public treasury, paying it on his own behalf because the matter of his father had become unclear to him. He said:

As a result, strife, estrangement, and a rupture arose between him and his brother. His brother said, “You have disgraced us. What need did you have to do what you did?”

[Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAyyāsh]

Abū Yūsuf said: I used to hear our companions say, “The knowledge of Syria is with Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAyyāsh and al-Walīd ibn Muslim.”

I heard Abū al-Yamān say: I copied Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAyyāsh’s books, leaving none of them on the sheets. A man from Khurāsān came and asked Ismāʿīl to arrange for him to buy a copy and read it back to him. Ismāʿīl called me and said, “Ḥakam, you have not performed the pilgrimage. Would you sell the books to this man from Khurāsān, go on pilgrimage, return, and copy them (133b), and I will read them back to you?” I said, “Perhaps you will die.” He replied, “Ask God to guide you; if you accept my proposal, do as I say.” He said: I sold the books to him—they were on sheets—for thirty dinars. We performed the pilgrimage, I returned, and copied the books for a few dirhams; he read them back to me.

He said: Our companions were eager for knowledge and pursued it intensely in Syria, Medina, and Mecca. They used to say, “We exert ourselves in seeking it, wear out our bodies, and are away; then, when we return, we find everything we copied with Ismāʿīl.”

“As for al-Walīd, he followed his way, held in high regard by the scholars, precise and sound, sound in knowledge.” Some people criticized Ismāʿīl, but Ismāʿīl is trustworthy and upright, the most knowledgeable of people about Syrian traditions; no one can refute him. The most they said in criticism was: “He relates unusual reports from trustworthy Medinans and Meccans.”

[Baḳiyya ibn al-Walīd]

Baḳiyya comes close to Ismāʿīl and al-Walīd. If he is like al-Walīd in the traditions of the Syrians, then he is trustworthy; when he relates from a trustworthy narrator, his report stands as proof. “He is known for his retention, except that he favors amusing and curious traditions, and relates from shaykhs who have some weakness. He was fond of hadith, so he would give a kunyah to a weak narrator known by his name, and call a well-known narrator by his name when he was known by his kunyah.

I heard Isḥāq ibn Ibrāhīm ibn Rāhawayh say: Ibn al-Mubārak said, “Baḳiyya baffled me: he gave the names kunyahs and the kunyahs names.” [He said:] “Abū Saʿīd al-Wuḥāẓī related to me.”

It is in fact ʿAbd al-Quddūs.

The scholars have said: “When Baḳiyya does not name the person from whom he relates, but gives him a kunyah, then his report is not worth anything—”

—then his hadith is worth nothing.”

Abū al-Yamān related to us: Ṣafwān ibn ʿAmr al-Saksakī related to us, from Yazīd ibn Ḥumayr al-Raḥabī, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Busr al-Māzinī.

Abū al-Walīd, Sulaymān, and Abū ʿUmar related to us. They said: Shuʿba related to us, saying: Yazīd ibn Khumayr informed me, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Busr, of Banū Sulaym, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ came to my father and stayed with him.

Yazīd was a Syrian who came to Wāsiṭ. Shuʿba heard from him in Wāsiṭ, and his hadith is sound.

(134a) Abū al-Walīd and Abū ʿUmar related to us. They said: Shuʿba related to us, from Abū al-Fayḍ, who said: I heard Sulaym ibn ʿĀmir, a man of Ḥimyar.

Abū al-Fayḍ was a Syrian with fine traditions, and “Sulaym ibn ʿĀmir was a well-known, trustworthy man,” a Kalāʿī Khubāʾirī.

Muḥammad ibn Bashshār related to us: Abū Dāwūd related to us, saying: Shuʿba related to us. He said, “I heard—”

Abū Isḥāq say, “ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAṭāʾ related to me, from ʿUqba ibn ʿĀmir, a tradition from the Prophet ﷺ.” I met ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAṭāʾ and asked him about it. He said, “Ziyād ibn Mikh­rāq related it to me.” I came to Baṣra and asked Ziyād, “Who related this tradition to you?” He said, “A man of Banū Layth related it to me, from Shahr ibn Ḥawshab.” Although Ibn ʿAwn said that they had abandoned Shahr, he is trustworthy. This is a Syrian tradition—and Abū Qilāba, Shahr ibn Ḥawshab, and Maṭar al-Warrāq related many traditions from the people of Syria. Trustworthy Syrians related it with its chain from the Prophet ﷺ through sound lines of transmission, while Abū Qilāba, Shahr, and Maṭar transmitted it without naming the Prophet in the chain. Our companions ought to have accepted it with gratitude. As for Shahr’s version, Abū Ṣāliḥ, the righteous man, informed us: Muʿāwiya ibn Ṣāliḥ al-Ḥimṣī—a judge in al-Andalus—related to me, from Abū ʿUthmān, from Jubayr ibn Nufayr and Rabīʿa ibn Yazīd, from Abū Idrīs al-Khawlānī; and ʿAbd al-Wahhāb ibn Bukht, from al-Layth ibn Sulaym al-Juhanī. All of them relate from ʿUqba ibn ʿĀmir. ʿUqba said: We used to serve ourselves, and take turns tending the camels among us. My turn to tend the camels came, so I returned with them in the evening and caught up with the Messenger of God ﷺ as he stood addressing the people. I caught part of what he said, namely:

“Any one of you who performs ablution, completing the ablution, then stands and performs two rakʿahs, turning his heart and face toward them, will surely enter Paradise and be forgiven—”

—by virtue of them.” (134b) “A man who performs them will surely enter Paradise and be forgiven.” He said:

I said, “How excellent this is!” Someone said, “The one I performed before those, ʿUqba, is better.”74 I looked, and there was ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb. I said, “What is it, Abū Ḥafṣ?” He said, “Before you arrived, he said: ‘Any one of you who performs ablution, completing the ablution, and then says, “I bear witness that there is no god but God alone, without partner, and that Muḥammad is His servant and messenger,” the eight gates of Paradise will be opened to him, and he may enter through whichever one he wishes.’”

Abū al-Yamān related to us: Ḥurayz ibn ʿUthmān related to us, from Ibn Abī ʿAwf, from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ḥayy, who said: I attended the funeral of Shuraḥbīl ibn al-Simṭ with Ḥabīb ibn Maslama. Ḥabīb turned his face toward us, towering over us—as I mean by that, because of his height.

Abū al-Yamān related to us: Ḥurayz related to us, from Ḥabīb ibn ʿUbayd al-Raḥabī, who said: Abū Qabīla, Marthad ibn Wadāʿa al-Aʿmā, was standing and preaching.

Abū al-Yamān related to us: Ḥurayz related to us, from Ḥabīb ibn ʿUbayd, who traces it back to Abū Bishr; Abū Bishr traces it back to ʿAthāma ibn Qays—and ʿAthāma is ʿAthāma ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sufyān al-Azdī. Both were Companions of the Prophet ﷺ.

“Abū al-Yamān related to us, from Ḥurayz, from Abū al-Ḥasan ʿImrān ibn Nimrān, that Abū ʿUbayda ibn al-Jarrāḥ used to march with the army, saying: ‘How many a man whitens his clothes while soiling his religion! How many a man honors himself, only to be brought low by it tomorrow! So ward off old misdeeds—’”

—by means of recent good deeds.” If one of you were to commit sins reaching from here to the sky, then perform a good deed, it would rise above his sins until it overcame them.

Thawr ibn Yazīd is a Raḥabī. Abū al-Yamān related this to us from Ḥurayz.

Abū Ḥabīb al-Ḥārith ibn Muḥammad, the judge.

Abū al-Yamān related to us: Saʿīd related to us, from Makhūl, who said: I went over to Anas ibn Mālik from this mosque and asked him.

From Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz: He said: The name of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām was al-Ḥuṣayn, but the Messenger of God ﷺ renamed him ʿAbd Allāh. The name of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf was ʿAbd ʿAmr, but the Messenger of God ﷺ renamed him ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. The name of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl was al-Ḥubāb, but the Prophet ﷺ renamed him ʿAbd Allāh.

Muḥammad ibn Ziyād ibn al-Alhānī, whose kunyah is Abū Sufyān: Abū al-Yamān related this to me from Ṣafwān.

Khālid ibn Maʿdān is a Kalāʿī.

Abū al-Yamān, ʿĀmir ibn Luḥayy al-Hawzanī.

Abū al-Ṣalt, Shurayḥ ibn ʿUbayd.

Abū Ḥasana, Muslim ibn Akīs, the client of ʿAbd al-Dār.

ʿĀmir ibn Kurayz, from someone who mentioned that he entered to see Abū ʿUbayda.

And Umm Ṣafwān, Umm al-Hajras.

Azhar ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jamīʿ al-Ḥarāzī.

Ḥibbān ibn Zayd, Abū Khidāsh al-Sharʿabī. Abū al-Yamān related this to us from Ḥurayz.

Abū al-Yamān related to us: Ḥurayz related to us, from Muʿāwiya al-Hudhalī, a Companion of the Prophet ﷺ.

And from Ḥurayz, from Sulaym ibn ʿĀmir al-Khubāʾirī, from al-Ḥārith ibn Muʿāwiya al-Kindī, who heard him say: “I rode to ʿUmar.”

And from Sulaym, who said: ʿIyāḍ—or Ghuṭayf ibn ʿIyāḍ al-Kindī—came to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb with Ḥabīb ibn Maslama.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Maysara was a Ḥaḍramī; he heard from Abū Umāma.

ʿĀṣim ibn Ḥumayd was a Sakūnī, a Companion of Muʿādh. Rāshid ibn Saʿd related from him, from Muʿādh. Baḳiyya mentioned that Rāshid ibn Saʿd’s eye was injured on the day of Ṣiffīn. On the day of Ṣiffīn, ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī’s eye was put out. Abū Nuʿaym related this to us: Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to us, saying: Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn related to us: When ʿUthmān was killed, ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim said, “Not even two goats will butt heads over his killing.” When the day of Ṣiffīn came, his eye was put out.

He was asked, “Not even two goats will butt heads over ʿUthmān’s killing?” He replied, “Indeed—but many eyes will be put out.”

Abū al-Yamān related to us: Ḥurayz related to us, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Maysara, from Jubayr ibn Nufayr (135b), from Bishr ibn Jiḥāsh al-Qurashī. I said to Abū al-Yamān, “Bishr ibn Jiḥāsh?” He said, “Yes, Bishr ibn Jiḥāsh.” He had confused it.

Abū al-Yamān and ʿAlī ibn ʿAyyāsh related to us. They said: Ḥurayz related to us, from Saʿīd ibn Marthad—who had witnessed Ṣiffīn—who said: I heard ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ḥawshab relate from Thawbān ibn Shahr, who said: I heard Kurayb ibn Abraha, while he was seated with ʿAbd al-Malik on the roof of the treasury, and they were speaking about arrogance. Kurayb said: I heard Abū Rayḥāna say, “I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: ‘No trace of arrogance will enter Paradise.’”

Someone said, “Messenger of God, I like to adorn myself with the strap of my whip and the thong of my sandal.”

The Prophet ﷺ said to him, “That is not arrogance. God is beautiful and loves beauty. Arrogance is only scorning the truth and looking down on people.” This is the wording of Abū al-Yamān.

Salmān is the son of Sumayya al-Alhānī. He relates from Ibn Ḥawāla; and Ibn Abī ʿAwf al-Jurashī relates from al-Miqdām ibn Maʿdīkarib and Shurāḥbīl ibn Shufʿa al-Raḥabī.

—from Ibn Nāsiḥ al-Ḥaḍramī; and from Abū al-Walīd Azhar al-Hawzī, from ʿUqba, a Companion of the Prophet ﷺ who used to seek refuge during his prayer from the tribulation of the West.

Ibn Abī Maryam: Abū Baḥriyya ʿAbd Allāh ibn Qays al-Tarāghumī.

Al-Haytham ibn Mālik al-Ṭāʾī.

Ḍamra ibn Ḥabīb ibn Ṣuhayb al-Ḥimṣī.

Al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Sufyān al-Ghassānī.

And from Abū Salama Sulaymān ibn Sulaym.

Abū Dharr ʿAbd Allāh ibn Faḍāla.

Al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Sufyān al-Ghassānī.

Ibn Bukayr said: Yazīd ibn Abī Ḥabīb did not hear from Ibn Shihāb or Nāfiʿ, and al-Awzāʿī did not hear from Nāfiʿ.

Sulaymān ibn Salama al-Ḥimṣī related to me: Baḳiyya related to us, saying: Yūsuf ibn al-Safr informed me, from al-Awzāʿī, from al-Zuhrī, from ʿUrwa, from ʿĀʾisha, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said, “God loves those who persist in supplication.” Yūsuf is from Beirut; his hadith is written down only for identification.

ʿUbāda ibn Awfā is a Syrian Numayrī.

Sulaymān ibn Salama al-Ḥimṣī related to me, saying: Baḳiyya related to us: Salāma ibn— ʿUmayra al-Munābijī—[from] a clan of Yemen—[reported] from Luqmān ibn ʿĀmir al-Wuṣābī—[from] a clan of Yemen—from [Abū] Umāma, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: “Every flock that goes out to graze and returns is forbidden to others besides its people.” He also said: Baqiyya related to us: Abū Khālid al-Sakūnī related to me—Buḥayr ibn Saʿīd, one of the trustworthy men of Ḥimṣ.

He said: Manīʿ ibn al-Sarī al-Ḥarāzī related to us: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥumayd al-Muzanī related to us, from Shurayḥ ibn Masrūq al-Hawzī, from Abū Zakariyyā, from Abū Umāma, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: “Kindness is fitting only for a man of religion, or a man of noble lineage, or a man of forbearance.” He said: Al-Muʾammal ibn ʿUmar—or Qaʿnab al-ʿUtabī—related to us: Yūsuf Abū ʿAnbasa, the servant of Abū Umāma, related to us: I heard Abū Umāma say: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: “Whoever does not recite behind the imam, his prayer is deficient.”

He said: Sulaymān ibn Nāshira al-Alhānī related to us: I heard ʿUmayr ibn Ziyād al-Alhānī say: Thawbān was our neighbor, and he used to enter the bathhouse. I said to him—

He said: The Prophet ﷺ used to enter the bathhouse. And he used to apply the depilatory.

He said: Thawbān was called Ibn Bajdad.

Hishām ibn ʿAmmār related to us, from Ṣadaqa ibn Khālid al-Qurashī, client of Umm al-Banīn—a Damascene, trustworthy—from Abū Ḥafṣ ʿUthmān ibn Abī al-ʿĀtika, who was the preacher of Damascus—“and his hadith is weak.”

Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Muqriʾ related to us: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ziyād ibn Anʿam related to us; he is counted among the Egyptians—“there is no harm in him”—though there is weakness in his hadith.

He said: Saʿīd ibn Abī Ayyūb related to us. Abū Ayyūb was Miqlāṣ, and al-Muqriʾ used to say that he was the client of Abū Hurayra. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿImrān—who was the son of Saʿīd’s daughter—rejected this and said: “We are clients of Khuzāʿa.” And he showed me—[the word is unclear]—his ancestors’ books; they are affiliated with Khuzāʿa. He was an Egyptian, trustworthy.

(136b) Aḥmad ibn Yūnus related to us: Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh related to us, from— Muṭarraḥ ibn Yazīd ibn al-Muhallab—who is weak—from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Zaḥr, who is weak.

[ʿAbd Allāh ibn Lahīʿa]

Abū al-Aswad al-Naḍr ibn ʿAbd al-Jabbār al-Murādī, the scribe of Ibn Lahīʿa—who was trustworthy—related to us: “I heard Aḥmad ibn Ṣāliḥ Abū Jaʿfar—one of the best of those who mastered their material—praise him. He said to me: ‘I wrote Abū al-Aswad’s hadith on parchment.’ I asked him to clarify, and he said to me: ‘I used to write down material from the Egyptians and others whose case gave me concern. When it became established for me, I transferred it to parchment. I wrote Abū al-Aswad’s hadith on parchment. How excellent his hadith from Ibn Lahīʿa is!’ I said to him: ‘Do they say there was an early audition and a late audition?’ He said to me: ‘There is nothing to that. Ibn Lahīʿa’s writing was sound. He brought out his books and dictated to the people until they wrote down his hadith from dictation. Whoever retained it accurately had good, sound hadith. The problem was that people who were precise and proficient would attend, while some people would attend and write without retaining the material accurately or checking it, and others would merely look on; still others heard along with other people. After that, Ibn Lahīʿa did not bring out a book, and no book of his was seen. Anyone who wanted to hear from him would go and copy from someone who had written from him, bring the copy, and read it back to him. Whoever came upon a correct copy had sound hadith; whoever copied from an inaccurate one introduced many errors into it. Then a group went [to him], and everyone who transmitted from him from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ had heard from ʿAṭāʾ. They would transmit from a man, from two men, or from three [men, all the way] from ʿAṭāʾ, but they omitted those between themselves and ʿAṭāʾ and made it [appear to be] from ʿAṭāʾ.’”

Abū Yūsuf said: “I had written, from Ibn Rumḥ, a book from Ibn Lahīʿa, and it contained something like what Aḥmad described.” He said: “This one had come upon a man who accurately retained Ibn Lahīʿa’s dictation.” I asked him about Ibn Lahīʿa’s hadith. He said: “He did not know my position regarding narrators: I hold that a transmitter’s hadith should not be abandoned until the people of his city unanimously agree to abandon (137a) his hadith.”

“I heard Ibn Abī Maryam say: Ibn Lahīʿa used to read from people’s books. A group of people from Egypt made the pilgrimage, then returned and went to Ibn Lahīʿa and exchanged reports with him. He said:

‘Have you written down any unusual hadith?’ One of them said to him: ‘The hadith of al-Qāsim al-ʿUmarī, from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “When you see a fire, proclaim God’s greatness.”’ Ibn Lahīʿa said: ‘This is an unusual hadith.’ Later, I saw a man come and ask him, ‘Did ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb relate it to you?’ He would say, ‘No; one of our companions—naming him—related it to us.’ Then they inserted [the report] into his hadith from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, so whenever they came upon this hadith he would say, ‘As God wills, this is the hadith of one of our companions from ʿAmr.’ Then he fell silent, and they continued inserting it into the body of the hadith of ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, changing it.”

Saʿīd said: “There is something else. Ḥaywa had appointed an executor, and his books were in the executor’s possession. Someone who did not fear God would go and copy from Ḥaywa’s books [the hadith] of the shaykhs whom Ibn Lahīʿa had also studied under, then take it to him and read it back to them.”

Abū al-Aswad related to me: Ibn Lahīʿa informed me, from Darāj ibn al-Samḥ, from Abū al-Haytham, from Abū Saʿīd.

I heard Ibn Bukayr say: Abū al-Haytham was the preacher of the congregation in Egypt during the days of the Umayyads. When the officials of the Abbasids arrived, they removed him from preaching. This weighed heavily on him, and he said: “Why are you removing me? I am only a preacher. If you tell me, ‘Add to your sermons,’ I will add; and if you tell me, ‘Make them shorter,’ I will make them shorter. So why are you removing me?”
