ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rajāʾ related to us: Isrāʾīl informed us, from Saʿīd, from Mundhir, who said: Bakr ibn Māʿiz related to us, from al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym: “Keep your tongue in check; [the remaining words are unclear]—for I distrust people where my religion is concerned.”85

Through the same chain, from al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym: When he prostrated during Sūrat al-Raʿd, he would say, “In willing submission, O our Lord…”

“…in willing submission, O our Lord.”

ʿUthmān ibn Zufar related to us: Rabīʿ related to us, from Mundhir al-Thawrī, from al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym, who said: “Everything for which God’s countenance is not sought will perish.”

ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Mūsā said: al-Aʿmash informed us, from Mundhir, who said: Al-Rabīʿ used to sweep out his privy. He was asked about it, and he replied, “I like to take a share of it.”

ʿUbayd Allāh related to us: al-Aʿmash related to us, from Ibrāhīm, who said: A woman passed by al-Rabīʿ. He did this and lowered his gaze, but did not close his eyes.

ʿUbayd Allāh related to us: al-Aʿmash related to us, from Mundhir, who said: Al-Rabīʿ said to his family, “Make me a sweet dish”—for he scarcely ever asked them for anything he craved. They made it. He then sent for a neighbor of his who was afflicted, and the man began eating, saliva running from his mouth. His family said, “He does not know what he has eaten.” Al-Rabīʿ said, “But God knows.”

Qabīṣa related to us, saying: Sufyān related to us, from the wife of al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym, who said: Al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym liked sweets, and would say, “Make me some food.” They made him a great deal of food, and he would call Farrūkh and so-and-so. Al-Rabīʿ would feed them with his own hand and give them drink, and he would drink from what they drank. She said: He would be asked, “Do they know what this is, and what you are feeding them?” He would reply:

“But God knows.”

Qabīṣa related to us, saying: Qays ibn Muslim related to us, from Ḥarrāb ibn ʿUbayd Allāh, who said:

Whenever a beggar came to al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym, he would say, “Give him sugar to eat, for I like sugar.”

ʿUthmān ibn Zufar related to us: Rabīʿ related to us, from his father—or from Saʿīd ibn Masrūq—who said: A beggar came to al-Rabīʿ, and he said, “Girl, give him sugar to eat.” She said, “What does he expect from sugar? He needs other things more.” Al-Rabīʿ said, “Al-Rabīʿ likes it, so give him something that al-Rabīʿ likes.”

Qabīṣa related to us, saying: Sufyān related to us, from Saʿīd (176b) ibn Masrūq, from Abū Yaʿlā, who said: Al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym saw me taking pleasure in written sheets. He said, “Abū Yaʿlā, I have never come to your door with a sheet bearing a seal from Muḥammad ﷺ.” Then he recited: “Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you” (6:151)…

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān related to us: ʿAbd Allāh informed us: Mālik ibn Mighwal informed us: Shaʿbī related to us, saying: Al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym never sat in a gathering or by the side of a road—such-and-such—saying, “I fear that a man might be wronged and I fail to support him; that one man might slander another and I be burdened with giving testimony against him; that someone might greet me and I fail to return his greeting; or that a pregnant woman might fall and I fail to help her carry her load.” He then began to mention more of such things. He said, “We used to visit him for a year.”86

Ibn ʿUthmān related to us: ʿAbd Allāh related to us: ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar informed us, saying: It seems that they mentioned something about people in al-Rabīʿ’s presence. Al-Rabīʿ said, “Remembering God is better than remembering people.”

He also informed us: ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar related to us: ʿAmr ibn Murra related to us: A man from among al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym’s household told me: “For twenty years, we have heard no word from Ibn Khuthaym that one could regard as disobedience to God.”

Ibn ʿUthmān related to us: ʿAbd Allāh related to us: ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar related to us: ʿAmr ibn Murra told me: Al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym passed by, and one of them said to a companion of al-Rabīʿ, “In what valley is this man wandering?” The companion replied, “By God, when we leave him, we do not know anything more than we knew when we sat down with him.” The man said, “Bring me in to see him, for I have hardly spoken with anyone without nearly discovering the sea from which he draws.” They went in to him and spoke with him. The man was skilled in disputation, and they discussed people’s disagreements and other matters. Then he asked God’s forgiveness and fell silent. Al-Rabīʿ then spoke, mentioning the central matter: Paradise and Hell, and things of that sort. Then he asked God’s forgiveness and fell silent. When we went out, the man said, “You blamed whoever among you said, ‘When I got up, I was no different from when I sat down.’”

Qabīṣa related to us: Sufyān related to us, from the wife of al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym, who said: Someone would come in to al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym while the Qurʾān was in his lap and he was reciting from it, and he would cover it up.

Muḥammad ibn Yazīd al-Kūfī related to us: Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym told me, from his paternal aunt, who said: I used to say to my father, “Father, will you not sleep?” He would reply, “My daughter, how can one who fears being overtaken by night sleep?”

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān related to us: ʿAbd Allāh informed us: Yūnus informed us, from Abū Isḥāq, from Bakr ibn Māʿiz, who said: A daughter of al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym came to him and said, “Father, may I go and play?” When she kept asking him, one of his companions said to him, “If only you would tell her to go.” He replied:

“God willing, it will not be recorded of me today that I ordered her to play.”

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān related to us: ʿAbd Allāh informed us: Ibn ʿAwn informed us, from Muslim, Abū ʿAbd Allāh, who said: Ibn Masʿūd, whenever he saw al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym, would say, “Give good tidings to…” (22:34)

“…those who are humble” (22:34).

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Sufyān related to us, from Abū Ḥayyān, from his father, who said: Al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym used to be led to the prayer, for he was afflicted by paralysis. He was told, “Abū Yazīd, you have been granted a concession in this matter.” He replied, “I hear ‘Come to success,’ so if you are able, come to it even crawling.”

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān related to us: ʿAbd Allāh informed us: Sufyān informed us, from his father, from Bakr ibn Māʿiz, who said: There was an affliction on al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym’s face, and its pus was running. Seeing the sorrow in my face, he said, “Bakr, I would not be pleased if what afflicts me were more rebellious against God than the most rebellious of the Daylamites.”87

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān related to us: ʿAbd Allāh informed us: Sufyān informed us, saying: Al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym was asked—he had been afflicted by paralysis—“Why do you not seek treatment?” He replied, “I was on the point of doing so, then I remembered ‘ʿĀd, Thamūd, the people of al-Rass, and generations between them, many indeed’ (25:38).” Among them were…

They had ailments, and they had physicians; yet neither healer nor patient remained without perishing.

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us: Sufyān related to us, saying: I heard Mālik ibn Mighwal relate from al-Shaʿbī, who said: “Since Rabīʿ first wrapped himself in a waistcloth, he has not sat in any gathering without saying, ‘I fear I may see a pregnant woman; I fear I may fail to return a greeting; I fear I may fail to lower my gaze.’”

He said: Sufyān related to us from Sālim ibn Abī Ḥafṣa and another—I think it was from Mundhir—who said: “When ʿAbd Allāh saw al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym, he would say, ‘And give good tidings to the humble.’ And, ‘Were the Messenger of God ﷺ to see you, he would love you.’”

He said: Sufyān related to us from Sālim or someone else, from someone who had heard it from Mundhir or another, that al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym was stricken with paralysis. One of his children or members of his household, when they saw him, seemed distressed.

He said: Rabīʿ replied, “I would not wish that this were the most rebellious of the Daylam against God.”

Saʿīd related to us: Sufyān related from Nusayr ibn Dhuʿlūq, from al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym, who said: “I have never seen anyone praying voluntary prayers in the neighborhood mosque except on one occasion.”

Abū Bakr related to us: Sufyān related to us: Misʿar related from ʿAmr ibn Murra, who said: I heard— Al-Shaʿbī say: “Al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym related to us here by this pillar; he was one of the wellsprings of truthfulness.”

Ibn Numayr related to us: Abū Bakr, one of the descendants of al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym, related to us from his mother, who said: “When al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym received his stipend, he would distribute it and keep for himself only enough to suffice him.”

Yaḥyā ibn Abī ʿUmar related to us: Sufyān related from Misʿar, from ʿAmr ibn Murra, who said: I heard al-Shaʿbī say: “Al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym related to us—he was one of the wellsprings of truthfulness—who said: ‘Those to whom a debt is owed will press their claim more forcefully in the Hereafter than they do in this world. The debtor will be detained for them, and they will take it from him. He will say, “Lord, do You not see that I am barefoot and naked?” He will say, “Take from his good deeds in proportion to what they are owed.” If he has no good deeds, then add to his sins from their sins.’”

ʿAmr ibn Murra said: “Al-Shaʿbī was one of the wellsprings of truthfulness.” Misʿar said: “ʿAmr was one of the wellsprings of truthfulness.” Sufyān said: “Misʿar was one of the wellsprings of truthfulness.” Ibn Abī ʿUmar said: “Sufyān was one of the wellsprings of truthfulness.”

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr related to us: Abū Muʿāwiya related to us: al-Aʿmash related from Ibrāhīm al-Taymī, from his father, who said: “He used to wear a mantle that reached his buttocks at the back and his knees in front. I said, ‘Father, why not get a mantle wider than this?’ He replied, ‘My son, you have not told me that before. By God, there is no morsel on earth that I have eaten as wholesome food without wishing it had been in the mouth of the person I hate most.’” (178a)

Yazīd ibn Mihrān al-Kūfī related to us: Abū Bakr related from al-Aʿmash, from Ibrāhīm al-Taymī, who said: “Sometimes I would go a month without tasting anything. Had my family not made me eat a grape, I would not have eaten it. I felt its pain in my stomach, though I was buying their provisions for them.”

[ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Nuʿm]

Yazīd related to us: Abū Bakr related from Mughīra, who said: “ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Nuʿm would fast continuously for fifteen [days], eating nothing.” He said: “He would be visited as though he were ill.”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us: Sufyān related to us, saying: I heard Sālim ibn Abī Ḥafṣa say: “ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Nuʿm would remain in a state of consecration for pilgrimage from one year to the next.” Sālim said: “People used to say that he was showing off. I heard him reciting the pilgrim’s response in the market, saying, ‘At Your service!’ [Even] had it been ostentation, it would have vanished.”

Ibn Bukayr related to us: Abū Bakr related to us from Mughīra, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Nuʿm, who said that he stood before al-Ḥajjāj and said: “Do not go to excess in killing; he was supported [by God].” Al-Ḥajjāj said: “May God give me power over your blood.” He replied: “Those in her womb are more numerous than those on her back.”

[And [Abū] Wāʾil, Shaqīq ibn Salama]

Muḥammad ibn al-Muthannā related to us: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to us from Shuʿba, from Yazīd ibn Abī Ziyād: Abū Wāʾil was asked, “Are you older, or al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym?” He said, “I was—” older than he in years, and he is greater than I in understanding.

Yazīd ibn Mihrān related to us: Abū Bakr related from ʿĀṣim: “Abū Wāʾil would pass through the market and hear the price of a qīrāṭ or a dāniq, but not know what it was.”

Aḥmad ibn Yūnus related to us: Abū Bakr related to us from al-Aʿmash, who said: “When I was late in coming to Abū Wāʾil, he would say, ‘Solomon, where have you been? Indeed, it is no more hateful to me than for you not to come to me.’”

Bakr ibn al-Aswad related to us: Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh related to us from al-Aʿmash, who said:

Shaqīq ibn Salama said to me, “What keeps you from coming to us more often than you do?” He disliked saying, “I would like you to come to us more often than you do,” lest he be lying.

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us: Sufyān related to us: ʿUmar ibn Saʿīd related from his father, who said: I came to Abū Wāʾil, and he said, “Who are you from?” I replied, “From Banū Nūr.” (178b) He said, “I have many a close friend from Banū Thawr.” I asked him, “Are you older, or al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym?” He said, “I am older by birth, and he is greater than I in understanding.”

“Jāmiʿ ibn Ṣubayḥ al-Ramlī related to us: Abū Bakr related to us from ʿĀṣim, who said:

‘Zirr was older than Abū Wāʾil. Whenever the two sat together, Abū Wāʾil would not speak in Zirr’s presence.’”

“in Zirr’s presence.”

“Yūsuf ibn Muḥammad al-Muṣaffā related to me: Abū Bakr related to us from ʿĀṣim, who said:

‘When Abū Wāʾil was alone, he would sob. Even if the whole world were offered to him on condition that he do that while someone watched him, he would not do it.’”

Ibn Numayr related to me: Abū Muʿāwiya related to us from al-Aʿmash, from Ibrāhīm, who said: “Hammām arose anxious, and someone among the people said to him, ‘Hammām’s flesh tells you that he did not rest his side against it last night.’”

Yaḥyā ibn Sulaymān related to us: Sufyān related to us from al-Aʿmash, from Ibrāhīm al-Taymī, who said: “There were among us sixty elders who were companions of ʿAbd Allāh.”

Qabīṣa related to us: Sufyān related to us from al-ʿAlāʾ ibn al-Musayyib, from Abū Yaʿlā, who said: “Among Banū Thawr were thirty men, none of them inferior to al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym.”

He said: Sufyān related to us from his father, who said: “We had an elder named ʿAzra who would say, ‘We belong to God and to Him we return.’ They would ask him, ‘What is the matter with you?’ He would reply, ‘I knew elders of ours in whose company we were thieves.’”

He said: “I was told that he once said, ‘If there is a civil strife, we have seen and experienced [one before].’ That reached al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym, who said: ‘What is Ibn Abī ʿAzra saying? “If there is a civil strife, we have seen and experienced [one before].” What if God were to bring one that is deaf and dumb!’”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us: Sufyān related to us from Mālik ibn Mighwal, who said: Abū Ḥuṣayn said to me, “If you had seen what we experienced, your liver would have burned.”

Abū Bakr related to us: Sufyān related to us, saying: I heard Mālik say: Al-Shaʿbī said:

“I have never seen people with more knowledge, greater forbearance, or greater abstinence from worldly things than the companions of ʿAbd Allāh. Were it not that the Companions of Muḥammad ﷺ had preceded them, we would have placed no one above them.”

He said: Sufyān related to us from Mālik, who said: Asīr ibn Jābir came to Baṣra. When the people heard him speak, (179a) they said: “If this is what he is like, then what must the one from whom he learned be like—or the ocean from which he learned!”

Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb related to us: Ḥammād ibn Zayd related to us from someone who mentioned it, from Muḥammad, who said: “Among the black-headed people, I have never seen a group more learned in jurisprudence than the people of Kūfa, though they are a people with audacity.”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us: Sufyān related to us: Ismāʿīl related to us, saying: I heard al-Shaʿbī say: “Among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ no companion was more learned in jurisprudence than ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd.”

Qabīṣa related to us: Sufyān related to us from ʿUmāra ibn al-Qaʿqāʿ, who said: I heard Ibn Shubrumah say: “I have never seen any neighborhood in Kūfa with more elderly men who were learned in jurisprudence and devoted to worship than Banū Thawr.”

He said: Sufyān related to us from Abū Bakr al-Zubaydī, from his father, who said: “I have never seen any neighborhood with more people sitting in the mosque than the Thawrīs and the ʿUranīs.”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us: Sufyān related to us, saying: I heard ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib say: “I saw Murra al-Hamdānī’s place of prayer; it was like a camel’s resting place.”

Sufyān said: ʿAṭāʾ or someone else said: “He used to pray six hundred rakʿas every day.”

He said: Sufyān related to us, saying: I heard ʿAṭāʾ say: “When Zādhān spread out a garment, he would offer the buyer the poorer of its two sides, then bargain for a single price.”

Sufyān said: “I think ʿAṭāʾ mentioned this from Maysara and Sālim the cloth-seller, or one of them.”

Or one of the two.

“He said: Sufyān related to us, saying: I heard Yazīd ibn Abī Ziyād say: Ibn Abī Laylā and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Shaddād ibn al-Hādī met and discussed hadith. I heard one of them say to the other, ‘May God have mercy on you! How many a hadith you have revived in my heart, after it had died!’”

(182a) “Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us, saying: Sufyān related to us, saying:

Yazīd ibn Abī Ziyād related to us, saying: ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith said, ‘Bring me together with Ibn Abī Laylā.’ So I brought them together, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith said, ‘I would never have imagined that women could give birth to the like of this!’”

Sufyān related to us, saying: Yaḥyā al-Jābir related to me that he heard Abū Mājid. Sufyān said: I asked Yaḥyā, “Who is Abū Mājid?” He replied, “A newcomer who came to us.”

Ṣāʿiqa Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥīm related to me from ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī, who said: “As for what is related from others besides Abū Mājid, Yaḥyā al-Jābir is [reliable]. Abū Mājid, however, is unknown and unrecognized. As for his hadith from others, there is no fault in it.”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us, saying: Sufyān related to us, saying: Ibn Sawqa related to us, saying: I heard Mundhir say, “This Nabataean has prevailed over us with my father.” Sufyān said:88 Mundhir about what was said to him.

He said: Sufyān related to us from Misʿar, from someone who related to him, who said: Masrūq ibn Maʿqil’s striving in worship was mentioned, and Masrūq said: “How does his striving compare with his father’s? He forbade himself a bed. Then he went to ʿAbd Allāh and asked him, and ʿAbd Allāh recited to him: ‘O you who believe, do not forbid the good things God has made lawful for you’ (5:87).” He said, “I read it last night; that is why I came to you.” He replied, “You are well-off, so free a slave.”

Abū Bakr related to us, saying: Sufyān related to us, saying: Idrīs ibn Yazīd al-Awdī related to us, saying: Saʿīd ibn Abī Burda brought out for us ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb’s letter to Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī and said, “This is ʿUmar’s letter to Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī.”

He said: Saʿīd ibn Abī Burda was his father’s executor. (182b)

Sufyān related to us, saying: Khalaf ibn Ḥawshab related to us, saying: “Māymūn ibn Mihrān and I hired mounts to take us to such-and-such a place. Māymūn said, ‘Were it not that we had hired the mounts, we would have stopped by the family of so-and-so.’”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us, saying: Sufyān related to us, saying: Khalaf related to us, saying:

“Jawwāb would tremble when he heard the mention of God. Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī said, ‘If you can control it, I do not mind not counting you among us; but if you cannot control it, then you have opposed someone better than you.’”

Sufyān related to us, saying: Mujālid related to us, saying: I heard al-Shaʿbī say to al-Mughīra ibn Saʿīd, “Mughīra, from whom do you relate these hadiths?” He replied, “I relate from so-and-so.” Al-Shaʿbī said, “That man was a liar.” He said, “And I relate from so-and-so.” Al-Shaʿbī said, “That man was a liar.”

He said, “I relate from al-Ḥārith.” Al-Shaʿbī replied, “He taught me the laws of inheritance and arithmetic.” He said, “And I relate from Ṣaʿṣaʿa.” Al-Shaʿbī said, “If you wish, I will tell you everything I heard from Ṣaʿṣaʿa. Al-Mughīra ibn Shuʿba sent for him and asked him about ʿUthmān. Ṣaʿṣaʿa mentioned the Messenger of God ﷺ honored him, and praised him as he deserved. Then he mentioned Abū Bakr and said, ‘He was the first to compile the codex and to assign inheritance to the person without direct heirs.’ Then he mentioned ʿUmar and said, ‘He was the first to establish the registers and found the garrison towns, and to combine severity with gentleness.’ Then he mentioned ʿUthmān and said, ‘His rule was decreed, and his killing—’”

89 …, and al-Mughīrah said to him, “Be quiet. His rule was by decree, and his killing was by decree.” Ṣaʿṣaʿah ibn Ṣawḥān said to him, “You summoned me, and I answered; you asked me to speak, and I spoke; you silenced me, and I fell silent.”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī narrated to us, saying: Sufyān narrated to us, saying: Ismāʿīl narrated to us, saying:

“Qays ibn Abī Ḥāzim led us in prayer so-and-so many times, but I never saw him praying voluntary prayers in our mosque, where he used to lead us.”

Qabīṣah narrated to us, saying: Sufyān narrated to us from al-Nuʿmān ibn Qays, from ʿUbaydah al-Salmānī, who said: “I never saw him praying voluntary prayers in al-Ḥasan’s mosque.”

Qabīṣah narrated to us, saying: Sufyān narrated to us from al-Nuʿmān ibn Qays (183a), who said:

“ʿUbaydah called for his books when he was dying and erased them. He said, ‘I fear that someone may write them down after me and put them in the wrong place.’”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī narrated to us, saying: Sufyān narrated to us, saying: Misʿar narrated to us from Abū Ḥuṣayn, who said: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Maʿqil met me and said, “Trade has kept you busy.” I replied:

“And governance has kept you busy.”

Sufyān narrated to us, saying: al-Aʿmash narrated to us, saying: I heard Thumāmah ibn ʿUqbah al-Malḥamī. Al-Aʿmash mentioned that he was a Bedouin, not a hadith specialist.

Ibn Numayr narrated to us, saying: Ibn Idrīs narrated to us from Ashʿath, from ʿAlī ibn Mudrik, who said: ʿAbd Allāh used to say, “I certainly know …90 al-Nakhaʿ.”

He also said: Ibn Idrīs narrated to us from his uncle, from Kirdūs, that he was alive in al-Ḥajjāj’s time.

He also said: Ibn Idrīs narrated to us from Mālik, who said: Murrah al-Hamdānī, when he had grown old, was asked, “How much of your prayer remains for you?” He replied, “Half: two hundred and fifty rakʿahs.”

Ibn Numayr narrated to us, saying: Abū Bakr narrated to us from Mughīrah, who said: “Al-Ḥakam was a man who kept a muṣḥaf.”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī narrated to us, saying: Sufyān narrated to us, saying: Mālik—meaning Ibn Mighwal—narrated to us, saying: Ṭalḥah informed me, saying: Khaythamah said to me, “I know a man who ought to die twice in a year.” Ṭalḥah said: We thought he meant himself. Ṭalḥah said: “There were no two men in Kūfah more beloved to me than Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī and Khaythamah.”

He also said: Sufyān narrated to us, saying: A man said to Mālik ibn Mighwal, “Fear God.”

So he placed his cheek on the ground.

He said: Muḥammad Ṣāʿiqah narrated to me, saying: ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī said: Yaḥyā said:

Shuʿbah said: “Al-Ḥakam heard four hadiths from Miqsam: the report on the resolve concerning divorce, the witr prayer, hunting, and the report on the qunūt—the qunūt of ʿUmar in the two sūrahs—and the report about a menstruating woman, from ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd. The rest came from a book.”

Abū Saʿīd al-Ashajj narrated to us, saying: Jābir ibn Nūḥ al-Ḥammānī narrated to us from al-ʿAlāʾ ibn ʿAbd al-Karīm al-Yāmī. He said: I laughed, and Ṭalḥah said to me, “You laugh like a man who was not present at al-Jamājim.” He said: He was asked, “Abū Muḥammad, were you present there?”

He replied, “Yes, and I shot arrows there—though none reached their mark. I wish my hand had been cut off from here”—and he pointed to his shoulder (183b)—“and that I had not been present there.”

[Al-Qāsim ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān]

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī narrated to us: Sufyān narrated to us, saying: Misʿar narrated to us from Muḥārib, who said: “We kept company with al-Qāsim ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, but he surpassed us in three things: abundant prayer, lengthy silence, and generosity of spirit.”

Abū Bakr narrated to us, saying: Sufyān narrated to us, saying: I asked Misʿar, “Who was the most scrupulous about hadith among those you saw—”

—out of scrupulousness regarding hadith?” He replied, “Al-Qāsim ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and ʿAmr ibn Dīnār.”

He also said: Sufyān narrated to us from Misʿar, from Muzāḥim, who said: I came to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, and he asked me, “Who is in charge of judging among you?” I replied, “Al-Qāsim ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān.”

He asked, “How is his knowledge?” I replied, “In what he understands.” He asked, “Then who is the most learned of the people of Kūfah?” I replied:

“The most God-fearing among them.”

[ʿAmr ibn ʿUtbah ibn Farqad]

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd Allāh informed us, saying: ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar informed us, saying: Ḥawṭ ibn Rāfiʿ narrated to me that ʿAmr ibn ʿUtbah used to stipulate to his companions that he would serve them. He said: One hot day he went out to pasture. One of his companions came upon him, and there he was, standing beneath a cloud that shaded him. The man said to him, “Rejoice, ʿAmr!” ʿAmr made him promise not to tell anyone about it.

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr narrated to us, saying: Abū Muʿāwiyah narrated to us, saying: al-Aʿmash narrated to us from Mālik ibn al-Ḥārith, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rabīʿah—who said that he was sitting with ʿUtbah ibn Farqad—who said: ʿUtbah said, “ʿAbd Allāh, will you not help me with your nephew ʿAmr ibn ʿUtbah”—meaning, with the work I am engaged in? ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rabīʿah replied, “Obey your father.” ʿAmr looked at Muʿaḍḍid al-ʿIjlī. He said, “What do you say?” He replied, “Do not obey them; prostrate and draw near.”

ʿAmr said, “Father, I am only a servant working to ransom my own neck.” ʿUtbah wept and said:

“My son, I love you with two loves: a father’s love for his child, and love for God, mighty and exalted.” He replied:

“Father, you once brought me wealth amounting to seventy thousand. If you are asking me about it, here it is; take it. I have no need of it.” He said, “My son, spend it.” So he spent it until not a single dirham remained.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd Allāh informed us, saying: ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar informed us, saying: ʿAmr ibn ʿUtbah ibn Farqad would ride out on his horse at night and stop by the graves, saying, “People of the graves, the records have been rolled up, and deeds have been raised.”

Then he would weep and stand with his feet together (184a) until morning. Then he would return and attend the dawn prayer.

[Shurayḥ ibn al-Ḥārith, the Judge]

Abū Nuʿaym narrated to us, saying: Umm Dāwūd al-Wābishiyyah narrated to us. She said: “My husband died, so I brought my dispute with them before Shurayḥ.” She said: “Shurayḥ had no beard.”

Abū al-Nuʿmān narrated to us, saying: Ḥammād ibn Zayd narrated to us from Ayyūb, from Muḥammad, who said: “Shurayḥ was a kawsaj.”

Ibn Numayr narrated to us, saying: Abū Bakr narrated to us from ʿĀṣim, from Abū Wāʾil, who said: “I never saw Shurayḥ in the company of ʿAbd Allāh.” He said: “The only thing that kept him from visiting him was that he felt no need of him.”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī narrated to us, saying: Sufyān narrated to us, saying: ʿAmr narrated to us from Abū al-Shaʿthāʾ, who said: “Ziyād brought Shurayḥ to us, and he judged among us for a year. No one before or after him judged among us as he did.”

Mūsā ibn Masʿūd narrated to us, saying: Sufyān narrated to us from Abū Isḥāq, from Hubayrah who said: ʿAlī said, “Bring the Qurʾān readers to me.” They gathered in the mosque’s courtyard. He said:

“I am about to part from you.” Then he began asking them, “What do you say about such-and-such? What do you say about such-and-such?” until they had all departed and Shurayḥ remained. He kept questioning him, and when he had finished, he said, “Go; you are among the best of people”—or, “among the best of the Arabs.”

Abū Nuʿaym narrated to us, saying: Abū ʿĀṣim Muḥammad ibn Abī Ayyūb al-Thaqafī narrated to us, saying: ʿĀmir narrated to me. I asked him about walāʾ, saying, “Abū ʿAmr, how does one inherit through walāʾ?” He replied, “Shurayḥ treated it as property.” I said, “The people of Medina do not say that.” He replied, “Indeed, the people of Medina treat it as lineage.” I asked:

“From whom did Shurayḥ transmit?” He replied, “He was held in such high esteem by us that we would not ask him from whom he transmitted.”

Qabīṣah narrated to us, saying: Sufyān narrated to us from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Aʿyan, from al-Shaʿbī, who said:

“Masrūq had greater knowledge of legal opinions than Shurayḥ, and Shurayḥ had greater knowledge of adjudication than Masrūq. Shurayḥ would consult Masrūq, but Masrūq would not consult Shurayḥ.”

Abū Nuʿaym and Qabīṣah narrated to us, saying: Sufyān narrated to us from Abū Ḥayyān, from his father, who said: “Shurayḥ would have a drain only in his own house, and he would bury a cat only in his own house—when it died.”

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr narrated to us, saying: Ismāʿīl ibn Ibrāhīm narrated to us, saying: Abū Ḥayyān al-Taymī narrated to us from his father, who said: (184b) “Shurayḥ had no drain except one that opened onto the street in his house. When one of his family’s cats died, he would order it buried in his house, to avoid causing harm to a Muslim.”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī narrated to us, saying: Sufyān narrated to us, saying: ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib narrated to us, saying: I came to Shurayḥ during the time of ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān—he was judge at the time—and said, “Father, give me a legal opinion.” He replied, “Nephew, I am only a judge, not a jurisconsult.” I said, “By God, I have not come seeking to bring a dispute before you. A man from the tribe has made his house a ḥabs.” ʿAṭāʾ said: He entered through the door from the mosque into the enclosed prayer area; I heard him as he entered. I followed him, and he was saying to Ḥabīb—the man who brought litigants before him—“Well done, man! Is a dwelling to be made a ḥabs from the land of God?”91

[Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī]

Sufyān narrated to us, saying: I heard ʿAṭāʾ say: I said to Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān—who was an ʿUthmānī—“It seems you have little regard for what you heard from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.” Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān replied, “What I heard from ʿAlī is dearer to me than red camels.”

Sufyān narrated to us, saying: I heard ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib say: “I saw Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. When he taught people to recite, he would begin with the people of the marketplace.”

He also said: Sufyān narrated to us from ʿAṭāʾ, from Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, who said: “When we learned ten verses, we would not move on to others until we knew what we had been commanded to do.”

Abū al-Nuʿmān narrated to us, saying: Ḥammād narrated to us from ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib, who said: “We went to encourage Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī as he lay dying. He said, ‘I do hope so; I have fasted eighty Ramadans for its sake.’”

Al-Ḥajjāj, Muslim ibn Ibrāhīm, Abū al-Walīd al-Ṭayālisī, Abū ʿUmar, and Ādam narrated to us; they said: Shuʿbah narrated to us, saying: ʿAlqamah ibn Marthad informed me, saying:

I heard Saʿd ibn ʿUbaydah, from Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī, from ʿUthmān, from the Prophet ﷺ—who said: “The best of you are those who learn the Qurʾān and teach it.” He said: Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī taught Qurʾān recitation during ʿUthmān’s rule and continued until al-Ḥajjāj’s time. He said, “That is what seated me in this place.”

[Tamīm ibn Ḥadhlam]

Al-Ḥumaydī narrated to us, saying: Sufyān narrated to us, saying: Ibn Shubrumah narrated to us (185a) and others—who said: Tamīm ibn Ḥadhlam recited before ʿAbd Allāh, and he corrected him in only two places in the Qurʾān. He recited, “Until, when the messengers despaired and thought that they had been denied,” (12:110) and ʿAbd Allāh said to him, “They were denied.” He also recited before him, “And all of them came to Him in submission,” (27:87) and ʿAbd Allāh said:

“‘All came to Him in submission’ (27:87)?”

Qubayṣah related to us: Sufyān related to us, from Jaḥsh ibn Ziyād, from Tamīm ibn Ḥadhlam, who said: ʿAbd Allāh had me learn two readings: “Until, when the messengers despaired and thought that they had been denied” (12:110); and he had me learn: “And all of them will come to Him humbled” (27:87).

[ʿĀmir al-Shaʿbī]

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Sufyān related to us, from Ṣāliḥ, who said: I heard al-Shaʿbī say: “I would love to come away from it with neither gain nor loss.”

Qubayṣah related to us—Sufyān related to us, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī al-Safar, from al-Shaʿbī, who said:

A time came upon me when there was no place I loved sitting in more than this mosque. But today, I would rather sit on a heap of rubbish than sit in this mosque. He said: When he passed them, he would say, “What are these muʿāniqah saying?”—or he said, “sons of their buttocks”; Qubayṣah was unsure. “Whatever they tell you from their own opinions, reject it; but whatever they relate to you from the Companions of Muḥammad ﷺ accept it.”

Qubayṣah related to us: Sufyān related to us, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī al-Safar, who said: Al-Shaʿbī said, “I am no scholar, and I do not leave behind a scholar. Abū Ḥuṣayn is a righteous man.”

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: ʿĪsā ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to us, saying: I saw al-Shaʿbī reciting poetry in the mosque of Kūfah, and I saw him wearing a red wrap and a yellow waistcloth.

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us: Sufyān related to us, saying: Ibn Shubrumah informed us: I heard al-Shaʿbī say to Shibāk, “I’ll return it to you. I have never asked anyone to return it to me.”

Abū Saʿīd Aḥmad ibn Dāwūd al-Ḥaddād related to us: Ibn Fuḍayl related to us, from Ibn Shubrumah, who said: Ibn Hubayrah appointed al-Shaʿbī as judge and required him to keep him company at night. Al-Shaʿbī said to him, “I cannot manage both the judgeship and staying up at night.”

He said: Sufyān related to us, saying: I heard Ibn Shubrumah say: When al-Shaʿbī was asked about a question that involved blame, he would say, “We are only in the crossing, not among the she-camels.”

(185 b) He said: Sufyān related to us, saying: Ibn Shubrumah related to us: I heard al-Shaʿbī, when asked about a difficult question, say, “The shaggy wool is excessive; it will neither be led nor driven.”

If the Companions of Muḥammad ﷺ were asked about it, it would prove too difficult for them.

He said: Sufyān related to us: Ibn Shubrumah related to us: I heard al-Shaʿbī say, “Give me the easiest thing available and the greatest thing missing”—meaning water.

He said: Sufyān related to us—he said: Ibn Shubrumah related to us: I heard al-Shaʿbī say:

“When the circle grows large, it is only confidential talk or a shout.”

He said: Sufyān related to us: I heard Ibn Shubrumah say: Al-Shaʿbī was asked about something but did not answer. A man there said, “Abū ʿAmr says such-and-such about it.”

Al-Shaʿbī said, “You are lying about me while I am alive; you will lie about me even more when I am dead.”

He said: Sufyān related to us—he said: Ibn Shubrumah related to us: I heard al-Shaʿbī say to Abū al-Zinād, “Son of Dhakwān, by God, you bring them counterfeit and leave with them genuine.” Sufyān sometimes said, “and return with them sound”—meaning the legal opinions of the people of Medina.

He said: Sufyān related to us: I heard Ibn Shubrumah say: Al-Shaʿbī passed by—

…along a road, and I was with him, with a man who was saying, “Al-Shaʿbī’s legal opinion, when—” Then, when al-Shaʿbī saw him, it was as though… Al-Shaʿbī said, “He raised his gaze toward her.”

Then Sufyān said: He ruled unjustly against the litigant and did not rule against her.

Abū Bakr related to us: Sufyān related to us: I heard Sālim say: Whenever al-Shaʿbī saw me, he would say:

“God’s policewoman, stop and fly,

as a barley grain flies.”

Sālim said: He was making fun of me.

He said: Sufyān related to us: Mālik related to us, saying: There was a man in Kūfah who had a cow—Abū Yūsuf said, “He mentioned something that escaped me,” then returned to the report—and he used to say, “I have never seen people in any age with thicker necks or finer clothes than theirs.” He used to sit with al-Shaʿbī. The man would go out to the market on an errand, pass by the mosque, and say, “I’ll go in and pray two cycles, then go out and take care of my errand.” Then he would see al-Shaʿbī relating reports, sit with him until his errand passed him by (186 a) and the market closed. This man would say to al-Shaʿbī, “You who ruin people’s errands!” The man also used to say, “Half your judgment belongs to your brother.”

Yazīd ibn Khālid ibn Yazīd ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mawhab al-Filasṭīnī related to me, saying:

Yaḥyā ibn Zakariyyā ibn Abī Zāʾidah related to us: Mujālid informed us, from al-Shaʿbī— He said: ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān wrote to al-Ḥajjāj, “Send me a man from your side who is a great scholar.” He said: Al-Ḥajjāj summoned me and sent me to him. I arrived in Syria during the pilgrimage season of ʿAbd al-Malik, who had appointed his brother ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz as his deputy. He said: I went in to see ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. He said:

“Are you al-Shaʿbī?” I said, “Yes.” He said, “I have heard of you. I was still a boy, and I have wanted to meet you.” He said: I used to visit him with Muḥarrir ibn Abī Hurayrah. He would say, “Relate to us, al-Shaʿbī. By God, we have had everything in this world except a fine report.” He said: One day al-Akhṭal came in to see him and began reciting the poems he had composed in praise of them. I turned to Muḥarrir ibn Abī Hurayrah and said, “May God fight al-Nābighah, when he says:

This lad, handsome in face,

is headed for good, swift to fulfillment.

Al-Ḥārith the Elder, and al-Ḥārith

the Younger, and al-Ḥārith, best of humankind;

then Hind and Hind, and their leader,

who outstripped them in good deeds;

six forefathers belonging to them, who are

the best of those who drink the clouds’ flow.”

ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz turned to me and said, “How does it go?” I recited it to him. He said, “Akhṭal, why don’t you say something like this?” Al-Akhṭal said, “I seek refuge in God from associating partners with Him, al-Shaʿbī! By God, I had not sought refuge from associating partners with Him today until I came to the bayʿah to draw near.”

Yaḥyā said: Someone—either Mujālid or another—related to me, saying: When ʿAbd al-Malik came to power, I used to sit with him and relate reports to him. Sometimes I would relate a report while he had raised a morsel to his mouth; he would hold it in his hand, turn toward me, and listen. I would say, “Please eat it, may God set you right; the report will still be there.” He would say, “By God, your report is dearer to me than it.”

Yaḥyā said: ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Abjar informed me (186 b): I heard al-Shaʿbī say: When I arrived in Syria, I stayed with ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Marwān. One day, as I was sitting in the mosque, a short, red-faced, bald, completely hairless old man entered. People craned their necks to look at him and said, “This is the standard-bearer of the scholars.” He began sitting in the study circles and moving from one to another. I said, “O God, bring him to me.” He came and sat in the circle where I was. He said, “The man of the two scriptures related to us that the sky rests on the shoulder of an angel.” I said, “God’s Book has declared you a liar.” They nearly sprang up—or did spring up—then said, “What do you want with the Commander of the Faithful’s guest?” He said: They held one another back.

Then he said, “The man of the two scriptures related to us that there is a Trumpet in the East and a Trumpet in the West. One is blown, and people die; the other is blown, and they come to life.” I said, “God’s Book has declared you a liar.” They nearly sprang up—or did spring up—then held one another back and said, “What do you want with the Commander of the Faithful’s guest?” He said: I turned to them and said, “Why are you surprised that I call a liar the one whom God, mighty and majestic, calls a liar? This man claims that the sky rests on the shoulder of an angel, while God, mighty and majestic, says: ‘He raised the heavens without pillars that you can see’ (13:2). And this man claims there is a Trumpet in the East and a Trumpet in the West, one of which is blown and people die, and the other is blown and they come to life, while God, mighty and majestic, says: “The Trumpet will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on earth will fall unconscious, except whom God wills. Then it will be blown again” (39:68). It is only one.”

He said: He asked me, “Where are you from?” I told him. He said, “The man of the two scriptures also related to us that your women are evil, and that they will be brought and made to stand on the steps, with their shins uncovered.”

He said: I hope this last claim will be like the first two.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yūsuf related to us: ʿĪsā ibn Yūnus related to us, from ʿAbbād ibn Mūsā, from al-Shaʿbī, who said: Al-Ḥajjāj had me brought to him in chains. When he reached me at the palace gate, Qaysī Yazīd ibn Abī Muslim said, “We belong to God, al-Shaʿbī, considering the knowledge you hold between your two covers. This is no day for intercession. Acknowledge to the emir that you are guilty of polytheism and hypocrisy, and perhaps you will escape.” Then Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥajjāj met me and said the same thing as Yazīd. When I entered (187 a) before al-Ḥajjāj, he said, “And you, al-Shaʿbī, were among those who rebelled against us and swelled their ranks!” I said:

“May God set the emir right. Our dwelling brought us sorrow, the land grew barren around us, the road narrowed, we applied sleeplessness like kohl, fear became our constant garment, and we fell into ruin. We were neither righteous, God-fearing men nor powerful, wicked men.”

He said, “By God, you speak truly. They were not righteous when they rebelled against us, nor were they strong enough to prevail over us when they acted wickedly. Release him!”

Then he needed my advice on a prescribed inheritance share, so I came to him. He said, “What do you say about a sister, a mother, and a grandfather?” I said, “Five of the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ differed over it: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās, Zayd, ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd.” He said, “What did Ibn ʿAbbās say about it, since he was a jurist?” I said— “He made the grandfather a father, gave the sister nothing, and gave the mother one-third.”

He said, “What did Zayd say about it?” I said, “He divided it into nine shares: he gave the mother three, the grandfather four, and the sister two.” He said, “What did the Commander of the Faithful”—meaning ʿUthmān—“say about it?” I said, “He made it three shares.” He said, “What did Ibn Masʿūd say about it?” I said:

“He divided it into six shares: he gave the sister three, the grandfather two, and the mother one.” He said, “What did Abū Turāb say about it?” I said, “He divided it into six shares: he gave the sister three, the mother two, and the grandfather one.”

Just then the chamberlain came in and said, “There are messengers at the door.” He said, “Let them in.” They entered, their turbans wrapped around their waists, their swords on their shoulders, and their letters in their right hands. A man of Banū Sulaym, called Sayyābah ibn ʿĀṣim, entered. He asked, “Where are you from?” He replied, “Syria.” He asked, “How is the Commander of the Faithful? How is his retinue?” He told him. He said, “Was there rain behind you?” He replied:

“Yes. Three rain clouds passed over me between here and the Commander of the Faithful.”

He said, “Describe for me how the rain fell, what its effects were, and what signs it left.”

He said, “A cloud came upon me at Ḥawrān. Some drops fell small and some large; the large ones were a mass alongside the small ones. A widespread, successive rain fell—the downpour I had heard about. One valley was flowing, and another was a torrent, and land turned toward fertility, and land turned away from it. A cloud came upon me at Sawāʾ—or al-Qarnayn—I do not know which of the two watering places; ʿĪsā was unsure—and softened the lowlands (folio 187 b), sent water over the hard ground, washed down the ravines, and exposed the places where truffles grew.

A cloud came upon me at Sawāʾ—or al-Qarnayn—ʿĪsā was unsure—and the earth settled after being watered, the pools filled, the valleys brimmed, and I came to you in a burrow like a hyena’s den.” Then he said, “Let him in.”

A man from the people of al-Yamāmah entered. He asked, “Was there rain behind you?” He replied, “Yes. I heard the scouts calling others to inspect their route, and I heard someone say, ‘Come, I’ll lead you to a place where fires are put out, women complain, and the she-goats compete.’” Al-Shaʿbī said: Al-Ḥajjāj did not understand what he meant.

He said, “Woe to you! You are speaking to the people of Syria; make it clear to them.”

He said, “May God set the emir right. The people prospered, and there were dates, clarified butter, fresh butter, and milk; so no fire was lit for baking bread— As for the women’s complaint, a woman spends the day pouring out her worry and churning her milk, [then passes the night] with her arms aching, as though they did not belong to her. As for the she-goats’ competition, they see varieties of trees, colors of fruit, and blossoming plants that fill their bellies but do not satisfy their eyes. They spend the night with their bellies full, yet the burning from their distension is like the water of al-Ḥarrah, until the milk lets down.

He said, “Let him in.” A man from among the mawālī entered, one of the strongest people of that time. He asked, “Was there rain behind you?”

He replied, “Yes, but I cannot speak as those men did.”

He said, “Say it as you can.”

He replied, “A cloud came upon me at Ḥulwān, and I kept walking in its wake until I reached the emir.”

He said, “Though you were the briefest of them in your speech about the rain, you will be the longest in your stride with the sword.”

Qubayṣah related to us: Sufyān related to us: Someone who heard al-Shaʿbī informed me— “...to say: ‘Would that I might emerge from my knowledge with neither gain nor blame for me.’”

Abū ʿĀṣim related to us; he said: I think it was from Ibn ʿAwn, who said: When al-Shaʿbī was asked, he would say, “And he said.”

Abū Nuʿaym related to us; he said: Sufyān related to us, saying: Al-Shaʿbī said: “I never struck a slave of mine, nor ever imposed a tax on him.”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us; he said: Sufyān related to us; he said: Muṭarrif related to us, from al-Shaʿbī, who said: “I saw ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib bare an arm of his, with hair on it, and say: ‘No,’ until he shook it with it.”92

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Numayr related to us; he said: Ibn Idrīs related to us, from Mālik ibn Mighwal, from Zayd ibn Iyās al-Hamdānī, who said: Among his sayings was: “Half your intelligence belongs to your brother.” He also used to say: “I have seen no Qurʾān reciters with necks more imposing, clothes finer, or a greater appetite for the choicest food than the reciters of this age.” When he passed al-Shaʿbī, he would say: “O frustrator of people’s needs!”

Salama related to us, from Aḥmad: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī related to us; he said:

ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak informed me, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yazīd, from Makḥūl, who said:

“I have seen no one more knowledgeable than al-Shaʿbī about an established Sunna.”

Hishām ibn ʿAmmār related to us; he said: Al-Walīd ibn Muslim related to us; he said: Tamīm related to me; he said: I heard Makḥūl say: “I came to Kūfa and kept attending Shurayḥ’s sessions for six months without asking him about anything; I contented myself with what he judged.”

Ibn Numayr related to us; he said: Isḥāq al-Azraq related to us, from al-Aʿmash, who said: A man came to al-Shaʿbī and asked: “What is the name of Iblīs’s wife?” He replied: “That was a wedding I did not attend.”

Ibn Numayr related to us; he said: ʿĪsā ibn Yūnus related to us, from al-Aʿmash, who said: “I passed by al-Shaʿbī, who was an eloquent Arab.”

ʿUthmān ibn Abī Shayba related to us; he said: Muʿāwiya related to us; he said: I heard al-Aʿmash say: Al-Shaʿbī said: “Do you not find it astonishing that this one-eyed man comes to me at night and asks me questions, and [unclear] during the day”—meaning Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī.

Abū Bishr related to us; he said: Saʿīd ibn ʿĀmir related to us; he said: Shuʿba related to us, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī al-Safar, who said: Al-Shaʿbī said: “By God, there is no verse about which I have not asked, but it is a report from God, Mighty and Majestic”—or he said, “about God, Mighty and Majestic.”

“ʿAlī ibn ʿUthmān ibn Nufayl related to me; he said: Abū Mushir related to us; he said: Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to us, from Makḥūl, who said: ‘I have never met anyone like al-Shaʿbī.’”

I heard someone report from Abū Mushir, who said: “The report of Tamīm ibn ʿAṭiyya is not preserved, because if Makḥūl had attended Shurayḥ’s sessions, he would not have said, ‘I have never met anyone like al-Shaʿbī.’”

“Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmar related to us, from Sufyān, from Dāwūd, who said:

‘I have never sat with anyone more knowledgeable than al-Shaʿbī.’”

[Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī]

Qabīṣa ibn ʿUqba and Abū Nuʿaym related to us; both said: Sufyān related to us, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAmr, who said: Ibrāhīm said: “I have never disputed with a man.”

“And they both said: Sufyān related to us, from Mughīra: ‘We stood in awe of Ibrāhīm as we stood in awe of the ruler.’”

And the two said: Sufyān related to us, from his father, who said: “Sometimes I heard Ibrāhīm take delight in the saying, ‘I was needed, I was needed.’”

Qabīṣa related to us; he said: Sufyān related to us, from ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Abjar, from Zubayd, who said: “Whenever I asked Ibrāhīm about anything, I could always sense his aversion to it.”

“And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Abū Ḥuṣayn, who said: ‘I asked Ibrāhīm about something, and he said: “Could you find no one else to ask about this matter between you and me?”’”

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from al-Aʿmash, who said: “Sometimes I saw Ibrāhīm praying, then he would come to us and stay for an hour during the day as though he were ill.”

Abū Nuʿaym related to us; he said: Muḥill ibn Muḥriz ibn Khalīfa al-Ḍabbī, the blind man, related to us; he said: “I entered upon Ibrāhīm”—meaning al-Nakhaʿī—“with Mughīra, and with us was a man an Irjāʾ adherent. We mentioned some of their views to him, and he said: ‘Do not speak to them or sit with them.’ He also said:

‘Let me know: when you leave me, do not come back to me.’”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us; he said: Sufyān related to us; he said: I heard al-Aʿmash say: “We tried hard to get Ibrāhīm to sit beside a pillar, but he refused.”

Ibn Numayr related to us; he said: Wakīʿ related to us, from al-Aʿmash, who said: I said to Ibrāhīm:

“I am going out to a spring, wearing a garment dyed with saffron.” Ibrāhīm said: “That is not how they used to pursue worldly things.”

Ibn Numayr related to us; he said: Ibn Idrīs related to me, from al-Aʿmash, who said: A man said to Ibrāhīm: “I passed by so-and-so, and he said such-and-such about you.” Al-Aʿmash said: I said:

“He had no need of you.” When Ibrāhīm saw that I was angry, he said: “Perhaps, had the person spoken about heard what was said, he would not have defended himself.”

Ibn Numayr related to us; he said: Wakīʿ related to us; he said: I heard al-Aʿmash say:

“A man asked permission to enter while Ibrāhīm was reading from the codex. He covered it and said: ‘He must not see that I read from it at every moment.’”

Qabīṣa related to us; he said: Sufyān related to us, from al-Aʿmash, who said: “I never related a report to Ibrāhīm without his adding something to it for me.”

Ibn Numayr related to us; he said: Yaḥyā ibn ʿĪsā related to us, from al-Aʿmash. Ibrāhīm was mentioned in his presence, and he said: “He did not have what people claim he had”—meaning expertise in jurisprudence.

Ibn Numayr related to us; he said: Wakīʿ related to us; and I heard al-Aʿmash say: “If I held Ibrāhīm’s opinion, I would have brought you a load.”

“Ibn Numayr and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Maslama related to us; both said: ʿĪsā ibn Yūnus related to us, from al-Aʿmash, from Ibrāhīm, who said: ‘I hear a report, take from it what can be acted upon, and leave the rest.’”

Ibn Numayr and Bakr ibn Khalaf related to us; both said: Abū Usāma related to us, from al-Aʿmash, who said: “Ibrāhīm was a money-changer in hadith.”

Through the same chain, from al-Aʿmash, who said: “Ibrāhīm used to avoid fame and would not sit beside a pillar. He would sit among the people, and when a man came, he would make room for him. But if the gathering forced him to sit beside a pillar, he would get up.”

Ibn Numayr related to us; he said: Abū Usāma related to us, from al-Aʿmash, who said: Khaythama said to me:

“Why do you sit with Ibrāhīm in the gathering where he sits with the leading men?” I mentioned this to Ibrāhīm, and he said: “Are you telling me to withdraw from people? They speak about whatever they wish, and we speak about whatever we wish.”

Abū ʿĀṣim related to us, from Ibn ʿAwn, who said: Al-Shaʿbī said to me: “Did you witness this man’s death?” I said: “Yes.” He said: “Know that he has left no one like himself.”

I said: “In Kūfa?” He said: “No: in Kūfa, nor in such-and-such, nor in such-and-such.”

Abū ʿĀṣim was asked: “So-and-so related from Ibn ʿAwn that he said: ‘Neither in Kūfa nor in Baṣra.’” He said: “That is a mistake. Ibn ʿAwn did not name Baṣra.”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us; he said: Sufyān related to us; he said: I heard Ibn Shubrumah say: “When Ibrāhīm died, people kept saying, ‘Ibrāhīm said this,’ and ‘Ibrāhīm said that.’”

Al-Shaʿbī said: “Dead, he is more learned in jurisprudence than he was alive.”

Abū Bakr related to us; he said: Sufyān related to us; he said: I heard Ibn Shubrumah relate from Shibbāk, who said: Al-Shaʿbī said: “Has the man died?”—meaning Ibrāhīm. I said: “Yes.”

He said: “He left no one like himself.” (189b)

“Ibn Numayr related to us; he said: Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh related to us, from al-Ḥasan ibn…”

“ʿUbayd Allāh said: I asked Ibrāhīm: ‘Did you hear everything you issue legal opinions about?’ He said: ‘No. Rather, I heard some things, then used them as the basis for analogical reasoning about what I had not heard.’”

Salama related to us, from Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, who said: Ḥajjāj related to us; he said: I heard Shuʿba relate from Manṣūr, who said: Ibrāhīm said: “I never wrote anything down.” Manṣūr said: “I wish I had written things down, even if I had to pay such-and-such; knowledge like mine has been lost.”

Abū Bishr related to us; he said: Saʿīd ibn ʿĀmir related to us; Shuʿba said: “Sulaymān related to us; he said:

I said to Ibrāhīm: ‘Give the chain of transmission, for it comes from more than one person.’”

Saʿīd ibn Asad related to me; he said: Ḍamra related to us, from Rajāʾ ibn Abī Salama, from Ibn ʿAwn, who said: I mentioned Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī to Ibn Sīrīn, and he put his hand over his eye without saying “the one-eyed man.” I said: “Yes.” He said: “I used to see him attending those gatherings.”

Al-ʿAbbās ibn Muḥammad related to us; he said: Shādhān related to us; he said: Abū Bakr ibn…

“ʿAyyāsh, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAmr al-Fuqaymī, from Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī: He used to buy geese, fatten them, and give them as gifts to the rulers.”

Ibn Numayr related to us; he said: Ibn Fuḍayl related to us, from al-Aʿmash, from Ismāʿīl ibn Rajāʾ, who said: “He used to go to the children at the writing school, gather them together, and relate hadith to them so that he would not forget his hadith.”

“ʿUqba ibn Mukram related to us; Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿAdī related to us; Shuʿba informed us, from Hushaym, from al-Mughīra, from Ibrāhīm: He saw no harm in eating the fish set aside for him by the fish-trap maker, even if it died in it.

Through the same chain, from Shuʿba, from Hushaym, from Mughīra, from Ibrāhīm—as far as I know—concerning a man who said to his wife, ‘You are no wife of mine.’ He said: ‘That means nothing.’ He said: Al-Shaʿbī said:

‘Even a milder expression than this is counted as divorce.’

ʿUqba ibn Mukram related to us; Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿAdī related to us; Shuʿba informed us, from Hushaym, from Mughīra, from Ibrāhīm, who said: If a man says to his wife, ‘Go and marry someone else’—

he said: “That means nothing.” Al-Shaʿbī said: “Even something milder than this is counted as divorce.”

Through the same chain, from Ibrāhīm, who said: “They used to say: When the heat grows severe, prostrate on a man’s back”—meaning during Friday prayer. (30a)”

[Ibn Shubrumah]

Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb related to us; he said: Ḥammād ibn Zayd related to us; he said: “I have seen no Kūfan more learned in jurisprudence than Ibn Shubrumah.”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us; he said: Sufyān related to us; he said: Ibn Shubrumah related to us, saying: “I saw al-Shaʿbī entering the mosque, heading toward Jarīr. I offered him my hand and said: ‘By God, if I did not receive more from you than you receive from me, I would not have offered you my hand.’”

Through the same chain, he said: Ibn Shubrumah related to me, saying: Ibn Hubayra said to me: “Why did you work for Yūsuf and not for me?” I said to him: “May God set you right: I am not someone who will work for you unless you break my back and keep me imprisoned for a long time.”

Through the same chain, from Ibn Shubrumah, who said: ʿĪsā ibn Mūsā said: “You will surely take charge of the Kūfan police for me.” I said: “May God set you right: the Kūfan police are such-and-such. And Ziyād said, ‘I cannot manage the trifling matter until I cut into living flesh.’”

(190a) Through the same chain, Ibn Shubrumah said: “Jābir met me and said: ‘What prevents you from seeking advice?’ I said: ‘About what I know, or about what I do not know?’ Had he said to me, ‘About what you know,’ I would have said:

‘Why should I seek advice about what I know?’ And had he said to me, ‘About what you do not know,’ I would have said: ‘Why should I judge about what I do not know?’

“Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb related to us; he said: Ḥammād ibn Zayd related to us; he said: I heard Ibn Shubrumah say: ‘Among legal questions are some that it is unbecoming for the questioner to ask, or for the person asked…’” that he answer.”

“Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us: Sufyān related to us: Ibn Shubrumah was asked about a legal question and gave an answer, but he was wrong. Nūḥ ibn Darraj said to him, ‘Consider it again and make sure, Abū Shubrumah.’ He realized he had been wrong, and Ibn Shubrumah said, ‘Bring the man back to me.’

Then he began to recite:

His foot almost slipped from a lofty place,

had Nūḥ ibn Darraj not caught it in time.”

Al-Ḥumaydī related to us: Sufyān related to us: Whenever Ibn Shubrumah was asked about bloodshed, he would swear that he knew nothing about it.

Sufyān related to us: Ibn Shubrumah had been sent with a man to Yemen as an official, to serve alongside him like a vizier. They summoned a man to serve as judge, one who had been appointed to such a post before. Sufyān said: Ibn Shubrumah held the office of judge in very high regard. He said to the man, “We have summoned you for a grave matter.”

The man said, “What is it?” He replied, “Judging.” The man said, “There is nothing about it that I cannot do well.” Ibn Shubrumah said to him, “If you were asked about an eighth of a dirham, you could not handle it well. What would you say about a man who struck a ewe in the belly, causing it to miscarry what was in its womb?” The man did not know.

“According to him, Ibn Shubrumah said:

Judge by what is prescribed in the Book of God,

and judge by analogous cases and by qiyās.”

Ibn Shubrumah related the report about the man of Aylah, but it did not please him. He said, “Had I been there, I would have said to the son: ‘You are as your father said.’ If he said, ‘Yes,’ I would have prescribed the legal penalty for the son; if he said, ‘No,’ I would have prescribed it for the father.”

He said: I heard Ibn Shubrumah say, “What could be better than a banner fluttering above your head?”

According to him, Ibn Shubrumah caught up with us at Sarif while riding a horse. He mentioned that he intended to travel to Mecca. My father said to him, “We have twelve camels with us.” He said, “I have never performed the pilgrimage, and I have plenty and ample means. I dislike taking from others, and would rather spend from my own means.” We hired a camel for him from a Bedouin.

Salamah related to us, from Aḥmad, who said: ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us, from Maʿmar, who said: When they removed Ibn Shubrumah from office—I mean, when he was dismissed from the judgeship—I escorted him. When the people had gone back and the journey left just the two of us, with no one else in our company, he looked at me and said, “Abū ʿUrwah, praise be to God: I have not replaced this shirt with another since I entered that place.” Then he was silent for a while, and said to me, “Abū ʿUrwah, I speak to you only of what is lawful; as for what is unlawful, there is no way to it.”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us: Sufyān related to us, from Ibn Shubrumah, who said:

Al-Shaʿbī was asked about a man who had vowed to divorce his wife. He said, “That is nothing.” Ibn Shubrumah said, “I corrected al-Shaʿbī, and al-Shaʿbī said, ‘Bring the man back to me.’” He then said to him, “Your vow will remain upon your neck until the Day of Resurrection.”

Sufyān related to us: Ibn Shubrumah related to us: I saw al-Shaʿbī entering the mosque, heading toward Jarīr. I offered him my hand and said to him, “By God, were it not that I gain more from you than you gain from me, I would not have offered you my hand. What do you say about a group of people in consecration, some of whom pointed out game and others hunted it?”93

Some of them pointed out game, and others hunted it. He said, “Each one of them owes an equivalent penalty.”

Ibn Shubrumah said: I said to him, “Ḥammād says that they owe a single penalty.” Al-Shaʿbī stopped as we were walking and said, “By God, does he say that?!” I said, “Yes.” He said, “If he says that, then he has gone mad.”

Ibn Shubrumah said: Then I went to a gathering where we used to sit together—Hubayrah, Shibbāk, and al-Ḥārith al-ʿUklī. None of my companions disagreed with me more strongly than he did. I told him what al-Shaʿbī had said and what Ḥammād had said. He replied, “The correct view is what Ḥammād said: they owe a single penalty. Do you not see that if a group of people accidentally killed a man, they would owe only one blood-money payment?” I said, “Rather, the correct view is what al-Shaʿbī said: each one of them owes a penalty. Do you not see that if a group of people accidentally killed a man, each one of them would owe an expiation: the freeing of a slave?” Ibn Shubrumah said, “Al-Shaʿbī reasoned by analogy from expiation, while Ḥammād and al-Ḥārith reasoned by analogy from blood-money.”

“Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Faḍl ibn Ziyād related to us: [Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal] related to us: Muḥammad ibn Fuḍayl related to us, from his father, who said: Ibn Shubrumah, al-Mughīrah, al-Ḥārith al-ʿUklī, al-Qaʿqāʿ ibn Yazīd, and others would stay up discussing jurisprudence; sometimes they did not get up even when the dawn call to prayer was made.”

Al-Faḍl related to us: Aḥmad related to us: Muḥammad ibn Fuḍayl related to us: I heard— Ibn Shubrumah say: Whenever al-Ḥārith and I agreed on a legal question, we did not care who disagreed with us about it.

Ibn Numayr related to us: Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh related to us, from ʿAmmār al-Duhnī, who said: I passed by Māhān when he had been crucified, while the people were looking at him. He said to me, “ʿAmmār, you too are among those who look and do nothing to change it!”

Abū ʿAlī Mujāhid ibn Mūsā related to us: Qirād, Abū Nūḥ, related to us: Shuʿbah related to us: “I have seen no shaykh in Kūfah better than Zubayd.”

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmmār related to us: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to us, from Shuʿbah, from al-Haytham, who said: Murrah used to perform two hundred rakʿahs of prayer each day.

[ʿAmr ibn Murrah]

Abū Bakr ibn Abī al-Naḍr related to me: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ghazwān, Abū Nūḥ, related to us, from Shuʿbah, who said: “We knew no shaykh in Kūfah better than Zubayd al-Yāmī,” and whenever I saw ʿAmr ibn Murrah at prayer, I thought that he would not finish until his supplication had been answered.

Abū ʿAlī Mujāhid related to us: Qirād, Abū Nūḥ, related to us: Shuʿbah related to us: “Whenever I saw ʿAmr ibn Murrah at prayer, I thought he would not depart until his supplication had been answered.”

Abū Bakr ibn Abī al-Naḍr related to us: Abū al-Naḍr related to us: ʿAbd Allāh al-Ashjaʿī related to us, from Misʿar ibn Kidām, from ʿAwn, who said: Whenever ʿAmr ibn Murrah raised his finger in supplication, we hoped that it would be answered.

Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmar related to us: Sufyān related to us, from Misʿar, from ʿAmr ibn Murrah, who said: When I wanted to recite the Qurʾān, I wondered which of the two things I should do: teach people ḥadīth or recite the Qurʾān. In a dream, I saw what seemed to be a man coming to the mosque with a fine garment. He reached the people of ḥadīth and passed them by, until he came to the people of the Qurʾān and gave it to them. So I began reciting the Qurʾān. Sufyān said: I asked Misʿar, “Who was the best person you ever saw?”

He said, “No one was better than ʿAmr ibn Murrah. Whenever I saw him point with his finger like this in supplication, I thought that his prayer would be answered.”

Abū Bakr ibn Abī Shaybah related to us: Abū Muʿāwiyah related to us: al-Aʿmash related to us, from Abū Isḥāq, who said: I stopped for the night and invited the companions of ʿAlī and the companions of ʿAbd Allāh. Among the companions of ʿAlī were ʿUmārah ibn ʿAbd, Hubayrah ibn Yarīm, and al-Ḥārith al-Aʿwar; and among the companions of ʿAbd Allāh were ʿAlqamah ibn Qays, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yazīd, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Duʾayb. I poured drink for them into the jars, and they drank from them. I asked, “Abū Isḥāq, could they see what was in them?” He said, “Yes. They could see it being drawn out with handled pitchers.”

Abū Yūsuf said, “Glory be to God! How astonishing this matter is. Perhaps it was something sweet.”

Chapter [ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Laylā]

Ibn Numayr related to us: Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh related to us, from al-Aʿmash, who said:

I saw al-Ḥajjāj summon ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Laylā and beat him while saying, “Revile the liars.” [ʿAbd al-Raḥmān would say:] “May God curse the liars.” Then he would be silent, and then say, “ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr, al-Mukhtār ibn Abī ʿUbayd.”

Abū Saʿīd al-Ashajj related to us: Ḥafṣ and Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh related to us, from al-Aʿmash, who said: I saw ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Laylā after al-Ḥajjāj had beaten him. He was an old man being brought before him, leaning on his son. They were saying to him, “Curse the liars,” and he would say, “May God curse the liars.” Then he would say, “God, God Almighty! ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr, al-Mukhtār ibn Abī ʿUbayd.” Al-Aʿmash said: The Syrians around him were like donkeys, not understanding what he was saying, while he was getting them out of the curse.

Abū Bakr ibn Abī Shaybah related to us: Muʿāwiyah ibn Hishām related to us:

Sufyān related to us, from al-Aʿmash, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Laylā, who used to pray; when someone entered, he would go to his bed and lean on it.

Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb related to us: Ḥammād ibn Zayd related to us, from Ayyūb, from Muḥammad, who said: I sat with ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Laylā. His companions treated him with such deference as though he were an emir. They mentioned the later of the two periods. I cited the ḥadīth of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUtbah concerning Subayʿah bint al-Ḥārith.94 He gestured to his companions, and I frowned. I said, “I would be eager to lie if you were lying about ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUtbah, when he is in the vicinity of Kūfah.”

He was embarrassed and said, “But his uncle did not say that.” I had not heard anything from him about ʿAbd Allāh. So I got up, met Abū ʿAṭiyyah Mālik ibn al-Ḥārith, and asked him about it. He began relating to me the ḥadīth of Subayʿah. I said, “That is not what I am asking you about. Did you hear anything about it from ʿAbd Allāh?” He said, “Yes. We were with ʿAbd Allāh and asked him about her. He said:

‘What do you think if she gives birth before four months and ten days have passed?’ We said, ‘She must wait until they have passed.’ He said:

‘What do you think if the four months and ten days fall short?’ We said, ‘She must wait until they have passed.’ He said, ‘What do you think if the four months and ten days come to an end before she gives birth?’ We said, ‘She must wait until she gives birth.’

He said, ‘You impose the stricter ruling on her but do not grant her the concession.’ Then the shorter sūrah of Women was revealed before the longer ones: “As for those who are pregnant, their term is until they deliver their burden”—the verse.”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us: Sufyān related to us: Ziyād ibn ʿAlāqah related to us: I heard al-Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah. “I pledged allegiance,” and the ḥadīth of Jarīr, and the ḥadīth of Usāmah ibn Sharīk, and the ḥadīth of Quṭbah ibn Mālik. Sufyān said: We heard these four ḥadīths from Ziyād in one sitting; we heard nothing else from him.

He said: Sufyān related to us: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sharīk related to us; he was one hundred years old.

He said: Sufyān related to us: Abū al-Zaʿrāʾ related to us: I heard Abū al-Aḥwaṣ say: Three brothers—one was killed on the Day of the Camel, another was killed on such-and-such a day, and what would happen to the third was unknown. Abū al-Aḥwaṣ went out to the Azāriqah, and was killed.

Sufyān related to us: Abū al-Zaʿrāʾ used to choose which military divisions to join during the civil war.

Sufyān said: ʿUmar ibn Saʿīd had related to me, from Abū al-Juwayriyah al-Jarmī, the ḥadīth about a found object. I asked him about it, but he did not transmit it fully to me, so I relate it from ʿUmar. Whenever we visited him, he would ask us about the civil war.

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us: Sufyān related to us: I heard Wahb—I mean Ibn ʿUqbah al-Bakkāʾī—say, “I was born with two years of ʿUthmān’s rule remaining.”

ʿImrān ibn Ẓabyān al-Ḥanafī—who had been so for sixty-six years—said: I heard these words from him in the year ninety-two.

Al-Ḥumaydī said: Sufyān related to us: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĪsā ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Laylā related to me. ʿAbd Allāh and his brother were older than their uncle, and the two of them would decide matters on behalf of their uncle Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān.

Al-Ḥumaydī said: Sufyān related to us: ʿĀmir ibn Shaqīq ibn Jamrah and Baḥr ibn Bālih related to us.

He said: Sufyān related to us: ʿAbd al-Malik ibn al-Ḥusayn related to us—he was a Shīʿī among us, a Rāfiḍī with independent views he heard it from Abū Ḥarb ibn Abī al-Aswad, who related from his father, who said: I heard ʿAlī say: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām came to me when I had put my foot in the stirrup. He said to me, “Where are you going?” I replied, “Iraq.” He said, “Know that if you go there, you will be struck there by the blade of the sword.” Then he said, “By God, I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ—say before that.” Abū Ḥarb said: I heard my father say: I was astonished by him and said, “A man who is going to fight—how can he relate something like this about himself?”

[Abū Isḥāq al-Sabīʿī]

Muḥammad ibn Bashshār related to us: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī ibn Ḥassān related to us: Sufyān ibn Isḥāq related to us, from Abū Isḥāq al-Hamdānī, who said: I saw ʿAlī preaching to the people at midday on Friday, his head and beard white.

Sufyān said: Or he mentioned one of the two.

Ibn Bashshār said: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to us: Isrāʾīl related to us, from Abū Isḥāq, who said: I was with my father on a Friday, and my father said to me, “My son, would you like to see the Commander of the Faithful?” I stood up and saw ʿAlī preaching to the people. He wore a waist-wrapper and a cloak; he was bald, with a large belly, and his head and beard were white. He did not raise his hands as they do, and he did not sit down before he descended.

Muḥammad ibn Fuḍayl related to me: Isḥāq al-Azraq related to us: Sufyān related to us, from Abū Isḥāq, from ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥārith ibn al-Muṣṭaliq, who said: The Messenger of God did not leave— The Messenger of God ﷺ left behind only weapons, land that he made a charitable endowment, and a white mule.

Muḥammad ibn Fuḍayl related to me: Abū Dāwūd al-Ḥafarī (193a) related to us: Sufyān related to us, from Abū Isḥāq, from Maṭar ibn ʿUkāmis, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said, “When God, Mighty and Majestic, decrees a servant’s death in a land, He gives him a need that will take him there.”

Abū Nuʿaym and Qabīṣa related to us, both saying: Sufyān related to us, from Abū Isḥāq, from Sulaymān ibn Ṣurad, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said on the day of the Confederates, “Now we shall raid them, and they shall not raid us.”

ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Muʿādh related to us: My father related to us: Shuʿba related to us, from Abū Isḥāq, who said: I heard al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr say: “The least severely punished of the people of the Fire is a man with two embers placed in the soles of his feet; his brain boils because of them.”

Through the same chain, from Abū Isḥāq, from al-Barāʾ, who said: Some people among the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ died while drinking wine, before it was forbidden. When it was forbidden, they said, “Our companions died while drinking wine.” Then was revealed: “Those who believe and do righteous deeds incur no blame for what they consumed” (5:93), “and God loves those who do good” (5:93). I said to Abū Isḥāq, “Did you hear it from him?” He said, “No.”

Through the same chain, from al-Barāʾ—and we did not hear it from al-Barāʾ—that they obtained donkeys on the day of Ḥunayn or Khaybar, and a herald of the Messenger of God ﷺ called out, “Turn over the cooking pots!”

Aḥmad ibn Yūnus related to us: Zuhayr related to us: Abū Isḥāq, ʿAmr ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUbayd al-Hamdānī al-Sabīʿī, related to us that his grandfather al-Khayyār passed by ʿUthmān. He asked, “How many dependants do you have with you, old man?” He replied, “I have sixty.” ʿUthmān said, “As for you, old man, we have assigned you fifteen, and one hundred each for your dependants.”

ʿAmr ibn Khālid al-Ḥarrānī related to us: Zuhayr related to us: Abū Isḥāq related to us, saying: I used to sit often with Rāfiʿ ibn Khadīj.

Through the same chain, from Abū Isḥāq, who said: I saw ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar wearing sandals, each with two straps.

Through the same chain, from Abū Isḥāq, who said: I used to sit with ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar.

Through the same chain, he said: Abū Isḥāq related to us, saying: I heard Ibn ʿUmar say, between al-Ṣafā and al-Marwa, “My Lord, forgive and have mercy; surely You are the Mighty, the Most Generous.”

Through the same chain, he said: Abū Isḥāq related to us, from Abū Burda: The Prophet ﷺ used to say, “O God, forgive me my sin, my ignorance, and my excess”—Zuhayr said, “I think he said, ‘in my affair’”—“O God, forgive me my jesting and my seriousness, my mistakes and my deliberate actions; all of that is in me.”95

Abū Bakr ibn Abī Shayba related to us: Abū Usāma related to us, from al-Aʿmash, who said: Abū Isḥāq related to us, from al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said, “The least severely punished of the people of the Fire is one who has two sandals and two straps of fire. His brain boils because of them as a pot boils. He thinks that no one is more severely punished than he, yet he is the least severely punished of them.”

Abū Bakr said: Abū Muʿāwiya related to us: al-Aʿmash related to us, from Abū Isḥāq, who said: I held a wedding feast and invited the companions of ʿAlī and the companions of ʿAbd Allāh. Among the companions of ʿAlī were ʿImāra ibn ʿAbd, Hubayra ibn Yarīm, and al-Ḥārith al-Aʿwar. Among the companions of ʿAbd Allāh were ʿAlqama ibn Qays, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yazīd, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Dhiʾb.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rajāʾ related to us: Isrāʾīl informed us, from Abū Isḥāq, from Ḥabashī ibn Junāda, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said, “O God, forgive those who shave their heads.” They said, “O Messenger of God, and those who shorten their hair?” He said, “O God, forgive those who shave their heads.” They said, “O Messenger of God, and those who shorten their hair?” He said, “And those who shorten their hair”—on the third occasion.

Abū Bakr ibn Abī Shayba related to me: Sharīk related to us, from Abū Isḥāq, from Ḥabashī ibn Junāda, Abū al-Janūb. Sharīk said: I asked Abū Isḥāq, “Where did you see him?” He said, “He stood before us in our gathering,” and said: “I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say, ‘ʿAlī is of me, and I am of him; none conveys [a message] on my behalf except ʿAlī.’”

Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā related to me: Ḥasan ibn Ḥusayn related to us: Ibrāhīm ibn Yūsuf ibn Abī Isḥāq related to us, from his father, from Abū Isḥāq, who said: I heard Ḥabashī ibn Junāda say: “I took part with the Messenger of God ﷺ in three campaigns, and I took part with ʿAlī in three campaigns; in my view, these were no less than those.” He said:

Abū Isḥāq said: Abū al-Janūb spoke truly; they were indeed comparable.

Abū al-Walīd Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik al-Bāhilī and Abū ʿUmar Ḥafṣ ibn ʿUmar al-Namarī related to us, both saying: Shuʿba related to us: Abū Isḥāq informed us, saying: I heard al-Barāʾ say:

“The first of the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ to arrive among us were Muṣʿab ibn ʿUmayr and Ibn Umm Maktūm. They used to teach the Qurʾān. Then ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, Bilāl, and Saʿd came; then ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb came with twenty men; then the Messenger of God ﷺ came. I never saw the people of Medina rejoice over anything as much as they rejoiced over him. I saw the young women and boys running in the road, saying, ‘The Messenger of God ﷺ has come!’ By the time he arrived in Medina, I had already recited ‘Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High’ in a sūra like it from the short sūras.”

ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Mūsā and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rajāʾ Abū ʿAmr al-Ghadānī related to us, from— Isrāʾīl, from Abū Isḥāq, from al-Barāʾ, who said: Abū Bakr bought a camel saddle from ʿĀzib for thirteen dirhams. Abū Bakr said to ʿĀzib, “Tell al-Barāʾ to bring my saddle to me.”

ʿĀzib said to him, “No, not until you tell us what you and the Messenger of God ﷺ did when you set out while the polytheists were pursuing you.” He said: “We left Mecca by night and traveled through the night and the day until it was midday and the height of the noon heat had arrived. I cast my eyes about to see whether there was any shade in which we could take shelter. Then I saw a rock, and I went to it. It had a patch of shade left, so I smoothed out the remaining shade. Then I spread a fur for the Messenger of God ﷺ and said, ‘Lie down, Messenger of God.’ He lay down. Then I went off, looking around me to see whether I could spot any of the pursuers. Suddenly, there was a shepherd driving his sheep toward the rock, wanting what I wanted from it—that is, the shade. I asked him, ‘Whose are you, young man?’

“He said, ‘A man of Quraysh’s.’ He named him, and I recognized him. I asked him, ‘Is there any milk among your sheep?’

“He said, ‘Yes.’ I said, ‘Will you milk some for me?’ He said, ‘Yes.’ I told him to restrain a ewe from his flock and told him to shake the dust from its udder. Then I told him to shake his hands. He said, ‘Like this,’ and struck one hand against the other. He milked a small amount of milk and said:
