Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb related to us, saying: Ḥammād ibn Zayd related to us, from al-Muthannā ibn— Saʿīd, from Abū al-Shaʿthāʾ, who said: I heard Ibn ʿAbbās say: “I ask God’s forgiveness for engaging in currency exchange.”

Sulaymān said: As for this Abū al-Shaʿthāʾ, Ibn al-Madīnī said that he was a freedman of Ibn Maʿmar, not Jābir ibn Zayd.

Ādam ibn Abī Iyās related to us, saying: Ḥammād ibn Zayd related to us, saying: Abū ʿAffān al-Muthannā ibn Saʿīd related to me, from a freedman of Ibn Maʿmar known by the kunyah Abū al-Shaʿthāʾ, who said: I heard Ibn ʿAbbās say: “I repent to God, Mighty and Majestic, for engaging in currency exchange. That was only an opinion I had formed. Here is Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī reporting from the Messenger of God ﷺ that he forbade it.”

Sulaymān related to us, saying: Wuhayb related to us, from Ayyūb, from Muḥammad, who said:

Ḥafṣa related to me that Sīrīn held a wedding feast in Medina and prepared food. He invited people for seven days. Among those he invited was Ubayy ibn Kaʿb. He came while fasting, prayed for them to be blessed, and left.

Sulaymān related to us, saying: Ḥammād related to us, from Ayyūb, from Muḥammad, that his father held a wedding feast in Medina and invited people for seven days.

He said: Ḥammād related to us, saying: Yaʿlā ibn Ḥakīm died in Syria. He was a freedman of Thaqīf and lived here among the Jahāḍima. He left only a mother. Ayyūb would visit her, sit at her door for three days, and people would gather around him.

Hishām ibn ʿAmmār related to us, saying: Yaḥyā ibn Ḥamza related to us, saying: Yazīd ibn ʿUbayda related to us, saying: Abū ʿAbd Allāh Muslim ibn Mishkam related to me, from ʿAwf ibn Mālik, the one who relates from Abū al-Dardāʾ.

Abū ʿUmayr related to us, saying: Ḍamra related to us, from Ibn Shawdhab, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Qāsim, who said: We sat with ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abzā. He mentioned the call to prayer and the call to begin prayer for the two Festival prayers, criticized them, and said, “They are an innovation.” I said, “This is how we found people doing it.” He said, “My son, when did we ever find people doing anything?”

Abū ʿUmayr related to us, saying: Ḍamra said: ʿUqayl and Hishām accompanied Ibn Shihāb for four years.

Abū ʿUmayr said: Tamīm was not known to have a son; rather, he had a daughter named Ruqayya, and he was given his kunyah on her account.

Abū ʿUmayr related to us, saying: Ḍamra related to us, from Bilāl ibn Kaʿb al-ʿAtakī, who said:

We visited Yaḥyā ibn Ḥassān al-Bakrī, traveling from ʿAsqalān to Sanājiyya. I was with Ibn Qarīn, Ibn Adham, and Mūsā ibn Yasār. He brought us food, and Mūsā held back his hand. Yaḥyā said to him, “Eat. A man among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ gave us assurance in this mosque for twenty years. He was known by the kunyah Abū Qurṣāfa, and he used to fast one day and break his fast the next. A boy was born to me, so I went to him and invited him on a day when he was fasting, and he broke his fast.” Mūsā then reached out his hand and ate, while Ibn Adham got up and went to the mosque, sweeping it with his cloak.

He said: Ḍamra related to us, from Ibn Abī Ḥamla, who said: We were encamped at Ghuḍayriyāʾ with Nāfiʿ among us. He had a slave girl called Kawkab al-Ṣubḥ (“Morning Star”), and his slave girl would stay close to my slave girl because of all the washing.

Salama related to us, from Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, who said: Wakīʿ related to us, saying: They say that Sulaymān was the more accurate of the two in his reports and the more reliable—meaning the two sons of Burayda.

Muslim ibn Ibrāhīm related to us, saying: Shaddād ibn Saʿīd al-Rāsibī related to us, saying:

Jābir ibn ʿAmr Abū al-Wāziʿ related to us.

I heard Zayd ibn al-Mubārak mention, from Muḥammad ibn Thawr, from Maʿmar, who said: “My copy of al-Aʿmash’s written collection fell from me, so I can only recall his reports and relate them from memory.”

Salama related to us, from Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, who said: ʿAffān related to us, saying: Ḥammād ibn Salama related to us: Ḥajjāj al-Aḥwal borrowed Qays’s book from me and went to Mecca. He said it was lost. (274b) He said: Hishām said, “I wrote a booklet from ʿAṭāʾ.” He said, “It fell from me.”

Salama related to us, saying: Aḥmad related to us, saying: Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar related to us, saying:

Shuʿba related to us, saying: I heard Qays ibn ʿImrān ibn ʿUmayr relate from his father, from his grandfather, that he set out with ʿAbd Allāh, riding behind him on his mule, for a distance of four parasangs. He prayed the noon prayer as two units and the afternoon prayer as two units.

Shuʿbah said: “Qays told me, while his father was present.”

Salamah related to me, from Aḥmad, who said: ʿAbd al-Razzāq informed us: I said to Maʿmar:

“Why did you not narrate more from Ibn Sharwus?” He replied: “He used to garble the ḥadīth.”

Ismāʿīl ibn Sharwus was from the people of Ṣanʿāʾ, and his teknonym was Abū al-Miqdām.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq said: “I kept company with Maʿmar from the time between the eighth and the ninth.”

Salamah related to us, from Aḥmad, who said: ʿAffān related to us: Ḥammād ibn Zayd related to us, saying: “It befits a scholar to put dust on his head in humility before God, Mighty and Majestic.”

Salamah related to us, from Aḥmad, who said: Abū Qaṭan related to us, saying: A man mentioned to Shuʿbah:

“Al-Ḥakam, from Ibn Abī Laylā, from Bilāl: he commands me to make the second call at dawn and forbids me at the night prayer.” Shuʿbah said: “No, by God! He did not mention Ibn Abī Laylā; he mentioned only a weak chain of transmission.” He said: “I think Shuʿbah said: ‘I used to think he transmitted it from ʿImrān ibn Muslim.’”

He also said: Abū Qaṭan related to us, saying: Al-Masʿūdī said: “We never encountered anyone more given to the Shiʿite position than ʿAdī ibn Thābit.”

He also said: Abū Qaṭan related to us, saying: I heard Shuʿbah say: “I have secured myself against Qatādah by four [reports].” I thought he meant in ḥadīth, so ʿAbd Allāh said to me: “This is one of them”—meaning: “Make your rows straight.”

Salamah related to us, from Aḥmad, who said: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Idrīs related to us, saying: My father used to— “Tell me: ‘Memorize, and beware of writing. When you come, then write; for if one day you need it, or your mind is occupied, you will find your book.’ I never wrote down a single ḥadīth from Layth, Ashʿath, or al-Aʿmash.” (275a)

Salamah related to me, saying: Aḥmad related to us: I heard Ibn Idrīs say: I heard my father say: “I saw al-Ḥakam and Ḥammād, with Muḥārib between them. He was sitting as judge, with the litigants before him, and he would turn to this one at one moment and to the other at another.”

Salamah related to us, from Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, who said: ʿAffān related to us: Ḥammād ibn Salamah related to us, saying: Shuʿbah came to Ḥumayd and asked him about a ḥadīth he was relating. He said:

“Did you hear it?” He replied: “I think so.” Shuʿbah then made this gesture with his hand—meaning, “I don’t want it.”

He said: When Shuʿbah got up and left, Ḥumayd said: “I heard it from Anas, from Abū Jābir al-Bayāḍī.” He said: “Leave it.” I asked him about Shuʿbah, the client of Ibn ʿAbbās, and he said: “He was not one of the reciters.” I went to ask him, but when he saw me about to ask, he said: “Do not ask me; look in my book. Whatever is in it is what I transmit from him, and whatever is not in it, leave it.”

Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Faḍl ibn Ziyād related to me, saying: I heard Abū ʿAbd Allāh being asked: “Why did Mālik not transmit from Saʿd ibn Ibrāhīm?” He said: “He had an incident with Saʿd.” Then he said: “Saʿd does not mind if Mālik does not transmit from him.”

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Makhramī related to me, saying: Zakariyyā ibn ʿAdī related to us, saying:

Ibn Idrīs related to us, from Shuʿbah, who said: “I have never seen anyone disparage the men of the people of Medina more than Saʿd ibn Ibrāhīm. Whenever I put forward one of them to him, he called him a liar.” I asked him about that, and he said: “The people of Medina killed ʿUthmān.”

Aḥmad ibn al-Khalīl related to me, saying: Isḥāq related to us, saying: Yaḥyā informed us that Ibn Idrīs said: We were with Mālik ibn Anas when someone said to him: “Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq said: ‘ʿAbd Allāh was in al-Rayy,’ and he mentioned that your books were with him. He said: ‘Show them to me, for I am their farrier.’” Mālik said: “An impostor among impostors—and he is showing my books to him!” (275b)

Ibn Idrīs said: “I have never heard anyone else use the plural of dajjāl—dajājilah.”

ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī said: Al-Darāwardī said to me: “Tell Yūsuf al-Samtī to fear God, Mighty and Majestic, and return the book of Mūsā ibn ʿUqbah.”

ʿAlī said: Sufyān ibn Ḥabīb said: “I went to Mūsā ibn ʿUqbah and said: ‘Relate to me.’”

A woman who was with him said: “Do as two men who passed by us did: they took his book, then said, ‘We will not transmit from you,’ and went away.” I said: “Who were they?” He said: “Fuḍayl ibn Sulaymān and Yūsuf ibn Khālid.”

ʿAlī said: A man who used to ask Mālik questions and read to him related to me, saying: “Al-Darāwardī, Ibn Abī Ḥāzim, and Ibn Kinānah each gave me a dinar to ask Mālik about three men of Medina from whom he had not transmitted. I went in to see him and said: ‘I have married, but I have no flour or parched flour. My people have given me a dinar to ask you about something.’ He said: ‘As God wills; there is no power except through God’—he used to say this often—then said: ‘How welcome is the good God, Mighty and Majestic, has brought your way. Ask.’”

I said: “So-and-so, so-and-so, and so-and-so—you have not transmitted from them. What is their standing?” I had asked leave to see him while al-Darāwardī, Ibn Abī Ḥāzim, and Ibn Abī Kinānah were with him. He said to me: “This is not the time for that.” I said to him: “I have come to you about a matter.” He lowered his head for a while, then said:

“As God wills; there is no power except through God. I encountered seventy shaykhs in this mosque, all of whom had heard from the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ and from those after them. We took this matter only from its people.”

ʿAlī said: Bishr ibn ʿUmar informed me, saying: I asked Mālik about Shuʿbah, the client of Ibn ʿAbbās. He said: “He did not resemble the reciters.” He said: “I asked him about Ṣāliḥ, the client of al-Tawʾamah, Abū al-Ḥārith, and Abū Jābir al-Bayāḍī. He said: ‘They are not fit for this.’” He said: “I asked him about Ibn Abī Yaḥyā al-Aslamī, and he said: ‘He is not trustworthy in his religion.’” He said: “I asked him about a man, and he said: ‘Do you see anything from him in my books? If I had considered him trustworthy, you would have seen something from him in my books.’ I said to him: ‘Was Ibn Abī Najīḥ a Muʿtazilī?’ He said: ‘Yes.’” Ayyūb said: “What men they corrupted!” He said: “He used to hold a vile, reprehensible opinion. Ḥurayth ibn al-Salmānī said that the Prophet ﷺ killed a Muslim in retaliation for a protected non-Muslim. It is transmitted only on the authority of Ibn Abī Yaḥyā; it is not through Ḥajjāj—he only took it from him.”

ʿAlī said: Shuʿbah used to say: “Dāwūd ibn Farāhīj related to us”—and he was weak.

ʿAlī said: Yaḥyā did not take anything from Ḥajjāj that he had seen in Mecca. In Yaḥyā’s view, Ḥajjāj’s ḥadīth was confused, so he did not take from him; so-and-so did take from him.

ʿAlī said: Yaḥyā said about something: “Then it is Mahdī ibn Hilāl; they all agree on him.”

He said: “Sometimes I would see Yaḥyā with his cheek against the door, with no one with him.”

ʿAlī said: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān said: “I arrived in Basra, and its ḥadīth scholars were four. The most prolific of them, and the one with the smallest following, was Hishām al-Dastawāʾī. The following was with ʿUthmān al-Barrī, al-Ḥasan ibn Dīnār, and Abū Juzʾ.” ʿAlī said: I said to him: “What about Ḥammād ibn Salamah?”

He said: “People had not yet come to him.” He said: “Abū Juzʾ once arrived and sat in the mosque of Banū ʿAdī. The mosque could not contain the crowd, and he could not sit down.”

ʿAlī said: Hishām al-Dastawāʾī was Abū Bakr, and his father’s name was Sanbar.

Chapter: Those from whom people are advised against transmitting

Abū Yūsuf said: “I used to hear our companions declare them weak.”

Among the Kufans and those of their standing from other regions:

Among them are:

[al-Ḥasan ibn ʿUmārah].

Abū Maryam ʿAbd al-Ghaffār ibn al-Qāsim al-Anṣārī.

Al-Ḥakam ibn Ẓuhayr.

And [Sulaymān ibn Arqam].

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh.

Al-Muʿallā ibn Ghazwān, who was a soothsayer on the road to Mecca.

[And] Sulaymān ibn Yasīr.

Dāwūd ibn al-Zibriqān.

Yaḥyā ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Taymī.

Bakr ibn Khunays.

Juwaybir. (276b)

Al-Kalbī, Muḥammad ibn al-Sāʾib.

ʿUbaydah al-Ḍabbī.

Mūsā ibn ʿUthmān, who transmits from al-Ḥakam.

ʿAmr ibn Abī al-Miqdām.

Ḥammād ibn Saʿīd al-Ḥummānī.

[Talīd ibn Afṣā—a vile man. I heard ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Mūsā say to his son Muḥammad: “Have I not told you not to write down this ḥadīth of Talīd?”]

Abū Mālik al-Nakhaʿī.

Jābir al-Juʿfī.

Abū Mikhnaf.

Al-Waqqāṣī.

Muḥammad ibn al-Furāt.

Abū Isḥāq al-Kūfī, from whom Hushaym transmits; he is ʿAbd Allāh ibn Maysarah.

[Qays ibn al-Rabīʿ].

ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Abī Ḥumayd al-Hudhalī.

[Ismāʿīl al-Azraq, who is Ibn Salmān].

Yaḥyā ibn Salamah ibn Kuhayl.

ʿAmr ibn Khālid.

[[And] Ḥārithah ibn Abī al-Rijāl].

[Dahtham ibn Qurān].

[ʿAbd al-Wahhāb ibn Mujāhid, a Meccan].

[ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Isḥāq al-Kūfī].

[Abū Sufyān Ṭarīf al-Saʿdī].

[Abān ibn Abī ʿAyyāsh].

[ʿAbd Allāh ibn Samʿān al-Madanī].

[Yazīd ibn ʿIyāḍ, a Medinan].

[Khārijah ibn Muṣʿab al-Sarakhsī].

[al-Hayyāj ibn Bisṭām].

[Muqātil ibn Sulaymān].

[ʿUmar ibn Shabīb al-Kūfī]. I think he was Aḥmasī.

Yāsīn al-Zayyāt.

Saʿd the cobbler.

Abū Farwah Yazīd ibn Sinān.

Sayf ibn Hārūn.

Suwār ibn Muṣʿab.

ʿAmr ibn Shaym.

Sulaym ibn Muslim al-Makkī al-Khashshāb, the client of Banū ʿAbd al-Dār, and a son of his whom I saw. He was not fit for ḥadīth, and nothing should be written down from him. He fell ill, and people and his peers came in to see him. He used to relate what he had not heard. Then he recovered and went back to relating those ḥadīths which, during his illness, he had said he had not heard from them.

Abū al-Jārūd Ziyād ibn al-Mundhir.

[Sayf ibn Muḥammad].

[Abū Saʿd al-Ṣanʿānī].

Sulaym, the client of al-Shaʿbī.

Muḥammad ibn Sālim.

Al-Sarī ibn Ismāʿīl.

Saʿd ibn Ṭarīf.

Al-Aṣbagh ibn Nubātah.

Abū al-Yaqẓān ʿUthmān ibn ʿUmayr.

Sayf ibn ʿUmar al-Ḍabbī.

Sayf ibn Muḥammad, the nephew of Sufyān.

[ʿAmr ibn Jumayʿ, who was judge of Ḥulwān].

[ʿĪsā ibn Abī ʿĪsā, a Kufan], who settled in Medina. He was called al-Ḥannāṭ. A ḥannāṭ is one who deals in wheat and grain.

Muḥammad ibn Abān.

[al-Minhal ibn Khalīfah].

And Abū Qays (277a), the Damascene.

[And Jaʿfar ibn Maymūn, a Basran].

[And ʿAlī ibn Nizār].

And Salām ibn Abī ʿAmrah.

And ʿĪsā ibn Maymūn, who narrates from al-Qāsim.

And Muḥammad ibn Abī Ḥumayd, a Medinan.

And Ibrāhīm ibn Ismāʿīl al-Makkī.

And Ṣāliḥ ibn Abī al-Akhḍar.

And Ṭalḥah ibn ʿAmr.

And Abū Bakr al-Sabarī, a Medinan.

And Abū Bakr ibn Nāfiʿ.

[And Ismāʿīl ibn Rāfiʿ al-Makkī].

[And ʿAbd al-Razzāq ibn ʿUmar, a Syrian].

[And Ibn Abī Labībah], from whom Wakīʿ narrates.

And Ibn Abī Fudayk.

And Dāwūd ibn ʿAbd al-Jabbār.

And Bakr ibn al-Sharūd, a Ṣanʿānī.

And ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿīd ibn Abī Saʿīd.

And Zamʿah ibn Ṣāliḥ.

[And Ibrāhīm ibn al-Ḥakam ibn Abān].

And Maynāʾ, client of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf; ʿAbd al-Razzāq narrates from him, from his father, from Maynāʾ.

And ʿUmar ibn Qays, who is Sindal, the brother of Ḥumayd ibn Qays. [And Ḥumayd is trustworthy].

[And ʿUmar ibn ʿAṭāʾ ibn Warāz, from whom Ibn Jurayj narrates; and he narrates from ʿUmar ibn ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī al-Khuwwār, who is trustworthy].

[And Yaʿqūb ibn al-Walīd].

[And Ibrāhīm ibn Yazīd al-Khawzī].

And Zanfil al-ʿUrafī.

He said: I heard al-Ḥumaydī say, “Our companions would mention him,” then he said, “He used to play with beads for children in the road.”

And Zarzar, a Meccan—a shaykh from among the people of Mecca, of Banū Makhzūm.

He said: Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah narrated from Zarzar. A man said, “Abū Muḥammad, Zarzar!” They disapproved of his narrating from him, so he said, “We narrated two words from him, so enough!”119 And Ṣāliḥ al-Ṭalḥī is a Kūfan.

[And Usāmah ibn Zayd ibn Aslam]: his hadith is recorded only for the sake of familiarity, and his narration is not used as proof.

And Marwān ibn Sālim, from the people of Qarqīsiyāʾ, from whom ʿAbd al-Majīd narrated: his hadith is objectionable; his narration is not used as proof, and the people of knowledge record his hadith only for the sake of familiarity.

And Yaḥyā ibn Abī Unaysah—his hadith is abandoned—and his brother Zayd ibn Abī Unaysah is trustworthy.

Al-Faḍl related to me, saying: Aḥmad related to us, saying: Hushaym related to us, saying: al-Kalbī informed me, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that the Messenger of God ﷺ assigned on the day of Ḥunayn two shares to the horse and one share to the man.

Abū ʿAbd Allāh Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal said: Hushaym related to us, saying: ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, from the Prophet ﷺ related the same.

Aḥmad said: Were it not for the hadith of ʿUbayd Allāh, I would not have narrated the hadith. (277b) ʿAbd Allāh ibn Zayd ibn Aslam and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam are brothers. As for Usāmah ibn Zayd al-Laythī, Yaḥyā al-Qaṭṭān criticized him and refrained from using his hadith. Among the people of Medina and our companions, however, he is trustworthy and reliable.

And Munkadir ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir.

[And Zakariyyā ibn Manẓūr, a Medinan].

And al-Qāsim ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar.

And al-Ḥasan ibn Ḍumayrah ibn Abī Ḍumayrah.

[And ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd ibn Sulaymān, the brother of Fulayḥ ibn Sulaymān].

And Ayyūb ibn Yasār.

And Rishdayn ibn Kurayb.

And Ibrāhīm ibn al-Faḍl.

And Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Mujabbir.

And ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir al-Aslamī.

[And Khālid ibn Ilyās]: we wrote down his hadith, but he did not read it aloud to us.

[And] Abū Nuʿaym.

And Abū al-Bakhtarī, the judge.

And al-Ḥakam ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Aylī.

And Fāʾid, Abū al-Warqāʾ.

And ʿAbd al-Jabbār ibn ʿUmar al-Aylī.

And Isḥāq ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Farwah.

And Muṭarrif ibn Māzin, a Ṣanʿānī.

And ʿAbd al-Karīm, Abū Umayyah, a weak Basran.

And Ghālib ibn ʿUbayd [Allāh] al-Jazarī.

And Abū al-ʿAṭūf.

And Maslamah ibn ʿAlī.

And Nāṣiḥ ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-ʿAjamī, the companion of Simāk.

And Nāṣiḥ al-Baṣrī.

[And Saʿīd ibn Muḥammad al-Warrāq, a Baghdadi].

[I heard Isḥāq ibn Ibrāhīm say: Ibn al-Mubārak said, “Baqiyyah baffled me: he would narrate to us, saying, ‘Abū Saʿīd al-Wuḥāẓī related to us,’ but it turned out to be ʿAbd al-Quddūs”].

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥīm related to me, saying: ʿAlī informed us, saying: He said— ʿAbd al-Raḥmān: “Hushaym ibn Abī Isḥāq al-Kūfī baffled me, until he said something about ʿIkrimah.” ʿAlī said: “We used to think he was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Maysarah, Abū Laylā. He gave him a kunyah derived from one of his sons.”

Al-ʿAbbās ibn Muḥammad related to me, saying: Muslim ibn Ibrāhīm related to us, saying:

Shuʿbah related to us, saying: “I saw Abū al-Muhazzam in Thābit’s session. If someone gave him a coin, he would narrate ninety hadiths to him.”

ʿAlī said: “I have abandoned the hadith of Muḥammad ibn al-Qāsim, Abū Ibrāhīm; I do not narrate from him.”

[ʿAlī said: “ʿAbd al-Raḥmān crossed out the hadith of Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAyyāsh and the hadith of al-Mubārak ibn Faḍālah”].

[I heard (278a) Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb say: “I used to sit with al-Mubārak ibn Faḍālah on Fridays. He would narrate to us, and I would write. Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī Jaʿfar al-Jaʿfarī used to sit with him, and he would say to me, ‘Boy, look at what you write down from al-Mubārak ibn Faḍālah, gather it, and write it out for me.’ So I would gather what he would narrate as if it were a verse in a collection, write it down, and take it to him.”].

Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb related to us, saying: Ḥammād ibn Zayd related to us, from al-Jalad ibn Ayyūb, from Muʿāwiyah ibn Qurrah, from Anas ibn Mālik, who said: “The interval of the woman suffering from prolonged bleeding is three, five, seven, or ten.”

Sulaymān said: “Ḥammād considered al-Jalad weak and would say, ‘He did not understand the hadith—’” of hadith.”

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr related to us, saying: Ismāʿīl ibn Ibrāhīm related to us, saying: Khālid ibn Ayyūb related to us, from Muʿāwiyah ibn Qurrah, who said: Anas ibn Mālik said: “The interval of the menstruating woman is five, six, seven, eight, or ten; then she bathes, fasts, and prays.”

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr related to us, saying: Ḥammād related to us, saying: al-Jalad ibn Ayyūb related to us, from Muʿāwiyah ibn Qurrah, from Anas ibn Mālik, who said: “The woman suffering from prolonged bleeding waits three, five, seven, nine, or ten.” Sufyān narrated from him, saying: “Menstruation is ten days; anything beyond that makes her a woman suffering from prolonged bleeding.”

Ibn ʿUthmān related to us, saying: ʿAbd Allāh said: “The people of Basra reject the hadith of al-Jalad ibn Ayyūb and say, ‘He is a shaykh, but not a hadith scholar.’”

Ibn al-Mubārak said: “The people of his own town know him better than others.”

I heard Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb, Ṣadaqah ibn al-Faḍl, and Isḥāq ibn Ibrāhīm, and it reached me that Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, too, considered al-Jalad ibn Ayyūb weak and did not regard him as fit to serve as proof.

ʿAlī said: “It reached me that Ḥammād ibn Zayd said: ‘There was a shaykh here who did not know whether it was the interval of menstruation or of prolonged bleeding.’” He said: “They kept at him until—meaning al-Jalad ibn Ayyūb—”

ʿAlī said: “The mursal reports of Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib and al-Shaʿbī are dearer to me than Dāwūd ibn al-Ḥuṣayn’s report from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbās.”

[ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salamah al-Afṭas]

I heard Isḥāq ibn Ibrāhīm al-Ḥanẓalī say: “Aḥmad al-Marwazī and I entered upon ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salamah al-Afṭas, and we opened a conversation with him. He said, ‘Can there be anyone in Khurasan who hears this subject!’ He spoke freely with us and said, ‘Write down this matter—’”

(That is,) Aḥmad al-Marwazī and I entered upon ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salamah al-Afṭas, and we opened a conversation with him. He said: “Can there be anyone in Khurasan who hears this subject!” He spoke freely with us and said: “Write down this matter—this matter in which Sufyān and so-and-so lied, though he was a counterpart to Sufyān.” Isḥāq said: “It was a matter of Ibn Jurayj from ʿAṭāʾ, with a chain of narrators in which each narrator reported from the preceding one; Sufyān abbreviated it. Isḥāq mentioned this only to show the man’s misconduct and lack of scrupulousness.

I heard al-Ḥumaydī say: “Ghundar and al-Afṭas arrived among us, and one of them lodged near the other. Al-Ḥuwayṭī, our companions, and I went there. Ghundar had a crowd of hadith scholars around him at the lodging where he had settled, while al-Afṭas sat on a bench in the road opposite Ghundar’s lodging. We gathered around him, and he began to make mocking gestures. While we were there, Ghundar appeared with a book. He had sprung up, with that crowd around him. He had read to them from his book, and one said, ‘This one will give me the book so we can copy it’; another said, ‘No, he should hand it to me.’ They argued, so Ghundar sprang up, the book in his hand. He held it aloft while those around him shouted, and Ghundar had raised his hand, the book in it. Al-Afṭas looked at him and said, ‘I heard ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAwn say, “I heard Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn say: This knowledge is religion, so consider from whom you take your religion”—’” He was alluding to Ghundar.

Al-Ḥumaydī said: “Glory be to God, who raised Ghundar up and caused al-Afṭas’s reputation to disappear.”

Al-Ḥumaydī also said: “In addressing al-Ḥuwayṭī, he said, ‘Enemy of yourself! Could you not find anyone else besides Ubayy ibn Kaʿb to use as an example and make light of—’”

Ubayy ibn Kaʿb?” He said: “The hadith scholars turned against him.” He then began saying, “I only said Ubayy ibn Khalaf.” Al-Ḥuwayṭī kept saying, “You lie! You said Ubayy ibn Kaʿb.”

Al-Ḥumaydī said: “I heard him say to his companions, ‘Get up and prepare to leave, for this is no place for us.’”

I heard Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb al-ʿAnbarī say: Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd said to me: “Al-Afṭas came to me and said, ‘Hand over to me the book of so-and-so’—one of Yaḥyā’s shaykhs. I refused him, and he threatened me. I said—hoping to soften the matter—‘I have promised some people that I would narrate to them, and they are waiting for me.’ He said, ‘I will certainly do this, and I will certainly do that.’ I said, ‘Sit down,’ and went to my father and told him. He said, ‘Give it to him, so no harm comes to us from him.’ I think he said, ‘If you don’t, what may happen will happen.’”

Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb said: “Yaḥyā invited a group of his brethren and invited al-Afṭas with them. When they left, someone met him and asked, ‘Where are you coming from?’ He replied, ‘This cross-eyed man invited us, and brought out a little dog or a cat he had roasted and fed us.’” (279a) Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Anṣārī said to me: “One day al-Afṭas met me and said:

‘Where are you coming from?’ I said, ‘From Ibn Dāwūd.’ He said to me, ‘When you go to him, carry a piece of bread in your sleeve and show it to him. Then move it and show it to him; he will follow you wherever you go.’”

[And ʿUthmān ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Qurashī—one of the descendants of Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ—was called al-Waqqāṣī. The people of knowledge record his hadith only for the sake of familiarity and do not use it as proof—]

“...by his narration.”

Marwān ibn Sālim was from the people of Qarqīsiyāʾ. ʿAbd al-Majīd narrated from him. He is objectionable in hadith; his narrations are not to be relied upon, and scholars record his hadith only for purposes of identification.

Yaḥyā ibn Abī Unaysah is abandoned in hadith, while his brother Zayd ibn Abī Unaysah is reliable.

Al-Faḍl related to me; he said: Aḥmad related to us; he said: Hushaym related to us; he said: al-Kalbī informed me, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that the Messenger of God ﷺ allotted two shares to a horse and one share to a foot soldier on the day of Ḥunayn.

Abū ʿAbd Allāh Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal said: Hushaym also related to us, saying: ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, from the Prophet ﷺ, reported the same.

Aḥmad said: Were it not for the report of ʿUbayd Allāh, I would not have narrated the report of al-Kalbī.

Aḥmad ibn al-Khalīl related to me; he said: Aḥmad ibn Sulaymān related to us; he said:

Jarīr related to us; he said: al-Aʿmash related to us; he said: I asked al-Mughīrah ibn Saʿīd, “Can you bring the dead to life?” He replied, “No.” I asked, “And ʿAlī?” He replied, “By Him by whom I swear, had he wished, he could have brought ʿĀd, Thamūd, and many generations between them back to life.”

ʿAlī ibn Ṣāliḥ related to me, from Ibn Abī Zāʾidah, from Mujālid, from al-Shaʿbī, from Rashīd al-Hajarī: “A bad doctrine.”

Muslim ibn Khālid, whose byname was Zinjī, was a Meccan. “I heard the shaykhs of Mecca say: He had a study circle in the days of Ibn Jurayj and would seek out and hear reports, but did not write them down. He made his audition notes into a suftajah. When people needed him and he began narrating, he would take up the reports he had heard but had since forgotten.” ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī used to consider him weak. One day he left his home and went to the mosque. Some hadith scholars entered the mosque and were discussing his reports. He said, “You would do well to occupy yourselves with someone else”—or words to that effect.

Muḥammad ibn Abī Ḥafṣah was a Basran who narrated from al-Zuhrī. He is weak, though superior to Ṣāliḥ ibn Abī al-Akhḍar.

“Yaḥyā ibn Sulaym al-Ṭāʾifī was a Sunnī, a pious man, and his book was sound. When he narrated from his book, his hadith was good; when he narrated from memory, some of it was recognized and some rejected.” He and al-Qaddāḥ had testified against Sulaym al-Khashshāb, the client of the Shaybayn. He settled—

...with Sulaym, and was treated harshly. Sulaym said, “As for Yaḥyā, he is an upright man. He did not know what I said or what he testified to, so he is absolved. But al-Qaddāḥ testified against me falsely, knowingly and deliberately. May God judge between him and me.”

“ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rajāʾ al-Makkī al-Muzanī is reliable. I heard Ṣadaqah praise him highly and declare him reliable.”

ʿAbd al-Majīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz was an obstinate innovator who called others to his doctrine. I heard Ḥammād ibn Ḥafṣ say: I heard Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Qaṭṭān say, “A liar”—meaning ʿAbd al-Majīd.

“Muʾammal ibn Ismāʿīl was a Sunnī and a venerable shaykh. I heard Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb praise him highly, saying: ‘Our shaykhs recognized his standing and recommended him. But his hadith does not resemble that of his peers, to the point that he might say120 He had no business narrating. Scholars may even be obliged to refrain from his hadith and to limit their transmission from him, for he is objectionable and relates objectionable reports from our reliable shaykhs. This is worse: had these objectionable reports come from weak transmitters, we would have made an allowance for him.’”

Ibrāhīm ibn Ismāʿīl was a Meccan.

“Muḥammad ibn Abī Ḥumayd was Medinan.”

“Ṣāliḥ ibn Abī al-Akhḍar was Basran.

Ṭalḥah ibn ʿAmr was Meccan.

...and Ismāʿīl ibn Rāfiʿ: there is weakness in them. They are not abandoned, but their hadith does not serve as proof.”

Saʿīd related to us, from Sufyān, from Saʿīd ibn Saʿīd, a Meccan who is unobjectionable.

I heard ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ibrāhīm say: ʿAbd al-Razzāq ibn ʿUmar had written down reports from al-Zuhrī, but his book was lost. He then gathered al-Zuhrī’s reports from here and there, and his hadith is worthless. So-and-so said: ʿAbd al-Razzāq told me, “I have gathered al-Zuhrī’s reports.”

He said: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yazīd ibn Tamīm’s reports from al-Zuhrī are objectionable.

He said: His father had a book of reports from his father, from al-Zuhrī, but he had not examined it. (280a)

Ibn Abī Labībah—Wakīʿ narrated from him.

Ibn Abī Fudayk is weak.

“Dāwūd ibn ʿAbd al-Jabbār—I think he was Kufan—is objectionable in hadith; his hadith should not be written down.”

Bakr ibn al-Shurūs was Ṣanʿānī and weak.

“ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muslim ibn Hurmuz was Meccan and weak.”

“ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿīd al-Maqburī was weak.”

“Yazīd ibn ʿIyāḍ ibn Juʿdubah: Mālik branded him a liar.”

The same applies to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ziyād ibn Samʿān.

“Ibrāhīm ibn al-Ḥakam ibn Abān’s weakness is undisputed.”

ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Zanjawayh related to me, from ʿAbd al-Razzāq, from his father, from Maynā, the client of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf: “He is neither reliable nor trustworthy.” His hadith must not be written down.

“ʿUmar ibn Qays Sandal was a Meccan; his hadith is not to be written down.” I heard a reliable shaykh from among the shaykhs of Mecca say: I wrote down some questions from him on the authority of ʿAṭāʾ. Someone took them to him and said, “These were related by Ibn Jurayj from ʿAṭāʾ”—though there had been a falling-out between him and Ibn Jurayj. He read them aloud to him, and he said, “This is false; it is worthless.” “He was a wastrel, and they tell vile, indecent stories about him.” These things took place between him and Mālik ibn Anas.

“Saʿīd ibn Sālim al-Qaddāḥ held a bad doctrine, and he called others to it. His hadith and reports are to be avoided.”

Yāsīn al-Zayyāt: Abū ʿĀṣim related to us from him, and he is weak. His hadith is not written down except for purposes of identification. He used to live in al-Yamāmah.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us from Yāsīn al-ʿIjlī, and there is no objection to him.

Muḥammad ibn Abī Yaḥyā, Saḥbal, and Unays are reliable. Their brother, Ibrāhīm ibn Abī Yaḥyā, was a Jahmī, Qadarī, Muʿtazilī, and Rāfiḍī, and was accused of lying.

“Among the family of Abū Farwah, everyone from whom reports are transmitted is reliable, except Isḥāq ibn Abī Farwah; his hadith is not to be written down.”

Muḥammad ibn Kathīr related to us from “Abū al-Miqdām Hishām ibn Ziyād, who is weak and whose hadith is not to be welcomed.”

Saʿīd ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Abī Saʿīd [ibn] al-Muʿallā al-Anṣārī: Fulayḥ narrates from him.

Ibn Numayr said: Abū Saʿīd ibn al-Muʿallā’s name is Rāfiʿ ibn al-Muʿallā, and he is reliable. But I overlooked that and wrote him here as “reliable.”

ʿAbd Allāh, ʿAbd al-Ḥakam, (280b) and ʿAbd al-Aʿlā, the sons of Abū Farwah, are reliable.

Abū ʿAlqamah Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Farwah is reliable.

“Al-Naḍr ibn Ismāʿīl al-Bajalī is weak.”

Abū Ḥafṣ al-Ghanawī is weak.

“Al-Walīd ibn Abī Thawr and Abū Ḥamzah al-Thumālī are weak.”

“Nūḥ ibn Darāj and ʿAlī ibn Ẓabyān: their hadith is not to be written down.”

“Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan al-Hamdānī and Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan al-Asadī are weak.”

ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Hārūn ibn ʿAntarah is weak; his hadith is worthless.

“I heard it from Ibn Maʿīn: Nūḥ ibn Darāj is a wicked liar. He served as judge for two years while blind.”

“Al-Ḥasan al-Luʾluʾī is a liar.”

“Al-Haytham ibn ʿAdī is a liar.”

“I heard al-Ḥasan ibn al-Rabīʿ say: Ibn al-Mubārak said, ‘Al-Muʿallā ibn Hilāl is—’”

“...except that when he gets to hadith, he lies.” One of the Ṣūfīs said, “Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, you are backbiting!” He replied, “Should I keep quiet? If we do not explain, how will truth be distinguished from falsehood?”—or words to that effect.

Sulaymān ibn Arqam Abū Muʿādh related to us. I was told from Yaḥyā that he said, “He is not worth a penny.”

“Abū Dāwūd al-Nakhaʿī’s name was Sulaymān ibn ʿAmr. He was a Qadarī, a wicked man, a liar who would challenge his interlocutor to dispute him.” Isḥāq said: We went to him and asked, “What do you know about the shortest and longest duration of menstruation, and the interval of purity between two menstrual periods?” He replied, “God is greatest! Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd related to me from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, from the Prophet ﷺ; and Abū Ṭuwālah related to us from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, and Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: ‘The shortest menstruation is three days, and the longest is ten. The shortest interval of purity between two menstrual periods is fifteen days.’” He and Abū al-Bukhtarī used to fabricate hadith.

“ʿAṭāʾ ibn ʿAjlān was Kufan and weak; his hadith is worth nothing.”

Al-Fayḍ ibn al-ʿAbbās, the client of Bujaylah, related to me; he said: Sālim ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā al-Awdī related to us; he said: Nāfiʿ, the client of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, related to us; he said: When ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar sent me on an errand, he would tell me to tie a reminder of the errand to my hand—to my finger.

Ibn Idrīs also narrated this from Sālim, and called him Abū al-Fayḍ. Some people narrated this report from him and attributed it to the Prophet ﷺ: “Whenever he feared he might forget an errand, he would tie a thread around his hand.” Al-Fayḍ and Sālim are weak, and their hadith is not to be welcomed.

ʿUbayd ibn Isḥāq related to me; he said: Sayf ibn ʿUmar related to us; he said: I was with Saʿd al-Iskāf, when his son came to him crying and said, “The teacher beat me.” He replied, “By God, I will disgrace them!” He then said, “ʿIkrimah related to me, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: ‘The teachers of your children are the worst of you: they are the least merciful toward orphans and the harshest toward the poor.’” Sayf and Saʿd al-Iskāf are worthless in their hadith and reports.

ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Mūsā related to us; he said: Abū Saʿd al-Baqqāl, Saʿīd ibn al-Marzubān, informed us, from Anas ibn Mālik. He is weak, and his hadith is not to be welcomed.

ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Sulamī is objectionable in hadith. Abū al-Walīd related reports to us from him, and I was told that Abū Nuʿaym had related reports from him. Abū Bishr Bakr ibn Khalaf related reports to me from him.

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr related to us, from Abū Muʿāwiyah, from Shaybah ibn Naʿāmah, who is weak.

“ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Isḥāq is weak.”

Al-Madanī is unobjectionable.

Abū ʿĀṣim related to us from Ḥusām ibn Miṣakk ibn Shayṭān. One of our companions asked him, “What is he like, Abū ʿĀṣim?” He replied, “Take me to Banū Shayṭān so we can ask them about him.” He is weak.

I heard Bakr ibn Khalaf say: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī said, when they asked for the Musnad: “How good this is! But I fear that this will lead them to write from those who are not reliable.”

Yamān ibn al-Mughīra is a Baṣran, weak.

Abū ʿAqīl al-Dawraqī is reliable.

Abū ʿAqīl Hāshim ibn Bilāl, the judge of Wāsiṭ, is reliable.

“Al-Ḥārith ibn Wajīh is a Baṣran; his hadith is soft.”

“Bakkār ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Abī Bakra: Mūsā ibn Ismāʿīl related to us from him, and he is weak.”

“Yūsuf ibn ʿAṭiyya al-Ṣaffār’s hadith is soft.”

Ayyūb ibn ʿUtba is weak.

“Ayyūb ibn Jābir is weak.”

“Muḥammad ibn Jābir is weak.”

“Rūḥ ibn Musāfir is abandoned in hadith, weak.”

“Al-Rabīʿ ibn Badr is weak, abandoned.”

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Nibrās is a Baṣran; his hadith is soft. Muslim related to us from him.

ʿAbbād ibn Manṣūr (281b): his hadith is soft.

“Ayyūb ibn Mudrik is weak.”

“ʿIkrima ibn Ibrāhīm was a judge; his hadith is objectionable.”

ʿAdī ibn al-Faḍl and al-Ḥārith ibn Nabḥān are weak, and so is ʿUqba ibn al-Aṣamm.

ʿAbd al-Wāḥid ibn Zayd: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī refrained from relating from him.

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥīm related to me, saying: ʿAlī said: Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd said:

“We took exception to Ibn Abī ʿArūba before Ibrāhīm’s defeat. The defeat took place in the year 145.”

Yaḥyā said: “The first thing about which we took exception was when he said: ‘Qatāda from Muʿādha,’ or ‘Muʿādha—”

“—from Qatāda.”

He said: ʿAlī said: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī said: “I went to Saʿīd and said, ‘I will ask him about something in which there can be no confusion.’ So I said to him, ‘Did you perform the pilgrimage with Qatāda?’ He said, ‘I performed the pilgrimage with Qatāda!’ He did not know. He said: ‘He lived for a long time after the confusion, until the year 158.’”

He said: “When Abū Juzʾ fell ill, he retracted some hadiths. He said: ‘The hadith of Simāk from Tamīm ibn Ṭarafa—the hadith of the she-camel—I did not hear it.’” ʿAbd al-Ṣamad ibn ʿAbd al-Wārith said:

“I went in to see him, and he told me this and other things. I then related that to the people. When he recovered, he denied it and complained about me to my father.”

ʿAlī said: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān said: “ʿUthmān al-Burrī is more firmly established than al-ʿUmarī.”

I said to him, “What keeps you from relating from him?” He said, “Your weakness.”

A group gathered at Mūsā ibn Ismāʿīl’s, and they jostled one another. Each of them had with him hadiths from the hadiths of Abān al-ʿAṭṭār. He said: “Glory be to God! Most of what I used to hear from Abān was when we were driven away. Whenever he drove me away, I would say, ‘Where shall I go?’”

“I went?” So I went to Abān al-ʿAṭṭār.

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥīm related to me, saying: I heard ʿAlī say: Abū Usāma said: “Al-Ḥasan ibn Dīnār said to me: ‘I heard sixteen hadiths from Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn.’”

ʿAlī said: ʿAbd al-Ṣamad related to me, saying: “I wrote down a thousand reports from al-Ḥasan ibn Dīnār, from Muḥammad.” I said to him, “Perhaps he was transmitting them without naming his source.” He said, “He does not say, ‘Muḥammad related to us.’”

ʿAlī said: “Al-Ḥasan ibn Dīnār was the most firmly established of people in four [transmitters]; had he confined himself to them, and had he known them best, he would have been the most knowledgeable of people about Muʿāwiya ibn Qurra. He transmitted from him with a connected chain, from ʿĀʾidh (282a) ibn ʿAmr, and from Maʿqil ibn Yasār, from his father. He was the most knowledgeable of people about Ḥumayd ibn Hilāl. I was told that he used to come to the mosque of Banū ʿAdī and ask, ‘What did he speak about today?’ They would say, ‘Such-and-such.’ He would say, ‘I heard him speak of that.’ He was also the most knowledgeable of people about al-Jurayrī and Isḥāq ibn Suwayd. Al-Ḥasan ibn Dīnār was not Dīnār’s son; he was Wāṣil’s son.”

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Wāqid, who relates from Qatāda, is weak.

“Al-Ṣalt ibn Dīnār is a Murjiʾī, weak.”

Ḥabīb ibn Ḥassān is a Kūfan; his hadith is nothing.

ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥazwar, Saʿd ibn Ṭarīf, “ʿAbs ibn Qurṭās”, and Naṣr Abū ʿAmr al-Khazzāz: their hadiths are not to be cited, nor written down except for purposes of identification.

Salama related to me, saying: Aḥmad related to us, saying: Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd related to us, saying:

Kahmas said to me: “We took exception to him”—meaning al-Jurayrī—“during the days of the plague.”

Aḥmad ibn al-Khalīl related to me, saying: Surayj ibn Yūnus related to us, saying: ʿUbayd ibn al-Qāsim related to us, saying: “Al-Aʿmash used to criticize al-Ḥasan ibn ʿUmāra. A gift was sent to him, and the next morning he was praising him. Abū ʿĀṣim al-Thaqafī said to him: ‘You were criticizing him yesterday and praising him today?’ Al-Aʿmash replied: ‘Do you not know that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Hearts are formed with two inclinations: love for whoever does good to them, and blame for whoever does them harm.”’ I heard my companions say: ‘It was said to al-Aʿmash: “Al-Ḥasan ibn ʿUmāra has been put in charge of redressing grievances.” He said: “We seek refuge in God from a time when an oppressor is appointed over the redress of grievances.”’ It reached al-Ḥasan, so he sent him wheat. The next morning [al-Aʿmash] said: ‘People will remain in a good state as long as they entrust their affairs to people of honor and standing, who know people’s worth’”—and he mentioned something like his earlier statement.

ʿAlī said: Abū Dāwūd related from Shuʿba, who said: “Al-Ḥasan ibn ʿUmāra said—”

“—from al-Ḥakam, from Mujāhid, from Ibn ʿAbbās, such-and-such.” I asked al-Ḥakam, and he said:

“From Mujāhid,” then he enumerated things he had mentioned.

“Abū Ḥamza al-Aʿwar is not abandoned, but he is not an authority.”

ʿUthmān ibn ʿUmayr, Abū al-Yaqẓān, is a Kūfan. Al-Thawrī related from him, and he is weak.

“ʿAbd al-Aʿlā ibn ʿĀmir al-Thaʿlabī, who relates from Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya, is considered weak. They say: ‘It is only a written sheet.’”

“ʿIsl ibn Sufyān is not abandoned, but he is not an authority.” (282b) “Ibn Abī Ṭalḥa, Abū al-Ḥasan al-Hāshimī, is a Syrian; he is not abandoned, but he is not an authority.”

ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Abī Ḥumayd, Abū al-Khaṭṭāb al-Hudhalī, is weak, weak.

Sulaymān ibn Qusaym, Abū al-Ṣabāḥ, is weak. Sufyān used to call him that in order to disguise him, saying, “Abū al-Ṣabāḥ ibn Qusaym related to me.”

“Muḥammad ibn Sālim is weak; his hadith is not to be welcomed.”

Sufyān related from Bukayr al-Ḍabbī, who said: “I saw Jarīr al-Ḍabbī. He was a reprehensible local chief; his hadith is not to be taken into account.”

ʿAmr ibn Wāqid is a Syrian; his hadith is nothing.

Rushdayn ibn Kurayb and Muḥammad ibn Kurayb have weak hadiths.

“Rushdayn ibn Saʿd al-Miṣrī is weaker and weaker still.”

ʿAbd al-Wāḥid ibn Maymūn, Abū Ḥamza, relates from ʿUrwa; his hadith is recognized and rejected.

Saʿd ibn Ṭarīf, Aṣbagh ibn Nubāta, Saʿd al-Iskāf, and “Ismāʿīl ibn Muslim al-Makkī”: their hadith is recognized and rejected.

Volume Three

The teknonyms, the names, and those known by their teknonyms!

Abū Yūsuf related to us, saying: Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥīm Ṣāʿiqa related to me, saying:

ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī said: “The name of Abū al-ʿAwwām from whom Ḥammād ibn Salama relates is:

Fāʾid ibn Kaysān.

“Abū al-ʿAwwām al-Sadūsī’s name is Shaybān; Qatāda related from him.

“Abū al-ʿAwwām al-Bāhilī is ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Rabīʿ; Wakīʿ and more than one of the Baṣrans related from him.

“The name of Abū Shaykh is Khaywān ibn Khālid al-Hanāʾī.

“They say that Ḥayyān is the name of Abū Madīna, from whom Thābit al-Bunānī related. ʿAlī claimed that he is not the same person as the one from whom Qatāda related.

“ʿAlī said: Sufyān said: ‘I said to Abū al-Zinād, “O Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān!”’

“ʿAlī said: ‘His teknonym was Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. He used to get angry when addressed as Abū al-Zinād.’

“The name of Abū al-Ṣiddīq al-Nājī is Bakr.

“The name of Abū Ṣādiq is ʿAbd Allāh ibn Nājid; he is the brother of Rabīʿa ibn Nājid.

“Abū al-Juwayriyya al-Jarmī is Ḥaṭṭān ibn Khifāf.

“The name of Abū Maryam, the associate of Nuʿaym ibn Ḥakīm, is ʿUbayda.

“The name of Abū Maryam al-Anṣārī (283a) is ʿAbd al-Ghaffār ibn al-Qāsim. Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Anṣārī, Shuʿba, and Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq related from him.

“I heard Muḥammad ibn Numayr say: ‘When the hadith of Abū Maryam was abandoned, we lost out, and he almost became a Rāfiḍī.’”

Ibn Fuḍayl related to me, saying: ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to us, saying: Shuʿba related to us, saying:

“I heard Simāk al-Ḥanafī say: ‘I heard Ibn ʿAbbās say: “The fifth [of the spoils] belongs to us, but we have been wronged.”’ He said: Abū Maryam, who was with me, said, ‘He spoke truly.’ Simāk al-Ḥanafī said, ‘You have lied, and so has so-and-so with you.’” I thought that Ibn al-Mubārak had related from him, except that his name was not made clear; thus, he is like one abandoned.

Iyās ibn Ṣubayḥ, Abū Maryam al-Ḥanafī, was a judge over Baṣra, and Abū Mūsā appointed him as judge.

Abū Maryam al-Salūlī’s name is Mālik ibn Rabīʿa; he was a Companion.

The name of Abū Naʿāma al-Saʿdī is ʿAbd Rabbihi.

Abū Naʿāma al-ʿAdawī is ʿAmr ibn ʿĪsā ibn Suwayd ibn Hubayra.

The name of Abū Naʿāma al-Ḥanafī is Qays ibn ʿAbāya.

The name of Abū Naʿāma al-Ḍabbī is Shayba ibn Naʿāma; Sufyān and Jarīr related from him.

The name of Abū Ṣadaqa al-ʿIjlī is Sulaymān ibn Kindīr.

The name of Abū al-Muḥajjal al-Rudaynī is Murra.

Abū Wāʾil Sufyān ibn Salama set Abū Razīn free.

The name of Abū Razīn is Masʿūd; he was a non-Arab.

Abū Razīn, Laqīṭ ibn ʿĀmir ibn al-Muntafiq.

The name of Abū al-Ṣiddīq al-Nājī is Bakr.

The name of Abū Burda ibn Abī Mūsā is ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Qays.

The name of Abū al-Mutawakkil al-Nājī is ʿAlī ibn Dāwūd.

Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī is Ẓālim ibn ʿAmr ibn Sufyān; he is best known by his teknonym.

Abū Ḥarb—that is his name.

Abū Naḍra is Mundhir ibn Mālik ibn Quṭʿa.

The name of Abū al-ʿUbaydayn is Muʿāwiya ibn Sabura ibn Ḥuṣayn al-Numayrī.

Abū ʿAyyāsh al-Zuraqī is Zayd ibn Muʿāwiya; it is also said: Zayd ibn Ṣāmit.

Abū Rifāʿa is Tamīm ibn Asad.

Abū Qatāda al-ʿAdawī is Tamīm ibn Nadhīr.

Ṣirma al-Māzinī is Mālik ibn Qays.

Furāt al-Qazzāz is Furāt ibn [Abī] ʿAbd al-Raḥmān.

Suwayd ibn Hubayra was not a Companion.

Isḥāq ibn Suwayd ibn Hubayra.

And Ḥumayd ibn Hilāl ibn Hubayrah.

And Sinān ibn Salamah, Abū Jubayr.

Jabalah ibn Suḥaym, Abū Surayrah.

Abū Shurayḥ is ʿAmr ibn Khuwaylid.

The name of Abū Khaldah al-Ḥanafī is Sulayṭ ibn ʿAṭiyyah. (283 b) The name of Abū al-Sawwār al-ʿAdawī is Ḥassān ibn Ḥurayth.

Abū Salamah ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān is his name; it is also said that his name was ʿAbd Allāh.

The name of Abū al-Jūdī is al-Ḥārith ibn ʿUmayr, a Syrian.

Ismāʿīl from Qays ibn Abī Ḥāzim; the name of Abū Ḥāzim is ʿAwf ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥārith.

Ḥujr ibn Qays al-Madrī.

The name of Abū al-Zinbāʿ is Ṣadaqah ibn Ṣāliḥ.

Abū Sulayṭ al-Badrī is Usayrah ibn ʿAmr.

Abū Ḥayyān al-Taymī is Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd.

Abū Ḥayyān, from whom ʿAbd Allāh narrated, is named Mundhir al-Ashjaʿī.

Abū Khālid al-Wālibī is named Hurm.

Abū al-ʿAnbas is Saʿīd ibn Kathīr ibn ʿUbayd. ʿUbayd is Abū Saʿīd, the foster-brother of ʿĀʾishah; Ibn ʿAwn and Shuʿayb ibn al-Ḥabḥāb narrated from him.

Abū al-Jald is Jaylān ibn Farwah.

Abū al-ʿAjfāʾ al-Sulamī is Haram ibn Nusayb.

Abū Maʿbad, the client of Ibn ʿAbbās, is Nāfidh.

Abū al-Zaʿrāʾ is Yaḥyā ibn al-Walīd ibn Musayr al-Ṭāʾī.

Ayyūb ibn Kaysān, Abū Bakr al-Sakhtiyānī; Kaysān is Abū Tamīmah, the client of ʿAnazah.

Dāwūd ibn Abī Hind.

Dīnār ibn al-ʿAdhāfir, the client of Banū Qushayr.

And Dīnār, a client of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir ibn Kurayz.

Khālid al-Ḥadhdhāʾ ibn Mihrān, Abū Mubārak.

“ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī said: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Mahdī said: ‘The Yazīd al-Fārisī from whom ʿAwf narrated is Yazīd ibn Hurmuz.’ He said: ‘Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd said, “Ask him from whom he heard it.”’ He said: ‘So I asked him, and he said, “We have always heard it.”’

Al-Faḍl ibn Ziyād related to me: Aḥmad related to us: ʿAbd al-Ṣamad related to us: Sallām ibn Miskīn related to us: ʿAwn ibn Rabīʿah related to us from Yazīd al-Fārisī, who was a scribe for Ibn ʿAbbās.” Aḥmad said: “He is Yazīd ibn—”

Hurmuz.

Abū Thaʿlabah al-Khushanī is Jurhum ibn Nāshim.

Isrāʾīl, from Abū Fazārah, Rāshid ibn Kaysān.

Abū ʿImrān al-Jawnī is ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Ḥabīb ibn Khunays.

Abū al-Jawzāʾ is Aws ibn ʿAbd Allāh.

Abū Ḥabrah is Shīḥah ibn ʿAbd Allāh.

Abū Rajāʾ al-ʿUṭāridī is ʿImrān ibn Taym; they have also said Milḥān.

Abū al-Malīḥ al-Hudhalī is ʿĀmir ibn Usāmah ibn ʿUmayr al-Hudhalī.

Nubayḥ al-ʿAnzī, Abū ʿAmr.

Abū al-ʿAsharāʾ is Usāmah ibn Mālik ibn Qaḥṭam.

And they have said: ʿUṭārid ibn Barz.

And they have said: Sayyār, or Ibn Sayyār ibn Bilz.

And Abū Tamīmah is Ṭarīf ibn Mujālid.

Abū Bakrah is Nufayʿ ibn al-Ḥārith. (284 a) Nāfiʿ, Nufayʿ, and Ziyād are the sons of Sumayyah, and they are brothers.

ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ. The name of Abū Rabāḥ is Aslam, the client of Ḥabībah bint Maysarah ibn [Abī] Khaytham.

Abū Isḥāq, from al-Tamīmī, whose name is Arbadah.

Abū Ḥurayz, the judge of Sijistān, is ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥusayn.

Abū Bulj is named Jāriyah ibn Bulj; he narrated to us from al-Ḥārith.

Abū Bulj, from whom Hushaym narrated, is Yaḥyā ibn Abī Sulaym.

Abū al-Muhallab is named ʿAmr ibn Muʿāwiyah.

The name of Abū Ramthah is Rifāʿah ibn Yathribī.

And Abū Tamīm al-Jayshānī is ʿĪsā ibn Hānī.

The perfume-seller Abū al-Haytham is named ʿAdī.

Abū Murrah, the client of ʿAqīl ibn Abī Ṭālib, is Yazīd.

Abū Hayyāj al-Asadī is Ḥayyān ibn Ḥuṣayn.

Abū al-ʿAdbas is Manīʿ ibn Sulaymān.

Abū Ibrāhīm is ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb.

ʿAmr ibn Murrah, Abū ʿAbd Allāh.

Ḥabīb ibn Ṣahbān, Abū Mālik.

Nāfiʿ ibn Jubayr, Abū Muḥammad.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Aswad, Abū Ḥafṣ.

Abū ʿĀṣim is Rifāʿah ibn Shaddād.

Abū ʿĀṣim is ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr ibn Qatādah al-Laythī.

Abū ʿĀṣim is al-Qāsim ibn Abī Bazzah.

Abū Saʿīd is ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mughāffal.

ʿĀʾidh ibn ʿAmr, Abū Hubayrah.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Aʿraj, Abū Dāwūd.

ʿUmayr ibn Saʿīd, Abū Yaḥyā.

Usayd ibn Ḥuḍayr, Abū Yaḥyā.

Ḥabīb ibn Abī Thābit; the name of Abū Thābit is Hind.

Abū Bakr ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yazīd, the brother of al-Aswad ibn Yazīd.

Abū Baḥr Maymūn ibn Siyāh.

Abū Baḥr al-Aḥnaf ibn Qays.

Abū Baḥr al-Furāt ibn Aḥnaf, Abū Baḥr al-Hilālī.

Ismāʿīl ibn Sharwas, Abū al-Miqdām al-Ṣanʿānī.

Sudayr ibn Ḥukaym al-Ṣayrafī, a Kufan.

Ghālib ibn Khaṭṭāf al-Qaṭṭān.

Ḥabbah ibn Juwayn al-ʿArabī.

Muḥammad ibn Qays al-Asadī: Abū Nuʿaym related to us from him, and al-Thawrī and Ibn ʿUyaynah narrated from him. He is trustworthy.

“And Muḥammad ibn Qays al-Murhibī, who is weak.”

“And Muḥammad ibn Qays the storyteller, the storyteller of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, is Medinan and trustworthy.”

And Muḥammad ibn Qays al-Zayyāt is Medinan; Abū ʿĀmir and ʿUthmān ibn ʿUmar.

And Muḥammad ibn Qays ibn Makhramah, from whom Ibn Jurayj narrated.

Muslim ibn Maḥbūq, from whom al-Thawrī narrated. Shuʿbah gave him the teknonym Abū Maymūnah.

Muslim ibn Kaysān al-Aʿwar, Abū al-Haytham.

ʿAmmār, the man of the reeds.

Abū Yaḥyā Ziyād, from whom ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib and Ḥuṣayn narrated (284 b), is named Ziyād al-Makkī.

Abū Māwiyah is ʿAntarah, from whom al-Shaybānī narrated. The Abū Māwiyah from whom Dāwūd ibn Abī Hind narrated is not this man; he is another.

Abū al-ʿUbaydayn is Muʿāwiyah ibn Saburah.

Abū Isḥāq ʿAmr ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Sabīʿī lived until the governorship of Yūsuf ibn ʿUmar. His sons took him to al-Ḥīrah when he had grown old, and he defecated on the mount during the journey.

“Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah said: ‘Abū Isḥāq related to us in his mosque—there was no third person with us.’ Some people of knowledge said: ‘He had become confused; they only stopped taking from him when he was with Ibn ʿUyaynah because of his confusion.’” Yūsuf ibn ʿUmar was the one who crucified Zayd ibn ʿAlī, and he did not— Abū Isḥāq heard nothing from ʿAlqamah, though he saw Zayd ibn ʿAlī.

Ibn al-Madīnī said: “The name of Abū al-Miḥjal al-Rudaynī is Murrah, and the name of Abū ʿUrūbah—Abū Saʿīd ibn Abī ʿUrūbah—is Mihrān.”

Abū Hānīʾ al-Khawlānī is Ḥumayd ibn Hānīʾ.

Umm al-Dardāʾ the elder is Khayrah, and Umm al-Dardāʾ the younger is Hujaymah. Yaḥyā ibn Maʿīn related a contrary account from Abū Misʿhar.

Ibrāhīm al-Taymī, Abū Asmāʾ.

And Abū al-Wāziʿ Zuhayr ibn Mālik, from whom Sufyān and Isrāʾīl narrated.

And Abū al-Wāziʿ al-Baṣrī al-Rāsibī, Jābir ibn ʿAmr.

Abū al-Kunūd, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAwf.

Abū ʿAṭiyyah al-Wādiʿī, Mālik ibn ʿĀmir, a Hamdānī.

Abū Iyās, ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbdah, a Bajalī.

Abū Thābit, Ayman ibn Thābit.

Marthad ibn Ghifārah, Abū al-Muthannā, a Kufan.

Sufyān and Misʿar narrated from ʿImrān ibn Muslim ibn Riyāḥ, a Kufan.

And ʿImrān ibn Muslim al-Juʿfī, a Kufan, the companion of Suwayd ibn Ghafalah.

And ʿImrān ibn Muslim al-Qaṣīr, a Basran, from whom Muʿādh ibn Muʿādh narrated.

And Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Sulamī was the maternal half-brother of Manṣūr ibn al-Muʿtamir.

Ḥuṣayn ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī.

Abū ʿAmr Manṣūr ibn Zādhān, a Wasitian, trustworthy, very trustworthy. Hushaym and Shuʿbah narrated from him, but al-Thawrī did not hear from him.

I heard (285 a) Abū al-Ṣalt al-Harawī, from Ibn al-Mubārak, say: “I asked Hushaym, ‘Who is Manṣūr ibn Zādhān?’ He said: ‘He used to pray the dawn prayer and speak to no one until the sun rose. When the sun rose, he would stand and pray until around midday, then enter his home. Then he would go out for the noon prayer and pray between noon and afternoon. Then he would pray the afternoon prayer and greet us, saying, “Is anyone ill? Is there a funeral?” If there was, he would go and follow the funeral or visit the sick person. Then he would pray sunset, pray between sunset and nightfall, then pray nightfall and enter his home.’ I asked, ‘How long was this his practice?’ He said, ‘Forty years.’”

I asked, “From what did he earn his living?” He said, “He had—”

Al-ʿAbbās ibn Muḥammad related to me, saying: Yaḥyā ibn Abī Bukayr related to us:

Shuʿbah related to us from Hishām ibn Ḥassān, who said: “I prayed beside Manṣūr ibn Zādhān between sunset and nightfall, and he recited the Qurʾān; in the second unit of prayer he reached Sūrat al-Naḥl.”

Al-Ḥajjāj related to us, saying: Ḥammād ibn Salamah related to us from Thābit, from Anas:

“The Prophet ﷺ—said to Saʿd ibn Muʿādh: ‘O Abū ʿAmr, why is Thābit ibn Qays—’”

“Thābit ibn Qays is not seen.” Ḥammād said, reporting from Zayd ibn Aslam: “A man came and called out, asking permission for Abū ʿĪsā to enter upon the Commander of the Faithful. ʿUmar said, ‘Who is Abū ʿĪsā?’ Al-Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah said, ‘I am.’

“ʿUmar said, ‘Does ʿĪsā have a father?’ So he gave him the teknonym Abū ʿAbd Allāh.”

And he said: “Ḥammād related to us from Saʿīd ibn Juhmān, from Safīnah, Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān.”

He said: “ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī said: ‘Abū Kurayz al-Zubaydī ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Jumhān.’”

ʿAlī was asked, “What is the name of Abū Rāfiʿ the goldsmith?” He said, “I do not know a name for him.”

He said: “ʿUmar ibn Ḥafṣ related to us, saying: My father related to us, saying: al-Aʿmash related to us:

“Abū al-Safar related to us from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr, who said: ‘The Messenger of God ﷺ—passed by me while I was repairing a reed shelter of ours. He said, “What are you doing?” I said, “I am repairing a reed shelter of ours, O Messenger of God.” He said, “The matter will come sooner than that.”’”

Abū Nuʿaym related to us, saying: Shuʿbah related to us, saying: “I heard Abū al-Safar say: ‘I saw a gold ring on al-Barāʾ.’”

The name of Abū al-Safar is Saʿīd ibn Aḥmad. In the speech of the people of Yemen, when they say Aḥmad, they say Yuḥmad; they turn the alif into a yāʾ. His wife was Umm Ḥayyah, the mother of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Safar. Yūnus ibn Abī Isḥāq and Mālik ibn Mughawwil narrated from Abū al-Safar; Sufyān and Shuʿbah narrated from his son ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Safar. He was from Hamdān, Thawr, and they were a family of learning.

Abū al-Nuʿmān related to us, saying: Ḥammād ibn Zayd related to us from Ayyūb and Hishām and Yaḥyā ibn ʿAtīq, from Muḥammad, that “Shurayḥ would not declare himself free of an illness until we showed it to him.” Yaḥyā said: “He would say, ‘I have recovered from such-and-such,’ so put this among (288 b) those things; he would not declare himself free of it until we showed him that defect.”

Abū Yūsuf said: “This is a sound chain of transmission, the soundest there can be, and a ruling that may not be opposed. This is Shurayḥ the judge, son of Sharaḥbīl—they also say Sharāḥīl—and these are one and the same.”

And Shurayḥ ibn Hānīʾ.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us, saying: Zakariyyā related to us from ʿĀmir, who said: “Shurayḥ ibn Hānīʾ related to me, saying: ʿĀʾishah related to me that the Messenger of God ﷺ—said: ‘Whoever loves meeting God, mighty and exalted, God, mighty and exalted, loves meeting him; and whoever dislikes meeting God, mighty and exalted, God, mighty and exalted, dislikes meeting him. And death is before meeting God, mighty and exalted.’”

And Shurayḥ ibn Arṭāʾah, who was trustworthy.

And Shurayḥ ibn al-Nuʿmān al-Ṣāʾidī, from whom Abū Isḥāq narrated, from ʿAlī: “The Messenger of God ﷺ—commanded us to inspect the eye and the ear.”

Qabīṣah related to us, saying: Sufyān related to us from ʿImrān ibn Muslim al-Juʿfī, from Suwayd ibn Ghafalah, who said: “There is nothing more aggravating to him than seeking refuge”—meaning Iblīs, may God curse him.

Qabīṣah related to us, saying: Sufyān related to us, saying: Yazīd ibn Abī Ziyād related to us from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Laylā, from al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib, who said: “When the Messenger of God ﷺ”

When he ﷺ—said the takbīr, he raised his hands until his thumbs could be seen near his ears. Bakr ibn Khalaf and Muḥammad ibn al-Muthannā related to us; they said: Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar related to us, from Shuʿbah, from Yazīd ibn Abī Ziyād, who said: I heard Ibn Abī Laylā say: I heard al-Barāʾ relating to a group of people among whom was Kaʿb ibn ʿUjrah. He said: I saw the Messenger of God ﷺ—raise his hands when he began the prayer.

Abū ʿUmar al-Numarī related to us; he said: Khālid related to us; he said: Yazīd ibn Abī Ziyād informed us, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Laylā, from al-Barāʾ, that when the Messenger of God ﷺ—stood for prayer, he said the takbīr and raised his hands. Saʿīd related to us; he said: Khālid related to us with the same chain of transmission, with a similar report. He said: I saw the Messenger of God ﷺ—say the takbīr and raise his hands when he stood for prayer.

He also said: Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh related to us, from Yazīd ibn Abī Ziyād, from ʿAdī ibn Thābit, from al-Barāʾ, with a similar report.

He also said: ʿAlī ibn al-Mundhir related to us, from Ibn Fuḍayl, from Yazīd, with a similar report. (289a) He said: I saw the Messenger of God ﷺ—raise his hands when he stood for prayer, until they were at his shoulders, and his thumbs were level with his ears.

Saʿīd related to us; he said: Hushaym related to us; he said: Yazīd ibn Abī Ziyād related to us. He said:

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Laylā related to us, from al-Barāʾ, who said: I saw the Messenger of God ﷺ—say the takbīr and raise his hands when he began the prayer, until they nearly reached the level of his ears.

Ibn Abī Shaybah related to us, from Hushaym, with the same chain of transmission and a similar report.

Al-Ḥumaydī, Ibn Quʿnūb, and Saʿīd related to us; they said: Sufyān related to us. He said:

Yazīd ibn Abī Ziyād related to us—in Mecca—from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Laylā, from al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib, who said: I saw the Messenger of God ﷺ—raise his hands when he began the prayer. Sufyān said: When I came to Kūfah, I heard him narrate, and he added to it, “Then he did not do so again.” I suspected that they had prompted him to say this. At that time in Mecca, his memory was better than it was on the day I saw him in Kūfah. They told me that his memory had changed. This is al-Ḥumaydī’s wording.

I saw in Yaḥyā ibn Maʿīn’s book the following: “The report from al-Barāʾ that the Prophet ﷺ—used to raise his hands does not have a sound chain of transmission.” I suspect that the person who reported this did not accurately record Yaḥyā’s words, “because although people criticized Yazīd ibn Abī Ziyād for his decline late in life, he remained upright and reliable, even if he was not like Manṣūr and al-Ḥakam and al-Aʿmash. His statements are accepted; he is reliable.”

ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Mūsā related to us, from Isrāʾīl, from Abū Isḥāq, from Yarīm Abū al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Asʿad al-Hamdānī—Zuhayr ibn Muʿāwiyah said: “He was the imam of their mosque”—who said: I saw Qays ibn Saʿd while we were at Maskan. I saw him urinate and wipe over a pair of his boots made of Azīdaj, as though I could still see the mark of his fingers on the boots. Then he went forward and led us in prayer; we were ten thousand.

Zuhayr, from Abū Isḥāq—who said, “He was the imam of their mosque”—said:

I was with Qays ibn Saʿd ibn ʿUbādah in his contingent. They numbered ten thousand, and ʿAlī had sent him. He had been a servant of the Messenger of God ﷺ.

Abū Isḥāq said: Abū Maysarah was with me, and Abū Maysarah asked, “Did you see him, Abū al-ʿAlāʾ?” He said: “Yes.”

Ibrāhīm, the client of Banū Hāshim, is Ibrāhīm Quʿays.

Aḥmad ibn Manīʿ related to me, from ʿUbaydah, from al-ʿAlāʾ, from Ibrāhīm, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, from the Prophet ﷺ. In my view, he is objectionable in his reports.

Abū Ḥafṣ al-Abbār said: When I first began seeking hadith, I saw the scholars reject his reports. Likewise, with Ḥammād ibn Yaḥyā al-Abaḥḥ, I used to see these hadith scholars avoid the reports of both men and conceal their reports.

I likewise saw them regard Abū Yaḥyā al-Ḥummānī as burdensome and exercise caution regarding his reports.

“As for al-Ḥummānī, Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal held a poor opinion of him. Abū ʿAbd Allāh is scrupulous in his position, and Aḥmad’s position differs from that of others.”

As for Mujālid and al-Ajlaḥ, people criticized them both, though Mujālid was in a better state than al-Ajlaḥ.

As for Badr Abū Shujāʿ, I used to see the middle-aged hadith scholars exercise caution regarding his reports.

Ibn ʿUthmān related to us; he said: ʿAbd Allāh related to us; he said: ʿAnbasah ibn Saʿīd informed us. He was a reliable Kūfan with sound reports. He had been judge over al-Rayy. Ḥakkām ibn Sālim al-Rāzī related from him; “Ḥakkām is reliable.”

Abū Nuʿaym and Qabīṣah related to us; they said: Sufyān related to us, from Abū Rabāḥ, a Kūfan, from Abū ʿAmr al-Shaybānī, whose name was Saʿd ibn Iyās.

ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Mūsā related to us, from Abū Kibrān al-Ḥasan ibn ʿUqbah al-Murādī, who is reliable, from al-Shaʿbī, who said: If you hear something from me, write it down, even on a wall.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us, from al-Rabīʿ ibn Abī Ṣāliḥ, an Aslamī Kūfan, who is reliable.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us; he said: Abū Sinān Saʿīd ibn Sinān al-Shaybānī related to us. He said:

I heard ʿAntarah say: I heard ʿAlī say to the people, “Keep me away from this black crowd.” As for this younger one, he is reliable. The elder one—Abū Nuʿaym related to us from him, from Sufyān, from Abū Sinān— Ḍirār ibn Murrah, “who is among the best and is reliable.”

Abū Nuʿaym and ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Mūsā related to us; they said: ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Siyāh related to us; he said: Ḥabīb ibn Abī Thābit related to me, from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: I find nothing in this world that I regret except that I did not fight the transgressing faction. His son, Yazīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, relates from al-Aʿmash and is reliable.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us; he said: Sufyān related to us, from ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib. [A transmission variant.]

Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb related to us; he said: Shuʿbah related to us, from ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib. ʿAṭāʾ is reliable, and his hadith is authoritative. The reports narrated from him by Sufyān, Shuʿbah, and Ḥammād ibn Salamah are from their early period of hearing. ʿAṭāʾ’s condition changed later; therefore the reports of Jarīr, Ibn Fuḍayl, and their contemporaries are weak.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us; he said: Sufyān related to us, from ʿAlī ibn al-Aqmar, from “Abū Ḥudhayfah, whose name is Yazīd ibn Ṣuhaybah.” ʿAlī and Abū Ḥudhayfah are both reliable.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us; he said: Isrāʾīl related to us, from “Abū Isḥāq, who said: Abū Ḥudhayfah was Salamah ibn Ṣuhaybah.” That is how he said it. He was one of the companions of ʿAbd Allāh.

He said: He was with us on a journey and continued praying two rakʿahs until we returned.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us; he said: Sufyān related to us, from ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Rufayʿ. Ibn ʿUyaynah and Jarīr related from him. He had visited ʿĀʾishah.

Al-Ḥumaydī related to us; he said: Ḥafṣ ibn Ghiyāth related to us; he said: al-Shaybānī related to me, from ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Rufayʿ, who said: I saw Abū Maḥdhūrah arrive after someone else had given the call to prayer. He gave the call to prayer and then the iqāmah. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz is counted among the Meccans; he is reliable, and his hadith stands as authoritative proof.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us, from Sufyān, from Abū Isḥāq al-Hamdānī, then al-Sabīʿī, who is ʿAmr ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUbayd.

He also said: Sufyān related to us, from Manṣūr ibn al-Muʿtamir al-Sulamī.

Sufyān said: From Abū Muḥammad Sulaymān ibn Mihrān al-Aʿmash.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us; he said: Sufyān related to us, from Salamah ibn Kuhayl Abū Yaḥyā al-Ḥaḍramī.

He said: Sufyān related to us, from Ḥabīb ibn Abī Thābit Abū Yaḥyā.

Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid said, from Ḥabīb ibn Kindī—who is Ḥabīb ibn Abī Thābit, a reliable Kūfan.

He also said: Sufyān related to us, from ʿAmr ibn Murrah, a reliable Jamalī, except that he was a Murjiʾ. Aḥmad said: “He is vile.”

Sufyān said, from “Zubayd ibn al-Ḥārith al-Yāmī, reliable, reliable, among the best, except that he used to lean toward Shīʿism.”

He also said: Sufyān related to us, from Abū Qays, who is acceptable.

He also said: Sufyān related to us, from Wāṣil al-Aḥdab (290b), who is reliable.

He also said: Sufyān related to us, from ʿImrān ibn Muslim al-Juʿfī, a reliable Kūfan.

He also said: Sufyān related to us, from “Ziyād ibn al-Fayyāḍ, reliable, reliable, a Kūfan.”

He also said: Sufyān related to us, from “Qays ibn Muslim, reliable, reliable, a Kūfan Murjiʾ.”

He also said: Sufyān related to us, from ʿAlī ibn al-Aqmar. Manṣūr and Shuʿbah related from him; he is a reliable Kūfan.

Qabīṣah related to me; he said: Sufyān related to us, from Ashʿath ibn Abī al-Shaʿthāʾ, from al-Aswad ibn Hilāl, from Thaʿlabah ibn Zahdam al-Ḥanẓalī, who said: A group of us from Banū Tamīm came to the Prophet ﷺ. He said: We reached him as he was saying, “The giver’s hand is the upper one. Begin with those you support: your mother and father, your sister and brother, then the next closest, and the next.” A man from the Anṣār said: “Messenger of God, these are the Banū Thaʿlabah ibn Yarbuʿ, who killed so-and-so in the pre-Islamic period.” The Prophet ﷺ—called out, “Indeed, no soul bears the guilt of another.”

Aḥmad ibn al-Khalīl related to me; he said: Aḥmad ibn ʿImrān related to us; he said: I heard— Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh say: Abū Isḥāq al-Sabīʿī used to say: “Go to Simāk ibn Ḥarb and ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿUmayr, for they are early authorities.”

Abū Nuʿaym, Abū ʿĀṣim, and Qabīṣah related to us; they said: Sufyān related to us, from ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿUmayr, a Laḫmī, a memorizer and fluent narrator. Shuʿbah and Misʿar related from him. He is reliable.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us; he said: Sufyān related to us, from “al-Aswad ibn Qays, a reliable Kūfan.”

He said: Sufyān related to us, from “al-Zubayr ibn ʿAdī, a reliable Kūfan.”

He also said: Sufyān related to us, from ʿAmmār al-Duhnī, from Abū Muʿāwiyah al-Bajalī, the sāburī cloth seller, a Kūfan who is acceptable. His son Muʿāwiyah is also acceptable.

He also said: Sufyān related to us, from Nuṣayr ibn Dhuʿlūq Abū Ṭuʿmah, a reliable Kūfan.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us; he said: Sufyān related to us, from Usayd ibn Ismāʿīl, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Karīmah, the client of Banū Hāshim.

He also said: Sufyān related to us, from Simāk ibn Ḥarb. Simāk related from Ḥanash al-Kinānī, who is Ibn al-Muʿtamir.

He also said: Sufyān related to us, from his father, Saʿīd ibn Masrūq ibn Ḥamzah al-Thawrī. Masrūq fought at the Battle of the Camel alongside ʿAlī ﵁. (291a)

He also said: Sufyān related to us, from ʿĀṣim ibn Abī al-Najūd—Abū al-Najūd was Bahdalah—from Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh Abū Maryam, a Kūfan.

He also said: Sufyān related to us, from “Abū Ḥuṣayn ʿUthmān ibn ʿĀṣim al-Asadī, distinguished, reliable, reliable, a Kūfan.”

Aḥmad ibn al-Khalīl related to us; he said: Yaḥyā ibn Ayyūb informed me; he said: Abū Bakr related to us; he said: I heard Abū Ḥuṣayn mention that he and ʿĀṣim ibn Abī al-Najūd were one year apart in age.

He also said: Sufyān related to us, from “Abū Sinān Ḍirār ibn Murrah al-Shaybānī—the elder one—reliable, reliable, a Kūfan.”

He also said: Sufyān related to us, from Sālim al-Afṭas, a Murjiʾ and client of Banū Umayyah, whose origin was Kūfan.

He also said: Sufyān related to us, from Abū Miskīn, who is acceptable.

He also said: Sufyān related to us, from Ibrāhīm ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā, who is acceptable.

He also said: Sufyān related to us, from Ḥukaym ibn al-Daylam, who is a reliable Kūfan and acceptable.

He also said: Sufyān related to us, from ʿAlqamah al-ʿAmī, who is acceptable.

He also said: Sufyān related to us, from ʿUthmān ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mawhab. Qabīṣah related it in the same way, from ʿUthmān ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mawhab, who said: I prayed over funeral biers with Abū Hurayrah.

Abū ʿUmar related to us, from Shuʿbah, who said: ʿUthmān ibn ʿAbd Allāh informed me:

I saw Abū Hurayrah pray over funeral biers.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us; he said: ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān ibn Mawhab related to us; he said: I heard Mūsā ibn Ṭalḥah mention, from Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī, that a Bedouin approached the Prophet ﷺ—at a pulpit of his and said: “Tell me what will bring me nearer to Paradise and keep me farther from Hell.” He replied: “Worship God, Mighty and Exalted, and associate nothing with Him; establish the prayer, pay the alms, and maintain ties of kinship.”

Abū Nuʿaym related to us; he said: Sufyān related to us, from Maʿbad ibn Khālid, who said: I heard Ḥārithah ibn Wahb say: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ. He is reliable, a Kūfan.

He also said: Sufyān related to us, from Shabīb ibn Gharqadah. Ibn ʿUyaynah related from him. He is a reliable Kūfan.

He also said: Sufyān related to us, from Thābit Abū al-Miqdām al-Ḥaddād. Al-Ḥakam, al-Aʿmash, and Shuʿbah related from him. He is a reliable Kūfan. (291b)

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Muḥārib ibn Dithār, who had served as judge of Kūfa. He is reliable, a Kūfan.

And he said: Sufyān ibn Ṣilah related to us, from Suḥaym, a Successor, a reliable Kūfan.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from ʿAyyāsh al-ʿĀmirī ibn Sulaym, a reliable Kūfan.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Hishām Abū Kulayb, a reliable Kūfan, among their righteous and best men.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from al-Rukayn ibn al-Rabīʿ al-Fazārī, a reliable Kūfan.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Aslam al-Munaqirī, a distinguished, reliable man.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Zayd ibn Jubayr, a reliable Kūfan.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Hilāl ibn Khabbāb. He used to reside in al-Madāʾin. He was reliable, except that he changed; age had its effect on him.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Ṣāliḥ al-Thawrī, who is acceptable.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from ʿĪsā ibn Abī ʿAzza, a reliable Kūfan.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Ṭāriq ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, a reliable Kūfan.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Ibn Abjar, who was among the reliable and best people of Kūfa.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Mūsā al-Juhanī, a reliable Kūfan. Mūsā is the son of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, and his teknonym is Abū ʿAbd Allāh.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Muḥammad ibn Sūqah, a Kūfan among the best and most reliable people of Kūfa.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Mūsā ibn Abī ʿĀʾishah, a reliable Kūfan.

Al-Ḥumaydī related to us: Sufyān said: “I went to see Mūsā. Whenever I saw him, I would think of what al-Zuhrī said: ‘If you had seen Ṭāwūs, you would have known that he does not lie.’” Sufyān mentioned him and praised him highly.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Sufyān related to us, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĪsā ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Laylā.

Al-Ḥumaydī related to us: Sufyān said: “ʿAbd Allāh was considered superior to his uncle, Ibn Abī Laylā.”

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Sufyān related to us, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī al-Safar. Abū al-Safar was Saʿīd ibn Aḥmad; Abū Isḥāq and al-Aʿmash related from him. He and his son are both reliable.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Ziyād Abū ʿUthmān al-Muṣaffir, the client of Muṣʿab, He was a reliable Kūfan.

And he said: (292a) Sufyān related to us, from Firās, who was the son of the son of Yaḥyā Khārifī. He was a Meccan, and there is some weakness in his hadith; he is reliable.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿUbayd Allāh, a reliable Nakhaʿī, one of the best people of Kūfa.

Muḥammad ibn Bashshār Bundār related to us: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to us: Sufyān related to us, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿUmar, from Ghālib ibn ʿAbbād, from Qays ibn Ḥabtar al-Nahshalī.

Abū Aḥmad related from Sufyān, from Ghālib, from Qays ibn Ḥabtar al-Nahshalī. Abū Aḥmad said: “A Dārī, from the household of Qays ibn Ḥabtar.”

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Sufyān related to us, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAmr al-Fuqaymī, from Ḥamzah ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qurashī. Wakīʿ says: “From Abū Ḥamzah, from his father”; Abū Nuʿaym’s version is more accurate here.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Ghālib Abū al-Hudhayl, a reliable man. Misʿar and Shuʿbah related from him.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from ʿUbayd al-Mukattib ibn Mihrān, a reliable man.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Ibrāhīm ibn Muhājir, a man of distinction and nobility; his hadith is somewhat weak; he is a Kūfan.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Abū al-Haytham, a reliable Kūfan, counted among the jurists.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Ḥuṣayn ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, a precise and reliable Kūfan. He used to reside in Wāsiṭ.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from al-ʿAlāʾ ibn al-Musayyib, a reliable Kūfan.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Ḥammād ibn Abī Sulaymān. Abū Sulaymān’s name was Muslim, and his clientage was to the Ashʿarīs. I heard Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh say that Sharīk said:

“I used to pass him by and go to someone else.”

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Sufyān related to us, from Mughīrah ibn Miqsam Abū Hishām, a reliable man.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Bayān, a reliable man.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Abū Isḥāq Sulaymān ibn Khāqān al-Shaybānī, a reliable man. He mentioned that he had gone out on the military expedition, while Ibrāhīm is not mentioned.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Muṭarrif ibn Ṭarīf, a reliable man.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib, whose teknonym was Abū Zayd.

Abū Yūsuf said: ʿUthmān related it to me, from Jarīr: His hadith, when related from him by Sufyān and Shuʿbah, stands as proof.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Sufyān related to us, from Yazīd ibn Abī Ziyād, that ʿAbd Allāh, the client of Banū Hāshim, was related from by Shuʿbah and Sharīk. He was a leading advocate among the people of Kūfa (292b), and he was reliable, except that he grew old and his memory changed.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Sufyān related to us, from ʿAbd al-Aʿlā ibn ʿĀmir, a noble elder, whose hadith is somewhat weak; he is a reliable Kūfan.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid Abū ʿAbd Allāh. Abū Khālid’s name was Hurmuz. He was unlettered, yet a retentive and reliable transmitter.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Abū Ḥayyān Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Taymī. The leading scholars of Kūfa related from him, and he is a reliable and trustworthy man. He was a Kūfan and related from Ayyūb ibn Kaysān.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from ʿUmar ibn Qays al-Mallāʾī, a reliable Kūfan.

He said: Sufyān related to us, from Ibn Abī Laylā, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān the judge: a jurist, reliable, upright, though there is some criticism of his hadith; his hadith is somewhat weak.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Abī Sulaymān al-ʿArzamī, a reliable, precise, and learned man.

Sufyān related to us, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Aṣbahānī, who is acceptable.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from ʿUmar ibn Qays al-Māṣir, a reliable man.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Mukhawwil ibn Rāshid, a reliable man.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Muʿāwiyah ibn Isḥāq, who is acceptable.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Abū Ṣakhrah Jāmiʿ ibn Shaddād, a precise and reliable man. Misʿar and Shuʿbah related from him.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Mujammiʿ ibn Ṣamghān al-Taymī, a reliable man.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from al-Miqdām ibn Shurayḥ ibn Hāniʾ ibn Yazīd. Misʿar and Shuʿbah related from him; he is a reliable Kūfan.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Bukayr ibn ʿAṭāʾ al-Laythī. Sufyān and Shuʿbah related from him; he is reliable.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from ʿĀṣim ibn Kulayb al-Jarmī. Shuʿbah, Zāʾidah, and the leading scholars related from him. He is a reliable Kūfan.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Sufyān related to us, from Salm ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Nakhaʿī, from Abū Zurʿah, from Abū Hurayrah, who said: “The Messenger of God ﷺ disliked a horse having shikāl markings.” Shuʿbah made an error in its chain of transmission: Ādam related to us: Shuʿbah related to us, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd al-Nakhaʿī, from Abū Zurʿah, from Abū Hurayrah. The established version is what Sufyān said.

Qabīṣah related to us: Sufyān related to us, from al-Maʿmar ibn Qays al-Murādī, a venerable elder, a reliable Kūfan.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Sufyān related to us, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Sāʾib (293a), an old and reliable elder; al-Aʿmash related from him.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Ādam ibn ʿAlī. The leading Kūfan scholars related from him; he is a reliable Kūfan.

Sufyān related to us, from Muḥammad ibn Qays al-Asadī, judge under ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. He is a precise and reliable man; Abū Nuʿaym related to us from him.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Ismāʿīl al-Asadī, from whom the leading Kūfan scholars related. He is a reliable Kūfan.

Abū ʿĀṣim related to us, from Sufyān, from Muḥammad ibn Qays al-Murhibī. His hadith is somewhat weak; Sharīk and others related from him.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Sufyān related to us, from Manṣūr ibn Ḥayyān, a reliable man, from whom Yazīd ibn Hārūn and Marwān related; he was a Kūfan.

Qabīṣah related to us: Sufyān related to us, from Maysarah al-Nahdī, a reliable Kūfan.

And Abū Nuʿaym said: Sufyān related to us, from Furāt ibn [Abī] ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Qazzāz.

And Sufyān said: from ʿĀmir ibn Shaqīq ibn Jamrah.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Abū Nahīk, whose name was al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad. Misʿar and Jarīr also related from him; he was a Kūfan.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Marzūq, who is acceptable.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Wāqid, who is acceptable.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from ʿUmārah ibn al-Qaʿqāʿ, a reliable man.

Qabīṣah related to us: Sufyān related to us, from the woman of al-Rabīʿ, who is acceptable.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Abū al-Jaḥḥāf.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Azhar, from Ibn ʿAwn.

And he said: Sufyān related to us, from Yūnus ibn Khabbāb. Ḥammād ibn Zayd, Mahdī ibn Maymūn, ʿAbbād ibn ʿAbbād, Manṣūr ibn al-Muʿtamir, and Shuʿbah ibn al-Ḥajjāj related from him.
