Ibn Numayr narrated to us, saying: my father narrated to us, from al-Aʿmash, from Ḥabīb ibn Abī Thābit, from Abū al-Bakhtarī, who said, “What excellent men Abū Bakr and ʿUmar are ﵄. Yet I find in ʿAlī ﵁—a striving that I do not find in those two.” We counted that as an elevation on his part.

ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Mūsā narrated to us, from Sayyār, from al-Aʿmash, from Sālim ibn Abī al-Jaʿd, from Sāriyah ibn ʿAbd Allāh, who said: ʿAbd Allāh said, “Whoever washes his head with marshmallow while in a state of major ritual impurity has fulfilled the requirement; let him wash the rest of his body.”

ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd Allāh narrated to us, saying: Yaḥyā ibn Ḥammād narrated to us, from Abū ʿAwānah, from Sulaymān ibn Mihrān al-Aʿmash, from Sālim ibn Abī al-Jaʿd, from Thābit ibn Quṭbah al-Thaqafī, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, who said, “If a man washes his head with marshmallow while in a state of major ritual impurity, that suffices, provided that he then washes the rest of his body.”

ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd Allāh narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī said: Abū ʿAwānah and Manṣūr ibn Abī al-Aswad (330b) narrated to us, from al-Aʿmash, from Sālim ibn Abī al-Jaʿd, from Thābit ibn Quṭbah, from ʿAbd Allāh.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān said, “Manṣūr told me, ‘Abū ʿAwānah and I heard it.’”

ʿAlī said, “The hadith is Sufyān’s hadith.”

ʿAlī narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān said: Sufyān narrated to us, from al-Aʿmash, from Sālim ibn Abī al-Jaʿd, from Sāriyah, from ʿAbd Allāh, who said, “If a person in a state of major ritual impurity washes his head with marshmallow, he has done enough—or he said, ‘It suffices for him.’”

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Maslamah narrated to us, saying: ʿĪsā ibn Yūnus narrated to us, from al-Aʿmash, from Abū Sufyān, who said, “We used to visit Jābir, who was staying in retreat for six months.”

Abū Nuʿaym and Qabīṣah narrated to us, both saying: Sufyān narrated to us, from [Wāṣil ibn Ḥayyān al-Aḥdab, a trustworthy Kūfī], and ʿImrān ibn Muslim ibn Riyāḥ; and from ʿAmmār ibn Abī Muʿāwiyah al-Bajalī al-Duhnī; and Nusayr ibn Dhiʿlūq, whose teknonym was Abū Ṭaʿmah.

Qabīṣah related to us: Sufyān ibn Saʿīd ibn Masrūq ibn Ḥamzah al-Thawrī—of Thawr of Tamīm—related from Abū Sinān Saʿīd ibn Sinān al-Shaybānī.

And from Sufyān, from Yaḥyā, from Hāniʾ ibn ʿUrwah, a reliable Kūfan.

Ibn Abī al-Sarī related to me, from ʿAbd al-Razzāq, from Sufyān, from Abū Fuzārah al-ʿAbsī.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Sufyān related to us, from ʿAyyāsh al-ʿĀmirī, from Muslim ibn Nudhayr al-Saʿdī.

Qabīṣah related to us: Sufyān related to us, from ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Abī Bashīr, who said: Fuḍālah ibn Abī Umayyah—who is Abū Mubārak ibn Fuḍālah—related to us.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Sufyān related to us, from Hishām, Abū Kulayb, a Kūfan, and al-Rukayn ibn al-Rabīʿ ibn ʿUsaylah, a Kūfan.

“Tawbah al-ʿAnbarī is their client.”

And Aslam al-Munaqqirī.

And Zayd ibn Jubayr.

And Ajlaḥ ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Kindī.

And Sālim al-Afṭas, a Murjiʾī.

And Sālim ibn Abī Ḥafṣah, a Shīʿī.

And Ḥasan ibn ʿUbayd Allāh, a Nakhaʿī.

And Ḥasan ibn ʿAmr, a Fuqaymī.

Qabīṣah related to us: Sufyān related to us, from Abū Hāshim Mughīrah—who is Mughīrah ibn Miqsam al-Ḍabbī.

And Muḥall ibn Muḥriz al-Ḍabbī.

And al-Mughīrah ibn Ziyād, Abū Hāshim.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Sufyān related to us, from Salamah ibn Tammām, Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Shaqrī.

“Qabīṣah related to us: Sufyān related to us, from Abū Yazīd Waqāʾ ibn Iyās al-Asadī, a Kūfan of acceptable standing; and from Sufyān, from Ziyād Abū ʿUthmān al-Muṣaffir, a Kūfan client of Muṣʿab.

Abū Jamrah al-Ḍabʿī, Naṣr ibn ʿImrān, a Baṣran.

Abū Ḥamzah Maymūn ibn Kathīr, a Meccan.

Abū Hāshim al-Rummānī, whose name is Yaḥyā ibn Dīnār.

Shawdhāb, Abū Muʿādh, a Kūfan.

Abū Hārūn al-Ghanawī, Ibrāhīm ibn al-ʿAlāʾ, a Baṣran.

Ghālib ibn al-Hudhayl, Abū al-Hudhayl.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Sufyān said: Abū Ṣakhrah Jāmiʿ ibn Shaddād—al-Aʿmash also related from him—a reliable Kūfan, related to us.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Muḥammad ibn Abī Ayyūb, Abū ʿĀṣim—who is reliable—related to us. He said: Ibrāhīm said to me, “Do you know the laws of inheritance?” I replied, “Yes.” He said, “Do you know how to distribute the shares?” I replied, “Yes.” He said, “Do you know the rules of bequests?” I replied, “Yes.” He said, “What do you think of a man who bequeathed one-third of his estate to one man, one-fourth of his estate to another man, and half his estate to someone else?”

I did not know, so I said, “That is not permissible; only one-third of his estate is permissible for him to bequeath.” He said:

“What if the heirs approve it?” I replied, “I do not know.” He said, “Shall I teach you?” I replied, “Yes.”

He said, “Consider an amount of property that has a half, a third, and a quarter.” I said, “That would be twelve.” He said:

“Yes. You take half of it, six; a third of it, four; and a quarter of it, three. That makes thirteen shares.

“Divide the estate into thirteen shares. Give the beneficiary of the half what corresponds to six shares, the beneficiary of the third what corresponds to four shares, and the beneficiary of the quarter what corresponds to three shares. Is that how it works?” I replied, “Yes.”

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: ʿĪsā ibn al-Musayyab related to us. He was from Bajīlah; Asad ibn ʿAbd Allāh appointed him judge in Khurāsān. He is weak.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Umayy al-Ṣayrafī—who is reliable—related to us, from Ibrāhīm, the associate of al-Qaṣab. He said: Ibrāhīm appointed al-Ḥakam and me as executors of his will. He said, “When four people have gathered, do not wait for a fifth before carrying me in the funeral procession.”

“Abū Nuʿaym related to us: ʿĪsā ibn Ṭahmān, a reliable Kūfan, related to us”. He said:

I heard Anas ibn Mālik say: The Prophet of God ﷺ said, “Whoever deliberately lies about me, let him take his seat in the Fire.” And, “The Messenger of God ﷺ served bread and meat at the wedding feast for Zaynab daughter of Jaḥsh.”

“Abū Nuʿaym related to us [folio 331b]: Yūsuf ibn Ṣuhayb, who is reliable, related to us”. Ḥabīb ibn Yasār related to me, from Zayd ibn Arqam, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said, “Whoever does not trim his moustache is not one of us.”

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Muḥammad ibn Qays al-Asadī—who is reliable—related to us, from Muslim ibn Ṣubayḥ, Abū al-Ḍuḥā, who said: I heard Jarīr ibn ʿAbd Allāh addressing the people. I heard him say: The Messenger of God ﷺ said, “Whoever establishes a good practice in Islam will have a reward like that of everyone who acts upon it, without anything being deducted from their rewards. And whoever establishes a bad practice in Islam will bear a burden like that of everyone who acts upon it, without anything being deducted from their burdens.”

Muḥammad ibn Qays al-Murhibī is weak. He is the one who relates the ḥadīth of Ibn Abī Mulaykah, from Ibn ʿAbbās, about the two girls who were stripped.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Maʿmar ibn Yaḥyā ibn Sām, who is reliable, related to us. Al-Aʿmash related from his father, Yaḥyā ibn Sām.

The sons of Abū al-Jaʿd are Sālim, ʿUbayd Allāh, and Ziyād, sons of Abū al-Jaʿd. Ibrāhīm ibn Abī al-Jaʿd, from whom Ḥakkām al-Rāzī relates, has nothing to do with these men.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rajāʾ al-Ghudānī al-Baṣrī related to us, and I heard Abū al-Walīd. al-Ṭayālisī say: “Abū Ḥamzah is not in the mosque”—meaning the congregational mosque—“of the three who desire him.”

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rajāʾ related to us: Kāmil ibn al-ʿAlāʾ, who is reliable, related to us.

ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Mūsā related to us, from Usāmah ibn Zayd al-Laythī, who is reliable and Medinan. Yaḥyā made a mistake concerning him and refrained from relating his ḥadīths, but he is not as Yaḥyā supposed.

Misʿar related from Thawr al-Hamdānī, from Ibrāhīm al-Taymī, who is reliable.

Thuwair ibn Abī Fākhitah is weak.

Shuʿbah related from Manṣūr al-Ashall, who is al-Ghudānī, a reliable Sunnī.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: ʿUbādah ibn Muslim al-Fazārī, who is reliable, related to us.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Ismāʿīl ibn Ibrāhīm ibn Muhājir related to us. Neither of them is strong, nor are they abandoned; they are between those two ranks.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us, from Isrāʾīl, from Ḥakīm ibn Jubayr ibn Ḥakīm. Ḥukaym is disparaged; it is said that he is a Rāfiḍī, among the extremists in rejectionism.

I was told on the authority of Yaḥyā ibn Ādam that Sufyān said, “Does Shuʿbah relate from Ḥakīm ibn Jubayr?” He was told, “He intended to relate from him.” He said, “If he had, I would have related from him.” He said: Then Sufyān said, “He has indeed related to us— Zubayd.” This is a far-fetched account. If the ḥadīth of Ḥakīm ibn Jubayr, from Abū Khālid, from Abū ʿĪsā—who is Yaḥyā ibn Rāfiʿ—were [the report in question, it says]: “I was told that when the Lord, mighty and exalted, established Himself upon the Throne, an angel fell prostrate and has remained prostrate until the Day of Resurrection. He will not raise his head until the Hour comes. When the Day of Resurrection comes, he will raise his head and say, ‘Glory be to You! I have not worshipped You as You deserve to be worshipped, except that I have not associated anything with You, nor taken any protector besides You.’”

Ibn Numayr related to us, from his father, from Nahshal—and he declared him very weak.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Ashras, the client of Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ, who is reliable, related to us.

Abū Rabīʿ related to us, from Abū ʿAwānah, from Hārūn ibn Saʿd ibn al-ʿĀliyah, concerning the seven.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Sufyān related to us, from Ḥuraysh the scribe, from his father, from— ʿAlī ﵁ assigned inheritances to two men killed at Ṣiffīn, one of whom was the other’s son.

And Sufyān related to us, from Ziyād ibn Ismāʿīl, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbbād al-Makhzūmī, from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Quraysh polytheists came to the Messenger of God ﷺ disputing with him about predestination. Then the verse was revealed: “Indeed, We created everything according to a measure” (54:49).

Ziyād was a client of one of the clients of Mecca, weak, and his ḥadīth is not a source of satisfaction.

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbbād is a Makhzūmī, among the finest of them, a Meccan known for his retention, sound judgment, mastery, and nobility.

Manṣūr related from Layth ibn Abī Ruqayyah, a Syrian scribe who used to be with ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz.

Abū Sufyān, the companion of al-Aʿmash, is Ṭalḥah ibn Nāfiʿ al-Makkī.

Abū Sufyān Ṭarīf al-Saʿdī was related from by Sharīk, Abū Muʿāwiyah, and Marwān.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Sufyān related to us, from Abū Bakr ibn Abī al-Jahm. Abū al-Jahm’s name was Ṣukhayr, and Abū Bakr heard from Fāṭimah daughter of Qays.

Ibn Numayr related to us, from Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh, from al-Aʿmash, from Sālim ibn Abī al-Jaʿd, from Thawbān. Sālim did not hear from Thawbān; this is only tadlīs.

Al-Ḥumaydī related to us: Sufyān related to us, from Ibrāhīm ibn Maymūn, a reliable Kūfan client of the family of Samurah.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us [folio 332b]: Saʿīd ibn Yazīd al-Aḥmasī, a reliable Kūfan, related to us.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Qays, a Kūfan of acceptable standing, related to us.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Maslamah ibn Nawfal ibn ʿUrwah ibn al-Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah related to us. Abū al-Mughīrah al-Thaqafī said to me: My father told me that he was with his father at Minā when he heard a crier calling, “O people, hold back the riding animals, for the foot is fettered and the hand is suspended.” I said to my father, “Who is that?” He said, “ʿUmar.” Maslamah is a reliable Kūfan.

ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Mūsā related to us: Abū al-Minhal Naṣr ibn Aws al-Ṭāʾī—a reliable Kūfan—related to us, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Zayd. I asked Abū Hurayrah about the offspring of the hyena. He said:

“That is the farʿul, a ewe among sheep.”

“ʿUbayd Allāh related to us: Abū Kibrān al-Murādī—a reliable Kūfan—related to us. He said: I heard al-Shaʿbī say, ‘When you hear anything from me, write it down, even on a wall.’”

Qabīṣah related to us: Sufyān related to us, from al-Mughīrah, from al-Haytham ibn Badr, on the terms of the people of al-Rayy.

Abū Nuʿaym and Qabīṣah related to us; they said: Sufyān related to us, from Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid, from— Abū al-Ashhab: The Prophet ﷺ saw a garment on ʿUmar.

Ibn Idrīs heard from Abū al-Ashhab, a Kūfan shaykh whose name was Jaʿfar ibn al-Ḥārith al-Nakhaʿī; he is weak.

Ḥanẓalah ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-ʿĀṣī was related from by Wakīʿ and Abū Nuʿaym; he is weak.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Ṣaghdī, the seller of al-ḥulqān, of acceptable standing, related to us.

And Ṣaghdī al-Baṣrī, from whom al-Zaman and others related, has weak ḥadīth.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Sufyān related to us, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān ibn Mawhib, a reliable Kūfan, and his brother ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān, who is reliable.

“Abū Nuʿaym related to us: ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān ibn Mawhib related to us”.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us: Sufyān related to us, from Maʿbad ibn Khālid al-Jadalī, from Yaḥyā ibn Hāniʾ al-Murādī, from Shabīb ibn Gharqadah al-ʿAjalī, from ʿAyyāsh al-ʿĀmirī, from ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Abī Bashīr, from Hishām Abū Kulayb, from ʿĪsā ibn Abī ʿAzzah, from Ṭāriq ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, and from [folio 333a] Ibn— Abjar, from Mūsā al-Juhanī, from Muḥammad ibn Sūqah, from Mūsā ibn Abī ʿĀʾishah, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĪsā ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Laylā, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī al-Safar, from Ziyād Abū ʿUthmān al-Muṣaffir, the client of Muṣʿab, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿUbayd Allāh al-Nakhaʿī, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAmr al-Fuqaymī, from Ghālib Abū al-Hudhayl, from ʿUbayd the copyist, from Abū al-Haytham, the associate of al-Qaṣab, whose name was ʿAmmār, from al-ʿAlāʾ ibn al-Musayyib, from Sulaymān ibn Khāqān, Abū Isḥāq al-Shaybānī, from Muṭarrif ibn Ṭarīf, from ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib, from Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid, from Abū Ḥayyān Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Taymī, “from ʿAmr ibn Qays”, from ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Abī Sulaymān, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Aṣbahānī, from Mukhawwal ibn Rāshid, from Muʿāwiyah ibn Isḥāq, from ʿAwn ibn Abī Juḥayfah, from Bukayr ibn ʿAṭāʾ al-Laythī, and from al-Miqdām ibn Shurayḥ ibn Hāniʾ al-Nakhaʿī—and all of these are reliable Kūfans—and ʿAbd al-Wāḥid, a client of Balʿanbar, and Ismāʿīl ibn Ibrāhīm, a client of Banū Asad. I asked him about it, and he informed me of this.

“Al-Faḍl related to me: I heard Abū ʿAbd Allāh say: ‘The mursal reports of Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib are the soundest of the mursal reports; the mursal reports of Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī are acceptable. Among mursal reports, none are weaker than the mursal reports of al-Ḥasan and ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī— Rabbāḥ, for the two of them accept reports from everyone.”

Yaʿqūb said: ʿAlī disagreed with Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal on this.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us; he said: Saʿīd ibn Ḥassān al-Makhzūmī related to us. He was a trustworthy Meccan.

Saʿīd related to us; he said: Sufyān related to us, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿAlqama. He was a trustworthy Meccan, a Kinānī and one of their notables.

Ibn Jurayj transmitted from Sulaymān, the client of Umm ʿAlī, from Mujāhid. There is no harm in him. Ibn Jurayj and Muḥammad ibn Muslim al-Ṭāʾifī transmitted from him. He is the one from whom ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Abī Sulaymān transmits, mentioning him by his teknonym but not by name: he gives him the teknonym Abū ʿAbd Allāh. He was one of the shaykhs of Mecca; there is no harm in him.

“Yaʿlā ibn Ḥakīm and Yaʿlā ibn Muslim are Meccans, sound in their ḥadīth.”

Ibn ʿUthmān related to us; he said: ʿAbd Allāh related to us; he said: ʿAmr ibn Abī Sufyān al-Jumaḥī related to us. He and Ḥanẓala ibn Abī Sufyān are both trustworthy (333b).

Abū Nuʿaym related to us; he said: Sufyān related to us, from ʿAmr ibn Abī Sufyān al-Jumaḥī, who said: Ibn al-Zubayr was brought a thief whose hand had been cut off. Abān ibn ʿUthmān said:

“Cauterize it.” He replied, “You are indeed compassionate.” Abān said, “That is the Sunna.”

Abū Ghassān Mālik ibn Ismāʿīl related to us—trustworthy, trustworthy, though inclined toward Shiʿism. He said: Masʿūd ibn Saʿd al-Juʿfī related to us. He was a trustworthy and reliable Kūfan; ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī transmitted from him.

Muḥammad ibn Fuḍayl related to us, from Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī al-Juʿfī, a trustworthy Kūfan, from al-Rabīʿ ibn Saʿd. Wakīʿ transmitted from him.

Marwān was trustworthy and Kūfan.

Ibn Bashshār related to us; he said: Abū Aḥmad al-Zubayrī related to us; he said: Sufyān related to us, from Manṣūr: “I never wrote down a ḥadīth; I used to memorize.”

Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us; he said: Sufyān related to us; he said: Abū Isrāʾīl related to us. He was a Kūfan, trustworthy, who settled in Baṣra.

ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Rufayʿ was a Kūfan who settled in Mecca, and he was trustworthy.

Qabīṣa related to us; he said: Sufyān related to us, from al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥuṣayn al-Azdī. He was a Shiʿite, above Sālim al-Afṭas, who was Sālim ibn ʿAjlān, the client of Muḥammad ibn Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam: “a defiant Murjiʾ.”

Abū Nuʿaym related to us; he said: Sufyān related to us, from Sālim ibn Abī Ḥafṣa, who was a Shiʿite.

He said: Yaḥyā ibn ʿUbayd al-Bahrānī was a trustworthy Kūfan.

Qabīṣa related to us; he said: Sufyān related to us, from Ādam ibn Sulaymān, who was Abū Yaḥyā ibn Ādam, and [reading uncertain]. Yaʿqūb.

Qabīṣa and Muḥammad ibn Kathīr related to us, from Sufyān, from ʿAmr ibn Murra, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith, from Ṭulayq ibn Qays, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ used to supplicate.

Ibn Fuḍayl related to us; he said: Wakīʿ related to us; he said: Sufyān related to us; he said: ʿAmr ibn Murra related to us, during the governorship of Khālid al-Qasrī, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith al-Muktab, from Ṭulayq ibn Qays al-Ḥanafī, from Ibn ʿAbbās—and from the Prophet ﷺ—who said this in his supplication.

They say that Ṭulayq ibn Qays was the brother of Abū Ṣāliḥ al-Ḥanafī, who transmitted from his brother Ṭulayq ibn Qays.

More than one of our companions related to us, from Marwān, from Abū Ṣāliḥ ibn Masʿūd al-Jadalī, from Abū Juḥayfa, who was trustworthy.

He said: Abū Nuʿaym transmitted from Abū al-Mughīra, who was Yazīd ibn Ṭahmān. Abū Nuʿaym related to us from him, and he was trustworthy (334a).

Abū Nuʿaym related to us; he said: Quṭrī al-Khashshāb related to us.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us; he said: Yazīd ibn Mardānaba, the client of ʿAmr ibn Ḥurayth, related to us. He was trustworthy, and he was the maternal grandfather of the children of al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad al-Kūfī.

Yaʿqūb related to us; he said: Abū Nuʿaym and ʿUbayd Allāh related to us, from Saʿīd ibn ʿUbayd al-Ṭāʾī, one of the trustworthy men, a Kūfan.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us; he said: Saʿīd ibn Ṣāliḥ al-Asadī related to us. He was trustworthy.

ʿUbayd Allāh related to us, from Saʿīd ibn ʿUbayd, from ʿĀfiya ibn ʿUbayd, who said: I saw Anas.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us; he said: Muḥammad ibn al-Jaʿd, a shaykh who belonged to Banū al-Waṣṣāb, related to us; he said: I asked al-Shaʿbī about the dust of the goldsmiths. He replied: “It is gharar [uncertainty].”

And he was trustworthy.

Abū Nuʿaym related to us; he said: Qays ibn Sulaym al-ʿAnbarī related to us; he said: ʿUmayr ibn Saʿīd related to me. Qays and ʿUmayr were both trustworthy.

And Yaḥyā ibn [Abī] al-Haytham al-ʿAṭṭār, who was trustworthy.

Qulaywa: the leading scholars of Kūfa, al-Aʿmash and his peers, transmitted from him; he was trustworthy.

Ibn ʿUthmān related to us; he said: ʿAbd Allāh related to us; he said: Abū ʿAwāna related to us, from Sulaymān al-Shaybānī, who said: Asīr ibn ʿUmayr related to us and said:

“When there had been as much killing among the people as there had been, I heard that Abū Masʿūd had set out, so I caught up with him at al-Saylaḥīn. There he was in a garden, having performed ablutions. I went up to him and sat him down. He praised God, Mighty and Majestic, and extolled Him. Then I said: ‘You had two companions to whom you could turn for refuge: Ḥudhayfa and Abū Mūsā. I heard of your journey and followed you, and I am glad I did. I adjure you by God, Mighty and Majestic, and by Islam: if you have heard anything from the Messenger of God ﷺ about these civil wars, tell it to me; and if you have heard nothing, then exert your judgment on my behalf.’ He replied: ‘You must fear God, Mighty and Majestic, and adhere to the main body of Muḥammad’s community ﷺ. For God, Mighty and Majestic, would never unite his community ﷺ upon error. Be patient until a righteous person finds rest, or a wicked person is rid of.’”

“Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr related to us; Abū Muʿāwiya related to us; he said: Abū Isḥāq al-Shaybānī related to us, from Yusayr ibn ʿAmr, from Abū Masʿūd al-Anṣārī, who said: I said to him,

‘Give me your counsel’—when he was about to depart for Medina. He replied: ‘I counsel you to fear God, Mighty and Majestic, and to adhere to the community, for God, Mighty and Majestic, would never unite Muḥammad’s community—’”

God bless him and grant him peace, upon error. Be patient until (334b) a righteous person finds rest, or a wicked person is rid of.’”

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr related to us; he said: Khalaf ibn Khalīfa related to us, from ʿArīf al-Shaybānī, from Yusayr ibn ʿAmr, who said:

“Abū Masʿūd set out in this direction, and I went with him. When we reached al-Saylaḥīn, he dismounted, and I dismounted with him. When I saw that he was alone, I went over to him and said: ‘Abū Masʿūd, there were three Companions of Muḥammad ﷺ among us. Ḥudhayfa has died, Abū Mūsā has gone to Syria, and you have set out in this direction. You see what has happened with this campaign.’

“He said to me: ‘Yusayr, I am sincerely advising you: adhere to the community, for God, Mighty and Majestic, would never unite Muḥammad’s community ﷺ upon error, until a righteous person finds rest, or a wicked person is rid of.’”

The Book of Knowledge and History is complete. Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds. May God bless Muḥammad the Prophet and his family, and grant them abundant peace. God is sufficient for us, and He is the best disposer of affairs. How excellent a Patron and how excellent a Helper.

Texts quoted from the missing volume of the Book of Knowledge and History (the annals)

Texts quoted by the sources from the first volume of the Book of Knowledge and History

1—Chronology arranged by the years, beginning with the earliest

The extent of the earth:

Abū al-Qāsim Ismāʿīl ibn Aḥmad ibn ʿUmar ibn Abī al-Ashʿath, the ḥadīth scholar, informed us—I read to him in Baghdad. He said: Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn Hibat Allāh ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Manṣūr ibn al-Lālakāʾī informed us. He said: Abū al-Ḥusayn Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Faḍl al-Mutawthī al-Qaṭṭān informed us. He said: Abū Muḥammad ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar ibn Durustawayh the grammarian informed us. He said: Abū Yūsuf Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān ibn Jawwān al-Fasawī informed us: I was told, from al-Aṣmaʿī, from al-Nimr ibn Hilāl, from Qatāda, from Abū al-Khald, who said:

“The earth is twenty-four thousand parasangs; one thousand parasangs belong to the Arabs, and the rest to all other people.”

The age of the world:

Abū al-Qāsim Ismāʿīl ibn Aḥmad al-Samarqandī informed us. He said: Muḥammad ibn Hibat Allāh ibn al-Ḥasan informed us. He said: Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Faḍl informed us. He said: Abū Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar informed us. Yaʿqūb related to us; Qabīṣa related to us; Sufyān related to us, from al-Aʿmash, from Kaʿb, who said: “The world is six thousand years old.” That is how he said it, but al-Aʿmash in fact transmits it from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Kaʿb.

The number of days in which He created it:

Abū al-Qāsim Ismāʿīl ibn Aḥmad al-Samarqandī informed us. Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn Hibat Allāh ibn al-Ḥasan informed us. Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl informed us. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed us. Yaʿqūb related to us; Ibn Numayr related to us; Wakīʿ related to us; al-Aʿmash related to us, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Kaʿb, who said:

“The creation of the heavens and the earth began on Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday; then He assigned a thousand years to each day.”

The number of years between the prophets:

Abū al-Qāsim al-Samarqandī informed us. Muḥammad ibn Hibat Allāh ibn al-Ḥusayn informed us. Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn informed us. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed us. Yaʿqūb related to us; our companions related to us, from Yūnus ibn Bukayr, from Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, who said:

“Between Adam and Noah were one thousand two hundred years; between Noah and Abraham, one thousand one hundred and forty-two years; between Abraham and Moses, five hundred and sixty-five years; between Moses and David, five hundred and sixty-nine years; between David and Jesus, one thousand three hundred and fifty-six years; and between Jesus and Muḥammad ﷺ six hundred years. That makes five thousand four hundred and thirty-two years.

“This reckoning is correct.

“That makes five thousand four hundred and twenty-six years.

“This total is not correct.”

The Prophetic Biography

The Beginning of the Hijrī Era:

Abū al-Qāsim ibn al-Samarqandī informed us; Muḥammad ibn Hibat Allāh informed us; Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl informed us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed us; Yaʿqūb narrated to us; Abū Ṭāhir and Yūnus narrated to us, saying: Ibn Wahb narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from Ibn Shihāb, who said:

The dating began on the day the Prophet ﷺ came to Medina as an emigrant. Ibn Wahb said: I asked Mālik, “When did dating begin?” He said: “From the Prophet’s arrival.”

The Meccan Period

The Year of the Prophet’s Birth

... Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān narrated to us: Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir narrated to us: ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Abī Thābit narrated to us: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān ibn Abī Sulaymān al-Nawfalī narrated to me, from his father, from Muḥammad ibn Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim, who said:

The Messenger of God ﷺ was born in the Year of the Elephant. ʿUkāẓ took place fifteen years after it, and the House was built twenty-five years after the Elephant. The Messenger of God ﷺ was commissioned as a prophet forty years after the Elephant.

Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir narrated to us: Muḥammad ibn Fulayḥ narrated to us, from Mūsā ibn ʿUqba, from Ibn Shihāb, who said: God sent Muḥammad as a messenger fifteen years after the Kaʿba was built, and between the Prophet’s mission and the People of the Elephant there were seventy years.

Abū Isḥāq Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir said: “This is an error. None of our scholars doubts that the Messenger of God ﷺ was born in the Year of the Elephant and was commissioned forty years after the Elephant.”

Ibn Lahīʿa said, from Khālid ibn Abī ʿImrān, from Ḥanash, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: “Your Prophet ﷺ was born on Monday, commissioned on Monday, departed from Mecca on Monday, conquered Mecca on Monday, and Sūrat al-Māʾida was revealed on Monday; he died on Monday.” Al-Fasawī recorded it.

ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib’s Care for the Prophet ﷺ:

I read to Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad al-Maqdisī, the ascetic. He said: Abū Isḥāq Ibrāhīm ibn ʿUthmān informed you, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Bāqī, from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥusayn. Abū Isḥāq said: And Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Ṣāliḥ informed me. He said: Abū Bakr Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥusayn informed us. Both said: Abū ʿAlī ibn Shādhān informed us. He said: Ibn Durustawayh informed us. He said: Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān informed us. Abū al-Ḥasan Mahdī ibn ʿĪsā narrated to us. He said: Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Wāsiṭī informed us, from Dāwūd ibn Abī Hind, from al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Kandīr ibn Saʿīd, from his father, who said:

I performed the pilgrimage in the pre-Islamic period. While I was circumambulating the House, a man said:

“Return my mount to me—Muḥammad!

“May my Lord return him and grant me a favor through him.”

I said, “Who is that?” He replied, “ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib ibn Hāshim. He sent his son after some camels of his that had strayed. Whenever he sent him to fetch something, he came back with it.”

He said: “I stayed there until he came back with the camels. Then he said, ‘My son, I was so worried about you that I shall never again let you out of my sight.’”

They said: Umm Ayman used to tell the following story: “I was caring for the Messenger of God ﷺ. One day I was distracted, and suddenly ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib was standing over me, saying, ‘Baraka!’ I said, ‘At your service.’ He said, ‘Do you know where I found my son?’ I said,

‘I do not know.’ He said, ‘I found him with some boys near the lote tree. Do not neglect my son, for the People of the Book claim that my son is the prophet of this community, and I do not feel safe about him around them.’ Whenever he ate, he would say, ‘Bring my son to me,’ and they would bring him.”

The Building of the Kaʿba:

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Aṣbagh ibn Faraj informed me. He said: Ibn Wahb informed me, from Yūnus, from Ibn Shihāb, who said:

When the Messenger of God ﷺ reached maturity, a woman fumigated the Kaʿba. A spark flew from her censer onto the Kaʿba’s coverings, and they caught fire. They demolished it, and when they had rebuilt it as far as the place of the Corner, Quraysh disputed over the Corner: which tribe would have the honor of raising it? They said, “Come, let us accept the judgment of the first person who appears to us.” The Messenger of God ﷺ appeared to them. He was a boy wearing a striped mantle. They accepted his judgment, and he ordered that the Corner be placed in a cloth. Then he summoned the chief of each tribe and gave him one side of the cloth. He himself then climbed up, and they raised the Corner to him; he was the one who set it in place. He had not grown beyond ...132 until they called him “the Trustworthy.” Thereafter, whenever they slaughtered a camel, they would seek him out so that he might bless it for them.

His Marriage to Khadīja:

Al-Bayhaqī said: Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl al-Qaṭṭān informed us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed us; Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān narrated to us: Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir narrated to me: ʿUmar ibn Abī Bakr al-Muʾamlī narrated to me: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī ʿUbayd ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir narrated to me, from his father, from Miqsam ibn Abī al-Qāsim, the freedman of ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Nawfal, that ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith told him that whenever ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir heard people talking about the Messenger of God’s marriage to Khadīja ﷺ and making much of it, he would say: “I know more than anyone about his marriage to her. I was his age-mate, and I was his companion and close friend. One day I went out with the Messenger of God ﷺ. When we reached al-Ḥazwara, we passed by Khadīja’s sister, who was sitting on some hides to sell them. She called me, so I turned toward her, while the Messenger of God ﷺ stopped for me. She said, ‘Does your companion have any interest in marrying Khadīja?’ ʿAmmār said: I went back to him and told him. He said, ‘Yes, by my life.’ I told her what the Messenger of God ﷺ had said. She said, ‘Come to us tomorrow morning.’ We went to them in the morning and found that they had slaughtered a cow, dressed Khadīja’s father in a robe, and dyed his beard. I spoke to her brother, and he spoke to his father—who had been given wine to drink—and mentioned to him the Messenger of God ﷺ and his standing, then asked him to marry him to Khadīja. He married him to Khadīja, and they prepared food from the cow, which we ate. Her father slept, then woke up sober and said:

“What is this robe, this dye, and this food?” His daughter, the one who had spoken to ʿAmmār, said to him, “This is a robe given to you by Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh, your son-in-law, and a cow he gave you as a gift. We slaughtered it when he married Khadīja.” He denied having married her to him and went out shouting until he reached the Black Stone. The Banū Hāshim came out with the Messenger of God ﷺ and went to him to speak with him. He said, “Where is your companion, whom you claim I married to Khadīja?” The Messenger of God ﷺ came forward. When he saw him, he said, “If I married her to him, then let it be so; and if I did not, then I have now married her to him.”

Al-Ṣiddīq’s Conversion to Islam:

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said in his History: Al-Ḥumaydī narrated to us; Sufyān narrated to us; Hishām narrated to us, from his father: Abū Bakr became Muslim while he had forty thousand [dirhams], and he spent them in God’s cause. He freed seven people, all of whom were being tortured for God’s sake: Bilāl, ʿĀmir ibn Fuhayra, Nadhīra, al-Nahdiyya and her daughter, the slave girl of the Banū al-Muʾammal, and Umm ʿUbays.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī narrated to us; Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna narrated to us, from Mālik ibn Mughawwal, from a man, who said: Ibn ʿAbbās was asked, “Who was the first to believe?”

He replied, “Abū Bakr. Have you not heard Ḥassān’s words?”

“When you recall a sorrow from a trusted friend,

remember your brother Abū Bakr for what he did, the best of creation, the truest and most just,

after the Prophet, and the foremost to bear the burden.

The second in succession, whose deeds are praised,

and the first among them to affirm the messengers.

He lived with honor, following God’s command,

following the command of his companion, who had gone before and never turned back.”

ʿUthmān’s Emigration to Abyssinia:

Yaʿqūb al-Fasawī said in his History: Al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAẓīm al-ʿAnbarī narrated to me: Bashshār ibn Mūsā al-Khaffāf narrated to me: al-Ḥasan ibn Ziyād al-Barjamī—the imam of the mosque of Muḥammad ibn Wāsiʿ—narrated to us: Qatāda narrated to us, who said:

“The first to emigrate to God, exalted is He, with his family was ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān. I heard al-Naḍr ibn Anas say: I heard Abū Ḥamza—meaning Anas ibn Mālik—say: ʿUthmān set out for Abyssinia with Ruqayya, the daughter of the Messenger of God ﷺ. News of them was delayed. Then a Qurayshī woman arrived and said, ‘Muḥammad, I saw your son-in-law with his wife.’ He said, ‘In what condition did you see them?’ She replied, ‘I saw him carrying his wife on a donkey of this kind133 and driving it.’ The Messenger of God ﷺ said, ‘May God accompany them. ʿUthmān is the first to emigrate with his family after Lot.’”

Khadīja’s Death:

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Abū Ṣāliḥ narrated to us; al-Layth narrated to us; ʿUqayl narrated to me, from Ibn Shihāb, who said that ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr said:

Khadīja had died before the prayer was prescribed.

Then he related, by another chain, from al-Zuhrī, who said:

Khadīja died in Mecca before the Messenger of God ﷺ departed for Medina, and before the prayer was prescribed.

Naming Those Present at the Second ʿAqaba:

Abū al-Qāsim ibn al-Samarqandī informed us; Abū Bakr ibn al-Ṭabarī informed us; Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl informed us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed us; Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān narrated to us in Naming Those Present at the ʿAqaba on the Second Occasion:

ʿAmr ibn Khālid, Ḥassān ibn ʿAbd Allāh, and ʿUthmān ibn Ṣāliḥ, from Ibn Lahīʿa, from Abū al-Aswad—namely, Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān—from ʿUrwa, who said:

Among the Banū al-Ḥārith ibn al-Khazraj: Bashīr ibn Saʿd.

The Medinan Period

Naming Those Who Were Present at Badr:

I heard Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb say: ʿAlī was present at Badr when he was twenty years old, and was present at the Conquest when he was twenty-eight years old.

... Yaʿqūb narrated to us: ʿAmr ibn Khālid, Ḥassān, and ʿUthmān narrated to us, from Ibn Lahīʿa, from Abū al-Aswad, from ʿUrwa, who said: Among the Banū al-Ḥārith ibn Fihr who were present at Badr was Abū ʿUbayda ibn al-Jarrāḥ.

Abū al-Qāsim ibn al-Samarqandī informed us; Abū Bakr ibn al-Ṭabarī informed us; Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl informed us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed us; Yaʿqūb narrated to us. In Naming Those Who Were Present at Badr, he said: Thābit ibn Aqram ibn Thaʿlaba ibn ʿAdī ibn ʿAjlān.

In Naming Those Who Were Present at Badr, he also said:

Among the Banū Zayd ibn Mālik ibn Thaʿlaba ibn Kaʿb ibn al-Ḥārith ibn al-Khazraj:

Bashīr ibn Saʿd ibn Thaʿlaba ibn Khallās.

The Change of the Qibla:

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related in his History, by way of Ibn Shihāb, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kaʿb, that Kaʿb said: “Al-Barāʾ ibn Maʿrūr was the first living person to face the Kaʿba. When he was near death, before the Messenger of God ﷺ had turned to face it, the Messenger of God was informed of this and ordered him to face the Bayt al-Maqdis, and he obeyed. When he was near death, he instructed his family to turn him toward the Kaʿba.”

The Battle of Uḥud:

There is no disagreement that Uḥud took place in Shawwāl of the year three, except according to the view that the Hijra era began in Muḥarram of the second year of the Hijra, and that the remaining months of the Hijra year, from Rabīʿ al-Awwal to its end, were not counted, as al-Bayhaqī related. This was also Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān’s view. He stated explicitly that Badr took place in the first year, Uḥud in the year two, Badr al-Mawʿid in Shaʿbān of the year three, and the Trench in Shawwāl of the year four.

Al-Bayhaqī said: “This is the well-known account among those who write about the campaigns: they remained at seven hundred fighters.” He said: “The well-known account from al-Zuhrī is that they remained at four hundred fighters.” Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related it in the same way, from Aṣbagh, from Ibn Wahb, from Yūnus, from al-Zuhrī. It is also said of him, through this chain, that they were seven hundred. God knows best.

Al-Ḥudaybiya:

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Ismāʿīl ibn al-Khalīl narrated to us, from ʿAlī ibn Mushir: Hishām ibn ʿUrwa informed me, from his father, who said:

The Messenger of God ﷺ set out for al-Ḥudaybiya in Ramaḍān, and al-Ḥudaybiya took place in Shawwāl.

Muʾta:

... Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān narrated to us. He said:

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥa ibn Mālik ibn Imruʾ al-Qays ibn al-Ḥārith ibn al-Khazraj. Then, from the Banū Imruʾ al-Qays ibn Thaʿlaba ibn Kaʿb ibn al-Khazraj ibn al-Ḥārith ibn al-Khazraj: chief of the Banū al-Ḥārith ibn al-Khazraj; present at Badr, he was killed on the day of Muʾta alongside Jaʿfar ibn Abī Ṭālib.

... Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān narrated to us. Abū Ṣāliḥ and Ibn Bukayr narrated to us, saying: al-Layth narrated to us; Yūnus narrated to me, from Ibn Shihāb: al-Haytham ibn Abī Sinān informed me that he heard Abū Hurayra, while delivering his sermons and mentioning the Messenger of God ﷺ say: “A brother of yours who does not speak obscenely”—by this he meant ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥa—“said:

“Among us is the Messenger of God, reciting His Book,

when from the dawn’s cleft a familiar light shines.

He showed us guidance after our blindness, and our hearts,

through him, are certain that what he said will come to pass.

He spends the night keeping his side from his bed,

when the beds grow heavy for the unbelievers.”

The Conquest of Mecca:

Al-Bayhaqī related, from Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar, from Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān, from al-Ḥasan ibn al-Rabīʿ, from Ibn Idrīs, from Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, from al-Zuhrī, Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn, ʿĀṣim ibn ʿUmar ibn Qatāda, ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Bakr, and others, who said:

The Conquest of Mecca took place with ten days of Ramaḍān remaining in the year eight.

Then al-Bayhaqī related, by way of Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān, from Jābir, from Yaḥyā, from Ṣadaqa, from Ibn Isḥāq, that he said:

The Messenger of God ﷺ set out when ten days of Ramaḍān had passed in the year eight—that is, for the conquest of Mecca.

The shaykh, the traditionist, Abū Bakr Aḥmad ibn ʿAlī ibn Thābit al-Baghdādī, dictated to us, saying: Abū al-Ḥusayn Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl read to us, and I heard him say: Abū Muḥammad ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar ibn Durustawayh read to us in the year 346. He said: Abū Yūsuf Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us; Ṣafwān ibn Ṣāliḥ related to me; al-Walīd—I mean Ibn Muslim—related to us. He said: ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd ibn ʿAdī al-Juhanī related to me, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥumayd al-Juhanī. He said: A man from Juhayna named Bishr ibn ʿUrfuṭa ibn al-Khashkhāsh said in a poem of his:

On the morning of the conquest, we were with Muḥammad;

we appeared before the people, a thousand in the vanguard.

We added many more men, and found

no thousand among the people before us who had accepted Islam.

By the favor of the Lord of the Glorious Throne, our Lord

guided us to piety—how excellent His gift!

We fought in al-Baṭḥāʾ, defending Muḥammad,

against companies of men who were more disobedient and more unjust.

When we draw them one day for battle,

they are not sheathed, nor do they fail to draw blood.

The Expedition of Ḥunayn:

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Abū Sufyān related to us; Abū Saʿīd ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ibrāhīm related to us; al-Walīd ibn Muslim related to us. Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Shuʿaythī related to me, from al-Ḥārith ibn [Sulaymān ibn] Badal al-Naṣrī, from a man of his people—who had witnessed that day at Ḥunayn—and ʿAmr ibn Sufyān al-Thaqafī. They said:

The Muslims were routed on the day of Ḥunayn, and none remained with the Messenger of God ﷺ except al-ʿAbbās and Abū Sufyān ibn al-Ḥārith. He said: The Messenger of God ﷺ took up a handful of pebbles and cast them into their faces. He said: We were routed, and it seemed to us that every stone and every tree was a horseman pursuing us.

Al-Thaqafī said: I spurred my horse until I entered Ṭāʾif.

The Number of Expeditions:

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Muḥammad ibn ʿUthmān al-Dimashqī al-Tanūkhī related to us; al-Haytham ibn Ḥumayd related to us; al-Nuʿmān informed me, from Makḥūl, that the Messenger of God ﷺ went on eighteen expeditions and fought in eight of them. The first was Badr, then Uḥud, then the Confederates, then Qurayẓa, then Biʾr Maʿūna, then the expedition against Banū al-Muṣṭaliq of Khuzāʿa, then the expedition of Khaybar, then the expedition to Mecca, then Ḥunayn and Ṭāʾif.

Yaʿqūb said: Salama ibn Shabīb related to us; ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us; Maʿmar informed us, from al-Zuhrī: I heard Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib say, “The Messenger of God ﷺ went on eighteen expeditions.” I heard him say another time, “Twenty-four.” I do not know whether that was a mistake or something he heard afterward.

The Apostasy of al-Aswad al-ʿAnsī:

Among those who included this account was Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān in his History. He said: Zayd ibn al-Mubārak and others related to us; Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan al-Ṣanʿānī related to us; Sulaymān ibn Wahb related to us, from al-Nuʿmān ibn Burzuj, who said:

Al-Aswad al-ʿAnsī came forth. He recounted the story of how he gained control of Ṣanʿāʾ in Yemen, killed Bādhām, the Prophet’s governor, and took his wife, al-Marzubāna, for himself and married her. She loathed him because of what he had done to her people. He said: She sent for Dādhawayh—Bādhām’s deputy—and for Fayrūz, Kharzādh ibn Burzuj, and Jarjast, the two Persians. They conspired to kill al-Aswad. A thousand men guarded his gate. Al-Marzubāna kept giving him wine; whenever he said to her, “Mix it for me,” she gave it to him neat, until he became drunk and went in to lie down on a feather bed. Dādhawayh and his companions went to the wall and wetted it with vinegar. They dug through it with an iron tool until they made an opening. Dādhawayh and Jarjast went in but were afraid to kill him. Fayrūz and Ibn Burzuj entered, and the woman signaled to them that he was on the bed. Fayrūz seized his head, wrung his neck, and broke it; Kharzādh stabbed him with a dagger, split him open, then cut off his head, and they went out.

Al-Bayhaqī included it in al-Dalāʾil through this chain of transmission.

The Messenger’s Illness and Death:

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Aḥmad ibn Yūnus related to us; Abū Maʿshar related to us, from Muḥammad ibn Qays, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ was ill for thirteen days. When he felt some relief, he prayed; when his illness grew heavier, Abū Bakr prayed.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said, from Yaḥyā ibn Bukayr, from al-Layth, that he said: The Messenger of God died on Monday, on the first night of Rabīʿ al-Awwal. He had arrived in Medina at the beginning of the tenth year after his arrival.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related, from ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd ibn Bakkār, from Muḥammad ibn Shuʿayb, and from Ṣafwān, from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Wāḥid—both from al-Awzāʿī—that he said:

The Messenger of God ﷺ died on Monday before midday.

… Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us; Yaḥyā ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bukayr related to us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Lahīʿa related to me, from Khālid ibn Ḥanash, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: Your Prophet ﷺ was born on Monday; he left Mecca on Monday; entered Medina on Monday; Sūrat al-Māʾida was revealed on Monday—“Today I have perfected your religion for you” (5:3); the Corner was raised on Monday; and he died on Monday.

Yaʿqūb said: Sufyān related to us; Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr related to us; Sufyān related to us, from Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from his father, and from Ibn Jurayj, from Abū Jaʿfar:

The Messenger of God died on Monday, and remained that day, that night, and Tuesday until the end of the day.

[This is an unusual report; the well-known position of the majority is what we have stated earlier: he ﷺ died on Monday and was buried on Tuesday night. Among the other unusual reports on this subject is that which was related] by Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān, from ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd ibn Bakkār, from Muḥammad ibn Shuʿayb, from al-Nuʿmān, from Makḥūl, who said:

The Messenger of God was born on Monday, received revelation on Monday, emigrated on Monday, and died on Monday at the age of sixty-two and a half years. He remained unburied for three days, with people coming in to visit him in groups, praying without forming rows, and no one leading them in prayer over him.

Al-Bayhaqī related, from al-Ḥākim, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar, from Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān, from Abū Bakr ibn Abī Shayba: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Idrīs related to us, from Ismāʿīl ibn [Abī] Khālid, from Qays ibn Abī Ḥāzim, from Jarīr ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd al-Bajalī, who said: I was in Yemen, and we met two men from Yemen, Dhū Kilaʿ and Dhū ʿAmr. I began telling them about the Messenger of God. They said to me, “If what you say is true then your companion has been dead for three days.” He said: I set out, and they set out with me. When we were partway along the road, a party of riders from Medina came into view. We asked them, and they said, “The Messenger of God ﷺ has died; Abū Bakr has been appointed as his successor, and the people are in good order.” He said:

They said to me, “Tell your companion that we have come; perhaps we will return, if God, Mighty and Glorious, wills.”

He said: They returned to Yemen. When I arrived, I told Abū Bakr what they had said.

He said, “Why did you not bring them?” Later Dhū ʿAmr said to me, “Jarīr, you have a claim on me, and I shall tell you something. You Arabs will remain in a good state as long as, whenever a ruler dies, you appoint another in his place. But when rule is by the sword, you become kings: you grow angry as kings do and are pleased as kings are”.

His Age:

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related, from Muḥammad ibn al-Muthannā, from Muʿādh ibn Hishām, from his father, from Qatāda, who said:

The Messenger of God ﷺ died at the age of sixty-two.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related, from ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd ibn Bakkār, from Muḥammad ibn Shuʿayb, from al-Nuʿmān ibn al-Mundhir, from Makḥūl, who said:

The Messenger of God ﷺ died at the age of sixty-two and a half.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related in his History, from Saʿīd ibn Abī Maryam, from Nāfiʿ ibn Yazīd, from ʿUmāra ibn Ghaziyya, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān, that his mother Fāṭima, daughter of al-Ḥusayn, told him that ʿĀʾisha used to say: Fāṭima informed me that the Messenger of God ﷺ told her, “There was no prophet after whom another prophet came who did not live half the lifetime of the prophet before him. He told me that Jesus son of Mary lived for one hundred and twenty years, so I can only expect to depart at sixty”.

Names of the Messenger ﷺ

… Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us: Abū Ṣāliḥ ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṣāliḥ related to us; al-Layth related to us; Khālid ibn Yazīd related to me, from Saʿīd ibn Abī Hilāl, from ʿUqba ibn Muslim, from Nāfiʿ ibn Jubayr, that he visited ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān, who said to him, “Can you enumerate the names of the Messenger of God ﷺ which Jubayr used to count?” He said, “Yes. They are six: Muḥammad, Aḥmad, Khātim, Ḥāshir, ʿĀqib, and Māḥ. As for Ḥāshir, he was sent with the Hour, before a severe punishment; ʿĀqib is the one who came last among the prophets; and Māḥ means that through him God effaced the sins of those who followed him”.

His Mothers, Wet Nurses, and Grandmothers:

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us: al-Ḥajjāj ibn Abī Manīʿ related to us; my grandfather related to us, from al-Zubayrī, who said: The mother of the Messenger of God ﷺ who gave birth to him was Āmina, daughter of Wahb ibn ʿAbd Manāf ibn Zuhra ibn Kilāb. Her mother was Barra, daughter of ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā ibn ʿUthmān ibn ʿAbd al-Dār ibn Quṣayy ibn Kilāb ibn Murra. Her mother was Umm Sufyān, daughter of Asad ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā ibn Quṣayy ibn Kilāb ibn Murra. Her mother was Barra, daughter of ʿAwf ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUwayj ibn ʿAdī ibn Kaʿb ibn Luʾayy ibn Ghālib ibn Fihr. Her mother was Qulāba, daughter of al-Ḥārith ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿa, of Banū ʿĀdiya ibn Liḥyān ibn Hudhayl. Her mother was a daughter of Mālik ibn Ghanm, of Banū Liḥyān.

The mother of the Messenger of God ﷺ who nursed him until he grew up was Ḥalīma, daughter of al-Ḥārith ibn Shijna al-Saʿdiyya, of Banū Saʿd ibn Bakr ibn Hawāzin ibn Manṣūr ibn ʿIkrima ibn Khaṣafa ibn Qays ibn ʿAylān ibn Muḍar.

Ḥalīma’s husband was al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā.

Thus the Messenger of God ﷺ grew up among these people.

The Messenger of God ﷺ was also nursed by Thuwayba, the client of Abū Lahab; Abū Lahab’s name was ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā.

The Messenger of God’s grandmother, the mother of his father ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, was:

Fāṭima, daughter of ʿAmr ibn ʿĀʾidh ibn ʿImrān ibn Makhzūm. Her mother was Ṣakhra, daughter of ʿAbd ibn ʿImrān ibn Makhzūm. Her mother was Takhmur, daughter of ʿAbd ibn Quṣayy ibn Kilāb ibn Murra. Her mother was Salmā, daughter of ʿĀmira ibn ʿUmayra, daughter of Wadīʿa ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Fihr. Her mother was a sister of Banū Wāʾila ibn ʿAdwān ibn Qays.

His Wives:

Khadīja:

… Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us: al-Ḥajjāj ibn Abī Manīʿ related to me; my grandfather—ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Ziyād al-Ruṣāfī—related to me, from al-Zuhrī, who said:

The first woman whom the Messenger of God ﷺ married was Khadīja, daughter of Khuwaylid ibn Asad ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā ibn Quṣayy. Her father gave her to him in marriage before the beginning of the prophetic mission.

Before the Messenger of God ﷺ Khadīja had been married to two men. The first was ʿAtīq ibn ʿĀʾidh ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Makhzūm. She bore him a daughter, the mother of Muḥammad ibn Ṣayfī. Then, after ʿAtīq—Yaʿqūb adds: “daughter of Khuwaylid”—and the two say afterward, “ʿAtīq”—Ibn ʿĀʾidh, Abū Hāla al-Tamīmī, married Khadīja. He was of Banū Asad ibn ʿAmr ibn Tamīm. She bore him Hind, daughter of Hind.

ʿĀʾisha:

The Messenger of God ﷺ had been shown her in a dream twice. Yaʿqūb said, and the two say: He said, “She is your wife,” and ʿĀʾisha was at that time a daughter of … Yaʿqūb adds: The Messenger of God ﷺ consummated his marriage with ʿĀʾisha after he arrived in Medina. On the day the Messenger of God consummated the marriage with her, ʿĀʾisha was nine years old.

The traditionist Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: al-Ḥajjāj related to us; Ḥammād related to us, from Hishām ibn ʿUrwa, from his father, from ʿĀʾisha, who said:

The Messenger of God ﷺ married me after Khadīja had died and before he left Mecca, when I was seven—or six—years old. When we arrived in Medina, some women came to me while I was playing on a swing and my hair was combed. They prepared me and made me ready, then brought me to the Messenger of God ﷺ when I was nine years old.

The Kalābiyya and al-Jawniyya:

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related, from Ḥajjāj ibn Abī Manīʿ, from his grandfather, from al-Zuhrī, from ʿUrwa, from ʿĀʾisha: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Sufyān al-Kilābī was the one who suggested her to the Messenger of God ﷺ—I was listening from behind a curtain. He said, “Messenger of God, would you be interested in the sister of Umm Shabīb?” Umm Shabīb was al-Ḍaḥḥāk’s wife.

Through the same chain, al-Zuhrī said: The Messenger of God ﷺ married a woman from Banū ʿAmr ibn Kilāb. He was informed that she had leukoderma, so he divorced her without consummating the marriage.

He said: He married the sister of Banū al-Jawn al-Kindī, who were allies of Banū Fazāra. She sought refuge from him. He said, “You have sought refuge with someone mighty; go to your family.” He divorced her without consummating the marriage.

Māriya and Rayḥāna:

He said: The Messenger of God ﷺ had a concubine called Māriya. She bore him a son whom he named Ibrāhīm. He died after filling the cradle. He also had a bondwoman called Rayḥāna, daughter of Shamʿūn, one of the People of the Book, from Khunāfa, a branch of Banū Qurayẓa. The Messenger of God ﷺ freed her; they claim that she then observed the veil.

His Sons and Daughters:

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us: al-Ḥajjāj related to us; my grandfather related to us, from al-Zuhrī, who said: He married her—I mean Khadīja—in the pre-Islamic period, and her father, Khuwaylid ibn Asad, gave her to him in marriage. She bore the Messenger of God ﷺ al-Qāsim, after whom he was given his kunya al-Ṭāhir, Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthūm, and Fāṭimah ﵃ all.

As for Zaynab, daughter of the Messenger of God ﷺ she married Abū al-ʿĀṣ ibn al-Rabīʿ ibn ʿAbd Shams ibn ʿAbd Manāf in the pre-Islamic period. She bore Abū al-ʿĀṣ a daughter named Umāmah. After the daughter of the Messenger of God ﷺ died, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib married Umāmah. ʿAlī was killed while Umāmah was with him. After ʿAlī, al-Mughīrah ibn Nawfal ibn al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib ibn Hāshim married Umāmah; she died while with him. The mother of Abū al-ʿĀṣ ibn al-Rabīʿ was Hālah, daughter of Khuwaylid ibn Asad; Khadījah was his maternal aunt, the sister of Asad.

As for Ruqayyah, daughter of the Messenger of God ﷺ ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān married her in the pre-Islamic period. She bore him ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān, after whom ʿUthmān was first given the kunyah Abū ʿAbd Allāh. Later, he was given the kunyah Abū ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān, and he was known by both. Ruqayyah died at the time of Badr, and ʿUthmān stayed behind to bury her; that was what kept him from taking part at Badr. ʿUthmān had migrated to Abyssinia, and Ruqayyah, daughter of the Messenger of God ﷺ migrated with him. Ruqayyah, daughter of the Messenger of God ﷺ died on the day Zayd ibn Ḥārithah, the client of the Messenger of God ﷺ arrived with the good news of the victory at Badr.

As for Umm Kulthūm, daughter of the Messenger of God ﷺ he married her—Yaʿqūb adds—and she died while with him. She bore him no children.

As for Fāṭimah—Yaʿqūb adds: daughter of the Messenger of God ﷺ—and the two say: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib married her, and she bore him al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī the elder, and Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī, who was killed in Iraq at al-Ṭaff.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān related to us: Jarīr related to us, from Yazīd ibn Abī Ziyād, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith, who said:

Fāṭimah lived for eight months after the death of the Prophet ﷺ.

He said: Yaʿqūb related to us: Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us: Sufyān related to us: ʿAmr related to us, from Ibn Shihāb, who said: Fāṭimah, daughter of the Messenger of God ﷺ lived for three months after the Prophet ﷺ.

He said: ʿAmr ibn Dīnār related to us, from Abū Jaʿfar, who said: She lived for six months after him.

Places where prophethood was revealed:

Al-Qaṭṭān informed us; Ibn Durustawayh informed us; Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us; Abū Saʿīd ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ibrāhīm related to us; al-Walīd ibn Muslim related to us; ʿUfayr ibn Maʿdān related to us, from Sulaym ibn ʿĀmir, from Abū Umāmah ﵁ that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: “Prophethood was revealed in three places: in Mecca, in Medina, and in Syria.”

Proofs of prophethood:

Al-Bayhaqī related, through Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān, from Abū Nuʿaym—that is, al-Faḍl ibn Dukayn—who said: Misʿar related to us, from ʿAbd al-Jabbār ibn Wāʾil ibn Ḥujr, who said: [My family] related to me from my father: The Messenger of God ﷺ was brought a bucket of water. He drank from it, then spat into the bucket, and then poured it into the well. Or: he drank from the bucket, then spat into the well, and the scent of musk wafted from it.

Al-Bayhaqī and al-Ḥākim related, from the report of Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān, from Aḥmad ibn Shabīb ibn Saʿīd al-Ḥabaṭī, from his father, from Rūḥ ibn al-Qāsim, from Abū Jaʿfar al-Madanī, from Abū Umāmah ibn Sahl ibn Ḥunayf, who said: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ. A blind man came to him and complained that his sight was gone. He said, “Messenger of God, I have no guide, and it is a hardship for me.” The Messenger of God ﷺ said: “Go to the place for ablution, perform ablution, then pray two cycles, and then say: ‘O God, I ask You and turn to You through Your Prophet Muḥammad, the Prophet of mercy. O Muḥammad, I turn through you to my Lord, that my sight may be restored. O God, accept his intercession for me, and accept my intercession for myself.’” ʿUthmān said: By God, we had not dispersed, nor had our conversation lasted long, before the man came in as though he had never suffered any affliction at all.

(The account of Salmān al-Fārisī):

… Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān al-Fasawī related to us: Zakariyyā al-Arsūfī related to us: al-Sirrī ibn Yaḥyā related to us, from Sulaymān al-Taymī, from Abū ʿUthmān al-Nahdī, who said:

Salmān was from Ramhurmuz. A monk came to its mountains to worship, and the son of the village headman used to visit him. I noticed this and said to him, “Take me with you.”

He said, “Not until I ask his permission.” He asked his permission, and the monk said, “Bring him with you.” We used to visit him regularly, until the people of the village noticed. They said, “Monk, you have settled among us, and we have treated you well. We see that you intend to corrupt our young men, so leave our land.” He said:

So he left, and I left with him. The higher he went through the land, the more his knowledge and honor increased, until he reached Mosul. There he came upon one of its mountains, where there were seven monks, each worshipping in a cave. They fasted for six days and nights, then, on the seventh day, they gathered to eat and talk. I said to my companion, “Leave me with these people.” But he refused and insisted that we go on. I said, “Then I will go with you.” He said: So I went with him. When we reached the gate of Jerusalem, there was a crippled man at the mosque gate. He said, “Servant of God, give alms to me.” My companion had nothing to give him. He entered the mosque and prayed for three days and nights. Then he went out, drew a line, and said, “When you see the shadow reach this line, wake me.” Then he slept. I felt sorry for him, because of how long he had stayed awake, and did not wake him until the shadow had passed the line. He awoke and said, “Did I not tell you?” I said, “I felt sorry for you, after you had stayed awake so long.” He said, “Woe to you! I am ashamed before God to let an hour of night or day pass without remembering Him.” Then he went out. The crippled man said, “You are a righteous man. You came in and went out without giving me alms.” My companion looked right and left and saw no one. He said, “Show me your hand. Stand, by God’s permission.” The man stood, with no ailment. I was so absorbed in looking at him that my companion went off through the alleys. I turned around, but could not see him, and set off to look for him. He said: A traveling party from Iraq passed by and took me along; they brought me to Medina. When the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Medina, I recalled what they had said: that he did not eat alms but accepted gifts. I brought him some food, and he said, “What is this?” I said, “Alms.” He said to his companions, “Eat,” but he did not taste it. Then I returned and gathered some food. He said, “What is this, Salmān?” I said, “A gift.” He ate.

I said, “Messenger of God, tell me about the Christians.” He said, “There is no good in them, nor in those who love them.” I got up, feeling burdened, and God Most High revealed: “You will surely find that the most hostile of people toward those who believe are the Jews and those who associate others with God; and you will surely find that the nearest of them in affection toward those who believe are those who say, ‘We are Christians.’” Q 5:82.

He sent for me and said, “Salmān, your companion—or your companions—are among those whom God Most High has mentioned.”

The account of Umm Maʿbad:

The tradition of Umm Maʿbad was related by the ḥāfiẓ Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān al-Fasawī and by the ḥāfiẓ Abū Nuʿaym in his book Proofs of Prophethood.

His description among the People of the Book:

The ḥāfiẓ Abū Bakr al-Bayhaqī said: Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl al-Qaṭṭān informed us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar related to us; Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us; Abū Ṣāliḥ related to us; al-Layth related to us; Khālid ibn Yazīd related to me, from Saʿīd ibn Abī Hilāl, from Usāmah, from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār, from Ibn Salām, who used to say:

“We find the description of the Messenger of God ﷺ in the words: ‘We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of glad tidings, and a protector for the unlettered. You are My servant and My messenger. I have named you the Trusting One. You are neither harsh nor coarse, nor do you shout in the marketplaces. You do not repay an evil with its like, but pardon and overlook. He will not take him until he has set upright through him the crooked community, so that they bear witness that there is no god but God. Through him He will open blind eyes, deaf ears, and covered hearts.’”

ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār said: The Lakhmī also informed me that he heard Kaʿb al-Aḥbār say the same as Ibn Salām.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Fayḍ al-Bajalī related to us; Salām ibn Miskīn related to us, from Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, who said: God, Mighty and Exalted, revealed to Jesus son of Mary: “Be earnest in My cause, listen and obey, son of the pure, virgin maiden. I created you without a male, and made you a sign for all the worlds. Worship Me, then explain in Syriac to the people of Sūrān. Tell those before you: ‘I am the enduring Truth, who does not pass away. Believe in the unlettered Arab Prophet, the owner of the camel, the coat of mail, the turban, the two sandals, and the staff—that is, the rod; the curly-haired one, with a smooth brow, eyebrows joined together, wide eyes, long eyelashes, dark eyes, an aquiline nose, clear cheeks, and a thick beard. His sweat on his face is like pearls, and the scent of musk wafts from him. His neck is like a silver ewer, and it is as though gold runs through his collarbones. From the hollow of his throat to his navel runs a line of hair, like a rod; he has no other hair on his belly. His hands and feet are thick. When he comes among people, he towers over them; when he walks, it is as though he were tearing himself free from rock and descending a slope. He has few offspring’”—apparently meaning male children from his loins. This is how al-Bayhaqī related it in Proofs of Prophethood, through Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān.

Abū Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl al-Makkī informed us, in a reading to him while I listened. He said: Abū ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī al-Maʿāmil ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, resident of Alexandria, informed us by audition— He said: Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad al-Shāfiʿī informed us, in a reading to him while I listened. He said: Aḥmad ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn informed us. He said: al-Ḥasan ibn Aḥmad informed us. He said: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed us. He said: Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān informed us: Yūsuf ibn Ḥammād al-Maʿnā related to us: ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us, from Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq.

We have also related it through al-Bakkāʾī, from Ibn Isḥāq; the two versions have the same meaning. This wording is al-Bakkāʾī’s version, from Ibn Isḥāq. He said: Ṣāliḥ ibn Ibrāhīm related to me, from Maḥmūd ibn Labīd, from Salamah ibn Salāmah ibn Waqsh, who was one of the Companions of Badr. He said:

We had a Jewish neighbor from Banū ʿAbd al-Ashhal. He spoke of the Resurrection, the raising of the dead, the Reckoning, the Balance, Paradise, and Hellfire. He said: “That is for a people who are polytheists and worship idols, who do not believe that there will be a raising after death.” They said to him, “Woe to you! Do you think this will happen—that people will be raised after their death to an abode where there is Paradise and Hellfire, and be recompensed there for their deeds?” He said:

“Yes, by the One by whom he swears. He would wish that, in exchange for his share of that Fire, he had the largest oven in his house, heated and then placed inside it, with its opening covered over him, so that he might escape that Fire tomorrow.”

They said to him, “Woe to you, so-and-so! What sign will there be of that?” He said, “A prophet will be sent from the direction of these lands,” and he pointed with his hand toward Mecca and Yemen. They said, “When do you think you will see him?” He looked at me—for I was the youngest of them—and said, “If this boy lives out his life, he will see him.”

Salamah said: By God, night and day had not passed before God sent His Messenger Muḥammad ﷺ while he was among us. We believed in him, but the man disbelieved out of spite and envy. We said to him, “Woe to you, so-and-so! Were you not the one who told us about him what you told us?”

His physical characteristics:

The seal of prophethood:

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related, from al-Ḥumaydī, from Yaḥyā ibn— Sulaym, from Ibn Khuthaym, from Saʿīd ibn Abī Rāshid, from al-Tanūkhī, whom Heraclius had sent to the Messenger of God ﷺ while he was at Tabūk… He related the report as we have given it earlier in the account of the Tabūk expedition, up to where he said: “He loosened the fold of his cloak from his back, then said, ‘Here is the mark of what I was commanded to seek.’” He said: “I looked closely at his back, and there was a seal in the place of the cartilage of the shoulder, like a large cupping glass.”

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Muslim ibn Ibrāhīm related to us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Maysarah related to us; ʿAttāb related to us: I heard Abū Saʿīd say: “The seal between the Prophet’s shoulders ﷺ was a raised piece of flesh.”

The color of his complexion:

Al-Bayhaqī cited, with his chain of transmission, from Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān: ʿAmr ibn ʿAwn and Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr related to me; the two said: Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh related to us, from Ḥumayd al-Ṭawīl, from Anas ibn Mālik, who said: “The Messenger of God ﷺ was dark-complexioned.”

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān al-Fasawī said: ʿAmr ibn ʿAwn and Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr related to me; the two said: Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh related to us, from al-Jurayrī, from Abū al-Ṭufayl, who said: “I saw the face of the Prophet ﷺ and no one who saw him remains besides me.”

I said to him, “Describe the Messenger of God ﷺ to us.” He said, “He had a fair, handsome face.”

Yaʿqūb al-Fasawī said: Isḥāq ibn Ibrāhīm ibn al-ʿAlāʾ related to us; ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥārith related to me; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sālim related to me, from al-Zubaydī. Muḥammad ibn Muslim informed me, from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, that he heard Abū Hurayrah describe the Prophet ﷺ saying: “He was very fair-complexioned.”

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Ibn al-Aṣbahānī related to us; Sharīk related to us, from ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿUmayr, from Nāfiʿ ibn Jubayr, who said: “The Prophet ﷺ was described to us as fair-complexioned with a reddish tinge.” Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr related to us; Nūḥ ibn Qays al-Ḥarrānī related to us; Khālid ibn Khālid al-Tamīmī related to us, from Yūsuf ibn Māzin al-Māzinī, that a man said to ʿAlī:

“Commander of the Faithful, describe the Messenger of God ﷺ to us.” He said: “He was fair-complexioned with a reddish tinge, large-headed, radiant, with a clear brow and long eyelashes.” Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr related to us; Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh related to us, from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿUmar ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: ʿAlī was asked—or someone said to him, “Describe the Messenger of God ﷺ to us.” He said: “He was fair-complexioned, his fairness tinged with red; his pupils were black and his eyelashes long.” Yaʿqūb said: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Maslamah and Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr related to us; the two said— ʿĪsā ibn Yūnus related to us; ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd Allāh, the client of Ghufrah, related to us, from Ibrāhīm ibn Muḥammad, from a descendant of ʿAlī, who said: When ʿAlī described the Messenger of God, he would say: “His face was rounded and fair; his eyes were dark and his eyelashes long.” Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related, from al-Ḥumaydī, from Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah, from Ismāʿīl ibn Umayyah, from a client of theirs—Muzāḥim ibn Abī Muzāḥim—from ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Khālid ibn Asīd, from a man of Khuzāʿah called Muḥarrish or Mukharrish—Sufyān was unsure of his name, and sometimes said Muḥarrish, though I did not hear him say so—that the Prophet ﷺ went out from al-Jiʿrānah by night to perform the lesser pilgrimage, then returned and was there at dawn as one who had spent the night there. I looked at his back, and it was like a bar of silver.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Isḥāq ibn Ibrāhīm ibn al-ʿAlāʾ related to us; ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥārith related to me; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sālim related to me, from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, who heard Abū Hurayrah describe the Messenger of God ﷺ saying: “He was very fair-complexioned.”

Description of his eyes:

Yaʿqūb related to us; Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr related to us; Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh related to us, from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿUmar ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: ʿAlī was asked, “Describe the Messenger of God ﷺ to us.” He said: “He was dark-eyed the pupil. The shaykh, the preacher, the ḥāfiẓ Abū Bakr Aḥmad ibn ʿAlī ibn Thābit al-Baghdādī, dictated to us: Abū al-Ḥusayn Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Faḍl recited to him, and he said: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar ibn Durustawayh recited to him in the year 346. He said: Abū Yūsuf Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān al-Fasawī related to us: ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Muʿādh related to us: my father related to us. And Muḥammad ibn al-Muthannā and Ibn Bashshār related to us, saying: Muḥammad—meaning Ibn Jaʿfar, Ghundar—related to us. Both reports are from Shuʿbah, from Simāk, who said: I heard Jābir ibn Samurah—and in ʿUbayd Allāh’s report, “I asked Jābir ibn Samurah”—about the description of the Prophet’s eye. He said: “He had a broad mouth and eyes with a touch of brown.”

He said: “His eye was long in its slit.” I asked, “What does ‘hollow-heeled’ mean?” He replied, “Having little flesh on the heel”.

His eyelashes:

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Ādam and ʿĀṣim ibn ʿAlī related to us; they said: Ibn Abī Dhiʾb related to us; Ṣāliḥ, the client of al-Tawʾamah, related to us. He said: Abū Hurayrah used to describe the Messenger of God ﷺ saying: “His arms were long and slender, his shoulders far apart, and his eyelashes long”.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Isḥāq ibn Ibrāhīm related to us: ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥārith related to me: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sālim related to me, from al-Zubaydī, who said: al-Zuhrī related to me, from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, that he heard Abū Hurayrah describing the Messenger of God. He said: “His forehead was broad, and his eyelashes long.”

His hair:

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Maslamah and Yaḥyā ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd related to us; they said: Sufyān related to us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, who said: Umm Hāniʾ said, “The Prophet came to Mecca on one of his visits with four locks of hair”—meaning braids.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān related to us, from Abū Ḥamzah al-Sukkarī, from ʿUthmān ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mawhib al-Qurashī. He said: “We went in to see Umm Salamah, and she brought out for us some of the Messenger of God’s hair. It was reddish, dyed with henna and katam”.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Abū Nuʿaym related to us: ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Iyād related to us: Iyād related to me, from Abū Rimthah, who said: “I set out with my father toward the Messenger of God ﷺ. When I saw him, my father said, ‘Do you know who this is?’ I said, ‘No.’ He said, ‘This is the Messenger of God ﷺ.’ I shuddered when he said this. I had thought that the Messenger of God ﷺ would be something unlike other people, but there he was, a human being with abundant hair, dyed with henna, wearing two green mantles”.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Makhramī, from Abū Sufyān al-Ḥimyarī, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Ḥamrah, from Ghaylān ibn Jāmiʿ, from Iyād ibn Laqīṭ, from Abū Rimthah: “The Messenger of God ﷺ dyed his hair with henna and katam, and his hair reached his shoulders or his shoulder blades”.

Al-Bayhaqī said: Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl informed us: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed us: Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us: Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Walīd al-Kindī al-Kūfī related to me: Yaḥyā ibn Ādam related to us: Sharīk related to us, from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: “The Messenger of God ﷺ had about twenty gray hairs”.

Description of his face:

The ḥāfiẓ Abū Bakr al-Bayhaqī said in al-Dalāʾil: Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl al-Qaṭṭān informed us in Baghdad: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar ibn Durustawayh informed us: Abū Yūsuf Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us: Abū Nuʿaym and ʿUbayd Allāh related to us, from Isrāʾīl, from Simāk, who said: He heard Jābir ibn Samurah say that a man asked him, “Was the Messenger of God’s ﷺ face like a sword?” He replied, “No, rather it was round like the sun and the moon”.

Yaʿqūb al-Fasawī said: Saʿīd related to us: Yūnus ibn Abī Yaʿfūr al-ʿAbdī related to us, from Abū Isḥāq al-Hamdānī, from a woman of Hamdān whom he named. She said: “I performed the pilgrimage with the Prophet ﷺ. I saw him riding his camel as he circumambulated the Kaʿbah, with a hooked staff in his hand.” I said to her, “Describe him.” She replied, “Like the full moon; I have never seen anyone like him, before or after”.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Saʿīd related to us: Yūnus ibn Abī Yaʿfūr al-ʿAbdī related to us, from Abū Isḥāq al-Hamdānī, from a woman of Hamdān whom he named. She said: “I performed the pilgrimage with the Messenger of God ﷺ. I saw him riding his camel as he circumambulated the Kaʿbah, with a hooked staff in his hand” and wearing two red mantles that nearly touched his shoulders. Whenever he passed the Black Stone, he touched it with the hooked staff, then raised the staff to himself and kissed it.

Abū Isḥāq said: I asked her, “Describe him.” She replied, “Like the full moon; I have never seen anyone like him, before or after”.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir related to us: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mūsā al-Taymī related to us: Usāmah ibn Zayd related to us, from Abū ʿUbaydah ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, who said:

I said to al-Rubayyiʿ bint Muʿawwidh, “Describe the Messenger of God ﷺ for us.” She said:

“My son, had you seen him, you would have seen the sun rising”.

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib’s description of him:

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Maslamah al-Qaʿnabī and Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr related to us: ʿUmar ibn Yūnus related to us: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd Allāh, the client of Ghufrah, related to us: Ibrāhīm ibn Muḥammad, one of ʿAlī’s descendants, related to me. He said: When ʿAlī described the Messenger of God ﷺ he would say: “He was neither excessively tall nor short and stocky, but of medium height among the people. His hair was neither tightly curled nor straight; it was wavy. He was neither bulky nor round-faced. His face was rounded, fair with a touch of color; his eyes were dark and his eyelashes long. His shoulder joints and upper back were prominent; his chest was broad, with a line of hair running down it. His palms and feet were coarse. When he walked, he lifted his feet as if walking downhill; when he turned, he turned his whole body. Between his shoulders was the Seal of Prophethood. He was the most generous of people, the broadest in chest, the truest in speech, the most faithful to his pledges, the gentlest in temperament, and the best companion. Whoever saw him unexpectedly stood in awe of him, and whoever came to know him loved him. Anyone describing him would say: ‘I have never seen anyone like him, before or after’”.

Hind ibn Abī Hālah’s description of him:

The ḥāfiẓ Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān al-Fasawī said: Saʿīd ibn Ḥammād al-Anṣārī al-Miṣrī and Abū Ghassān Mālik ibn Ismāʿīl al-Hindī related to us. They said: Jamīʿ ibn ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-ʿAjalī related to us: a man in Mecca related to me, from a son of Abū Hālah al-Tamīmī, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, who said: I asked my maternal uncle, Hind ibn Abī Hālah—who was a skilled describer—about the appearance of the Messenger of God ﷺ. I longed for him to describe something of it to me that I could hold on to. He said: “The Messenger of God ﷺ was imposing and majestic; his face shone like the moon on the night of the full moon. He was taller than a man of medium height and shorter than one exceptionally tall. He had a large head and wavy hair. If his hair parted naturally, he parted it; otherwise it did not reach beyond his earlobes. He had abundant hair. His complexion was luminous, his forehead broad, his eyebrows arched and long but not joined; between them was a vein that swelled when he was angry. His nose was aquiline, with a light above it; one who did not examine him closely might think his nose was raised. He had a thick beard, dark eyes, smooth cheeks, a wide mouth, a slight overbite, and a fine line of hair from chest to navel. His neck was like the neck of a statue, clear and gleaming—meaning, like silver. His build was well-proportioned, plump yet firm; his belly and chest were even. He had a broad chest and wide-set shoulders, prominent joints, and a radiant body. A line of hair ran from the hollow at the base of his throat to his navel, like a thread. His breasts and belly were hairless, apart from that; his arms, shoulders, and upper chest were hairy. His forearms were long, his palms broad, his fingers long and supple, and his palms and feet coarse. His limbs were long and full; his soles were hollow, and his feet smooth, so that water ran off them. When he moved, he lifted his feet with force; when he walked, he leaned forward slightly. He walked gently, with long strides, as if descending a slope. When he turned, he turned his whole body. His gaze was lowered; he looked at the ground longer than at the sky, and most of his looking was by glancing. He led” his companions, and was first to greet anyone he met. I said, “Describe his speech to me.” He said: “The Messenger of God ﷺ was continually sorrowful and always reflective. He knew no rest. He spoke only when necessary, and was long in silence. He began and ended his speech at the corners of his mouth. He spoke with concise, comprehensive words, clear and without excess or deficiency. He was gentle, neither harsh nor demeaning. He honored blessings, however small; he neither disparaged nor praised them. When something of right was at stake, nothing could stand against his anger until he prevailed for it—and according to one report:

‘The world and its affairs did not anger him. But when a matter of right was at stake, no one could recognize him, and nothing could stand against his anger until he prevailed for it.’ He did not become angry on his own behalf nor seek victory for himself. When he gestured, he gestured with his whole hand; when he was surprised, he turned his palm over. When he spoke, he joined his hands, striking the back of his left thumb with his right palm. When angry, he turned away and looked aside; when pleased, he lowered his gaze. Most of his laughter was a smile, and his teeth showed like hailstones.”

Al-Ḥasan said: I kept this from al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī for a time, then told him. I found that he had already heard it: he had asked my maternal uncle what I had asked him, and had asked his father about his comings and goings, his gatherings, and his manner. He had left nothing out.
