Al-Ḥasan said: I asked my father about the Messenger of God’s entering his home. He said: “He had permission to enter for his own needs. When he retired to his home, he divided his time into three parts: one for God, one for his family, and one for himself. Then he divided the part set aside for himself between himself and the people, sharing it with the common people and the distinguished; he withheld nothing from them. His practice in the portion devoted to the community was to give precedence, through his consideration, to those of merit, apportioning his time according to their standing in religion. Some had one need, some two, and some many needs; he would attend to them and engage them in what would set them and the community right. He would ask them about their affairs and inform them of what they ought to know, saying: ‘Let those present convey this to those absent, and bring me the need of anyone unable to bring it to me himself. Whoever conveys to a ruler the need of one unable to bring it to him, God will make his feet firm on the Day of Resurrection.’ Only such matters were raised in his presence, and he accepted nothing else from anyone. They came to him as visitors and departed only after taking nourishment—and according to one report, ‘after tasting’—and they left as guides, meaning as learned men.”

He said: I asked him how he conducted himself when he went out. He replied: “The Messenger of God ﷺ restrained his tongue except in matters that benefited and brought people together, not drove them away. He honored the distinguished person of every people and appointed him over them. He was cautious of people and guarded against them, without concealing his good humor or his smile from anyone. He looked after his companions and asked people about the state of the people. He approved what was good and strengthened it; he disapproved of what was bad and weakened it. He was balanced in his affairs, never inconsistent. He was vigilant, lest they become heedless or stray. He was prepared for every circumstance. He neither fell short of the truth nor went beyond it. The best of people were those closest to him; the most esteemed in his sight were those most sincere in counsel, and the highest in rank with him were those most generous in support and assistance.”

He said: I asked him about his manner in gatherings. He replied: “The Messenger of God ﷺ never sat or stood without remembering God. He did not claim places for himself, and he forbade people from making a place their own. When he came to a group, he sat wherever the gathering ended, and he instructed others to do likewise. He gave each person sitting with him his due, so that no one sitting with him thought another was more honored by him. Whoever sat with him or stood with him to ask for something, he patiently stayed with him until that person departed. Whoever asked him for something was not turned away without receiving it, or at least a kind word. His generosity and good character extended to everyone; he became a father to them, and all were equal in his sight with regard to what was right. His gathering was one of forbearance, modesty, patience, and trustworthiness. Voices were not raised there; women’s honor was not impugned; nor were people’s slips spread about. They were balanced, yet excelled one another in piety; humble, honoring the old and showing mercy to the young; giving preference to the needy and looking after the stranger.”

He said: I asked him about his conduct with those who sat with him. He replied: “The Messenger of God ﷺ was always cheerful, easy in nature, and gentle. He was neither rude nor rough, neither loud nor foul-mouthed, neither fault-finding nor given to jesting. He overlooked what he disliked, did not let a petitioner lose hope, and did not disappoint him. He kept himself from three things: disputation, excessive speech, and what did not concern him. He kept people from three things: he did not disparage or reproach anyone, seek out anyone’s faults, or speak except in hope of reward. When he spoke, those sitting with him lowered their heads as though birds rested on them. When he fell silent, they spoke, but did not quarrel in his presence. He laughed at what they laughed at and marveled at what they marveled at. He patiently bore a stranger’s roughness in speech and questioning, so much so that his companions would invite the stranger to speak freely. He would say:

‘When you see someone asking for help, assist him.’ He accepted praise only from someone who had reciprocated a kindness, and he never interrupted anyone’s speech before that person had finished; then he would end it by speaking or rising.”

He said: I asked him how he kept silent. He replied: “His silence had four purposes: forbearance, caution, deliberation, and reflection. His deliberation lay in giving people equal attention in his gaze and listening. His reflection—or, he said, his thought—concerned what endures and what perishes. God had joined forbearance and patience in him, so nothing could anger or provoke him. Caution was joined in him in four things: his choosing the gentlest course, and his attending to them in all that had been gathered for them in this world and the next.” ﷺ.

… Yaʿqūb said: Abū Bishr and Ibn Qaʿnab related to us: Isḥāq ibn Ṣāliḥ related to me al-Makhzūmī, from Yaʿqūb al-Taymī, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās, who said to Hind ibn Abī Hālah al-Tamīmī—who was skilled at describing the Messenger of God ﷺ—“Describe the Messenger of God ﷺ for us, so that perhaps you may give us an intimate knowledge of him.” He said:

“May my father and mother be sacrificed for him: he was long in silence, always reflective, and continually sorrowful. When he spoke, he spoke with concise, comprehensive words, without excess or deficiency. When he narrated, he repeated himself; when he admonished, he was earnest and …. When contradicted, he turned away and looked aside. He found solace in talking with his companions. He honored blessings, however small. There had to be a taste of food. His smile was like hailstones”.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir related to us: ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Abī Thābit al-Zuhrī related to us: Ismāʿīl ibn Ibrāhīm ibn ʿUqbah related to us, from his uncle Mūsā ibn ʿUqbah, from Kurayb, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: “The Messenger of God ﷺ had a slight gap between his two front teeth, and when he spoke, a light could be seen between them”.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Abū Bakr ibn Abī Shaybah related to us: ʿAbbād ibn Ḥajjāj related to us, from Simāk, from Jābir ibn Samurah, who said: “Whenever I looked at the Messenger of God ﷺ I would say, ‘His eyes are lined with kohl,’ though they were not. The Messenger of God’s shins were slender, and he never laughed except with a smile”.

His physical characteristics:

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Sulaymān related to us: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to us: al-Ḥasan ibn Yaḥyā related to us: Zayd ibn Wāqid related to us from Zayd ibn Wāqid, from Bishr ibn ʿUbayd Allāh, from Abū Idrīs al-Khawlānī, from Abū al-Dardāʾ, who said: I asked ʿĀʾishah about the character of the Messenger of God ﷺ. She replied: “His character was the Qurʾān: he was pleased by what pleased it and angered by what angered it”.

Al-Qaṭṭān informed us: Ibn Durustawayh informed us: Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us: Ādam and ʿĀṣim ibn ʿAlī related to us; they said: Ibn Abī Dhiʾb related to us: Ṣāliḥ, the client of al-Tawʾamah, related to us. He said: Abū Hurayrah ﵁ used to describe the Prophet ﷺ saying:

“He turned and moved away with his whole body—may my father and mother be sacrificed for him—and he was neither foul-mouthed nor given to foul speech, nor did he shout in the marketplaces.”

Ādam added: “I have never seen anyone like him, before him, nor shall I see anyone like him after him”.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Abū Nuʿaym related to us: ʿImrān ibn Zayd, Abū Yaḥyā al-Malāʾī, related to us: Zayd al-ʿAmī related to us, from Anas ibn Mālik, who said: “When a man shook hands with the Messenger of God ﷺ he would not withdraw his hand from the man’s hand until the man withdrew his. If a man faced him, he would not turn his face away until the man turned away. He was never seen putting his knee ahead of a companion seated with him”.

His being subjected to sorcery:

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Mūsā related to us, from Shaybān, from al-Aʿmash, from Thumāmah ibn ʿUqbah, from Zayd ibn Arqam, who said: “A man from the Anṣār used to visit the Prophet ﷺ. Two angels came to him when he was ill, and told him that so-and-so had tied a knot”

He had tied a knot for him and cast it into so-and-so’s well. That afflicted the Messenger of God ﷺ, and the water became yellow from the intensity of the spell. The Prophet ﷺ sent someone to retrieve the knot. They found that the water had turned yellow. He then untied the knot, and the Prophet slept. I saw the man afterward entering the Prophet’s presence, but I never saw him in the Prophet’s face again until he died.

Volume Three

The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The Caliphate of Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq

His hair dye:

Suwayd ibn Qays al-Tujībī related from Qays ibn Thawr that he migrated during the time of Abū Bakr. He said: “We stopped at al-Ḥarrah, and Abū Bakr came out to meet us. We saw that he had dyed the hair of his head and beard.” Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān included it in his History.

Fighting the apostates:

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān also related in his History, through al-Zuhrī, who said:

Abū Bakr set out on a campaign, then appointed Khālid and called the people to join him. He ordered him to travel through the open country of Muḍar, fighting those who had apostatized, and then to proceed to al-Yamāmah. He set out and fought Ṭulayḥah, whom God Most High defeated. The narrator then related the account.

The conquest of Syria:

Abū al-Qāsim informed us, saying: Abū Bakr ibn al-Ṭabarī informed us. He said: Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl informed us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed us; Yaʿqūb related to us; ʿAmmār related to us; Salamah related from Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, who said: Al-ʿAlāʾ ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to me, from a man of Banū Sahm, from Ibn Mājadah al-Sahmī, who said: “Abū Bakr came to perform the pilgrimage among us during his caliphate, in the year twelve.”

When Abū Bakr returned from the pilgrimage, he equipped armies for Syria: ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, Yazīd ibn Abī Sufyān, Abū ʿUbaydah ibn al-Jarrāḥ, and Shuraḥbīl ibn Ḥasanah.

Abū al-Qāsim ibn al-Samarqandī informed us; Abū Bakr ibn al-Ṭabarī informed us; Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl al-Qaṭṭān informed us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed us; Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us; ʿAmmār ibn al-Ḥasan related to us; Salamah related from Ibn Isḥāq:

The conquest of al-Yamāmah, Yemen, and al-Baḥrayn, and the dispatch of the armies to Syria, took place in the year twelve.

Abū al-Qāsim al-Shaḥḥāmī informed us; Abū Bakr al-Bayhaqī informed us. Ḥ.

Abū al-Qāsim ibn al-Samarqandī informed us; Abū Bakr al-Lālakāʾī informed us. They said: Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl al-Qaṭṭān informed us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed us; Yaʿqūb related to us; Abū al-Yamān al-Ḥakam ibn Nāfiʿ related to us; Ṣafwān ibn ʿAmr related from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Jubayr:

After the Prophet ﷺ, Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq equipped armies, placing Shuraḥbīl ibn Ḥasanah, Yazīd ibn Abī Sufyān, and ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ in command of some of them.

They marched until they reached Syria, where the Byzantines gathered immense forces against them. Abū Bakr was told of this, so he sent word to Khālid ibn al-Walīd, who was in Iraq, and wrote: “Set out with three thousand cavalrymen, reinforce your brothers in Syria, and hasten, hasten.” Khālid came swiftly at a gallop, cutting across the land with his men until he reached Ḍamīr. He found the Muslims encamped at al-Jābiyah. The Bedouins who were in the Byzantine realm heard about Khālid and were alarmed by him. One of them said these verses:

“Ho, our bright one, before Abū Bakr’s cavalry! Perhaps death is near, though we do not know.”

That is the end of al-Bayhaqī’s account. Ibn al-Lālakāʾī added: Khālid camped with Shuraḥbīl, Yazīd, and ʿAmr. These four commanders joined forces. The Byzantines marched from Antioch, Aleppo, Qinnasrīn, Ḥimṣ, and the places beyond them. Heraclius, reluctant to accompany their march, set out toward the Byzantines, while Bāhān the Byzantine, son of the Byzantine woman, marched against the people with those who were with him.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān al-Fasawī related: Hishām ibn ʿAmmār related to us; ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Muḥammad related to us; Rāshid ibn Dāwūd al-Ṣanʿānī related to us; Abū ʿUthmān al-Ṣanʿānī, Sharaḥīl ibn Marthad, related to me, saying: Abū Bakr sent Khālid ibn al-Walīd to the people of al-Yamāmah and sent Yazīd ibn Abī Sufyān to Syria. The narrator then mentioned Khālid’s campaign against the people of al-Yamāmah, until he said:

Abū Bakr died and ʿUmar was appointed caliph. He sent Abū ʿUbaydah to Syria, and Abū ʿUbaydah arrived in Damascus. Abū ʿUbaydah asked ʿUmar for reinforcements, and ʿUmar wrote to Khālid ibn al-Walīd ordering him to march to Abū ʿUbaydah in Syria. The narrator then related Khālid’s march from Iraq to Syria, as mentioned earlier.

Abū Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Karīm ibn Ḥamzah al-Sulamī informed us; Abū Bakr al-Khaṭīb related to us. Ḥ. Abū al-Qāsim ibn al-Samarqandī informed us; Abū Bakr al-Lālakāʾī informed us. They said:

Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl informed us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed us; Yaʿqūb related to us; ʿAmmār related from Salamah, from Ibn Isḥāq, who said: Khālid marched until he raided Ghassān at Marj Rāhiṭ. Then he marched until he arrived at the watercourse of Buṣrā, where Abū ʿUbaydah ibn al-Jarrāḥ, Shuraḥbīl ibn Ḥasanah, and Yazīd ibn Abī Sufyān were. They joined forces and kept watch there until Buṣrā made peace on the basis of the jizyah. God granted the Muslims its conquest, and it was the first of the cities of Syria to be conquered during Abū Bakr’s caliphate.

Abū Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Karīm ibn Ḥamzah al-Sulamī informed us; Abū Bakr Aḥmad ibn ʿAlī ibn Thābit, the ḥāfiẓ, related to us. Ḥ. Abū al-Qāsim ibn al-Samarqandī informed us; Abū Bakr al-Lālakāʾī informed us. They said: Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl informed us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed us; Yaʿqūb related to us; Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir related to us; Ibn Fulayḥ related from Mūsā ibn ʿUqbah, from Ibn Shihāb, who said:

The battles of Ajnādayn and Faḥl took place in the year thirteen: Ajnādayn in Jumādā and Faḥl in Dhū al-Qaʿdah.

(The grant of land to ʿUyaynah and al-Aqraʿ, and its revocation):

Yaʿqūb related to us; Hārūn ibn Isḥāq al-Hamdānī related to us; al-Muḥāribī related from al-Ḥajjāj ibn Dīnār al-Wāsiṭī, from Ibn Sīrīn, from ʿAbīdah, who said:

ʿUyaynah ibn Ḥiṣn and al-Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis came to Abū Bakr and said: “O Successor of the Messenger of God, we have a barren tract of land with no pasture and no benefit. If you see fit to grant it to us, perhaps we can plow and sow it, and perhaps God will make it beneficial in time to come.” He said:

So he granted it to them, wrote them a document, and had it witnessed. ʿUmar was not among those present. They went to ʿUmar to ask him to witness it, and found him standing, tending a camel of his. They said: “Abū Bakr has asked you to witness what is in this document. Shall we read it to you, or will you read it?” He said: “You see the state I am in. If you wish, read it; if you wish, wait until I have finished, and then I will read it.” They said:

“We will read it.” They read it, and when he heard what was in the document, he took it from their hands, spat on it, and erased it. They were indignant and spoke harshly. He said: “The Messenger of God ﷺ used to win you over when Islam was weak. But God, Mighty and Majestic, has strengthened Islam. Go, then, and strive as hard as you can. May God not prosper you if you prosper.” He said:

They returned to Abū Bakr, still indignant, and said: “By God, we do not know whether you are the caliph or ʿUmar.” He said: “He is, if he so wishes.” ʿUmar came in anger and stood before Abū Bakr. He said: “Tell me about this land you granted to these two men: is it your own private land, or does it belong to the Muslims in general?” He said: “It belongs to the Muslims in general.”

He said: “Then what moved you to single these two out for it, rather than the body of the Muslims?” He said:

“I consulted those around me, and they advised me to do so.”

He said: “You consulted those around you—did you consult all the Muslims and obtain their consent?” Abū Bakr said: “I had told you that you were stronger than I in this affair, but you overpowered me”.

Yaʿqūb related to us; Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb related to us; Jarīr ibn Ḥāzim related from Nāfiʿ, that Abū Bakr granted al-Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis and al-Zibriqān a tract of land and wrote them a document. ʿUthmān said to them: “Have ʿUmar witness it; that will make your affair more secure, for he will be caliph after him.” He said: “We went to ʿUmar, who said to them: ‘Who wrote this document for you?’ They said: ‘Abū Bakr.’ He said:

‘No, by God—absolutely not! By God, he will make the Muslims’ faces meet swords and stones, and then you will get this!’” He said: “He spat on it and erased it. They went to Abū Bakr and said: ‘We do not know whether you are the caliph or ʿUmar.’ They told him what had happened, and he said: ‘Then we shall ratify only what ʿUmar ratifies’”.

Volume Three

The Caliphate of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

The year thirteen

(The battles of Faḥl and Ajnādayn)

Abū Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Karīm ibn Ḥamzah al-Sulamī informed us; Abū Bakr al-Khaṭīb related to us. Ḥ. Abū al-Qāsim ibn al-Samarqandī informed us; Abū Bakr ibn al-Ṭabarī informed us. They said:

Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl al-Qaṭṭān informed us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed us; Yaʿqūb related to us; Ḥāmid ibn Yaḥyā related to us; Ṣadaqah—meaning Ibn Sābiq—related from Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, who said: ʿUmar was appointed caliph twelve years, three months, and twenty-two days after the Hijrah of the Messenger of God ﷺ. Command of the forces in Syria had been given to Khālid ibn al-Walīd, and the commanders remained in their respective positions. They marched toward Faḥl in Jordan. Faḥl was in Dhū al-Qaʿdah of the year thirteen, six months into ʿUmar’s caliphate.

He said: Yaʿqūb related to us; Salamah related to me, from Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, from Isḥāq ibn ʿĪsā, from Abū Maʿshar, who said: Faḥl took place during ʿUmar’s rule, after six months had passed.

He said: Yaʿqūb related to us; Ibrāhīm related to us; Muḥammad ibn Fulayḥ related from Mūsā ibn ʿUqbah, from Ibn Shihāb. Ḥassān ibn ʿAbd Allāh related from Ibn Lahīʿah, from Abū al-Aswad, from ʿUrwah. Both said: The battles of Ajnādayn and Faḥl took place in Dhū al-Qaʿdah of the year thirteen. When Abū Bakr died and ʿUmar was appointed caliph, he removed Khālid ibn al-Walīd and appointed Abū ʿUbaydah ibn al-Jarrāḥ over the forces.

Abū al-Qāsim ibn al-Samarqandī informed us; Abū Bakr al-Ṭabarī informed us; Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl informed us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed us. Yaʿqūb said: Ajnādayn took place in Jumādā al-Ūlā of the year thirteen. Its commander was ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, with Khālid ibn al-Walīd, Yazīd ibn Abī Sufyān, and Shuraḥbīl ibn Ḥasanah alongside him. Faḥl and Ajnādayn took place in the same year, the year thirteen. Faḥl, however, was fifteen days into ʿUmar’s caliphate—that is, Faḥl took place in Rajab.

The year fourteen

(The conquest of Damascus):

Abū Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Karīm ibn Ḥamzah al-Sulamī informed us; Abū Bakr Aḥmad ibn ʿAlī ibn Thābit related to us. Ḥ. Abū al-Qāsim ibn al-Samarqandī informed us; Abū Bakr ibn al-Ṭabarī informed us. They said: Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl informed us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed us; Yaʿqūb related to us; Ḥāmid ibn Yaḥyā related to us; Ṣadaqah—meaning Ibn Isḥāq—related from Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, who said: Then they marched to Damascus. Khālid was in command of the people, though ʿUmar had already removed him and appointed Abū ʿUbaydah. They kept watch there until God, Mighty and Majestic, granted its conquest. When the letter appointing Abū ʿUbaydah and removing Khālid arrived, Abū ʿUbaydah was too embarrassed to read the letter to Khālid before Damascus had been conquered. This was in Rajab of the year fourteen.

He said: Abū ʿUbaydah made his appointment known and removed Khālid. Then Abū ʿUbaydah spent the winter—one copy reads: “his year”—in Damascus.

He said: Yaʿqūb related to us; Salamah related to me, from Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, from Isḥāq ibn ʿĪsā, from Abū Maʿshar, who said: Damascus was conquered in the following year, in Rajab of the year fourteen. The Battle of al-Yarmūk took place in Rajab of the year fifteen.

Abū Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Karīm ibn Ḥamzah ibn al-Khiḍr al-Sulamī informed us; Abū Bakr Aḥmad ibn ʿAlī ibn Thābit related to us. Ḥ. Abū al-Qāsim ibn al-Samarqandī informed us; Abū Bakr ibn al-Ṭabarī informed us. They said: Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl al-Qaṭṭān informed us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar ibn Darastawayh informed us; Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us; [Hishām ibn ʿAmmār related to us;] ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Muḥammad related to us; Rāshid ibn Dāwūd al-Ṣanʿānī related to us; Abū ʿUthmān al-Ṣanʿānī, Sharaḥīl ibn Marthad, related to me, saying: Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq ﵁ sent Khālid ibn al-Walīd to the people of al-Yamāmah. When we arrived there, they fought us fiercely, but we defeated them. Abū Bakr died and ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb was appointed caliph. He sent Abū ʿUbaydah ibn al-Jarrāḥ to Syria and Damascus, and Abū ʿUbaydah asked ʿUmar for reinforcements. ʿUmar wrote to Khālid: “March to Abū ʿUbaydah in Syria.” Khālid ibn al-Walīd summoned the guide and asked: “How long will it take us to reach al-Ḥīrah?” The guide said: “Such and such a length of time.” Khālid made the camels thirsty, then gave them water; he drew water and watered the horses, then bound the camels’ mouths and hindquarters. The guide said to him:

“If you are at the tree by morning, you will have made it, and those with you will have made it.” Khālid marched with his men and, at the first light of dawn, arrived at the tree. He slaughtered the camels, gave the horses the water in their bellies, fed their meat to the people, and gave the Muslims water from the water-skins that they had been carrying with them. Then he came to al-Ḥīrah [or al-Kūfah]. Its bishop came to meet him at daybreak, and he made peace with him for seventy thousand dirhams. Then he marched until he reached ʿAyn al-Tamr, which ʿUmar used to call the village of the Arabs. They fought him fiercely, but the Muslims defeated them.

He said: The Banū ʿAbd Rabbih ibn Zaytūn who are in Jerusalem descend from those captives. Then Khālid and the Muslims marched until they reached ʿĀnāt. A Byzantine patrician heard of him while at Qarqīsiyāʾ and marched against him with around fifty thousand or thirty thousand men. When Khālid saw that, he led the Muslims along the cultivated lands, hastening toward Syria ahead of him. Khālid and the Muslims got ahead of him and reached the Pass of al-ʿUqāb. It was called the Pass of al-ʿUqāb because of Khālid’s standard.

His standard was called al-ʿUqāb. Khālid camped at the Gate of Kaysān, Yazīd ibn Abī Sufyān at the Small Gate, and Abū ʿUbaydah at the Gate of al-Jābiyah. Then the Muslims attacked them, and Yazīd ibn Abī Sufyān and those with him forced their way in through the Small Gate.

Khālid and the Muslims fought and took captives. When the Byzantines saw this, they lowered their bishop in a basket from the Eastern Gate to Khālid ibn al-Walīd. Khālid granted them a guarantee of safety, which they accepted, and they opened the Eastern Gate for him. Khālid and his men entered and reached al-Maqṣalāṭ. There, Khālid’s men met Yazīd’s men.

Khālid’s men said: “Wait! Khālid has granted them safe conduct.” Yazīd said: “No. We entered by force.” They disagreed, but when Abū ʿUbaydah saw this, he upheld Khālid’s safe conduct and made it binding. The Muslims had two garrison posts: one at Barzah, commanded by Abū al-Dardāʾ, where I was with him, and the other at ʿAyn Maysānūn. The Byzantine patrician Susnāq raided them from the pass of Beirut. Maysānūn was therefore called ʿAyn al-Shuhadāʾ.

(The conquest of Ḥimṣ and the Euphrates):

Abū al-Qāsim ibn al-Samarqandī informed us; Abū Bakr ibn al-Ṭabarī informed us. Ḥ.

Abū Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Karīm ibn Ḥamzah informed us; Abū Bakr al-Khaṭīb related to us. They said: Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl informed us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed us; Yaʿqūb related to us; Abū al-Jamāhir Muḥammad ibn ʿUthmān al-Ṣanʿānī informed us, saying: When God granted the conquest of Damascus, we went out with Abū al-Dardāʾ to the garrison post at Barzah. Then we advanced with Abū ʿUbaydah, and God granted us the conquest of Ḥimṣ.

He said: Then we advanced with Shuraḥbīl ibn al-Simṭ, and God enabled us to subdue the lands up to the river—that is, the Euphrates. We besieged ʿĀnāt, and we suffered hardship there. Salmān al-Khayr arrived with reinforcements for us.

The year fifteen

(The Battle of al-Yarmūk):

Abū Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Karīm ibn Ḥamzah al-Sulamī informed us; Abū Bakr al-Khaṭīb related to us. Ḥ. Abū al-Qāsim ibn al-Samarqandī informed us; Abū Bakr ibn al-Ṭabarī informed us. They said: Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl informed us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed us; Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us; Ibn Bukayr related to us; al-Layth ibn Saʿd related to me, saying: Al-Yarmūk took place in the year fifteen.

He said: Ibn Bukayr and Abū al-Ṭāhir related to us; they said: Ibn Wahb informed us. Ibn Lahīʿah said: The year of al-Yarmūk was fifteen, and ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb was caliph at the time. It is in the land of Jordan, and it is its river.

Yaʿqūb said: Al-Yarmūk took place in Rajab of the year fifteen.

And Abū al-Qāsim ibn al-Samarqandī informed us; Abū Bakr ibn al-Ṭabarī informed us. They said:

Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl informed us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed us; Yaʿqūb narrated to us. ʿAmmār related to me, from Salama, from Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, who said: “Al-Muthannā ibn Ḥāritha died, and Saʿd married his wife, Salmā bt. Ḥafṣ. This was in the year fourteen. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb led the people on that pilgrimage, and Abū ʿUbayda entered Damascus that year and spent the winter there. When the Romans were hard pressed, Heraclius marched with the Romans until he encamped at Antioch. With him were many Arabized tribesmen: Lakhm, Judhām, Balqayn, Baliyy, ʿĀmila, and those tribes of Quḍāʿa and Ghassān. With him, too, were many people from Armenia.

“When he encamped there, he stayed, and sent al-Ṣiqlār—one of his eunuchs—who marched with one hundred thousand fighters. With him were twelve thousand Armenians, under Jurja, and twelve thousand Arabized tribesmen from Ghassān and those tribes, under Abū ʿUbayda ibn al-Jarrāḥ. They met at the Yarmūk in Rajab of the year fifteen. The people fought fiercely, until they entered the Muslims’ camp. When the camp was entered, women of Quraysh fought with swords, among them Umm Ḥakīm bt. al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām, until they outstripped the men [in the fighting].”

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān and Ibn Saʿd related, with a sound chain of transmission, from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, from his father, who said: “The voices fell silent on the day of the Yarmūk, except for the voice of a man saying, ‘O victory from God, draw near!’ I looked, and there was Abū Sufyān beneath the banner of his son Yazīd.” It is said that his eye was put out that day.

Yaʿqūb also related, by way of Ibn Isḥāq, from Wahb ibn Kaysān, from Ibn al-Zubayr, who said: “I was with my father in the year of the Yarmūk. When the Muslims had drawn up for battle, al-Zubayr put on his armor, then mounted his horse and left me behind. I saw some people standing on a hill, fighting alongside the others. I took a shield, then went and joined them. There was Abū— Sufyān among a group of Quraysh elders. Whenever the Muslims gained the upper hand, they would say, ‘Strengthen him with the sons of the Yellow [People]’; and whenever the Romans gained the upper hand, they would say, ‘Alas for the sons of the Yellow [People]!’

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related the account of the Yarmūk from al-Uwaysī, from Ibrāhīm ibn Saʿd.

Year sixteen

(Al-Hurmuzān recounts to ʿUmar the reason for the Persians’ defeat before the Romans):

And Abū al-Qāsim al-Samarqandī informed us; Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn Hibat Allāh al-Ṭabarī informed us. He said: Abū al-Ḥusayn Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Faḍl al-Qaṭṭān informed us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar ibn Darastawayh informed us; Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān informed us, saying:

Abū al-Yamān related to us: Shuʿayb informed me.

He said: Al-Ḥajjāj ibn Abī Manīʿ related to us; my grandfather related to us—both from al-Zuhrī. He said: ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUtba ibn Masʿūd informed me that ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās told him that he heard ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb question al-Hurmuzān, the chief of al-Ahwāz, who had submitted to ʿUmar’s authority, embraced Islam, and been pardoned. ʿUmar asked him about the Persian armies that Kisrā had sent with Shahrbarāz, [or]—Ḥajjāj said—with Shāhyār, and about the war with the Romans, and what had caused the Persians to withdraw from them. Al-Hurmuzān said: “Kisrā sent Shahrbarāz, along with the Persian troops. He conquered Syria and Egypt, destroyed most of the Roman fortresses, and spent a long time in Syria, Egypt, and those lands. Kisrā began to think he was taking too long.”

Yaʿqūb said: Someone other than al-Zuhrī said: “Whenever Kisrā’s commander reached one of their fortresses, he built a fortress beside theirs, where he and his troops encamped. Then he besieged them with his troops and army and fought them. When the siege grew long, they would abandon the fortress to him and join those in the fortresses beyond it.—The account returns to al-Zuhrī’s narration from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from Ibn ʿAbbās.—Kisrā began to think Shahrbarāz was taking too long, and wrote to him: ‘If you wished to conquer a Roman city, you could do so, but you have contented yourself with your position and sought to prolong your rule.’ Kisrā sent him many letters about this, and Shahrbarāz repeatedly replied and made excuses. When this went on too long for Kisrā, he wrote to a Persian magnate who was with Shahrbarāz, ordering him to kill Shahrbarāz and take command of the troops. That magnate wrote back: ‘Shahrbarāz is a sincere fighter. Who is his equal in war?’ Kisrā wrote back, insisting that he kill him. The magnate wrote back again, saying: ‘You have no servant like Shahrbarāz. If you knew what he endured in outmaneuvering”—Ḥajjāj said: “outwitting”—“the Romans, you would excuse him.’ Kisrā wrote back, insisting that he kill him and take command of the armies. The magnate again wrote back to him.

“Kisrā grew angry and wrote to Shahrbarāz, ordering him to kill that magnate. Shahrbarāz sent for the Persian magnate and read Kisrā’s letter to him. The magnate said, ‘Reply to him.’ Shahrbarāz said, ‘You know that Kisrā does not take back his word, and you know how much I care for you, but I have received an order I cannot set aside.’ The man said, ‘Will you not let me return to my family, put my affairs in order, and leave my instructions to them?’ He replied, ‘Yes, that is what I can grant you.’ So the man went to his family, took the three letters Kisrā had written to him, and put them in his sleeve. Then he came back to Shahrbarāz and handed him the first letter. Shahrbarāz read it. Then the man handed him the second letter, and Shahrbarāz read it. He got down from his throne and said, ‘Sit on it.’ The man refused. Shahrbarāz said, ‘You are better than I.’ The man handed him the third letter, and Shahrbarāz read it. When he had finished, he said, ‘I swear by God, I will make Kisrā suffer.’ Shahrbarāz resolved to plot against Kisrā and corresponded with Heraclius, telling him that Kisrā had corrupted Persia, set its forces in motion, and afflicted him with his rule. He asked Heraclius to meet him at a place where they could settle the matter and make an agreement. Shahrbarāz would then withdraw the Persian troops and leave Heraclius free to march against Kisrā.

“When Shahrbarāz’s letter arrived, Heraclius summoned a group of Roman magnates. When they had sat down, he said to them, ‘Today I am either the most prudent of men or the most incapable. Something has come to me that you would not expect. I shall lay it before you, so advise me.’ Then he read Shahrbarāz’s letter to them. They disagreed in their counsel. Some said, ‘This is a trick by Kisrā.’ Others said, ‘This slave wants to meet you because he fears Kisrā and wants to risk his life through you; then he will not care what befalls him.’ Heraclius said, ‘The sound judgment is not where you have placed it. By my life, Kisrā would not willingly endure the insults I find in Shahrbarāz’s letter. Nor would Shahrbarāz have written such a letter while he held sway over most of my realm, unless something had happened between him and Kisrā. By God, I shall meet him.’

“Heraclius wrote to Shahrbarāz: ‘Your letter has reached me, and I understand what you have written in it. I will meet you at the appointed place, such-and-such. Come out with four thousand of your men, and I will come out with the same number. When you reach such-and-such place, leave five hundred of your men there; I will leave the same number at such-and-such place, until you and I meet with five hundred each.’ Heraclius sent messengers to Shahrbarāz and instructed them to stand by that agreement: if Shahrbarāz complied, they were not to send word to him; if he refused, they were to hurry back to Heraclius with the letter so that he could decide what to do. Shahrbarāz complied. Heraclius set out with the four thousand he had taken, leaving none behind, until they met at the appointed place. Heraclius had four thousand men with him, and Shahrbarāz had five hundred. When Shahrbarāz saw them, he sent to Heraclius:

“‘Have you betrayed me?’ Heraclius sent back: ‘I have not betrayed you, but I feared betrayal from you.’

“Heraclius ordered that a silk pavilion be pitched for them between the two battle lines. Heraclius dismounted, entered it, and brought his interpreter in with him. Shahrbarāz came forward and entered to meet him. The two conferred privately, with the interpreter between them, until they had settled their agreement, and each had secured the other’s pledge and guarantees. When they had finished their business, Heraclius came out and signaled to Shahrbarāz to kill the interpreter so that their affair and secret would remain hidden. Shahrbarāz killed him. Then Shahrbarāz withdrew and mustered the troops, while Heraclius’s army marched against Kisrā and raided him and those who remained with him. That was the beginning of Kisrā’s ruin. Heraclius kept his promise to Shahrbarāz and gave him whatever remained of the lands of Persia and their captives. When he withdrew and took power—Ḥajjāj said: ‘and Persia rebelled against Kisrā’—the Persians killed Kisrā, and Shahrbarāz reached Persia with the troops who were with him”.

Abū Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Karīm ibn Ḥamza al-Sulamī informed us; Abū Bakr Aḥmad ibn ʿAlī al-Khaṭīb informed us. And Abū al-Qāsim al-Samarqandī informed us; Abū Bakr ibn al-Ṭabarī informed us. They said: Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl al-Qaṭṭān informed us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed us; Yaʿqūb informed us. Abū Tuqī Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿImrān al-Yaḥṣubī al-Yazanī related to me: al-Walīd ibn Muslim related to us: Muḥammad ibn Muhājir al-Anṣārī related to me—and he mentioned Heraclius’s march to Jerusalem—saying: “Kisrā and Persia had prevailed over the Romans in Syria and as far as the Bosporus, and he marched with his armies until he encamped at the Bosporus. He began dumping stones and lime into it to make a dry passage. While he was occupied with this, word reached him that the king of India and the king of the Khazars had invaded his lands in Iraq.

“He turned back from Constantinople and left a governor over the Syrian cities he had conquered, together with a group of his armored cavalry and their horses. That governor encamped at Ḥimṣ and kept secure the territory Kisrā had left in his charge. Kisrā went on to Iraq, where he found that war had broken out between the king of India and the king of the Khazars. Both wrote to him, each asking him for support against the other, on condition that he return to whichever king he supported everything taken and captured from the other’s lands, and give him an additional” amount of such-and-such. Kisrā and his armored cavalry decided to support the king of the Khazars against the king of India, because the king of the Khazars was his neighbor and fought him every day, and because the king of India was fierce against him and would seize any opportunity if one arose. Kisrā allied himself with the king of the Khazars against the king of India. They defeated him, recovered everything he had taken from their lands, and plundered his camp. He came out defeated and routed. The king of the Khazars returned to Kisrā whatever he had taken from his lands, whether captives or anything else, and added a gift of thirty thousand male slaves—the men the king of the Khazars had left in his custody. He sent them to the lands beyond Constantinople and settled them there. Those lands were then in ruins.

Abū Tuqī said: Al-Walīd related to us, saying that Muḥammad ibn Muhājir al-Anṣārī said:

“They are now in Bajjān”.

(The conquest of al-Jābiya and Jerusalem):

Abū al-Qāsim ibn al-Samarqandī informed us; Abū Bakr ibn al-Ṭabarī informed us; Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl informed us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed us; Yaʿqūb informed us, saying: “The conquest of al-Jābiya and Īliyāʾ was completed in the year sixteen”.

(The death of Māriya ﵂:

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: “She”—meaning Māriya—“died in the year sixteen. May God have mercy on her”.

Year seventeen

He said: “ʿUtba ibn Ghazwān died at al-Baṣra in the year seventeen”.

Year eighteen

(The Year of Ashes and the Plague of ʿAmwās):

Abū Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Karīm ibn Ḥamza al-Sulamī informed us; Abū Bakr al-Khaṭīb informed us. And Abū al-Qāsim ibn al-Samarqandī informed us; Abū Bakr ibn al-Ṭabarī informed us. They said: Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl informed us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed us; Yaʿqūb informed us. Ibn Bukayr related to us: al-Layth ibn Saʿd related to me, saying: “Then came the Year of Ashes and the Plague of ʿAmwās, in the year eighteen.”

Yaʿqūb said: Salama related to me, from Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, from Isḥāq ibn ʿĪsā, from Abū Maʿshar, who said: “Then came ʿAmwās and al-Jābiya in the year sixteen, then Sargh in the year seventeen, then the Year of Ashes in the year eighteen. In that year there was the Plague of ʿAmwās”.

(The death of Abū ʿUbayda):

. .. Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us; al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Walīd ibn Ṣubḥ related to us; Abū Mushir related to us: Yaḥyā ibn Ḥamza related to me: ʿUrwa ibn Ruwaym related to me that Abū ʿUbayda ibn al-Jarrāḥ died at ʿAjall. He said: “Bury me beyond the river.” Then he said: “Bury me where I died”.

. .. Yaʿqūb related to us, saying: “In the year eighteen, Abū ʿUbayda ibn al-Jarrāḥ died. His name was ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Jarrāḥ”.

Year twenty

. .. Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: ʿAmmār related to me; Salama related to me, from Ibn Isḥāq, who said: “It is said that Bilāl, the Prophet’s caller to prayer, died in Damascus in the year twenty.”

In that year, ʿIyāḍ ibn Ghanm died.

Year twenty-one

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān transmitted, by way of Ibn Isḥāq, who said: “Abū Hāshim ibn ʿUtba made terms with the people of Antioch at the cemetery of Maṣṣīn and elsewhere, in the year twenty-one”.

Year twenty-three

(The expedition to ʿAmmūriyya):

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said in his Taʾrīkh: Ibn Bukayr related to us: al-Layth ibn Saʿd related to me, saying: “Then came the expedition to ʿAmmūriyya in the year twenty-three. The commander of the Egyptian army was Wahb ibn ʿUmayr al-Jumaḥī, and the commander of the Syrian army was Abū al-Aʿwar al-Sulamī”.

Abū Muḥammad al-Sulamī informed us; Abū Bakr al-Khaṭīb related to us. And Abū al-Qāsim ibn al-Samarqandī informed us; Abū Bakr al-Lālakāʾī informed us. They said: Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl informed us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed us; Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us; Ibn Bukayr related to us; al-Layth ibn Saʿd related to me, saying:

“In the year twenty-three, there was the expedition of Bisr ibn Arṭāʾ to Lūbiyya”.

ʿUmar’s appearance:

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān mentioned in his Taʾrīkh, with a good chain of transmission back to Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh, who said: “I saw ʿUmar: broad in the shoulders, bald, dark-complexioned, towering over the people as though he were on a mount.” He said:

“I mentioned this account to some of ʿUmar’s descendants, and one of them said: ‘We heard our elders say that ʿUmar was fair-skinned. But in the Year of Ashes, the year of famine, he gave up eating meat and clarified butter and ate olive oil constantly, until his complexion changed. He had been ruddy, but his complexion turned pale’”.

Miscellaneous reports:

Al-Qaṭṭān informed us; Ibn Darastawayh related to us; Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us; Abū Bakr—meaning ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr—al-Ḥumaydī related to us; Sufyān related to us; ʿAmr related to us: Muslim ibn Yasār informed me, saying: “I asked Ibn ʿUmar, ‘Did ʿUmar impose a tithe on the Muslims?’”

He said: “No.”

Sufyān said: “The one called Muslim ibn Sakara”—meaning Muslim ibn Yasār—.

. .. Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us, saying: It is related from al-Shaybānī, from Abū al-ʿAjfāʾ, who said: “It was said to ʿUmar, ‘If only you would appoint a successor!’ He replied, ‘If I had lived to see Khālid ibn al-Walīd, I would have put him in charge’”.

The caliphate of ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān

Year twenty-six

Abū Muḥammad al-Sulamī informed us; Abū Bakr al-Khaṭīb related to us. And Abū al- Qāsim ibn al-Samarqandī informed us; Abū Bakr al-Lālakāʾī informed us. They said: Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl informed us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed us; Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us; Ibn Bukayr related to us; al-Layth ibn Saʿd related to me, saying: “Then came Sābūr and the expedition of Bisr to Waddān, in the year twenty-six”.

Year twenty-nine

(The expedition to Ḥawr):

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān mentioned in his Taʾrīkh, by way of Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, who said: “Then came the expedition to Ḥawr, whose commander was ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir. He marched that day to Iṣṭakhr, with ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Maʿmar at the head of his vanguard. They killed him, and ʿUbayd Allāh was killed; the others returned”.

(The dismissal of al-Walīd ibn ʿUqba):

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said in his Taʾrīkh: ʿAmmār related to us, from Salama, from Ibn Isḥāq, who said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd Allāh related to me, from ʿUrwa, who said: “When the people of Iraq rose up”—meaning, against al-Walīd ibn ʿUqba—“there were five of them, one being al-Ṣaʿb ibn Jaththāma”.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: “Whoever says that al-Ṣaʿb ibn Jaththāma died during Abū Bakr’s caliphate is clearly mistaken”.

Year thirty-two

In that year, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd died in Medina, when he was in his early sixties, Before the killing of ʿUthmān ﵄.

The Year 33

Al-Fasawī said: He—meaning ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī—was born in the year 33.

The Year 34

Yaʿqūb related to us: In that year—meaning the year 34—ʿUbāda ibn al-Ṣāmit, Abū al-Walīd, died in Palestine, at the age of seventy-two.

The Year 35

The Civil Strife

Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī Bakr informed us; Ibn Durustawayh informed us; Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us; Muḥammad ibn ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Rūmī related to us; al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Kūfī related to us; Abū ʿAmr al-Madanī related to us, from al-Zuhrī, from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, who said:

One day, ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān looked out over the people and said, “Is Abū Muḥammad among you?”

He said this three times—meaning Ṭalḥa ibn ʿUbayd Allāh. Ṭalḥa said, “Here I am. What do you want?” ʿUthmān said, “Ṭalḥa, I adjure you by God: did you hear the Messenger of God ﷺ—say, ‘Every prophet has a companion in Paradise, and my companion there is ʿUthmān’?”

He said, “O God, yes.” Then Ṭalḥa rose from that gathering and was not seen there again.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir related to us; Ibn Wahb told me; Yūnus informed me, from Ibn Shihāb, who said: In the year ʿUthmān was killed, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās led the people on pilgrimage, by ʿUthmān’s order.

And from Yaḥyā ibn Bukayr, from al-Layth: the year 35.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Mūsā informed me; Saʿīd ibn Aws informed me, from Bilāl ibn Yaḥyā, who said: Ḥudhayfa lived for forty nights after ʿUthmān was killed.

ʿUthmān’s Appearance

… Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us; Abū al-Aswad al-Naḍr ibn ʿAbd al-Jabbār related to us; Ibn Lahīʿa related to us, from Abū al-Aswad, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh, the client of Shaddād ibn al-Hādī, who said: I saw ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān on Friday, on the pulpit. He wore a coarse ʿAdanī waist-wrapper, worth four or five dirhams, and a dark-dyed Kūfan cloak. He was well-built, with a long beard and a handsome face.

Volume Three

The Caliphate of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib

The Year 36

The Battle of the Camel

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related that al-Zubayr had a thousand servants who paid him the land tax, and he would give all of it away in charity, bringing none of it into his house.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related in his History, through Ḥuṣayn, from— ʿAmr ibn Jawwān, who said: When the two sides met, Kaʿb ibn Sūr stood holding a copy of the Qurʾān, adjuring them by God and Islam. It was not long before he was killed. When the two armies engaged, Ṭalḥa was the first to be killed. Al-Zubayr rode off on his horse. When al-Aḥnaf heard, he said, “He joined the Muslims, but when they began striking one another’s necks with swords, he wanted to go back to his sons.” ʿAmr ibn Jurmūz heard this, set out, came up behind al-Zubayr and stabbed him. Faḍāla ibn Ḥābis and Nufayʿ assisted him, and they killed al-Zubayr.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān transmitted, with a sound chain of transmission, from Qays ibn Abī Ḥāzim, that Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam saw Ṭalḥa among the cavalry and said, “This man helped bring about ʿUthmān’s death.” He shot him with an arrow in the knee, and the blood kept flowing until Ṭalḥa died.

… Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us: Abū Nuʿaym and Qabīṣa related to us; they said: Sufyān related to us, from Makhūl, from al-ʿAyzār ibn Ḥurayth, who said: Zayd ibn Ṣawḥān said, “Do not wash the blood from me, and do not remove any of my clothing except my two leather socks. Bury me in the earth as I am, for I am a man who argues.”

Abū Nuʿaym added: “I will argue on the Day of Resurrection.”

Yaʿqūb said: Zayd ibn Ṣawḥān was killed on the day of the Battle of the Camel, which took place in Jumādā I of the year 36.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Zayd ibn Ṣawḥān was one of the commanders on the day of the Battle of the Camel; he commanded ʿAbd al-Qays.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: He—that is, al-Mundhir ibn al-Jārūd—had taken part in the Battle of the Camel with ʿAlī.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: He—that is, Qabīṣa ibn Jābir ibn Wahb—took part in the Battle of the Camel with ʿAlī.

ʿAlī’s Commanders on the Day of the Battle of the Camel

Miʿqal ibn Qays al-Riyāḥī, Ḥujr ibn Yazīd al-Kindī, and ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī.

The Year 37

The Battle of Ṣiffīn

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: The Battle of Ṣiffīn took place in Rabīʿ I of the year 37.

Al-Bayhaqī related through Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān, from Abū al-Yamān, from Ṣafwān ibn ʿAmr: The people of Syria numbered sixty thousand, and twenty thousand of them were killed. The people of Iraq numbered one hundred and twenty thousand, and forty thousand of them were killed.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said, “But ʿAlī and his companions were closer to the truth than the two groups; Muʿāwiya’s companions were the ones who rebelled against them”—

… of the two factions, while Muʿāwiya’s companions were in rebellion against them.

Al-Bayhaqī said: Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl informed us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed us; Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us; Saʿīd ibn Abī Maryam related to me; Muḥammad ibn Muslim informed us; ʿAmr ibn Dīnār related to me; Ibn Shihāb informed me, from ʿIyāḍ ibn Khalīfa, from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, who said that he heard him say, while he was at Ṣiffīn: “The intellect is in the heart, compassion is in the liver, tenderness is in the spleen, and breath is in the lung”.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān transmitted from al-Zuhrī, who said: ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir and Hāshim ibn ʿUtba were killed on the day of Ṣiffīn.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Yūnus ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥīm related to us; Ḍamra related to us, from Yaḥyā ibn Zayd, who said: ʿAmmār took part in Ṣiffīn at the age of ninety. He rode a small mare, and a strap was used as the sword-belt for his sword.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related, with a sound chain of transmission, from Abū Wāʾil, who said: ʿAmr ibn Sharāḥīl dreamed that he had entered Paradise. There he saw pavilions pitched, and I said, “Who are these for?” They said, “For Dhū al-Kalāʿ and Ḥawshab.” I said, “And where is ʿAmmār?” They said, “Ahead of you.” I said, “How can that be, when some of them killed others?” They said, “They met God and found Him abundant in forgiveness”.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related by way of Muḍārib al-ʿIjlī, who said: Two men boasted—

… two men from Bakr ibn Wāʾil boasted, and took their dispute to a man from Hamdān. He said, “Which of you is Khālid ibn al-Muʿammar, whom Rabīʿa pledged to fight to the death on the day of Ṣiffīn?” Then he related the account.

Naming the Commanders Among ʿAlī’s Companions at Ṣiffīn

Yaʿqūb related to us in Naming the Commanders Among ʿAlī’s Companions on the Day of Ṣiffīn. Abū ʿUbayda said: Over Quraysh, Asad, and Kināna was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar. Ḥuḍayn ibn al-Mundhir, ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī.

The Year 38

The Battle of al-Nahrawān

… Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: ʿUbayd Allāh—that is, Ibn Muʿādh al-ʿAnbarī—related to me; he said: My father related to me, from ʿImrān ibn Ḥudayr, from Lāḥiq—that is, Abū Mujliz—who said:

Those who rose against ʿAlī at al-Nahrawān numbered four thousand, clad in armor. The Muslims attacked them and killed them; of the Muslims, only nine men were killed. If you wish, go to Abū Barza and ask him, for he witnessed it.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: al-Ḥumaydī related to us; Sufyān—namely, Ibn ʿUyayna—related to us; al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Abī ʿAyyāsh related to me that he heard Abū al-Ṭufayl relate, from Bakr ibn Qarwāsh, from Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ—mentioned Dhū al-Thudayya and said, “The devil of al-Radḥa, like a horse-herder, will be hunted down by a man from Bajīla called al-Ashhab or Ibn al-Ashhab, ʿAllāba, among a people of wrongdoing.” Sufyān said: ʿAmmār al-Duhnī informed me that a man called al-Ashhab came.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Muʿādh, from his father, from Shuʿba, from Abū Isḥāq, from Ḥāmid al-Hamdānī, who said: I heard Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ say:

“ʿAlī killed the devil of al-Radḥa”.

The Year 39

… Yaʿqūb related to us: In the year 39, Shayba ibn ʿUthmān ibn Ṭalḥa al-Ḥajabī led the people on pilgrimage.

The Year 40

The Martyrdom of ʿAlī

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā related to us; Sufyān related to us, from Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from his father, who said: ʿAlī was killed at the age of fifty-eight; Ḥasan died at that age, and Ḥusayn was killed at that age ﵃.

Volume Three

The Umayyad Period

The Caliphate of Muʿāwiya ibn Abī Sufyān

Al-Mughīra Leads the Pilgrimage

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Ibn Bukayr related to us, from al-Layth ibn Saʿd, who said: In the year 40, al-Mughīra ibn Shuʿba led the people on pilgrimage. Al-Mughīra had been staying apart at al-Ṭāʾif, so, in the year of the Community, he forged a letter appointing him to oversee the pilgrimage season. He brought the pilgrimage day forward, fearing that an appointed governor might arrive—

… and Ibn ʿUmar stayed behind, while most of the people went with Ibn ʿUmar. Nāfiʿ said:

“I saw us as we were leaving Minā, while they came toward us, returning from Jamʿ. We stayed at Minā one night after them”.

Ḥasan’s Pledge of Allegiance to Muʿāwiya

Al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAẓīm related to us; Aswad ibn ʿĀmir related to us; Zuhayr ibn Muʿāwiya related to us; Abū Rawq al-Hamdānī related to us; Abū al-Ghurayf related to us, who said:

We were in the vanguard of al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, twelve thousand men at Maskin, ready to die, our swords dripping with zeal to fight the people of Syria. Abū al-ʿAmrūṭa was our commander. When the peace settlement of al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī reached us, it was as if our backs had been broken with rage. When al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī arrived in Kūfa, one of our men, called Abū ʿĀmir Sufyān ibn Laylā—and Ibn al-Faḍl said: Sufyān ibn al-Layl—said to him, “Peace be upon you, humbler of the believers.” He replied, “Do not say that, Abū ʿĀmir. I am not the humbler of the believers, but I disliked killing them for the sake of sovereignty.”

This is the wording of al-Ḥakīmī’s report.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr related to us; ʿAwn ibn Mūsā related to us. I heard Hilāl ibn Khabbāb say:

Al-Ḥasan gathered the leaders of the people of Iraq in this palace—the palace of al-Madāʾin—and said, “You pledged allegiance to me on the condition that you make peace with those with whom I make peace, and fight those with whom I fight. I have made peace with Muʿāwiya, so hear and obey him”.

…and obey.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Abū Bakr ibn Abī Shayba and Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr related to us; they said: Abū Muʿāwiya related to us; al-Aʿmash related to us, from ʿAmr ibn Murra, from Saʿīd ibn Suwayd, who said:

Muʿāwiya led us in the Friday prayer at al-Nukhayla—that is, outside Kūfa—at midmorning. Then he addressed us, saying, “I did not fight you so that you would fast, pray, make pilgrimage, or give alms. I know that you do those things. I fought you only so that I would rule over you. God has granted me that, though you hate it”.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Abū Nuʿaym related to us; Muḥammad ibn Sulaymān al-Aṣbahānī related to us; Yūnus ibn Abī al-Nuʿmān related to us, from Umm Ḥakīm bint ʿAmr al-Jadaliyya, who said:

When Muʿāwiya arrived—that is, in Kūfa—and dismounted at al-Nukhayla, he entered through Bāb al-Fīl. Khālid ibn ʿUrfuṭa carried Muʿāwiya’s banner until he planted it in the mosque.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Ibn Bukayr related to us, from al-Layth ibn Saʿd, who said: Muʿāwiya was given the pledge of allegiance at Īliyāʾ in Ramaḍān, the pledge that brought unity; he entered Kūfa in the year 40.

The Year 44

The Death of Umm Ḥabība

Al-Fasawī said: Umm Ḥabība died in the year 44.

The Year 46

Abū Muḥammad al-Sulamī informed us; Abū Bakr al-Khaṭīb related to us. And Abū al-Qāsim ibn al-Samarqandī informed us; Abū Bakr al-Lālakāʾī informed us. They both said: Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn—

…al-Faḍl informed us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar related to us; Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us; Ibn Bukayr related to us; al-Layth ibn Saʿd related to me, who said: In the year 46, there was a raid by Bus[r] and Shurayk on Adhana.

Yaʿqūb said: He—that is, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Khālid ibn al-Walīd—died in the year 46.

The Year 49

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Ṣafwān ibn Ṣāliḥ related to us; al-Walīd related to us; Ibn Jābir related to us, that Abū Ayyūb did not refrain from military campaigns during the time of ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, and Muʿāwiya, and that he died during the campaign of Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya at Constantinople.

Al-Walīd said: A man from Palestine related to me that he saw a white little structure below the wall of Constantinople. They said, “This is the grave of Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī, the Companion of the Prophet ﷺ.” I went to that structure and saw his grave inside it, with a lamp hanging above it by a chain.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: She—that is, Maymūna bint al-Ḥārith al-Hilāliyya—died in the year 49.

The Year 51

Thābit related from Anas: Abū Ṭalḥa died while campaigning by sea. They found no island on which to bury him until seven days had passed, yet his body had not changed.

Al-Fasawī included it in his History, and its chain of transmission is sound.

The killing of Ḥujr ibn ʿAdī and his companions:

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related in his History, from Abū al-Aswad, who said: Muʿāwiya entered upon ʿĀʾisha, and she reproached him for killing Ḥujr and his companions. She said: “I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: ‘After me, people will be killed for whom God and the people of heaven will be angered.’”

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Ibn Bukayr related to us; Ibn Lahīʿa related to us; al-Ḥārith ibn Yazīd related to me, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn [Abī] Razīn al-Ghāfiqī, who said: I heard ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib say: “People of Iraq, seven men from among you will be killed at ʿAdhrāʾ. Their likeness is that of the Companions of the Trench.” Ḥujr ibn ʿAdī and his companions were killed.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Abū Nuʿaym said: Ziyād ibn Sumayya mentioned ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib on the pulpit. Ḥujr seized some gravel, then flung it, pelting Ziyād and those around him. Ziyād wrote to Muʿāwiya: “Ḥujr pelted me while I was on the pulpit.” Muʿāwiya wrote back ordering him to bring Ḥujr. When they neared Damascus, he sent someone to meet them. That person met them at ʿAdhrāʾ and killed them.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Ḥarmala related to us; Ibn Wahb related to us: Ibn Lahīʿa informed me, from Abū al-Aswad, who said: Muʿāwiya entered upon ʿĀʾisha, and she said: “What made you kill the people of ʿAdhrāʾ, Ḥujr and his companions?” He replied: “Mother of the Believers, I considered their killing” to be a reform for the community, and their survival to be corruption.” She said: “I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: ‘People will be killed at ʿAdhrāʾ for whom God and the people of heaven will be angered.’”

Yaʿqūb said: Ibn Lahīʿa related to me; al-Ḥārith ibn Yazīd related to me, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn [Abī] Razīn al-Ghāfiqī, who said: I heard ʿAlī say: “People of Iraq, seven men from among you will be killed at ʿAdhrāʾ. Their likeness is that of the Companions of the Trench.” He said: “Ḥujr and his companions will be killed.”

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: ʿAmr ibn ʿĀṣim related to us; Ḥammād ibn Salama related to us, from ʿAlī ibn Zayd, from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, from Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam, who said: I entered with Muʿāwiya upon the Mother of the Believers, ʿĀʾisha ﵂. She said: “Muʿāwiya, you killed Ḥujr and his companions and did what you did. Were you not afraid that I might conceal a man for you who would kill you?” He said: “No. I am in a house of safety, and I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: ‘Faith restrains treachery; a believer does not commit treachery, a believer does not commit treachery, Mother of the Believers.’”

“How am I, then, in the rest of your needs?” he asked. She said: “Well.” He said: “Then leave me and Ḥujr until we meet before our Lord, Mighty and Exalted.”

The year 52

Saʿīd—that is, ibn al-ʿĀṣ—led the people in the pilgrimage in the year 49 and the year 52, and remained thereafter. Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān mentioned this in his History, from Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr, from al-Layth.

The Year 54

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Ibn Bukayr said: Al-Layth said: In that year—that is, the year 54—Abū Qatāda al-Ḥārith ibn Ribʿī ibn al-Nuʿmān al-Anṣārī died.

The Year 56

In that year Juwayriya, the wife of the Prophet ﷺ died. Marwān performed the funeral prayer over her; Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam was governor of Medina that year.

The Year 58

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related, from Yaḥyā ibn Bukayr, who said: I think that he—that is, Kurayb ibn Abraha al-Aṣbaḥī—died in the year 58.

Al-Fasawī said: He—that is, ʿUbayd Allāh ibn al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib—died during Muʿāwiya’s time.

Yaʿqūb related to us, saying: In that year ʿĀʾisha, the wife of the Prophet ﷺ died.

The Year 59

The expedition to Rhodes:

Abū Muḥammad al-Sulamī informed us; Abū Bakr al-Khaṭīb related to us—ḥāʾ.

Abū al-Qāsim Ismāʿīl ibn Aḥmad informed us: Muḥammad ibn Hibat Allāh told us; both said: Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn informed us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed us; Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us; Zayd and ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to us, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us; al-Layth ibn Saʿd related to me, from Rashīd ibn Kaysān al-Fahmī, who said:

We were in Rhodes, and our commander was Junāda ibn Umayya al-Azdī. Muʿāwiya ibn Abī Sufyān wrote to us: “It is winter, and then more winter, so prepare yourselves for it.” Tabīʿ, the son of the woman married to Kaʿb al-Aḥbār, said: “You will return to your homes at such-and-such a time.” The people said: “How can we return when this is Muʿāwiya’s letter: ‘It is winter, and then more winter’?” One of the army’s close associates came to him and said:

“The people call you nothing but a liar, because you tell them of a return they do not expect.”

Tabīʿ said: “Their permission will come to them on such-and-such a day of such-and-such a month. Its sign will be that a wind comes and uproots this fig tree in their mosque.” His words spread among them, and that morning they gathered in their mosque, waiting for it. It was a day without wind. They waited until they needed to rest at midday and eat lunch, and grew weary, so they went back to their quarters or to their ships. Then, when midday had passed and only a few people remained in the mosque, a whirlwind came, surrounded the fig tree, and uprooted it. The people in their dwellings cried out: “The fig tree has fallen! The fig tree has fallen!” They came from every direction until they gathered on the shore. They saw something glimmering as it moved across the water, until they could make out that it was a boat. It brought them news of Muʿāwiya’s death, the pledge of allegiance to his son Yazīd, and their permission to return. They thanked Tabīʿ and praised him. Then they said: “There is one more thing: winter has set in, and we fear our ships will break apart.” Tabīʿ said: “No timber of yours that could harm you will break, and no rope of yours that could harm you will snap before you reach your homeland.” They set sail, and God, Mighty and Exalted, brought them safely home.

The Year 60

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Yaḥyā ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bukayr related to us, from al-Layth, who said:

Muʿāwiya died in Rajab, four nights having passed, in the year 60. His caliphate had lasted twenty years and five months.

The caliphate of Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya

Abū al-Qāsim ibn al-Samarqandī informed us; Abū Bakr ibn al-Ṭabarī informed us, saying: Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl informed us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed us; Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us, saying: It is also said that in the year 60 Bilāl ibn al-Ḥārith Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Muzanī died.

The Year 61

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Salama related to us, from Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, from Isḥāq ibn ʿĪsā, from Abū Maʿshar: Al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī was killed on the tenth night of Muḥarram in the year 61.

Yaʿqūb said: Abū Nuʿaym said: ʿAlqama—that is, ibn Qays al-Nakhaʿī—died in the year 61.

The year 62

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Abū Bakr al-Ḥumaydī related to us; Sufyān related to us; Shihāb ibn Khirāsh related to us, from a man of his people, who said: I was among the army Ibn Ziyād sent against al-Ḥusayn. They were four men, intended to fight the Daylamites, but Ibn Ziyād selected them and redirected them to fight al-Ḥusayn. I met Ḥusayn and saw that his head and beard were black. I said to him:

“Peace be upon you, Abū ʿAbd Allāh.” He replied: “And upon you, al-sarm”—he had a nasal twang. Then he said: “A band of thieves has spent the night among you since last night.” Shihāb said: I related this to Zayd ibn ʿAlī, and he liked it—he had a nasal twang. Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna said: This trait is found among the Ḥusaynids.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Abū Nuʿaym said: Masrūq ibn al-Ajdaʿ died in the year 62.

The Year 63

The Battle of al-Ḥarra:

Al-Zubayr mentioned that Muḥammad—that is, ibn Abī al-Jahm ibn Ḥudhayfa al-ʿAdawī—witnessed al-Ḥarra, and that Muslim ibn ʿUqba later executed him. Before that, he had gone as a delegate to Yazīd, who had granted him protection. When the people of Medina rebelled against Yazīd, Muḥammad testified against him that he drank wine and other things. Muslim ibn ʿUqba said to him: “By God, you will never again give false testimony.” Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān likewise mentioned this in his History, from Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḍaḥḥāk, from Mālik, adding: Al-Ḥarra took place in the year 63, and seven hundred of those who had memorized the Qurʾān were killed that day.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: I heard Saʿīd ibn Kathīr ibn ʿUfayr al-Anṣārī say: On the day of al-Ḥarra, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd al-Māzinī, Maʿqil ibn Sinān al-Ashjaʿī, and Muʿādh ibn al-Ḥārith al-Qāriʾ were killed; and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥanẓala ibn Abī ʿĀmir was killed.

Yaʿqūb said: Yaḥyā ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bukayr related to us, from al-Layth, who said: The Battle of al-Ḥarra took place on Wednesday, three nights remaining in Dhū al-Ḥijja of the year 63. Then Musrif ibn ʿUqba set out for Mecca, intending to kill ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr there because he had fled from the pledge of allegiance to Yazīd. In the meantime, Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya died, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr’s claim to the caliphate in the Ḥijāz grew strong. He then took Iraq and Egypt. After Yazīd, allegiance was pledged to his son Muʿāwiya ibn Yazīd. He was a righteous man, but his time in office did not last: he remained for forty days, or, it is said, twenty days, and then died ﵀. Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam seized Syria and took control of it. He remained for nine months, then died. His son ʿAbd al-Malik succeeded him, but ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd ibn al-Ashdaq contested his rule. ʿAmr had been governor of Medina from Muʿāwiya’s time, and throughout the days of Yazīd and Marwān. When Marwān died, ʿAmr claimed that Marwān had designated him to succeed, in preference to his son ʿAbd al-Malik. ʿAbd al-Malik was greatly troubled by him and persisted against him until, after ʿAmr’s power had grown strong in Damascus, he seized and killed him in the year 69; it is also said, in the year 70.

ʿAbd al-Malik’s reign continued until he overcame Ibn al-Zubayr in the year 73. Al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf al-Thaqafī killed him, under orders, in Mecca, after a lengthy siege that led to the catapult being set up against the Kaʿba, because Ibn al-Zubayr had taken refuge in the sanctuary. Al-Ḥajjāj continued against him until he killed him. Then ʿAbd al-Malik designated his four sons to succeed him, in this order: al-Walīd, then Sulaymān, then Yazīd, then Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir related to me; Ibn Fulayḥ related to me, from his father, from Ayyūb ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from Ayyūb ibn Bashīr al-Muʿāfirī, that the Messenger of God ﷺ went on one of his journeys. When he passed by the lava plain of Zahra, he stopped and said, “We belong to God and to Him we return.” His companions were distressed by this and thought it had to do with their journey.

ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said: “Messenger of God, what did you see?” The Messenger of God ﷺ said: “That has nothing to do with your journey.” ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said: “Messenger of God, what did you see?” The Messenger of God ﷺ said: “Indeed, that has nothing to do with this journey of yours.” They said: “Then what is it, Messenger of God?” He said: “The best of my community after my Companions will be killed on this lava plain.”

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān also said: Wahb ibn Jarīr said: Juwayriya related to me; Thawr ibn Yazīd related to me, from ʿIkrima, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: The interpretation of this verse came to pass at the head of sixty years: “Even if they had been entered upon from its outskirts, and then asked to commit sedition, they would have done so” (33:14). He said: “They would have given in”—that is, the people of al-Shām entering upon the people of Medina, the Banū Ḥāritha.

Abū Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Karīm ibn Ḥamza informed us; Abū Bakr Aḥmad ibn ʿAlī al-Ḥāfiẓ related to us—ḥāʾ.

Abū al-Qāsim ibn al-Samarqandī informed us; Muḥammad ibn Hibat Allāh ibn al-Ḥasan told us; both said: Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn al-Qaṭṭān informed us; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar related to us; Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us; al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Walīd ibn Ṣubḥ related to us; Marwān ibn Muḥammad related to me; Ibn Lahīʿa related to me; Wāhib ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Muʿāfirī related to me, who said: I came to Medina and went to the house of Zaynab daughter of Fāṭima, daughter of ʿAlī, to greet her. I entered the house and found a large group there. She was sitting unveiled, and she was a woman who was not [al-ḥalīla? Translator’s note: The word is unclear.] and had not advanced in age. I was moved by protective zeal and concern for her modesty, and I said: “Glory be to God! Your worth, your worth, your standing, your standing—and you sit before people, as I see you, unveiled [? Translator’s note: The source marks this word as uncertain.]” She said: “I have a story.” I said: “What is that story?” She said: “During the days of al-Ḥarra, the people of al-Shām came to Medina and did what they did there. At that time I had a son who was nearly of age.” She said: “One day, while I was sitting in my house, I suddenly saw him running, with Busr ibn Abī Arṭāʾ behind him. He came in to me and threw himself upon me, weeping so hard that it seemed his grief would split his liver. Busr said to me: ‘Hand him over to me, for I am better for him.’ I said to him: ‘Go with your uncle.’ He said: ‘No, by God, Mother, I will not go with him. By God, he will kill me.’ I said: ‘Do you think your uncle will kill you? No. Go with him.’ He said: ‘No, by God, Mother, I will not go with him. By God, he will kill me.’ And he was weeping so hard that it seemed his grief would split his liver.

“I continued to soothe him and calm him until he quieted down. Then Busr said to me: ‘Hand him over to me, for I am better for him.’ I said: ‘Go with your uncle.’ He stood and went with him. When he left the doorway, Busr said to the boy: ‘Walk in front of me.’ Then Busr drew his sword from beneath his clothes. When they came out into the lane, Busr lifted his garment from his shoulder and drew his sword on him from behind; then he struck him from behind with it. He kept striking him until he was dead. I heard a cry: ‘Come quickly, your son has been cut down!’ I got up, stumbling over my clothes, my senses gone. A group had gathered around him; there he was, killed and cut to pieces. I threw myself upon him and ordered that he be carried away. From that day I made a vow to God never to veil myself from anyone, for Busr was the first to violate my privacy and expose me to people. May God exact justice from him.”

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said in his History: A man from al-Shām, from al-Urdunn, entered upon him—that is, Muḥammad ibn Maslama al-Anṣārī—while he was in his house and killed him.

Some of those killed at al-Ḥarra:

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ḥāṭib ibn Abī Baltaʿa, and al-Sāʾib ibn Yazīd ibn Ukht al-Nimr.

The Year 64

Yaʿqūb al-Fasawī said: The people of al-Shām wanted al-Walīd ibn ʿUqba to take the caliphate, but he was stabbed and died after the death of Muʿāwiya ibn Yazīd.

The Year 66

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Yūsuf ibn Mūsā related to me, from Jarīr, from Yazīd ibn Abī Ziyād, who said: When the head of Ibn Marjāna and those with him were brought and placed before al-Mukhtār, a slender snake came. It wound its way among the heads until it entered Ibn Marjāna’s mouth and came out through his nostril; it entered his nostril and came out through his mouth. It kept entering and emerging from his head among the other heads.

Yaʿqūb dated his killing—that is, Rifāʿa ibn Rāfiʿ ibn Mālik ibn al-ʿAjlān—in The year sixty-six. It is related that al-Mukhtār ibn [Abī] ʿUbayd was the one who killed him.

The year sixty-seven

He was killed—that is, ʿUmar ibn Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ—in the year sixty-seven; Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said the same.

Al-Aḥnaf—that is, ibn Qays—died in the year sixty-seven, according to Yaʿqūb al-Fasawī.

The year sixty-eight

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Abū Nuʿaym said, “Ibn ʿAbbās died in the year sixty-eight”.

The year seventy

Abū al-Qāsim ibn al-Samarqandī informed us; Abū Bakr ibn al-Ṭabarī informed me; Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl informed me; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar related to us; Yaʿqūb related to us; Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr related to us; Ḥujr ibn al-Ḥārith al-Ghassānī, from the people of Ramla, related to us, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAwf al-Kinānī—who was an administrator for ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz in Ramla—who said:

“I was present when ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān said to Bashīr ibn ʿAqraba al-Juhanī, on the day ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ was killed:

“‘Abū al-Yamān, today I need you to speak. Stand up and speak.’

“He said: ‘I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ—say: “Whoever delivers a sermon, seeking nothing by it but ostentation and reputation, God will make him stand on the Day of Resurrection in a place of ostentation and reputation”’”.

The year seventy-two

Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb related to us; Ghassān ibn Muḍar related to me, from Saʿīd ibn Zayd, who said: ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ziyād ibn Ẓabyān attacked Muṣʿab and killed him at Dayr al-Jāthālīq, on the bank of a river called Dujayl, in the territory of Maskin. He severed his head, and al-Taymī took it to ʿAbd al-Malik. When ʿAbd al-Malik was brought his head, he prostrated.

ʿUbayd Allāh was a reckless and wicked man. He would lament, saying, “How is it that I did not kill ʿAbd al-Malik that day, when he prostrated, so that I might have killed the two kings of the Arabs?”

Al-Fasawī said: ʿĪsā, Muṣʿab’s son, was killed with him, and Muslim ibn ʿAmr al-Bāhilī was wounded. He said, “Carry me to Khālid ibn Yazīd.” He was carried to him, and Khālid sought a guarantee of safety for him.

Yaʿqūb said: In the year seventy-two, Muṣʿab ibn al-Zubayr was killed.

The year seventy-three

… Yaʿqūb related to us, saying: Ibn al-Zubayr was given the pledge of allegiance in the year sixty-four and ruled for nine years. He was killed in Jumādā in the year seventy-three.

Yaʿqūb related to us, saying: Ibn Bukayr said: Al-Layth said: Ibn al-Zubayr led the pilgrimage for the people—that is, in the years sixty-five, sixty-seven, sixty-eight, and sixty-nine and seventy, seventy-one, and seventy-two.

Yaʿqūb related to us, saying: Abū Bakr ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwām ibn Khuwālid ibn Asad ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā ibn Quṣayy ibn Kilāb ibn Murra ibn Kaʿb ibn Luʾayy ibn Ghālib ibn Fihr. Al-Ḥajjāj ibn Abī Manīʿ related this to us, from his grandfather, from al-Zuhrī.

Yaʿqūb said: Abū Nuʿaym said, “Ibn ʿUmar died in the year seventy-three”.

The year seventy-five

… Yaʿqūb related to us, saying: In that year—the year seventy-five—the Commander of the Faithful, ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān, performed the pilgrimage.

Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir related to us; Ibn Wahb related to me, from Yūnus, from Ibn Shihāb, who said:

“After the people united under his rule, ʿAbd al-Malik remained in power for a little more than ten years, less a few months. He performed the pilgrimage several times”.

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said, from Muḥammad ibn Ḥumayd: He died—that is, Nuʿaym ibn Maysara al-Naḥwī—in the year seventy-five or seventy-six.

The year seventy-nine

Al-Fasawī said: Mūsā took charge of Ifrīqiya in the year seventy-nine. He conquered many territories and was a man of resolve and sound judgment.

The year eighty-two

Abū al-Qāsim al-Samarqandī informed us; Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn Hibat Allāh informed me; …

Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn informed me; ʿAbd Allāh related to us; Yaʿqūb related to us; Ibn Bukayr related to us, saying: Al-Layth said: In the year eighty-two, Ibn Shihāb came to ʿAbd al-Malik.

With the preceding chain of transmission, Yaʿqūb related to us, saying: I heard Ibn Bukayr say: “Ibn Shihāb was born in the year fifty-six.” I said to him: “They claim that Ibn Shihāb said, ‘I went as a young man to Marwān.’” He said: “That is false. He went to ʿAbd al-Malik only in the year eighty-two.”

I said to him: “Does he relate from ʿAnbasa, the relative of Yūnus?” He said: “Only a madman, a fool, related from ʿAnbasa. ʿAnbasa was …134 … and he collected the land tax, and they sometimes employed him. Often he would hide in the lower part of my house. They had never approached him to write down hadith or learn from him”.

The year eighty-three

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said: Abū Nuʿaym said: Saʿīd, Abū al-Bukhtarī, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Laylā were killed at al-Jamājim in the year eighty-three.

The year eighty-six

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said, from Ibn Bukayr, from al-Layth ibn Saʿd, who said: It was— His death—that is, ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Marwān’s—occurred on the night of Monday, thirteen nights having passed in Jumādā al-Ūlā of the year eighty-six.

… Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us, saying: Ibn Bukayr said: Al-Layth said: In that year—that is, the year eighty-six—the Commander of the Faithful, ʿAbd al-Malik, died on Thursday, on the night of the full moon, fourteen nights having passed in Shawwāl.

Abū al-Qāsim ibn al-Samarqandī informed us; Abū Bakr ibn al-Ṭabarī informed me; Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl informed me; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed me, saying: Abū Yūsuf Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said:

“I read on gilded lapis-lazuli tablets at the qibla wall of the mosque of Damascus: ‘In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful. God—there is no god but He, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer. Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him. To Him belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is on earth. Who is it that can intercede with Him, except by His permission? He knows what lies before them and what lies behind them’ (2:255), to the end of the verse.

“‘There is no god but God alone; He has no partner, and we worship none but Him. Our Lord is God alone, our religion is Islam, and our Prophet is Muḥammad ﷺ.’

“ʿAbd Allāh al-Walīd, Commander of the Faithful, ordered this mosque to be built and the church that stood there to be demolished, in Dhū al-Qaʿda of the year eighty-six.

“On three tablets; and on the fourth:”

“Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful”, “Master of the Day of Judgment” (1:2–4), to the end of the sūra.

“Then [Sūrat] al-Nāziʿāt” to its end, then “[Sūrat] ʿAbasa” to its end, then “When the sun is folded up” (81:1).

Abū Yūsuf said: “I returned afterward and saw that this had been erased. This was before al-Maʾmūn”.

Abū al-Qāsim ibn al-Samarqandī informed us; Abū Bakr ibn al-Ṭabarī informed me; Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl informed me; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed me; Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān said:

“I asked Hishām ibn ʿAmmār about the story of the mosque of Damascus and the demolition of the church. He said:

“‘Al-Walīd said to the Christians of Damascus: “You may take the Church of Thomas by force and the Church of the Inner Quarter by treaty; we will demolish the Church of Thomas.”

“‘Hishām said: “That one was larger than the Inner Quarter.” He said: “They agreed that I should demolish the Church of the Inner Quarter and incorporate it into the mosque.”

“‘He said: “Its door was on the qibla side of the mosque. Today it is the miḥrāb where people pray.”

“‘He said: “The church was demolished at the beginning of al-Walīd’s caliphate, in the year eighty-six. They spent nine years building the mosque, until al-Walīd died before it was completed. Hishām completed it after him.”’

“That is what he said: Hishām! The correct name is Sulaymān.”

The year ninety-three

Yaʿqūb said, from Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir, from Maʿn ibn ʿĪsā: Anas ibn Mālik, ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn, ʿUrwa, and Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥārith died in the year ninety-three.

The year ninety-four

Abū al-Qāsim ibn al-Samarqandī informed us; Abū Bakr ibn al-Ṭabarī informed me; Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl informed me; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar informed me; Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān related to us, saying: Ibn Bukayr said: Al-Layth said: In the year ninety-four, Bashīr, the Commander of the Faithful’s son, brought the people of Syria to Egypt to raid by sea alongside the people of Egypt. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mālik ibn al-Abjar was in command of the people of Egypt.
